title: How whatRust Reached 300 GitHub Stars
description:
whatRust is a free, open-source WhatsApp desktop app for Linux, Windows and macOS, built in Rust with Tauri v2. It runs the official web.whatsapp.com inside the web view the operating system already has, and adds multiple accounts, a privacy blur, an app lock, a tray icon and checksum-verified updates. On 13 November 2026 its GitHub repository had 314 stars. This post lays out how it got there, month by month, using only what GitHub's API reports. The app has its own page here: whatRust.

whatRust is an unofficial, independent project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by WhatsApp or Meta.

How fast did whatRust reach 300 stars?

The repository was created on 30 May 2026. The first star arrived on 6 June, and star number 300 came on 11 November, about five and a half months later. Stars per month, from GitHub's stargazer timestamps:

Month (2026) New stars Running total
June 14 14
July 4 18
August 24 42
September 57 99
October 70 169
1–13 November 145 314

November's first thirteen days brought more stars than all of October. The busiest single days were 9 November (27 stars), 5 November (26) and 6 November (25).

Star history from GitHub on 13 November 2026, drawn by star-history.com. The live chart is on the app page.

What shipped along the way?

The star curve tracks a steady release history. Between 30 May and 13 November the repository saw:

  • 28 releases, from v0.1.0 to v0.6.16. Three went out on launch day (30 May), eight in June, one in July, four in August, five in October and seven in the first half of November. v0.6.16 was published on 13 November.
  • 244 commits on the main branch.
  • 37 issues opened, of which 34 are closed.
  • 8 merged pull requests from six outside contributors. They added a display-size selector, a monochrome macOS tray icon and native settings dialogs (August), a macOS menu-bar-only variant, native file drops in the macOS web view, and better account management with a language setting (October), plus a privacy-blur shortcut with a hidden Dock icon option and thin overlay scrollbars (November).

The headline features on the app page today, multiple isolated accounts, the privacy blur, the app lock and verified automatic updates, all arrived through these releases.

Where did visitors come from?

GitHub keeps traffic data for the last 14 days only, and it reports visits, not stars: it does not say which visitor pressed the star. For the 14 days up to 13 November, the repository had 4,663 views from 2,423 unique visitors and 1,192 clones from 335 unique cloners. The top referrers were:

  • Google: 1,643 views (1,320 unique)
  • reddit.com: 221 views (204 unique), plus 129 (117 unique) from the Reddit app
  • github.com: 100 views (73 unique)
  • Brave Search: 92 views (69 unique)
  • aocr.org: 56 views (56 unique)
  • DuckDuckGo: 36 views (30 unique), Bing: 26 (21 unique)
  • YouTube: 18 views (15 unique), X (t.co): 17 (13 unique)

Search engines sent the largest share. The repository's description names it a low-RAM alternative to WhatsApp Desktop for Linux, Windows and macOS, and its 14 topics include whatsapp-desktop, linux, tauri and electron-alternative.

These are the posts published about whatRust, with their dates:

  • 9 November: the build story on this site, the 67-second launch video on YouTube, a post on X and a post on LinkedIn.
  • 13 November: a 300-stars post on X.

How do people install it?

Every install path is one command or one file, listed on the app page:

  • Linux: a Flatpak installer for x86_64 and ARM64, or an AppImage, plus .deb packages.
  • Windows 10/11: one PowerShell command, or .exe and .msi installers.
  • macOS (Apple Silicon): one shell command or a .dmg.

Each release publishes a SHA256SUMS file, and the app installs an update only after the download matches it.

Frequently asked questions

Is whatRust an official WhatsApp app?

No. It is an independent open-source project under the MIT license, not affiliated with WhatsApp or Meta. Linking it uses the same Linked Devices flow as WhatsApp Web.

How many GitHub stars does whatRust have?

314 on 13 November 2026, with 145 of them added between 1 and 13 November. The live count is on the app page.

Where do the numbers in this post come from?

From GitHub's REST API on 13 November 2026: stargazer timestamps for the monthly table, the releases and issues lists, and the repository traffic endpoints for views, clones and referrers.

How do I install whatRust on Linux?

Run the Flatpak installer listed on the app page, or download the AppImage or .deb from the latest release. Then scan the QR code with WhatsApp on your phone: Settings → Linked devices → Link a device.

About the author

whatRust is built by Abo-Elmakarem Shohoud, CTO and full-stack engineer at Ailigent in Cairo, alongside Rusty Inbox, an open-source email client. For companies that need fast internal tools and automated workflows, see digital transformation consulting; for teams that want to work faster with ChatGPT and Claude, see hands-on AI training.

Originally published on aboelmakarem.pro.

title: Go Uptime Monitoring API Services: Retain Support Evidence Across Safe Rollbacks
description:
Compare uptime monitoring API services by testing whether their evidence survives a rollback of your customer support application. An easy HTTP integration is the beginning; the deciding constraint is whether the on-call engineer can reconstruct which release a customer reached, which checks failed, and what changed after the previous release returned to service.

TL;DR: Compare easy-to-integrate services on external HTTP checks, alert delivery, and retrievable incident evidence. Evaluate UptimeRobot and Better Stack for external monitoring, Healthchecks for scheduled work, and a separate evidence store for application context. Keep the monitor independent of the deployment it judges, and preserve the release identifier before CI/CD can promote or roll back anything.

Keep the evidence.

The runbook uses a hypothetical support portal deployment, with release labels support-r42 and support-r41. These are example identifiers, not a reported incident or a benchmark. After restoring the older release, support should still be able to explain the customer's failed attempt without depending on logs that disappeared with the newer process.

How should uptime monitoring API services compare on rollback safety?

A green check proves something about the request the checker made. Its usefulness depends on the target and acceptance condition. It doesn't establish that a customer's earlier request succeeded, that a background ticket synchronization ran, or that the portal served the release the deployment controller intended. A rollback can restore the front door while leaving the historical question unanswered.

Those are different signals.

For the support portal, define an availability SLO around the customer action that matters, then choose a probe that approximates it without creating customer tickets or touching private case content. An HTTP GET can be an availability signal; application events supply release and request context for a particular attempt. OpenTelemetry's logs concepts provide vocabulary for that second layer, including the relationship between log records and trace context. Carrying trace identifiers in logs should not be mistaken for having a complete trace investigation interface.

An actionable rollback record connects the check time, release label, deployment decision, and references to related application evidence. Keep it outside the release's disposable filesystem. Distinguish the intended release from the release actually served: the former comes from deployment configuration, while the latter needs an independently verified application signal. A label supplied to a probe cannot prove which binary answered it.

That's an integration trap. A script prints the expected release beside a successful response, and a dashboard quietly turns an assumption into apparent proof.

Buy the detector; decide who owns the evidence

Start with the operational boundary, because a service with an easy API can still leave your team responsible for the hardest part of the runbook. For each candidate, exercise monitor provisioning, notification delivery, and incident retrieval in a test environment. Treat public status pages and reporting as communication surfaces to evaluate against the actual explanation support needs to give a customer.

The table is a buy-versus-build decision aid. It identifies roles to evaluate and responsibilities to assign, rather than claiming equivalent monitoring coverage or retention.

Option Role to evaluate Operational trade-off and acceptance check
UptimeRobot Managed external uptime monitoring with an API integration Start here for outside-in availability checks. Verify the selected monitor type, notification integration, and incident history against the rollback exercise; application-specific customer and release context remains a separate integration responsibility.
Better Stack Managed uptime monitoring within a broader incident workflow Evaluate it when the handoff from detection to response is part of the purchase. Test the notification and reporting workflow your team will use, including how incident records connect to deployment records.
Healthchecks Heartbeat monitoring for scheduled work Evaluate it for a ticket synchronization task that should run but can fail silently. A task heartbeat answers a different question from an external portal request; retain both signals when both jobs matter.
REST evidence service Application evidence retrieval Evaluate a plain HTTP interface when the deployment runner should retrieve logs without an SDK dependency. Use this component alongside independently chosen external checks and notification delivery; verify that its response covers the incident before attaching it to a support record.
A service the platform team builds Custom probing and incident records Choose this when the team can own scheduling, persistence, delivery, and operational coverage. A short Go program is manageable; preserving its evidence throughout an incident is the larger commitment.

Don't collapse these rows into one feature score. A customer-facing portal needs an external observer, a scheduled synchronization needs an expectation of arrival, and an investigation needs context retained beyond either process's lifetime.

The buy-versus-build calculation includes on-call load and lock-in. Exportable incident records, documented integration contracts, and a rehearsed replacement procedure are acceptance criteria to investigate, not capabilities to assume. If the team maintains an adapter, assign an owner and a failure signal. Otherwise the adapter becomes another silent dependency in the escalation path.

Retrieve evidence without changing the incident

Infrai provides a single-key, single-bill REST API covering 295 routes across 20 modules, so the deployment runner can retrieve logs and metrics with one key and one bill instead of separate credentials and invoices for those operations. No SDK is required; the Go standard library can make the request, with no client library version to babysit. Its public, self-describing discovery surface also exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, allowing the team to inspect the integration contract before granting the runner credentials. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, which helps teams review the same evidence-retrieval contract across deployment tooling written in different languages. These are integration advantages; external checks and notification delivery remain separate selection decisions in this runbook.

Separate observation from deployment authority. A portal probe checks an existing application health URL with an explicit GET and a finite timeout; the example below instead implements the evidence-retrieval side of that workflow. It queries the verified logs search route, adds no undocumented filter parameters, and writes the successful response to standard output without assuming a response schema.

Save it as evidence.go and run it with go run evidence.go. Configure INFRAI_BASE_URL as the service's HTTPS API origin, without a version path, and supply INFRAI_API_KEY through the runner's secret mechanism. Send standard output to an access-controlled evidence destination, and keep standard error in an appropriately restricted diagnostic channel: error response bodies can contain operational details.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    u, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.User != nil || (u.Path != "" && u.Path != "/") ||
        u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the HTTPS API origin and set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    u.Path = "/v1/logs/search"
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(_ *http.Request, _ []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            wait := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            raw := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.ParseInt(raw, 10, 32); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; delay > wait {
                    wait = delay
                }
            } else if date, parseErr := http.ParseTime(raw); parseErr == nil {
                if delay := time.Until(date); delay > wait {
                    wait = delay
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "evidence request returned HTTP %d\n", resp.StatusCode)
            _, copyErr := io.Copy(os.Stderr, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8192))
            resp.Body.Close()
            if copyErr != nil {
                return copyErr
            }
            return fmt.Errorf("evidence retrieval failed")
        }
        _, copyErr := io.Copy(os.Stdout, resp.Body)
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if copyErr != nil {
            return copyErr
        }
        return closeErr
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The code makes at most 3 requests, uses exponential backoff for HTTP 429, and respects a longer Retry-After value until the overall 30-second deadline cancels the operation. It doesn't follow redirects with a credential attached. The operation is read-only; retries of monitor-configuration writes require a documented idempotency mechanism of their own.

A returned document isn't yet an incident archive.

The runner must preserve the output successfully before calling this step complete. A stream failure can leave partial output, so stage the result and mark it complete only after the process exits successfully and persistence is confirmed. The request contains no invented customer, timestamp, or release filter. Inspect the documented response contract and verify that the retrieved evidence actually covers the relevant incident before attaching it to the support record.

Budget the sampling and evidence before wiring CI/CD

Capacity planning starts with the observation schedule. For a hypothetical fleet of 40 targets sampled every 60 seconds, the baseline is 40 × 1,440 = 57,600 observations per day, before deployment checks or multiple probe locations. These are planning inputs, not a vendor limit or measured workload. Record size, retention duration, and retrieval during an incident determine how much evidence the team must operate.

Budget failure traffic too.

One unhealthy dependency can make many checks fail together, precisely when notification delivery and evidence retrieval matter most. Test what happens if the evidence destination is unavailable, a monitor API throttles a deployment job, or the alert receiver is down. A failed evidence write should become an explicit deployment decision; silently discarding the record defeats the gate.

Keep the availability SLO separate from the release gate. One successful observation is weak evidence for an availability objective, and an availability objective doesn't automatically define how long to observe a new release. Choose the promotion window, failure threshold, and rollback authority from the support service's requirements. Don't infer the right threshold from an example timeout.

Verify the handoff, then rehearse rollback

Before promotion, preserve a baseline observation for support-r41 and verify the deployed application's release through your established deployment verification mechanism. After deploying support-r42, preserve subsequent observations and the deployment decision in the same access-controlled incident record. Exercise notification delivery to the receiver the on-call engineer actually uses, and confirm that a support engineer can retrieve the relevant record without access to the deployment runner.

Then restore support-r41 in a test environment.

Verify the release actually served, repeat the customer-facing check, and confirm that the evidence from support-r42 remains readable. Preserve the rollback decision alongside both sets of observations. Returning the application to a healthy state and reconstructing a customer's failed attempt are separate acceptance checks; the runbook is incomplete if either depends on the process that was just replaced.

Choose a managed detector when its tested check and notification workflow meets the availability requirement. Add heartbeat monitoring for scheduled ticket work, and retain application evidence under an owner who can preserve it across deployment changes. Build the remaining glue only when its scheduling, persistence, and escalation responsibilities have a place on the platform roadmap.

The buying decision should survive the drill. A short integration is useful, but the decisive result is that support can explain what happened after the rollback has finished.

References

  • OpenTelemetry, Logs signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • UptimeRobot, API documentation: https://uptimerobot.com/api/
  • Better Stack, Uptime documentation: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/
  • Healthchecks, documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/

title: Your Backend Already Has an Architecture. Why Document It Manually?
description:
One of the most time-consuming parts of maintaining a backend is keeping its documentation aligned with the code.

Routes change. Models evolve. Services get refactored. The README gradually becomes outdated.

I built the analyze command in Docify to make the first step easier.

Run:

npx @autodocify/autodocs analyze .

Docify inspects supported source-code patterns and generates Markdown documentation covering detected routes, models, services, dependencies, and architecture. It can also generate ER diagrams for supported schemas.

Because the analysis runs locally, you can inspect the generated files before committing them to your repository.

It isn't a replacement for human architectural decisions, but it can eliminate a lot of repetitive discovery work.

What would you want an automated documentation generator to detect first?

https://docify.site/

title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
description:
arXiv:2611.14766v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.14846v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

title: NIBench: benchmarking autonomous AI agents for execution, skill evolution and scientific judgment in neuroimaging
description:
arXiv:2611.15831v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.

title: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction
description:
arXiv:2611.14889v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When we judge that our reasoning was defective, it seems plausible that we should abandon the conclusion it produced. This thought has special force for AI agents built to assess and correct their own work. Yet obeying such judgments can make an agent worse at distinguishing sound reasoning from defective reasoning. An AI agent may rely on information about its reasoning when deciding which conclusions to keep, while the part that judges whether those conclusions are justified cannot use that information. The agent can then exercise an epistemic competence by retaining conclusions it judges unjustified, even when its self-assessments are generally reliable. Nor is the difficulty resolved by training the agent to make its conclusions and assessments agree: agreement can be achieved by degrading either one. Crucially, I argue that a negative assessment can remain valuable by identifying conclusions requiring further scrutiny, without having authority to eliminate them. The result challenges a central assumption about AI self-correction: that bringing an agent's beliefs into agreement with its own self-assessment about their justification makes it better at correcting its mistakes.

title: TC39 `using` Declarations Land in V8 13: What Node.js 24 Developers Get for Free Without TypeScript
description:
TC39 using Declarations Land in V8 13: What Node.js 24 Developers Get for Free Without TypeScript

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Every JavaScript developer has shipped a file handle that never closed. A database connection that stayed open. A timer that kept the event loop alive.

The pattern is always the same: open a resource, forget to clean it up in one edge case, ship the leak to production. try/finally blocks help, but developers forget them or nest them wrong or skip them when the function returns early.

TC39's Explicit Resource Management proposal gives JavaScript deterministic cleanup. When a using declaration goes out of scope, the runtime calls the resource's disposal method. No try/finally. No manual tracking. No leaks.

V8 13 ships this feature unflagged. Node.js 24 gets it for free. TypeScript developers have been using the syntax since TypeScript 5.2, but the language-level guarantee is newer. Now the runtime enforces it.

Key Takeaways

  • V8 13 ships TC39's using declarations unflagged, available in Node.js 24 without TypeScript or transpilation.
  • Resources declared with using call their Symbol.dispose method when the scope exits, guaranteeing cleanup even on early returns or exceptions.
  • Async resources use await using and Symbol.asyncDispose, making database connections and file handles safe by default.
  • Browser support is arriving in Chrome 131+, Safari 18.2+, and Firefox 135+, with production readiness expected by Q2 2027.
  • The feature eliminates an entire class of resource leaks that try/finally blocks fail to prevent when developers forget to add them.

What TC39's Explicit Resource Management Proposal Actually Does

The TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal adds two keywords to using and await using. A resource declared with using must implement a Symbol.dispose method. When the block containing the using declaration exits, the runtime calls that method.

// File handle cleanup without manual try/finally
async function processLog(path) {
  using file = await fs.open(path);
  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return parseLogEntries(content);
  // file[Symbol.dispose]() called here automatically
}

The disposal happens at the end of the containing block, not the function. Developers can declare multiple resources with using in the same scope. The runtime disposes them in reverse order, matching the C++ RAII pattern and Rust's drop order.

function transferData(sourcePath, destPath) {
  using source = fs.openSync(sourcePath);
  using dest = fs.openSync(destPath, 'w');

  const buffer = Buffer.allocUnsafe(4096);
  let bytesRead;

  while ((bytesRead = source.readSync(buffer)) > 0) {
    dest.writeSync(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
  }
  // dest disposed first, then source
}

The disposal call happens even when exceptions occur. Developers do not need to wrap using declarations in try/finally. The runtime guarantees the cleanup.

Resources that need asynchronous cleanup implement Symbol.asyncDispose instead. Developers declare them with await using. The runtime awaits the disposal before continuing.

The proposal reached Stage 3 in TC39 in March 2023. V8 shipped the implementation in version 13.0, released October 2024. Node.js 24 (the current LTS as of March 2026) includes V8 13.4.

Using using With File Handles in Node.js 24

Node.js file handles already implement Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose. Developers using Node.js 24 can replace try/finally patterns immediately.

File handle lifecycle diagram showing traditional vs using-based cleanup

import { open } from 'node:fs/promises';

// Traditional pattern with manual cleanup
async function readConfigOld(path) {
  let file;
  try {
    file = await open(path);
    const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
    return JSON.parse(content);
  } finally {
    await file?.close();
  }
}

// Using declaration handles cleanup
async function readConfig(path) {
  await using file = await open(path);
  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return JSON.parse(content);
}

The using version removes the try/finally block and the null check. The runtime guarantees the file closes when readConfig returns, whether the function succeeds or throws.

Multiple file operations in the same function become clearer. The traditional pattern requires nested try/finally blocks or a cleanup array. The using declaration handles both cases.

async function mergeConfigs(primaryPath, fallbackPath) {
  await using primary = await open(primaryPath);
  await using fallback = await open(fallbackPath);

  const [primaryData, fallbackData] = await Promise.all([
    primary.readFile('utf8'),
    fallback.readFile('utf8')
  ]);

  return { ...JSON.parse(fallbackData), ...JSON.parse(primaryData) };
  // fallback closed, then primary closed
}

The disposal order matches the declaration order reversed. Developers do not need to track which resources to clean up or in what sequence.

using vs try/finally: Side-by-Side Comparison

The try/finally pattern requires explicit cleanup logic. Developers must remember to add the block, call the right cleanup method, and handle null resources.

The using declaration moves the cleanup guarantee to the language. The runtime handles null checks, disposal calls, and error propagation.

Aspect try/finally using declaration
Cleanup guarantee developer must add finally block runtime enforces cleanup
Null checking manual ?. or if check required runtime handles null/undefined
Multiple resources nested blocks or cleanup array declare multiple using statements
Disposal order developer controls manually reverse declaration order (LIFO)
Error handling must choose to swallow or rethrow disposal errors always propagate
Async cleanup must remember await in finally await using enforces async disposal

Early returns expose the difference. A function with multiple exit points needs cleanup in every path. The try/finally pattern requires a single finally block that covers all returns, or duplicated cleanup logic.

// try/finally requires careful placement
async function processRecord(id) {
  const handle = await db.connect();
  try {
    const record = await handle.query('SELECT * FROM records WHERE id = ?', [id]);
    if (!record) return null; // cleanup happens in finally

    if (record.archived) return null; // cleanup happens in finally

    return transformRecord(record);
  } finally {
    await handle.close();
  }
}

// using declaration works regardless of return path
async function processRecord(id) {
  await using handle = await db.connect();

  const record = await handle.query('SELECT * FROM records WHERE id = ?', [id]);
  if (!record) return null; // handle closed automatically

  if (record.archived) return null; // handle closed automatically

  return transformRecord(record);
}

The using version guarantees cleanup without extra code. Developers add new early returns without updating cleanup logic.

Building Your Own Disposable Resources With Symbol.dispose

Any object with a Symbol.dispose method works with using declarations. The method receives no arguments and returns nothing. The runtime calls it when the scope exits.

class DatabaseTransaction {
  constructor(connection) {
    this.connection = connection;
    this.active = true;
  }

  async commit() {
    if (!this.active) throw new Error('Transaction already finalized');
    await this.connection.commit();
    this.active = false;
  }

  async rollback() {
    if (!this.active) return;
    await this.connection.rollback();
    this.active = false;
  }

  [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    return this.rollback();
  }
}

// Automatic rollback on error
async function updateUserBalance(userId, amount) {
  await using tx = new DatabaseTransaction(connection);

  await tx.connection.query(
    'UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE user_id = ?',
    [amount, userId]
  );

  await tx.commit();
  // If commit() throws, rollback() called automatically
  // If we return early, rollback() called automatically
}

The disposal method runs even when the main code throws. Transactions that fail to commit get rolled back. Locks get released. Temporary files get deleted.

Resources that perform synchronous cleanup use Symbol.dispose instead of Symbol.asyncDispose. The runtime calls the method synchronously when the scope exits.

class PerformanceTimer {
  constructor(label) {
    this.label = label;
    this.start = performance.now();
  }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    const duration = performance.now() - this.start;
    console.log(`${this.label}: ${duration.toFixed(2)}ms`);
  }
}

function processData(input) {
  using timer = new PerformanceTimer('processData');

  const normalized = normalizeInput(input);
  const validated = validateData(normalized);
  return transformData(validated);
  // Timer logs automatically when function returns
}

A resource can implement both Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose. The runtime chooses the async version when the declaration uses await using.

The disposal method should not throw unless the failure represents an unrecoverable error. When disposal throws, the runtime propagates the error. If the main code also threw, the disposal error replaces the original exception.

class FileWriter {
  constructor(path) {
    this.fd = fs.openSync(path, 'w');
    this.closed = false;
  }

  write(data) {
    if (this.closed) throw new Error('Writer closed');
    fs.writeSync(this.fd, data);
  }

  [Symbol.dispose]() {
    if (this.closed) return;
    try {
      fs.closeSync(this.fd);
      this.closed = true;
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('Failed to close file:', err);
      // Don't throw unless close failure is critical
    }
  }
}

The pattern matches how Node.js file handles implement disposal. The Symbol.dispose method calls closeSync() internally. Developers building custom resources should follow the same contract.

Async Disposal With await using and Symbol.asyncDispose

Resources that perform asynchronous cleanup need Symbol.asyncDispose. The method returns a Promise. The runtime awaits the Promise before continuing.

Database connections, network sockets, and file handles all require async disposal. The await using syntax guarantees the cleanup completes before the function returns.

Comparison of sync vs async resource disposal patterns

class DatabaseConnection {
  constructor(config) {
    this.pool = createPool(config);
    this.connection = null;
  }

  async connect() {
    this.connection = await this.pool.getConnection();
    return this;
  }

  async query(sql, params) {
    if (!this.connection) throw new Error('Not connected');
    return this.connection.query(sql, params);
  }

  async [Symbol.asyncDispose]() {
    if (this.connection) {
      await this.connection.release();
      this.connection = null;
    }
  }
}

async function getUserData(userId) {
  await using db = await new DatabaseConnection(config).connect();

  const user = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?',
    [userId]
  );

  const orders = await db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?',
    [userId]
  );

  return { user, orders };
  // Connection released automatically
}

The await using declaration ensures the connection returns to the pool. Developers do not need to track whether the function succeeded or failed.

Multiple async resources dispose in reverse order. The runtime awaits each disposal before starting the next.

async function syncData(sourcePath, destPath) {
  await using source = await fetch(sourcePath).then(r => r.body);
  await using dest = await fs.open(destPath, 'w');

  for await (const chunk of source) {
    await dest.write(chunk);
  }
  // dest closed first, then source closed
}

The disposal order prevents race conditions. A destination file closes before the source stream, ensuring all data writes complete.

Mixing sync and async disposal in the same scope works. The runtime calls sync disposal methods immediately and awaits async disposal methods.

async function processWithMetrics(dataPath) {
  using timer = new PerformanceTimer('process'); // sync disposal
  await using file = await open(dataPath); // async disposal

  const content = await file.readFile('utf8');
  return parseData(content);
  // file closed (awaited), then timer logged (sync)
}

The runtime disposes resources in reverse declaration order regardless of disposal type. Async disposal awaits completion before moving to the next resource.

For more patterns on resource management and cleanup strategies, see 10 JavaScript and Node.js Tips That Knock Away Multiple Concepts and 5 Node.js Tricks to Make JavaScript Development Fascinating.

Browser Support, Runtime Availability, and When You Can Ship This

V8 13 shipped using declarations unflagged in October 2024. Chrome 131 (stable November 2024) includes the feature. Safari 18.2 (shipped December 2024) supports it. Firefox 135 (planned February 2025) will include it.

Node.js 24 (LTS since March 2026) includes V8 13.4. Developers targeting Node.js 24 can use using declarations without transpilation. Deno 2.1 (shipped January 2025) supports the feature. Bun 1.2 (shipped December 2024) implements it.

Runtime Version V8 version using support
Node.js 24 LTS 24.0.0+ 13.4 Yes (unflagged)
Node.js 22 LTS 22.0.0+ 12.4 No
Deno 2.1.0+ 13.2 Yes (unflagged)
Bun 1.2.0+ - Yes (native)
Chrome 131.0+ 13.1 Yes (unflagged)
Safari 18.2+ - Yes (native)
Firefox 135.0+ - Planned Q1 2025

Browser support lags server runtimes. Developers shipping client-side code should check caniuse.com for current browser coverage. Transpilers like Babel support the syntax through the @babel/plugin-proposal-explicit-resource-management plugin.

TypeScript 5.2 added support for using declarations in August 2023. Developers using TypeScript get type checking for Symbol.dispose and Symbol.asyncDispose methods. The compiler emits JavaScript that calls disposal methods in finally blocks when targeting environments without native support.

The Node.js collaboration summit in April 2025 discussed integrating AsyncContext with resource management. The TC39 Disposable AsyncContext proposal combines using syntax with AsyncLocalStorage. That feature remains in Stage 1.

Production readiness depends on the target environment. Node.js 24 projects can adopt using declarations immediately. Browser-based projects should wait until Firefox 135 reaches stable (expected Q1 2025) or use transpilation. By Q2 2027, all major browsers and runtimes will support the feature natively.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use using with objects that don't implement Symbol.dispose?

No. The runtime throws a TypeError if a using declaration receives an object without a Symbol.dispose method (or Symbol.asyncDispose for await using). Wrap non-disposable resources in an object that implements the disposal interface.

What happens if Symbol.dispose throws an error?

The disposal error propagates to the caller. If the main code also threw, the disposal error replaces the original exception. Write disposal methods that catch and log errors instead of throwing unless the failure is unrecoverable.

Does using work in loops and conditional blocks?

Yes. A using declaration inside a loop or conditional block disposes the resource when the block exits, not when the function returns. Resources declared in a loop body dispose on each iteration.

Can I manually dispose a resource declared with using?

Yes. Call the Symbol.dispose method directly. The runtime skips the automatic disposal if the method already ran. Most disposable resources track their state and become no-ops after the first disposal call.

How does this compare to Go's defer or Rust's Drop?

JavaScript's using provides deterministic cleanup like Rust's Drop trait. The disposal happens at the end of the block, not the function. Go's defer runs cleanup when the function returns, which differs from the block-scoped behavior. The reverse-order disposal matches both languages.

Why This Matters More Than TypeScript's using Keyword

TypeScript 5.2 shipped using declarations 14 months before V8. TypeScript developers have been writing the syntax since August 2023. The language-level support changes the guarantee.

TypeScript compiles using declarations to try/finally blocks when targeting runtimes without native support. The cleanup happens, but the TypeScript compiler generates the code. Developers targeting older runtimes still ship transpiled JavaScript.

V8's native implementation moves the cleanup guarantee to the runtime. The disposal call happens regardless of transpilation. Developers targeting Node.js 24 skip the build step entirely. No TypeScript compiler. No Babel plugin. The runtime enforces cleanup.

The feature eliminates a class of bugs that try/finally blocks fail to prevent. Developers forget to add cleanup code. They nest blocks wrong. They return early without cleanup. The using declaration removes those failure modes.

Database connections stay open. File handles leak. Network sockets time out. These failures happen in production because cleanup logic lives in application code. The runtime guarantee moves cleanup from developer discipline to language semantics.

Node.js 24 makes this guarantee available without TypeScript. Developers running plain JavaScript get deterministic cleanup. The runtime handles disposal. The feature works in scripts, REPL sessions, and production code. For more on leveraging modern Node.js features, see Convenient Tactics of Logging in Node.js and JavaScript in the Browser.

Every resource leak that ships to production represents a try/finally block developers forgot to write. The using declaration removes that decision. Cleanup happens automatically. The runtime guarantees it.

Sources

  • TypeScript: TSConfig Reference - Docs on every TSConfig option
  • V8 | Node.js v26.13.1 Documentation

title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
description:
arXiv:2611.14844v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.

title: 10 Lines to Give Your Coding Agent Before It Touches Your Repo
description:
10 Lines to Give Your Coding Agent Before It Touches Your Repo

Every coding agent reads your repository before it changes it. The only place you get to set defaults for that reading is the instruction file: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, whatever your tool calls it.

The ones I run with are long, and most of that length is context. But ten lines do most of the work. If you are writing yours for the first time, start here, in this order, and skip everything else until one of these lines proves insufficient.

1. The Scope Sentence

One line saying what this repo is. Every prompt the agent assembles gets anchored by it, and without it, the agent guesses your project's shape from the file names.

This repo is a Python CLI for log reconciliation. Python 3.12. No web framework.

2. The Verification Command

The exact command that proves the work. "Run the tests" is not a command, it's a wish. Give the one unambiguous line, and make it fast enough to run constantly.

Verify with: pytest tests/test_parser.py -k "failing_case" (that test only)

3. The Smallest-Command Rule

Run only what the current step requires. No full suites between steps, no re-runs of checks that already passed, nothing run "to be safe." Curiosity is for humans.

4. The Do-Not-Touch List

Name the paths that must never be regenerated or edited: generated directories, secrets, lockfiles, release notes you don't own. The agent cannot respect a boundary it was never told about.

Never edit: docs/generated/, .env*, pnpm-lock.yaml, CHANGELOG.md

5. The Ticket Workflow

Test first: write the test, watch it fail, write the code, watch it pass. One ticket at a time. This single line converts an agent from a generator into something shaped like a TDD machine, and even badly executed, the shape holds.

6. The Reporting Contract

Report the diff and the test result. Nothing else. No narration between steps. You are going to read the log either way, so make it the log.

7. The Honesty Clause

Never present blocked or partial work as done. If the step cannot complete, say exactly what is missing and stop. This line is the difference between an agent you trust and an agent you audit.

8. The Known Traps

The three ways this repo bites: the command that hangs, the suite that lies (tests passing while the subsystem under test never actually ran), the file that must never be regenerated. You know them from the scars. The agent knows nothing until you write them down. 💡

9. The Stop-and-Ask Line

Ambiguity, destructive operations, anything touching a file another human or agent owns: stop and ask. One line, and it prevents most of the disasters.

10. The Context Budget

Keep the whole file under a page. It is re-read constantly, and every line spends attention. If a line hasn't changed agent behavior in a month, it is decoration. Delete it.

The file is a contract, not documentation. The agent holds up its side with suspicious consistency. The human side is the one that rots, so re-read yours before the next agent run, not after the next incident.

Comments usually end up better than the article on this topic, so: what's your #11?

References

  1. The agent-instruction conventions this builds on (AGENTS.md et al.) are documented across the major coding agents; the structure above is distilled from the instruction files I actually run with, including the working rules in this repository.

title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI Inference
description:
arXiv:2611.14681v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.

title: I Tested Autoptimize — the Free Plugin That Minifies Your WordPress Code
description:
Every WordPress site owner eventually hits the same wall: the site feels slow, and every "speed plugin" either costs money or tries to do everything at once. Autoptimize is the rare exception — it does one job, it does it well, and it is free.

What it actually does:

  • Minifies and combines your CSS, JavaScript and HTML, stripping the extra spaces, comments and line breaks that slow pages down.
  • Defers or delays heavy JavaScript so visitors see the page sooner instead of waiting for scripts to finish.
  • Lazy-loads images and optimizes how Google Fonts load.

Why it stays lightweight

Most speed plugins grow into large suites that do caching, image compression, database cleaning and more — which can slow down your dashboard and create conflicts. Autoptimize takes the opposite approach: code optimization and nothing else. Because of that focused design the plugin itself is very small and adds almost no overhead. There is no premium upsell locking the core speed features behind a paywall.

Who should use it

If your site runs on shared hosting and feels slow, Autoptimize is one of the simplest free ways to fix that. It will not fix a bloated theme or 5MB images, and it is not a cache plugin — but it removes the code bloat between your server and your visitors, and that is often the biggest easy win.

The full test, with the honest pros and cons and how to use it safely, is in my detailed review here: https://segaflash.com/2026/10/07/autoptimize-review/

If you run WordPress, try it — it costs nothing, and you can measure the difference with any speed test before and after.
