title: Microsoft 365 Was Down for 25 Hours: The Health-Check Cascade That Took Email — and Your AI Connectors — With It
description:
Microsoft 365 was down for roughly 25 hours this week — and the outage didn't start with a server dying. It started with a health check doing exactly what it was designed to do.

The timeline, in short: the outage began on November 12 at 11:17 ET, ran about 25–26 hours, and was largely recovered by 13:00 ET on November 13. As of November 14, Microsoft still lists it as an open degradation. Downdetector recorded 130,000+ Outlook reports at the peak, across 70+ countries. Email delivery was delayed by up to 48 hours.

This post is about the failure mode behind those numbers — a cascade where the safety mechanism itself became the amplifier — and about the part nobody budgeted for: when Outlook went down, the ChatGPT and Claude email and calendar connectors went down with it, because they share the same failure domain.

The timeline

  • Nov 12, 11:17 ET — Outage begins. Incident IDs EX1550543 / MO1550821.
  • Nov 12–13 — Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, Intune, Planner, To Do, Defender XDR and Purview are all affected. Downdetector's Outlook reports peak above 130,000.
  • Nov 13, 13:00 ET — Broad recovery after roughly 25–26 hours.
  • Nov 14 — Still listed as an open degradation. Some mail is still catching up, with delivery delays stretching to 48 hours.

No company names were attached to the impact reports in the source material, and this post doesn't add any. The numbers above are the public ones.

The cascade: when the safety net pulls the floor out

Microsoft's preliminary account is short, and worth reading literally:

  1. An earlier network capacity upgrade introduced a defect.
  2. A recent network change made that defect surface.
  3. Health checks started failing on affected servers.
  4. Failing servers were removed from service — exactly as designed.
  5. The remaining servers took the load, and the secure-connection core process overloaded.

Step 4 is the one that matters. A health check is a binary decision: healthy or not, in or out. When the thing that makes servers look unhealthy is shared — a bad network change, not a bad server — the health checks fire everywhere at once. Each removal concentrates more load on the survivors, which makes their health checks more likely to fail, which removes more servers.

That is the cascade: the protection mechanism has no concept of "too many servers failing at once must mean the check is wrong." It just keeps doing its job, one server at a time, until there is nothing left to protect.

Two things Microsoft has ruled out, on the record: this was not a cyberattack, and it had nothing to do with AI.

The part nobody budgeted for: your AI connectors were in the blast radius

Here is the detail that turns an email outage into an agent outage. The ChatGPT and Claude email and calendar connectors stopped working during the same window — not because the models were down, but because the connectors live in the same failure domain as the mailbox they read from.

If your agent's morning routine is "read my email, check my calendar, draft the replies," then an Outlook outage is not a comms problem. It is a tooling outage. The agent loses its eyes and hands at the same time, and nothing in the agent's own error handling can tell the difference between "no new mail" and "the mailbox is unreachable."

The fix is not "add a retry." The fix is to treat the connector as a dependency with its own health signal, and to degrade in a way a human can see:

# Circuit breaker for a mailbox connector: fail loud, fail once
import time

class ConnectorBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failures_before_open=3, cooldown_seconds=300):
        self.failures = 0
        self.open_until = 0.0
        self.failures_before_open = failures_before_open
        self.cooldown_seconds = cooldown_seconds

    def call(self, fn, *args, **kwargs):
        if time.time() < self.open_until:
            # Don't hammer a sick service — and don't pretend it's fine
            raise RuntimeError("mail connector is in cooldown; showing stale data")
        try:
            result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.failures_before_open:
                self.open_until = time.time() + self.cooldown_seconds
                self.failures = 0
            raise
        self.failures = 0
        return result

Three failures, then stop calling for five minutes and say so out loud. The worst outcome in this outage was not the downtime — it was agents silently acting on an empty inbox as if nothing had happened.

Health checks need tiers, not just thresholds

The deeper lesson is about the health check itself. A single binary check cannot distinguish "this server is sick" from "the network is sick." Tiered checks can:

# Health-check tiers: a node-level failure and a fleet-level failure
# must trigger different responses
health_checks:
  - name: node_process
    scope: single_server
    on_fail: remove_server_from_rotation

  - name: fleet_connectivity
    scope: fleet_wide
    on_fail: freeze_removals_and_page_oncall
    # If >20% of servers fail checks within 5 minutes,
    # the check is suspect — stop removing servers, alert a human.
    fleet_failure_threshold: 0.20
    window_seconds: 300

The rule is simple: if a fifth of the fleet fails at once, the problem is almost certainly not the fleet. Freeze removals, page a human, and let the servers that are still up keep serving while someone looks at the shared cause.

Degradation checklist 

[ ] Map every AI connector to the service it reads from — the mailbox IS the dependency
[ ] Give connectors their own circuit breaker; never let an agent act on an empty inbox silently
[ ] Show staleness in the UI: "last successful sync" beats a silent empty state
[ ] Tier health checks: node-level failures remove servers, fleet-level failures freeze removals
[ ] Pre-write the comms: who tells users, and what the fallback workflow is, before the outage
[ ] After recovery, audit what the agent did during the gap — silent actions need a second look

Honest limitations

First, the root cause above is Microsoft's preliminary wording — a defect from a capacity upgrade, surfaced by a later network change, amplified by health-check removals. It is not an independent diagnosis, and the details may change as the investigation continues.

Second, the code samples are generic patterns written for this post, not Microsoft's code and not a reproduction of the failure. They illustrate the design principle; adapt them to your own stack.

Third, the outage was still listed as an open degradation at the time of writing, with mail delays up to 48 hours. If you are reading this later, check Microsoft's service health page for the final status.

The takeaway

The outage lasted a day. The lesson lasts longer: health checks are safety equipment, and safety equipment needs its own failure mode. A check that can remove every server, one by one, without ever asking whether the check itself is wrong, is not a safety net — it is a countdown.

And for anyone building agents on top of email and calendars: your connector is only as reliable as the mailbox behind it. Plan the degradation before the outage, not during it.

Has an outage ever taken out your agent's tools while the model itself was fine? What did your fallback look like — or did you find out the hard way that there wasn't one?

title: Build dashboard card grids that reduce columns before cards get cramped
description:
Responsive dashboard grids should usually change their column count before their cards become too narrow. A fixed track list, such as four fractional columns, keeps four columns even when the container no longer has room for four readable cards. The result is cramped content or horizontal overflow.

The implementation uses a repeating Grid track definition with auto-fit and a minimum-to-flexible range. The minimum is 180px, which represents the narrowest acceptable card in this fixture. The flexible maximum allows the tracks that remain on a row to share leftover space evenly.

The important decision is to put the readability threshold in the grid’s track sizing rule. auto-fit asks the browser to create as many tracks as fit. When another minimum-width track plus its gap no longer fits, Grid reduces the number of columns and reflows the same cards into another row. No card-specific breakpoint is needed for that transition.

With six cards, a wide container can resolve to four columns and two rows. At a middle width, it can resolve to two columns and three rows. At the narrow boundary, two 180px tracks and the gap fit at 376px but not at 375px, so the layout becomes one column. The markup and card count stay the same; only the track count changes.

Choose the minimum from the card’s real content, not from a generic device breakpoint. Short labels and values may work in a narrower card than summaries with supporting text, controls, or long localized labels.

This pattern solves an outer-layout problem. It does not make an unbreakable string, an oversized control, or poorly designed card internals shrink correctly. Those need their own content and overflow rules. It is also not the best fit for a strict comparison matrix or table where column alignment must remain fixed across rows.

Use this approach when cards are independent units that can move between rows without changing meaning. It keeps the responsive decision alongside the Grid sizing rule and lets available inline space, rather than a guessed viewport breakpoint, determine when a column disappears.

Working example 

export const MIN_CARD_WIDTH = 180;

const defaultCards = [
  'Revenue',
  'Active users',
  'Open tickets',
  'Conversion',
  'Deployments',
  'Uptime',
];

function escapeHtml(value) {
  return String(value)
    .replaceAll('&', '&')
    .replaceAll('<', '<')
    .replaceAll('>', '>')
    .replaceAll('"', '"')
    .replaceAll("'", ''');
}

export function dashboardHtml(cards = defaultCards) {
  const cardMarkup = cards
    .map(
      (title, index) => `
        <article class="card" data-card="${index}">
          <h2>${escapeHtml(title)}</h2>
          <p>Dashboard metric ${index + 1}</p>
        </article>`,
    )
    .join('');

  return `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <style>
      * { box-sizing: border-box; }
      html, body { margin: 0; }
      body {
        font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
        background: #e2e8f0;
      }
      .dashboard {
        display: grid;
        grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(${MIN_CARD_WIDTH}px, 1fr));
        gap: 16px;
        width: 100%;
      }
      .card {
        min-height: 72px;
        padding: 12px;
        border: 1px solid #94a3b8;
        border-radius: 8px;
        background: white;
      }
      h2 { margin: 0; font: 600 16px system-ui, sans-serif; }
      p { margin: 8px 0 0; font: 14px system-ui, sans-serif; }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main class="dashboard" aria-label="Dashboard cards">${cardMarkup}</main>
  </body>
</html>`;
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/grid-auto-fit-minmax-dashboard

title: Website Redesign Proposal Example
description:
Website Redesign Proposal Example

In the ever-evolving digital landscape, a website redesign is not merely an aesthetic update but a strategic imperative. This proposal outlines a comprehensive approach to redesigning your website, ensuring it aligns with modern user expectations and business objectives.

Analysis of Off-the-Shelf Templates and Generic Forms

  1. Lack of Brand Identity: Generic templates often fail to reflect a brand's unique voice and values, leading to a disjointed user experience.
  2. Poor User Experience: These templates are not optimized for user behavior, resulting in high bounce rates and reduced engagement.
  3. Inadequate Scalability: They lack the flexibility to adapt to future growth, technological advancements, and changing market dynamics.

Engineering Takeaways

  1. User-Centric Design: Prioritize intuitive navigation and responsive design to enhance user experience across all devices.
  2. Technical Architecture: Implement a robust backend with SEO best practices to improve search rankings and ensure future scalability.
  3. Performance Optimization: Optimize loading times and mobile responsiveness to meet user expectations and improve conversion rates.

Conclusion

A website redesign is a strategic investment in your digital presence. By focusing on user-centric design, robust architecture, and performance optimization, we can create a website that not only looks modern but also drives results.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:

https://vareli.info/blog/website-redesign-proposal-example

title: Wire it, don't configure it
description:
Where does a tool's configuration live? For a tool generated by go-tool-base it's always been a file you point it at with --config, and for plenty of tools that's all they'll ever need. But configuration has a habit of getting more involved depending on where a thing is run. One team keeps shared settings in Consul, another keeps secrets in Vault, a third has everything in AWS Parameter Store, and some platform or other drops a .env file in /etc and expects you to read it.

The estate has adapters for all of that, twenty-six of them in the go/config family (it's a big family). And until recently a generated project couldn't reach any of them.

Two awkward facts

When I came to bring them into the generator, the brief I gave the session was to work out how the adapters would manifest in a generated project "safely and most importantly securely". Two facts got in the way, and the spec (0204) put them plainly.

The first is that most of these adapters need a client the framework can't build for you. A chat provider is a blank import and a name in config. An S3 config store is a blank import and an authenticated client, with a region, a profile, a credential chain and all the baggage that comes with it.

The second is what worried me. A config source is itself configured, and whatever says where Consul lives can't come from Consul. Those pointers are every bit as sensitive as a token. A repository that sets config.sources.consul.address redirects all the keys the tool reads after that, not just one of them!

The stub I nearly shipped

The first version of the design, which I approved, had the generator write a little stub for each source, a file in the generated project with a comment along the lines of // TODO: build your Vault client here for the author to fill in. It's a common enough shape for a generator, and it seemed perfectly reasonable at the time.

Before building it I wanted a design document tracing how configuration would flow through a generated tool, and where it touched generated code. That paid for itself almost straight away... it showed the stub couldn't work: a file the generator owns is rewritten on every regenerate, a file the author owns has their code in it, and one file can't be both.

The obvious repair was to split it, a generated file plus some seeded files the author owned. I went the other way. The generator does the wiring, and the user must run an init command to fill in the config for each source they've enabled. The generator generates the dependencies and the wiring, the user configures it separately, and the connection details come out of the project's manifest altogether.

Pre-wired for a tow bar

You know how a new car can come pre-wired for a tow bar? The factory runs the loom and fits the socket, so the car's ready to tow, but what you hitch to it (a caravan, a bike rack, your neighbour's trailer) is your business, and the factory doesn't need to know.

That's the split now. The author decides what the tool can read. The generator turns that into a file of blank imports, generated and never edited, which links the code for each kind of source it declares. This is all of it for a tool declaring a Consul slot, a Vault slot and two fixed files, reading TOML as well as YAML:

// Code generated by gtb. DO NOT EDIT.

// Links the config formats this tool reads beyond YAML and the config
// source kinds it declares, one per line. Generated from properties.config.formats
// and properties.config.sources in .gtb/manifest.yaml; change those and regenerate.
package main

import (
    _ "gitlab.com/phpboyscout/go-tool-base/pkg/config/formats/toml"
    _ "gitlab.com/phpboyscout/go-tool-base/pkg/config/sources/consul"
    _ "gitlab.com/phpboyscout/go-tool-base/pkg/config/sources/file"
    _ "gitlab.com/phpboyscout/go-tool-base/pkg/config/sources/vault"
)

Alongside it the root command declares each source as a named slot with its place in the order of precedence (defaults lowest, flags highest, the sources in between), which I was insistent on: the author has to be able to say which source wins.

Each user then decides where a source connects. For each declared slot the tool grows a command, <tool> init config <name>, that asks for that slot's settings and writes them into the user's own config file under config.sources.<name>. For a Vault slot that's an address, a mount and a path, and the token comes from the usual places. Run the tool before you've configured a required slot and it tells you what to do about it:

ERROR failed to load configuration: "team" (consul): config source not configured
  hints="run `moo init config team`, or set config.sources.team in your config file or the tool's defaults"

(The original name was init source <name>, which I changed on sight. "Source" was the spec's word for a slot, and it means very little to someone reading --help.)

A clone can't rewire the car

Then there's the second awkward fact. A project-local config file, the kind that lives in a repository you've cloned, can't set config.sources any more, and that holds even when you've explicitly trusted the project. It's the only key in the tool where trust doesn't help. In the code:

// configSourcesKey is the subtree that says where configuration comes from
// (spec 0204 D5). A project file may never set it, trusted or not.
const configSourcesKey = "config.sources"

The test that holds it has a project file pointing a Consul slot at https://consul.attacker.example, which is about as subtle as a brick. Trusting a repository to set its own log level is a much smaller act than trusting it to choose your secret store, and the two shouldn't share a switch. The ordering mattered too: that rule landed hours before the first config source could exist, so a clone never had a window to point a tool at one.

Help text for someone who's never seen the code

The wizard had its own problem. With each source now a page of its own, there were a lot of pages, and very little on them explained why you'd choose anything. When I went through it, one note told me a source's settings were "these keys, under config.sources.file", followed by the single word path. Path to what?

I had to look at it as if I had no idea what the generator would produce, because that's who's reading it. In the end I wrote the text myself, and what ships now is close to my version: config isn't set here, this only wires in the adapter, each user runs init config <name>, here's what it writes and where, and here's how to give everyone a default instead. If the tool has no init command at all, the note says so and sends you to the defaults file. The format list stopped showing which Go packages each format would import (noise, to anyone choosing a format) and says whether the format can be written back.

The one that's waiting

Thirteen kinds of source made it through. The fourteenth, filekv, is on hold. It was built for reading a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret mounted as a directory, and I suspect the right pattern for that is to walk the directory and attach each file as a layer of its own, in an order the author chooses, instead of folding the whole directory into one. That's an open question for go/config first, so for now the generator refuses it, with a test to prove it does. I'd much rather that than ship it the wrong way round and have to take it back.

What the factory knows

So the generator doesn't ask for an address, a region, a prefix or a token any more. It wires in what the author says the tool can read and leaves the connecting to whoever runs it, in their own file, out of reach of anything they've cloned. The factory fits the socket, and what you tow is your business.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 14 November 2026.

title: AI Image Hand-off in Node.js: Presigned Parts, Multipart State, and Abort
description:
Short answer: for a large AI-generated image, let a trusted Node.js control plane create and authorize an upload session, let the worker send numbered bytes through short-lived presigned URLs, and finalize only an ordered manifest of returned ETags. Abort every session that will not finish.

This is a useful split because image generation and byte transfer fail differently. A generation retry can consume more model or accelerator work; a transfer retry should usually resend one part. Keeping those paths separate also keeps long-lived storage authority out of a browser or image worker.

How should a Node.js service presign multipart parts for AI-generated image uploads?

Start with two actors. The trusted API chooses the bucket and object key, binds them to a tenant and image job, starts the multipart session, and issues a presigned URL for one numbered part at a time. The worker holds the bytes, uploads each part, retains the response ETag, and asks the API to finalize or cancel. It does not choose a new key halfway through the transfer.

AWS describes a presigned URL as a way to grant time-limited access without giving the recipient storage credentials. Treat it as a bearer capability: keep its lifetime proportional to the transfer, do not put it in logs, and scope the application endpoint that asks for it. The effective lifetime can also be limited by the credentials that signed it, so an application deadline and URL expiry should be observed separately.

The application record needs more than a provider upload ID. Store the tenant, image-job ID, selected object key, session status, expiry, and an acknowledgement for each part number. Make the acknowledgement unique by session and part number. A duplicate acknowledgement with the same ETag is harmless; a different ETag for the same part should stop the finalization path until the conflict is understood.

Keep the authorization boring.

A small state machine before an SDK adapter

The storage adapter should be thin: it creates a session, produces a presigned part URL, finalizes a manifest, and aborts a session. The application owns the transitions. This Python model is runnable without selecting a storage vendor, and it makes the tests readable before an HTTP handler is involved.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum


class Status(str, Enum):
    OPEN = "open"
    COMPLETED = "completed"
    ABORTED = "aborted"


@dataclass
class UploadSession:
    session_id: str
    object_key: str
    status: Status = Status.OPEN
    etags: dict[int, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def acknowledge_part(self, part_number: int, etag: str) -> None:
        if self.status is not Status.OPEN:
            raise ValueError("upload session is closed")
        if part_number < 1 or not etag:
            raise ValueError("invalid part acknowledgement")

        previous = self.etags.get(part_number)
        if previous is not None and previous != etag:
            raise ValueError("part has conflicting ETags")
        self.etags[part_number] = etag

    def manifest(self) -> list[dict[str, int | str]]:
        numbers = sorted(self.etags)
        if self.status is not Status.OPEN or not numbers:
            raise ValueError("upload session cannot be completed")
        if numbers != list(range(1, len(numbers) + 1)):
            raise ValueError("part numbers must be contiguous")
        return [
            {"PartNumber": number, "ETag": self.etags[number]}
            for number in numbers
        ]

    def complete(self) -> list[dict[str, int | str]]:
        result = self.manifest()
        self.status = Status.COMPLETED
        return result

    def abort(self) -> None:
        if self.status is Status.COMPLETED:
            raise ValueError("completed uploads cannot be aborted")
        self.status = Status.ABORTED

I would put deterministic evals around this before connecting it to an endpoint: same-ETag duplicate acknowledgement, changed-ETag conflict, a missing part, finalization replay, cancellation, and two tenants probing one opaque session ID. Those checks are cheap, and they prevent a transfer bug from masquerading as a failed image-generation eval.

On the Node.js side, the handler maps its request into the same four commands: create, issue a URL for a known part, record the ETag, then complete or abort. The handler must validate ownership on every command. Its database transaction is the source of application intent; the object store is evidence of transferred bytes. Neither replaces the other.

Completion is a workflow boundary, not a successful request

An individual part response says something about that one upload request. It does not make a complete image available to a downstream RAG index, agent tool, or gallery. Finalization should submit the exact ordered part-number/ETag manifest recorded for the session. Only after finalization and a read-side verification appropriate to the chosen storage interface should the image job move into an available state.

That ordering is non-negotiable.

Consider the recovery path, because this is where a seemingly small shortcut becomes expensive. A worker can finish sending parts and lose the response from its request to finalize; meanwhile, a retry may arrive from the same job after a process restart. The trusted API should look up the stored session and manifest, enforce that the caller still owns the image job, and decide from recorded state whether it can safely repeat the finalize request or report that the image is already available. It should never rebuild a manifest from client guesses, accept a different object key, or turn a missing acknowledgement into an empty success. If the storage-side finalization is accepted, persist the terminal application state before publishing the image to the next pipeline stage. A verifier can then read the expected metadata through the storage interface and compare the object key, content type, byte length, and a generation-side checksum when that interface preserves comparable information. This gives operators a useful answer to a practical question: did generation produce bytes, did transfer assemble them, or did the publishing step withhold them? Those are distinct states, and collapsing them into one done flag turns an ordinary retry into a long debugging session. It also makes a transfer evaluation honest: the test can inject loss between requests without pretending that a successful HTTP status made an object readable.

That distinction matters for notebook-to-prod work. An image generator can emit the same bytes once, record a checksum and byte count, and hand transfer responsibility to a separate component. If a part needs another attempt, the system does not automatically request another generation. Token-cost accounting stays attached to generation, while retry count and transferred bytes remain transfer metrics.

Use three clocks: the URL lifetime, the application session deadline, and the cleanup schedule. Emit events for session creation, part acknowledgement, finalization requested, finalization recorded, verification recorded, and abort recorded. Include an opaque session ID, a hashed object key, elapsed time, part count, and byte count. Exclude the presigned URL itself.

I'm not sure a copied part size can be correct across different generated-image sizes and network conditions. Measure whole-object retry cost, memory pressure, request count, and tail latency with representative bytes. Small parts lower the amount resent after a failed part but create more acknowledgements; large parts reverse that trade-off.

When is direct multipart transfer the wrong choice?

The catch is that direct presigned multipart transfer is not suitable when a policy requires each byte to traverse an inspection service, when the client cannot retain the ETags needed for completion, or when a network intermediary prevents the worker from reading required response headers. Route bytes through a controlled service in those cases, accepting the bandwidth and buffering cost. A single-object upload is also a better fit when the generated images are small enough that repeating the full transfer is predictable and cheap.

Boundary Worker or client Trusted API
Object identity Holds an opaque session ID Selects and binds bucket plus object key
Authorization Presents application identity Checks tenant and image-job ownership
Part evidence Reads and submits the returned ETag Persists and validates the manifest
Terminal action Requests complete or cancel Finalizes, verifies, or aborts

Protocol compatibility is not a compliance claim. FedRAMP is a U.S. government program for standardized security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring; an S3-compatible interface alone does not establish a workload's authorization posture. Teams with an authorization requirement need to assess the deployed data flow, identities, locations, and operating controls with the responsible security organization.

There is a second operational boundary: abandoned sessions. A scheduled worker should select expired application sessions still marked open, request an abort through the adapter, and record the terminal transition. Keep it bounded and observable. Storage-layer lifecycle cleanup can provide defense in depth, but it cannot reconcile a job record or tell a user why their image is unavailable.

A release check for generated-image storage

Before release, run a fixed-byte transfer eval that covers a one-part success, several-part success, retry of one part, duplicate acknowledgement, missing acknowledgement, expired application deadline, cancellation, and finalization after the client lost its response. The acceptance condition is state you can inspect: an object becomes available only after verification, a cancelled session cannot later finalize, and each open session eventually reaches a terminal state or becomes eligible for cleanup.

Track generation latency, transfer latency, finalization latency, verification latency, retry count, bytes transferred, and age of open sessions separately. One blended job-duration chart hides the decision boundary that matters. Don't let an upload retry spend compute on a second image.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://www.fedramp.gov/

title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling
description:
arXiv:2611.14965v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.

title: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.15276v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent self-improvement requires feedback about task success, yet external feedback may be unavailable at test time. Agents must then infer success from observable evidence, and incomplete verification can misguide subsequent updates. We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), a method that co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task while keeping model weights fixed. The Evaluator actively inspects artifacts and environment state with tools; its findings ground an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators undergo comparative review on common candidates, while Actor updates require support from their own fresh outputs. Across AutomationBench, $\tau^3$ Banking, and selected GDPval tasks, VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods operating without external feedback, with gains of 3.3, 4.1, and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows that improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
description:
arXiv:2611.15309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

title: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.15109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. We introduce Structured Re-Decoding (SRD), a training-free framework that constructs local candidates from model scores, samples, or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection, and verifies reconstructed outputs. We show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction, and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool. External chemical templates further extend SRD to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization, and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments on a physical coherent Ising machine demonstrate the feasibility of hardware-based optimization, suggesting broader opportunities for quantum and quantum-inspired approaches to structured inference and combinatorial optimization across scientific domains.

title: A Failure Budget for Playwright Email Tests
description:
Email verification tests often look simple: submit a form, wait for a message, click a link, and confirm the account is active. In a real CI run, that short scenario crosses several systems. A browser submits the request, an API queues a message, a mail service accepts it, a mailbox exposes it, and Playwright reads the result.

When the test fails, the red line rarely tells you which system was late or wrong. A longer timeout can make the dashboard greener while making the diagnosis worse.

I use a failure budget instead. The idea is simple: define how much waiting and retrying each stage is allowed, then preserve evidence when that budget is spent. This gives a QA team a repeatable way to separate a slow email from a broken verification flow.

Why email tests need a budget

An email test has at least four clocks:

  1. The browser clock: how long the UI waits for a response.
  2. The application clock: how long the API takes to create and queue the message.
  3. The delivery clock: how long the message takes to reach the test mailbox.
  4. The processing clock: how long the test takes to parse the message and follow its link.

If these clocks are hidden inside one expect(...).toBeVisible() call, a failure is hard to classify. A burner email address may be valid, but the fixture can still be stale. A message may exist, but contain a link for a different test run. Or the application may never have queued anything.

The budget makes those possibilities visible. Give the API response, mailbox discovery, and link processing separate limits. The values are not universal; the useful part is assigning ownership to each wait.

Define the causal timeline

Before writing assertions, record the identifiers that connect the browser action to the message:

  • test run ID
  • user or fixture ID
  • message request ID, if the API returns one
  • mailbox address
  • verification token or message ID, when safe to expose in test logs

Then log milestones, not every polling attempt:

const timeline = {
  startedAt: Date.now(),
  requestSentAt: 0,
  messageFoundAt: 0,
  verificationClickedAt: 0,
};

await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
timeline.requestSentAt = Date.now();
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create account' }).click();

After the mailbox helper finds a message, add messageFoundAt. After the browser completes verification, add verificationClickedAt. If messageFoundAt is zero, the failure is probably delivery or fixture isolation. If the message is found but the link is rejected, inspect token ownership and application state.

The state model should be explicit too. A small union such as requested, delivered, opened, verified, and expired prevents a test from treating every non-success response as the same thing. See type-safe signup email states for a useful pattern.

Classify failures before retrying

Retries are useful only for failures that are plausibly transient. I put failures into three groups:

Application failure: the signup request returns an error, the message is never queued, or the verification endpoint rejects a token that was just issued. Retrying can hide a product bug, so capture the response and stop.

Delivery failure: the request succeeded, but no matching message appears before the mailbox budget expires. Keep the mailbox query, timestamps, and correlation IDs. Do not silently switch to another inbox.

Test-observer failure: the message exists and the token is valid, but the helper parsed the wrong element or the page assertion raced the navigation. Fix the observer or assertion; adding more delivery time will not help.

A retry should create a new fixture identity. Reusing the same address can pick up an earlier message, which makes the second attempt look successful for the wrong reason. This is where a test contract for email probes is useful: it can define matching rules, ownership, expiry, and what evidence a probe must return.

A Playwright implementation

Keep mailbox polling in a helper with a deadline rather than an unbounded loop:

async function waitForVerification(
  inbox: { messages: (address: string) => Promise<Array<{ subject: string; url: string }>> },
  address: string,
  deadlineMs = 30_000,
) {
  const deadline = Date.now() + deadlineMs;

  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    const messages = await inbox.messages(address);
    const match = messages.find((message) => message.subject.includes('Verify'));
    if (match) return match;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1_000));
  }

  throw new Error(`Verification email not found for ${address}`);
}

The helper should return structured data, not only a URL. Include the message ID, received time, subject, and a sanitized parse-failure reason. Avoid dumping full message bodies into CI logs because verification links can contain sensitive tokens.

Also assert the causal relationship. The message should belong to the current run, the link should target the expected environment, and the resulting account should match the fixture. A test that only checks that “some” verification link works is passing a weaker requirement than the product actually has.

A CI review checklist

When a Playwright email test fails, ask these questions in order:

  1. Did the browser request complete, and with which status?
  2. Was a message queued for this run and address?
  3. Did the mailbox return a matching message before the deadline?
  4. Was the link parsed from the expected message?
  5. Did the verification endpoint accept the token?
  6. Did the UI reach the expected state after navigation?

The wording in failure output matters. “Expected verified state” is vague. “No message for run abc after 30 seconds; request completed at 2.1 seconds” gives the next engineer somewhere to start.

Keep test data short-lived: a tem email or temp org mail fixture should be isolated and cleaned up after every run.

Common questions

Should I retry a missing email?

Only after recording that the application request succeeded and the message was queued. Use a bounded retry with a fresh fixture. If the queue event is absent, treat it as an application failure.

Is a longer Playwright timeout a solution?

Usually not. Increase a stage-specific budget only when delivery measurements support it. A global timeout hides which clock is slow and makes unrelated UI failures take longer.

What is the most valuable artifact after a failure?

A causal timeline with the run ID, fixture address, request result, mailbox result, and final browser state. It lets someone reproduce the reasoning without rerunning the whole job.

Reliable email testing is less about waiting longer and more about knowing what happened. Give every stage a budget, make state transitions explicit, and preserve enough evidence to tell a product failure from a delivery delay. That turns a flaky-looking Playwright test into a diagnostic tool for the whole verification system.

title: DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.15729v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.

title: ISO 20022 Structured Address Validator in Spring Boot
description:
From 15 November 2026, a pain.001 or pacs.008 message that carries only free-text address lines stops being accepted. You need structured fields, or the hybrid form with at least town and country as separate elements. If you are reading this on or after that date, treat it as a post-cutover checklist: the code below is what I would put in front of a payment gateway right now, and the last section covers what to watch in the first weeks.

I worked on this for a payments platform over several months, and the XML turned out to be the smaller problem. What actually hurt was an old customer table that nobody had ever cleaned.

I start with a plain explanation, then move toward architecture and Spring Boot code. Newer readers can stop after the first sections; people who already run payment gateways can jump to the parser. From the architecture onward I assume you know what an outbox and an idempotent consumer are.

The plain-language version

ISO 20022 is a message standard for payments, expressed in XML, which is a text format built from nested tags. Because every field has a fixed name and meaning, a bank in Frankfurt and a bank in Singapore read the same message the same way.

Two message types matter here. The names below are the official ones from the ISO 20022 catalogue:

  • pain.001, Customer Credit Transfer Initiation: your customer (or your corporate client) sends it to their bank to ask for payments. The version I worked with was pain.001.001.09; plenty of banks in the wild still accept .03, and the address block differs between them, so check which one your bank expects.
  • pacs.008, FI to FI Customer Credit Transfer: the bank-to-bank message that actually moves the money. The CBPR+ usage guideline I used targets pacs.008.001.08.

Both carry the payer's and the payee's postal address. For years that could be free text in a few AdrLine elements:

<PstlAdr>
  <AdrLine>Hauptstrasse 12</AdrLine>
  <AdrLine>10115 Berlin</AdrLine>
  <AdrLine>Germany</AdrLine>
</PstlAdr>

A person reads that without effort. Sanctions screening, name matching and routing software has to work out where the street stops and the town starts. The structured alternative names each part:

<PstlAdr>
  <StrtNm>Hauptstrasse</StrtNm>
  <BldgNb>12</BldgNb>
  <PstCd>10115</PstCd>
  <TwnNm>Berlin</TwnNm>
  <Ctry>DE</Ctry>
</PstlAdr>

The tag names are short on purpose: StrtNm is street name, BldgNb building number, PstCd postcode, TwnNm town name, Ctry the two-letter country code. The full element list in the schema is longer, and that matters later: Dept, SubDept, BldgNm, Flr, PstBx, Room, TwnLctnNm, DstrctNm and CtrySubDvsn all exist.

Which shapes survive the deadline

An address can arrive in three forms, and only two of them survive:

  1. Fully structured: every part in its own element. This is where you want to end up.
  2. Hybrid: TwnNm and Ctry are real elements, and up to two AdrLine entries of at most 70 characters each carry whatever remains. This is the temporary bridge for data you cannot split yet.
  3. Unstructured (rejected): only AdrLine. This is the form that no longer passes.

For cross-border traffic the rule comes from the CBPR+ usage guidelines (Cross-Border Payments and Reporting Plus), maintained for Swift's ISO 20022 migration and published through Swift MyStandards. For SEPA the equivalent sits in the EPC scheme rulebooks. I would not quote field lengths or the affected parties from memory: open the exact guideline or rulebook version your scheme membership points to and copy the rule from there. Which parties are covered, and the length limits, differ between schemes and versions.

Why the XML is rarely the failure point

Before writing any code I audited the existing system, expecting template bugs. What I found was this:

  • One address column, 255 characters, populated by a signup form that dated from 2016 and accepted anything.
  • Country stored as whatever the user typed: "Deutschland", "Germany", "GER", "DE " with a trailing space.
  • Lines pasted from PDF invoices, with a postcode on line 1, the town on line 3 and a phone number in between.

I am deliberately not quoting failure percentages from that client, because they are theirs and because your numbers will differ. The useful exercise is to run your own table through a parser and count. In my case the country column alone explained most of the rows that could not be resolved on the first pass.

Feed "c/o Mueller, Postfach 77 / 50667 Köln" into a flawless XML serializer and you still get a wrong or rejected message. So the repair has to happen before the message builder, in a translation layer between the legacy data and the new message model.

Build, buy, or fix the source

Three alternatives deserve a straight answer before you commit to writing a parser.

  • Fix the data at source. Migrate the column into structured fields and change the signup form. This is the right long-term move and I recommend it. It does not help with ten years of existing rows or with payees entered by third parties, so it complements a parser rather than replacing it.
  • Buy or embed a parser. libpostal is open source and statistical, covers many countries, but is a heavy native dependency with a large model download and gives you probabilities your compliance reviewer cannot trace. Google Address Validation and national postcode APIs give excellent results for the addresses they know, but each lookup sends customer personal data to a third party, which needs a data-processing and cross-border-transfer review that can take longer than writing the code. They also add latency and per-call cost on the payment path.
  • Write a rule-based parser for the countries you actually send to. It is narrow and needs maintenance, but every decision is a readable rule.

I chose the third for the first release, kept a hook so a library can be plugged in as a second opinion, and scheduled the source-data migration in parallel. In DDD vocabulary this is an anti-corruption layer; in practice it is simply a boundary where messy input gets translated and uncertainty gets labelled.

The architecture

The service runs four stages in sequence:

  1. Parse free text into a StructuredAddress plus a confidence score.
  2. Validate the outbound message against the structured and hybrid rules.
  3. Repair low-confidence cases through a queue, without losing or duplicating a payment.
  4. Measure everything so the cutover is visible.

I will go through each with code.

Stage 1: parser and confidence score

The parser never hands back a bare address. It hands back the address together with a confidence value and the reasons that lowered it, because a parse nobody can interrogate is something an operator ends up trusting blindly.

The model first. A thin record fails on real data, so this one carries the schema's building-level fields:

public record StructuredAddress(
        String department,
        String subDepartment,
        String streetName,
        String buildingNumber,
        String buildingName,
        String floor,
        String room,
        String postBox,
        String postCode,
        String townName,
        String districtName,
        String countrySubDivision,
        String countryCode,
        List<String> residualLines) {

    public boolean hasMandatoryHybridFields() {
        return notBlank(townName) && countryCode != null && countryCode.matches("[A-Z]{2}");
    }

    private static boolean notBlank(String s) {
        return s != null && !s.isBlank();
    }
}

public record ParseResult(StructuredAddress address, double confidence, List<String> reasons) {}

The parser is rule-based and selects a strategy per country. I avoided a machine-learning model in the first release because a compliance reviewer can read a regex and cannot audit a probability distribution.

@Component
public class PostalAddressParser {

    private final CountryResolver countries;
    private final Map<String, AddressStrategy> strategies;

    public PostalAddressParser(CountryResolver countries, List<AddressStrategy> all) {
        this.countries = countries;
        this.strategies = all.stream()
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(AddressStrategy::countryCode, Function.identity()));
    }

    public ParseResult parse(List<String> rawLines, String countryHint) {
        List<String> reasons = new ArrayList<>();
        double confidence = 1.0;

        String country = countries.toIso2(countryHint)
                .or(() -> countries.sniffFromLines(rawLines))
                .orElse(null);
        if (country == null) {
            reasons.add("COUNTRY_UNRESOLVED");
            confidence -= 0.5;
        }

        AddressStrategy strategy = strategies.getOrDefault(country, strategies.get("GENERIC"));
        AddressDraft d = strategy.apply(rawLines.stream().map(String::strip).toList(), countries);

        if (d.town() == null)   { reasons.add("TOWN_MISSING");   confidence -= 0.4; }
        if (d.street() == null && d.postBox() == null) {
            reasons.add("STREET_UNSPLIT");
            confidence -= 0.2;
        }
        if (d.postCode() != null && !strategy.postCodeValid(d.postCode())) {
            reasons.add("POSTCODE_FORMAT");
            confidence -= 0.15;
        }
        if (!d.residual().isEmpty()) {
            reasons.add("RESIDUAL_LINES");
            confidence -= 0.1;
        }

        return new ParseResult(d.toAddress(country), Math.max(confidence, 0.0), reasons);
    }
}

The weights (0.5, 0.4, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1) are not derived from anything clever. A missing town or an unresolved country makes a message unusable under the hybrid rule, so those two are penalised hard enough to push the score under the gate threshold on their own. Smaller defects such as leftover lines only nudge the score down, and two of them together should still land a parse in the repair queue. I tuned them by replaying a sample of real addresses and reading the borderline cases by hand.

Country conventions are where it gets real

Postcode position and house-number format change per country, which is why one regex fails:

@Component
class GermanStrategy implements AddressStrategy {
    private static final Pattern PLZ_TOWN = Pattern.compile("^(\\d{5})\\s+(.+)$");
    private static final Pattern STREET_NO =
            Pattern.compile("^(.+?(?:str\\.|straße|strasse|weg|platz|allee)?)\\s+(\\d+\\s?[a-zA-Z]?(?:[-/]\\d+)?)$",
                    Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
    private static final Pattern POSTFACH = Pattern.compile("^Postfach\\s+(\\d+)$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);

    public String countryCode() { return "DE"; }

    public AddressDraft apply(List<String> lines, CountryResolver c) {
        AddressDraft d = new AddressDraft();
        for (String line : lines) {
            Matcher pf = POSTFACH.matcher(line);
            Matcher pt = PLZ_TOWN.matcher(line);
            Matcher sn = STREET_NO.matcher(line);
            if (pf.matches())                          d.postBox(pf.group(1));
            else if (d.town() == null && pt.matches()) { d.postCode(pt.group(1)); d.town(pt.group(2)); }
            else if (d.street() == null && sn.matches()) { d.street(sn.group(1)); d.buildingNumber(sn.group(2)); }
            else if (!c.isCountryName(line))           d.residual(line);
        }
        return d;
    }
    public boolean postCodeValid(String pc) { return pc.matches("\\d{5}"); }
}

The Dutch case needs more care. Postcodes are four digits, a space, and two letters (1011 AB Amsterdam), and house numbers often carry an addition, as in Keizersgracht 12 bis or Prinsengracht 263-II. A German-style number pattern would drop the suffix into the street name.

@Component
class DutchStrategy implements AddressStrategy {
    private static final Pattern PC_TOWN = Pattern.compile("^(\\d{4}\\s?[A-Z]{2})\\s+(.+)$");
    // number, then optional addition: "12", "12a", "12 bis", "263-II", "12 3hg"
    private static final Pattern STREET_NO = Pattern.compile(
            "^(.+?)\\s+(\\d+)\\s*([a-zA-Z]{1,3}|[-/]\\w{1,4}|bis|ter|\\d{1,2}\\s?hg)?$",
            Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);

    public String countryCode() { return "NL"; }

    public AddressDraft apply(List<String> lines, CountryResolver c) {
        AddressDraft d = new AddressDraft();
        for (String line : lines) {
            Matcher pt = PC_TOWN.matcher(line);
            Matcher sn = STREET_NO.matcher(line);
            if (d.town() == null && pt.matches()) {
                d.postCode(pt.group(1).replace(" ", ""));   // keep canonical form: 1011AB
                d.town(pt.group(2));
            } else if (d.street() == null && sn.matches()) {
                d.street(sn.group(1));
                d.buildingNumber((sn.group(2) + (sn.group(3) == null ? "" : " " + sn.group(3))).trim());
            } else if (!c.isCountryName(line)) {
                d.residual(line);
            }
        }
        return d;
    }
    public boolean postCodeValid(String pc) { return pc.matches("\\d{4}[A-Z]{2}"); }
}

Singapore is different again. Addresses use a block number (Blk 123), a street, a unit in #04-56 form (floor 04, unit 56) and a six-digit postcode, and there is no state or province. Mapping that onto ISO 20022 means the block goes into BldgNb, the unit splits into Flr and Room, and the town is often just Singapore:

@Component
class SingaporeStrategy implements AddressStrategy {
    private static final Pattern BLK_STREET =
            Pattern.compile("^(?:Blk|Block)\\s+(\\d+[A-Z]?)\\s+(.+)$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
    private static final Pattern UNIT = Pattern.compile("^#(\\d{1,3})-(\\d{1,5}[A-Z]?)$");
    private static final Pattern SG_POSTCODE = Pattern.compile("^(?:Singapore\\s+)?(\\d{6})$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);

    public String countryCode() { return "SG"; }

    public AddressDraft apply(List<String> lines, CountryResolver c) {
        AddressDraft d = new AddressDraft();
        for (String line : lines) {
            Matcher b = BLK_STREET.matcher(line);
            Matcher u = UNIT.matcher(line);
            Matcher p = SG_POSTCODE.matcher(line);
            if (b.matches())      { d.buildingNumber(b.group(1)); d.street(b.group(2)); }
            else if (u.matches()) { d.floor(u.group(1)); d.room(u.group(2)); }
            else if (p.matches()) { d.postCode(p.group(1)); d.town("Singapore"); }
            else if (!c.isCountryName(line)) d.residual(line);
        }
        return d;
    }
    public boolean postCodeValid(String pc) { return pc.matches("\\d{6}"); }
}

Two traps I hit. In the Netherlands the postcode precedes the town while in the UK it comes last, so you cannot share the line-scan order between countries. And everything the strategies cannot place lands in residualLines, which is what the hybrid form's two AdrLine entries are for, so unplaceable text is preserved rather than thrown away.

Tests that pin the behaviour

Without tests a parser like this drifts. I keep a table of real-looking cases per country:

@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource(delimiter = '|', textBlock = """
    DE | Hauptstrasse 12;10115 Berlin            | Hauptstrasse | 12   | 10115  | Berlin
    NL | Keizersgracht 12 bis;1015 CJ Amsterdam  | Keizersgracht| 12 bis | 1015CJ | Amsterdam
    SG | Blk 123 Ang Mo Kio Ave 6;#04-56;Singapore 560123 | Ang Mo Kio Ave 6 | 123 | 560123 | Singapore
    """)
void parsesCountryConventions(String cc, String lines, String street, String no, String pc, String town) {
    ParseResult r = parser.parse(List.of(lines.split(";")), cc);
    assertThat(r.address().streetName()).isEqualTo(street.strip());
    assertThat(r.address().buildingNumber()).isEqualTo(no.strip());
    assertThat(r.address().postCode()).isEqualTo(pc.strip());
    assertThat(r.address().townName()).isEqualTo(town.strip());
    assertThat(r.confidence()).isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0.85);
}

@Test
void ambiguousInputFallsBelowGateThreshold() {
    ParseResult r = parser.parse(List.of("c/o Mueller", "Tel 0221 555 0101"), null);
    assertThat(r.reasons()).contains("COUNTRY_UNRESOLVED", "TOWN_MISSING");
    assertThat(r.confidence()).isLessThan(0.85);
}

The second test matters more than the first. A parser that scores garbage low is what makes the repair queue work at all.

The reasons list earns its keep when an operator opens a repair ticket: TOWN_MISSING tells them what to fix, confidence 0.6 does not. The same strings later become metric labels.

Stage 2: validating the outbound message

Parsing repairs data; validation guards the exit. A batch job somewhere will always build pain.001 by string concatenation and bypass your parser, so the last gate inspects the message, not the domain objects.

I validate in two layers. The official XSD enforces schema shape. A second set of business rules covers what an XSD cannot express, for example that hybrid allows at most two AdrLine entries of 70 characters and needs TwnNm and Ctry.

@Component
public class PostalAddressRules {

    public List<Violation> check(Element pstlAdr, String path) {
        List<Violation> out = new ArrayList<>();
        boolean hasStructured = hasAny(pstlAdr, "StrtNm", "BldgNb", "PstCd", "TwnNm", "Ctry");
        List<String> adrLines = texts(pstlAdr, "AdrLine");

        if (!hasStructured) {
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_UNSTRUCTURED",
                    "Only AdrLine present; TwnNm and Ctry are mandatory from 2026-11-15"));
            return out;
        }
        require(pstlAdr, "TwnNm", path, out);
        require(pstlAdr, "Ctry", path, out);

        if (adrLines.size() > 2)
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_HYBRID_TOO_MANY_LINES", "Max 2 AdrLine in hybrid"));
        adrLines.stream().filter(l -> l.length() > 70).forEach(l ->
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_LINE_TOO_LONG", "AdrLine exceeds 70 chars")));

        text(pstlAdr, "Ctry").filter(c -> !c.matches("[A-Z]{2}")).ifPresent(c ->
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_BAD_COUNTRY", "Ctry must be ISO 3166 alpha-2")));
        text(pstlAdr, "TwnNm").filter(t -> t.length() > 35).ifPresent(t ->
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_TOWN_TOO_LONG", "TwnNm exceeds 35 chars")));
        return out;
    }

    private void require(Element e, String tag, String path, List<Violation> out) {
        if (text(e, tag).filter(s -> !s.isBlank()).isEmpty())
            out.add(new Violation(path, "ADDR_MISSING_" + tag.toUpperCase(), tag + " is mandatory"));
    }
    // hasAny, texts, text: small DOM helpers, omitted for brevity
}

Two notes. Run the check on every PstlAdr in the message: debtor, creditor, ultimate debtor, ultimate creditor and any agents that carry an address. Ultimate parties are the ones people forget. And fail closed: a message with violations never reaches the transport layer, and the violation codes are stored so a decision can be reproduced later. That stored trail doubles as audit evidence, an idea I developed in DORA and NIS2 compliance evidence as code. I keep length limits in configuration instead of constants, because they varied between message versions while I was testing.

Stage 3: repair queue and outbox

Payments engineers should read this part twice. When confidence is low, guessing is the wrong move: a wrong address that gets through is worse than a late payment, since sanctions screening relies on it. So the payment is parked, a person fixes the address, and the payment resumes.

The risk is the dual write. Save the parked payment, then publish "needs repair" to a broker as two separate steps, and a crash between them leaves a payment nobody knows about, or a retry that opens two tickets. The transactional outbox removes that gap: the business change and the outgoing event commit in the same database transaction and a separate relay publishes the event. I covered the pattern, including idempotent consumers, in the transactional outbox guide for payment systems, so below is only what is specific to addresses.

@Service
public class AddressGateService {

    private static final double THRESHOLD = 0.85;
    private final PostalAddressParser parser;
    private final PaymentRepository payments;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    // constructor omitted

    @Transactional
    public GateDecision admit(PaymentInstruction p) {
        ParseResult r = parser.parse(p.creditorRawLines(), p.creditorCountry());

        if (r.confidence() >= THRESHOLD && r.address().hasMandatoryHybridFields()) {
            p.attachAddress(r.address());
            p.markReadyToSend();
            payments.save(p);
            meters.counter("address.gate", "outcome", "accepted").increment();
            return GateDecision.READY;
        }

        p.markPendingRepair(r.reasons());
        payments.save(p);
        outbox.save(OutboxEvent.of(
                "address-repair-requested",
                p.id().toString(),                       // aggregate key = ordering
                Map.of("paymentId", p.id(), "reasons", r.reasons(),
                       "dedupeKey", p.id() + ":addr:" + p.version())));
        r.reasons().forEach(reason ->
            meters.counter("address.gate", "outcome", "repair", "reason", reason).increment());
        return GateDecision.PARKED;
    }
}

On the 0.85 threshold: it comes out of the weights above. A parse missing only the street scores 0.8 and goes to repair; one with a clean town, postcode and street scores 1.0; a lone leftover line scores 0.9 and passes. I moved it once, from 0.80 to 0.85, after reading parked samples and finding that "street unsplit" cases were mostly addresses where the street really was missing, not parser misses. Treat the number as something to calibrate on your own data, not copy.

Three details matter more than they look:

  • One transaction. The payment's new state and the outbox row commit together or not at all.
  • A dedupe key from payment id plus version. The consumer that creates repair tickets skips a key it has seen, so a relay retry cannot produce a second ticket.
  • The same gate resumes the payment. When an operator submits a corrected address, the repair handler runs the validation again before the payment returns to READY. Human input gets no free pass; a mistyped country code is still a mistyped country code.

If your platform already has a streaming backbone, repair tickets also fit queue-style consumption well. I explored that in my notes on Kafka share groups for payment pipelines.

Stage 4: watching the cutover

Failures here are quiet. Nothing crashes; a share of payments comes back, seconds or hours later, with a reject reason code. If you cannot see that share by country, scheme and reason, customers will tell you first.

I export four metric families and one dashboard sits on top of them:

@Component
public class RejectionMetrics {

    private final MeterRegistry registry;

    public RejectionMetrics(MeterRegistry registry) { this.registry = registry; }

    public void outboundBlocked(String messageType, String code) {
        registry.counter("payments.outbound.blocked",
                "msg", messageType, "code", code).increment();
    }

    public void networkRejected(String scheme, String reasonCode, String country) {
        registry.counter("payments.network.rejected",
                "scheme", scheme, "reason", reasonCode, "country", country).increment();
    }

    public Timer repairLatency() {
        return Timer.builder("address.repair.latency")
                .publishPercentileHistogram().register(registry);
    }
}

The dashboard has to answer four questions:

  • What fraction of payments is parked for repair each day?
  • Which reason codes dominate? TOWN_MISSING points at bad legacy data; a growing STREET_UNSPLIT suggests missing parser rules.
  • What is the 95th percentile repair time? That is your cash-flow exposure.
  • How many messages passed my gate and were still rejected by the network? Anything above zero means my rules disagree with the scheme.

Keep country as a label but watch cardinality: a few dozen values are fine, free text never is. To follow a parked payment across services, the tracing setup in distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry in Spring Boot lets you correlate everything with one trace id.

First days after the cutover

If your platform is live or nearly live, this is the order I would work in:

  1. Use the hybrid format everywhere first. It needs only TwnNm and Ctry as real elements, and it is the cheapest route for messages with no structured source data.
  2. Make the gate fail closed for outbound messages with an explicit violation code, instead of finding out through downstream rejections.
  3. Back-fill country codes. Turning "Deutschland" into DE was the best-value data fix I made.
  4. Staff the repair queue. A queue nobody works is just a slower way to lose payments.
  5. Replay recent real traffic through the validator and count would-be rejections by reason. That count shows how far you are from compliant.

Deterministic replay of recorded traffic is a habit from my market-data work; the same idea carries over to payment messages, and I wrote the technique up in the replay and backtesting article.

Beyond addresses: VoP and the 2027 dates

Addresses are not the only euro-area change. The EU Instant Payments Regulation requires Verification of Payee (VoP): before a transfer is confirmed, the bank checks the entered name against the name on the receiving account and returns "match", "close match" or "no match". The EPC's VoP scheme rulebook defines the message exchange. The dates I worked to were October 2025 for payment service providers in the euro area and July 2027 for providers in EU member states outside it. Confirm them against the regulation and your national regulator, since that is my reading and not legal advice.

The link to this post is practical. Name matching works better when counterparty data is clean, so a pipeline that already produces normalised structured data gives you a head start. Treat the 2027 dates as a schedule for extending the same layer, not as a separate project. The same thinking applies to identity data; my EUDI wallet verifier build shows how verified attributes can feed a payment flow. For recurring mandates, where debtor and creditor details have to stay consistent over time, see Commercial VRP in Spring Boot.

In Singapore and elsewhere in Asia, local ISO 20022 migrations hit the same data problem, and the cross-border part follows the same CBPR+ guideline. A closely related routing problem is in my ASEAN QR payments post.

What I would tell my earlier self

This migration is a data quality project dressed up as an XML change. Teams that struggled spent their effort on schema validators while the address column kept supplying garbage. Teams that coped began with the data, measured it, and put a boundary in front of it that made uncertainty visible.

Three rules held up through all of the above:

  • Never guess silently. Every parse carries a confidence score and reasons.
  • Never lose a payment. The outbox ties state and events together in one transaction.
  • Never fly blind. Metrics by reason, country and scheme make a cutover observable.

One concrete step before you close this tab: export a day of real outbound payments and run them through a validator. The count of failures is your actual starting point.

FAQ

What is a structured postal address in ISO 20022?

It is an address split into separate labelled fields such as street name, building number, postcode, town and country, instead of one block of free text. Payment systems can then read each part reliably.

What changes on 15 November 2026?

Payment messages that carry only free-text address lines are no longer accepted on the Swift cross-border network and in SEPA schemes. You must send either fully structured fields or a hybrid form that has at least town and country as fields.

What is a hybrid address?

A hybrid address mixes the two styles. Town and country are filled in as proper fields, and up to two free-text lines can still hold the street and building details.

Why will payments be rejected even if the XML is correct?

Because the source data is often a single free-text customer address stored years ago. If it cannot be split reliably, the message has nothing valid to put in the structured fields.
