title: Modelling KEBS S-Mark Permits in an ERP: Product-Brand-Site Scope, Expiry Alerts and Label Validation
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

If you build or integrate an ERP for a food factory in Kenya, product certification is a data model problem hiding behind a certificate on the wall. The KEBS Standardization Mark (S-Mark) permit has a scope, a validity window and a label obligation, and most systems model none of them. Four design decisions matter:

  1. Scope as a composite key. KEBS issues permits per product, brand and production site, and they are not transferable. Model a certification_permit with (permit_type, permit_number) as identity and (product, brand, site) as its scope, then a many-to-many permit_sku table linking every finished SKU that prints that permit number.
  2. Validity as a date range with lead-time alerts. An S-Mark permit is valid for two years from issue. KEBS says acquisition can take about eight weeks when the manufacturer is ready. Store issued_on, expires_on and a renewal_due_on you compute with your own lead time, and surface the queue to the QA owner.
  3. Label artwork as a validated reference. KEBS requires the S-Mark logo and the permit number on the label. Make permit_number on artwork a foreign key, and validate on approval that the artwork's SKU, brand and site sit inside that permit's scope.
  4. Dependencies between permits. For wheat flour, dry milled maize products and edible fats and oils, the mandatory Fortification Mark requires an S-Mark or Diamond Mark first. That is a requires_permit_id relationship, not a note in a spreadsheet.

Everything below is the operational checklist those structures support.

Most food factories treat the KEBS Standardization Mark as a project. You apply, prepare for the inspection, pass, frame the permit and move on. Two years later someone notices the expiry date, or a new brand has been on the shelf for six months using a permit number that was never issued for it.

The S-Mark does not work like that. KEBS issues a permit per product, per brand and per production site. It is valid for two years. During that time KEBS carries out surveillance inspections in the factory and in the market. And the mark on your label is a statement that every batch carrying it complies with the relevant Kenya Standard, not only the batch that was sampled for the application.

It is also a live topic. In a public notice dated 16 October 2026, KEBS said it had revoked the certification permits of manufacturers found using permits issued for ordinary juices and drinks to market khat-infused beverages. On 12 November 2026, The Standard reported that KEBS is pushing for stronger regulation of imported and locally made products as Parliament reviews draft rules. KEBS consulted the public earlier this year on draft Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026, which are intended to replace the 1977 permit regulations.

This KEBS Standardization Mark permit checklist is written for dairies, millers, juice and water bottlers, bakeries, edible oil refiners, snack makers and other Kenyan and East African food and agro processors. It is not a guide to filling in the KIMS application form. KEBS publishes a user manual for that. It is about the operational side: how to know at any moment which permits you hold, what each one covers, when it expires, and whether the batches leaving your gate today could stand up to a surveillance visit.

It does not replace KEBS guidance, your QA consultant or your legal adviser. Fees, categories and procedures below are as KEBS publishes them at the time of writing; confirm the current position with KEBS before you act.

What KEBS and the law actually say

The Standardization Mark scheme. KEBS describes the Standardization Mark as a mandatory product certification scheme for locally manufactured products under section 10 of the Standards Act (Cap. 496). A permit certifies that a particular product conforms to an approved Kenya Standard or specification. Applications are made on the KIMS portal. KEBS officers inspect the production process, draw samples for analysis at KEBS or accredited/designated laboratories, and agree a scheme of supervision and control with the manufacturer. Once all requirements are met, a permit is issued with a unique permit number. The manufacturer must display the S-Mark logo and the permit number on the product label. The permit is valid for two years, and KEBS carries out surveillance in the factory and the market during that time.

Per product, brand and site. KEBS's quality assurance FAQ states that all permits (Standardization Mark, Fortification Mark and Diamond Mark) are issued per product, brand and manufacturing site, and are not transferable to other sites, branches or firms.

Fees and categories. KEBS's published fee schedule (two years, exclusive of VAT) charges an inspection fee per production site (KSh 40,000 for large, KSh 20,000 for medium and KSh 10,000 for small manufacturing enterprises) plus permit fees. Large enterprises pay KSh 15,000 per product, brand and site; medium and small enterprises' permit fees cover up to three products per site, with KSh 10,000 for each additional product. KEBS places alcoholic beverage manufacturers, animal feed millers, fortified maize and wheat millers, milk pasteurisers and bottlers, and containerised drinking water bottlers in the large category. A change request on a permit costs KSh 1,000 once evaluated and granted. KEBS says all its payments are now made through eCitizen.

Fortification Mark. For wheat flour, dry milled maize products and edible fats and oils, KEBS runs a mandatory fortification logo scheme on behalf of the Ministry of Health. The FAQ says a manufacturer must already hold the S-Mark or Diamond Mark before applying, and lists the fee as KSh 20,000 plus VAT per product, brand and site.

Test reports. KEBS accepts test reports from laboratories accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 (for example by KENAS), after evaluating them.

Renewal. The KIMS manufacturer user manual describes renewal from the "Awarded permits" view: open the permit, choose Renew, update the STA 10 details, submit and pay.

The law. Under section 10 of the Standards Act (Cap. 496), no person may apply a standardization mark to a commodity except under a permit issued by KEBS, and only if that commodity complies with the relevant Kenya Standard or approved specification. The Standardization Marks (Permits and Fees) Regulations say permits are not transferable, that the permit-holder must apply the mark to all commodities that comply, and that KEBS may carry out periodic tests and inspections and may suspend or revoke a permit, for example where the mark is used on commodities that do not comply or fees have not been paid.

What is changing. A summary of the draft Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026 by AO Wanga Advocates describes proposals for a public register of certified products, permit-holder obligations to keep production and quality records, cooperate with inspections, provide samples and report production stoppages, and wider KEBS powers to stop sales, order recalls and suspend or cancel permits. These are drafts. Track the final text.

Why this is an operations problem, not a certificate problem

A permit is a promise about every batch. The places where that promise usually breaks are not the inspection day. They are the ordinary decisions in between:

  • A new flavour or pack is launched under an existing brand and printed with the existing permit number.
  • Production moves a product to a second site for a few weeks to meet demand.
  • A contract packer runs your brand on their line.
  • The label artwork is redrawn and the permit number is dropped or mistyped.
  • The sample retention, lab results and release records that a surveillance officer might ask for exist only in a few notebooks.
  • Nobody owns the expiry dates, so renewal starts late.

Each of these is a data question: which product, which brand, which site, which permit, which standard, which batch.

The 12-point KEBS Standardization Mark permit checklist

1. Keep one permit register, owned by one person

List every S-Mark, Fortification Mark and Diamond Mark permit in one register: permit number, product, brand, site, Kenya Standard, issue date, expiry date and status. Name one owner, usually the QA manager, with finance as backup. If the only copy of your permits is the framed certificates in reception, you do not have a register.

2. Map every finished SKU to a permit, or to "no permit needed"

Go through your finished-goods list and link each SKU to the permit that covers it. Where a product is not covered by a mandatory standard, record that decision and its basis. Any SKU with neither a permit nor a recorded decision is a gap. Our item master data checklist explains why that list must be clean first.

3. Treat product, brand and site as the permit's scope

Because permits are issued per product, brand and site and are not transferable, any change to one of the three triggers a question before production, not after: does this need a new permit or a change request? Put that question into your new product and new brand approval steps.

4. Put expiry dates on a calendar with lead time

Permits run for two years. KEBS says acquisition can take about eight weeks from application when the manufacturer is ready. Set reminders well ahead of each expiry, assign the renewal owner, and check the STA 10 details you will need to update in KIMS. Budget the inspection and permit fees in the year they fall due.

5. Control the label: mark and permit number

KEBS requires the S-Mark logo and the permit number on the product label. Make the permit number a controlled field in label artwork approval, checked against the register for that exact product, brand and site. Our label control checklist covers artwork approval and line checks.

6. Keep the standard you are certified against on file

Hold a current copy of each Kenya Standard and code of practice your permits refer to (KEBS sells them through its webstore). Note the edition. When a standard is revised, review your specification, tests and labels against it.

7. Run the tests the standard calls for, at a defined frequency

Write down which parameters you test in-house, which go to an external ISO/IEC 17025 accredited lab, and how often. Keep the reports linked to batch numbers. A permit is easier to defend when you can show results across many batches, not only the application sample. Our calibration checklist covers the instruments behind in-house results.

8. Follow the scheme of supervision and control you signed

The scheme agreed with KEBS sets out your obligations. Keep a copy with the register, list the controls it commits you to, and check them in your internal audits.

9. Be surveillance-ready on any working day

KEBS surveillance can happen in the factory and in the market. Keep batch production records, QA release decisions, test results and retained samples where they can be produced quickly. Our food safety records checklist sets out which records to keep and how.

10. Add the Fortification Mark where it applies

If you mill maize or wheat flour or refine edible fats and oils, the fortification logo is a separate mandatory scheme that requires an S-Mark or Diamond Mark first. Track it in the same register, with premix purchases, dosing records and fortificant test results linked to batches.

11. Connect complaints and failures to the permit

A failed test, a customer complaint about quality, or a market sample that fails should be logged against the product, brand, site and permit, with corrective action and evidence. KEBS expects manufacturers to correct nonconformities and confirm the action taken. See our customer complaint handling checklist.

12. Review the register every quarter and watch the new regulations

Once a quarter, check the register against live SKUs, labels, sites and brands, and close any gaps. Keep an eye on the draft Standards (Product Certification) Regulations, 2026: if they are finalised, update the register for any new fees, forms and record-keeping obligations.

A simple permit register template

Field What to record
Permit type S-Mark / Fortification Mark / Diamond Mark
Permit number As issued by KEBS
Product Description as on the permit
Brand Brand name as on the permit
Production site Physical site the permit covers
Kenya Standard Standard number and edition
Linked SKUs Every finished SKU printed with this permit number
Issue / expiry Dates; renewal reminder date
Owner Named person and backup
Scheme of supervision Location of the signed copy; key obligations
Test plan Parameters, frequency, in-house or accredited lab
Surveillance log Visit dates, findings, corrective actions
Change requests Date, change, KEBS decision
Status Active / renewal in progress / expired / withdrawn

If you cannot say in one minute which permit covers the product on the pallet in front of you, a surveillance officer cannot either.

An illustration

This is an illustrative example, not a real case. A juice and water bottler holds S-Mark permits for its mango juice and its bottled water, both made at its main site. Over a year it adds a passion-fruit variant under the same juice brand, launches a second water brand for a supermarket, and moves part of the water production to a newer site to cope with demand. The labels for all three new lines are copied from existing artwork, so each carries an existing permit number.

On paper the business is "certified". In practice, three lines are carrying a permit number issued for a different product, brand or site. Nobody has broken a rule on purpose. The problem is that the permit register, the SKU list and the label artwork were never linked. Checks 2, 3, 5 and 12 would have raised the question before the first bottle was printed.

A minimal schema sketch 

CREATE TABLE certification_permit (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  permit_type   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (permit_type IN ('S_MARK','FORTIFICATION','DIAMOND')),
  permit_number TEXT NOT NULL,
  product_desc  TEXT NOT NULL,
  brand_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES brand(id),
  site_id       BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES site(id),
  standard_ref  TEXT NOT NULL,          -- Kenya Standard number + edition
  issued_on     DATE NOT NULL,
  expires_on    DATE NOT NULL,
  requires_permit_id BIGINT REFERENCES certification_permit(id), -- e.g. fortification needs S-Mark/D-Mark
  status        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  UNIQUE (permit_type, permit_number)
);

CREATE TABLE permit_sku (
  permit_id BIGINT REFERENCES certification_permit(id),
  sku_id    BIGINT REFERENCES item(id),
  PRIMARY KEY (permit_id, sku_id)
);

-- Gap report: finished SKUs with no permit and no recorded exemption decision
SELECT i.code, i.name
FROM item i
LEFT JOIN permit_sku ps ON ps.sku_id = i.id
WHERE i.item_type = 'FINISHED'
  AND ps.sku_id IS NULL
  AND i.certification_decision IS NULL;

The gap query is the one worth scheduling. It catches the new flavour printed with an old permit number before a surveillance officer does. Pair it with a check that every batch released under a permit was produced at the permit's site.

How FactoraERP helps

FactoraERP keeps one item master for purchasing, stores, production, QA and sales, with lot and expiry control on each item. Quality checks, non-conformances and batches sit in the same system, so a test result is recorded against the batch it belongs to and a deviation can be followed from the record to the product. Because production, stock and dispatch are in the same system, tracing a lot backwards and forwards does not mean pulling files from different shelves when a surveillance officer or a renewal asks for evidence. See factoraerp.com.

Free download: eTIMS readiness checklist for factories

Kenyan manufacturers increasingly need their records to tell one consistent story, for KEBS and for KRA. If you want a free eTIMS readiness checklist for factories, sign up for the FactoraERP Insights newsletter at https://isaacmuthui.substack.com. You will get practical operations notes for food and agro manufacturers. No spam; unsubscribe anytime. For background, see our HACCP CCP monitoring checklist and our guide to eTIMS for food and agro manufacturers.

FAQ

What is the KEBS Standardization Mark?

It is a product certification mark issued by KEBS under the Standards Act for products made in Kenya that conform to the relevant Kenya Standard or approved specification. KEBS describes it as mandatory for locally manufactured products covered by the scheme. It is also called the S-Mark or SM.

How long is a KEBS S-Mark permit valid?

Two years from the date of issue, and it is renewable. KEBS carries out surveillance in the factory and the market during that period.

Does one permit cover all my products?

No. KEBS issues permits per product, brand and manufacturing site, and they are not transferable to other sites, branches or firms. For medium and small enterprises, one permit fee covers up to three products per site, with a fee for each additional product.

How much does the S-Mark cost?

KEBS publishes a two-year fee schedule, exclusive of VAT: an inspection fee per production site of KSh 40,000, KSh 20,000 or KSh 10,000 depending on firm category, plus permit fees (KSh 15,000 per product, brand and site for large enterprises). Check KEBS's current schedule before budgeting.

What must appear on the label?

KEBS requires the Standardization Mark logo and the permit number on the product label.

Can KEBS withdraw a permit?

Yes. The 1977 regulations allow KEBS to suspend or revoke a permit, for example where the mark is used on products that do not comply or fees are unpaid. In October 2026 KEBS publicly said it had revoked permits it found being misused.

Do fortified flour and oil need a separate mark?

Yes. KEBS runs a mandatory fortification logo scheme for wheat flour, dry milled maize products and edible fats and oils, and requires an S-Mark or Diamond Mark first.

How can a buyer check a permit?

KEBS lists several ways: its website, the KEBS mobile app, an SMS of SM#permit number to 20023, or the toll-free number 1545.

Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd

title: Choosing a Futures Tick Database: Test Event Fidelity Before Query Speed
description:
Which database is best for futures tick data? Choose one that preserves the events your application needs before comparing query speed. Two trades can share a timestamp, continuous symbols can change their underlying contracts, and database deduplication rules differ. A small synthetic replay test can expose these mistakes before a fast query turns them into plausible but incorrect results.

For trade analytics, start with a trustworthy trade-event archive and a database whose duplicate and correction handling you can verify. For order-book reconstruction, trade records alone are insufficient: you also need the relevant book events and recovery rules. A fast database cannot reconstruct events that its upstream feed never supplied.

This is an evaluation method, not a database speed ranking or a claim that one market-data service covers every futures venue.

Separate the feed from the database

A market-data API delivers a documented representation of the market. A raw event log preserves what your collector received. A query database organizes that material for analysis. These responsibilities can share infrastructure, but they should have separate acceptance criteria.

TickDB is a useful example of the first layer. Its current documentation describes REST and WebSocket trade data for China and Hong Kong futures. That establishes a documented data-source option for those markets; it does not establish a user-queryable SQL database, exchange-native packet capture, or complete historical replay.

Preserve the original message, source, receive time and a durable collector receipt identifier before normalization. Keep source event time separately, with its documented unit and meaning. Receipt order can reproduce what your collector observed; sorting by event time answers a different question. Neither ordering should silently replace the other.

Suggested architecture: delivery, preservation and analytical queries are separate responsibilities, not a vendor architecture diagram.

Decide what identifies a futures event

A symbol plus a millisecond timestamp is not a universal event key. Two genuine trades can arrive with the same timestamp and price. Collapsing them can undercount volume while leaving a chart looking reasonable.

Use a documented event identifier within its documented scope when one exists. That scope may require a source, venue, session and instrument. Do not assume an ID is globally unique or survives a session reset. If the source provides no reliable identifier, preserve separate receipts and mark identity unresolved instead of silently deleting apparent duplicates.

The distinction matters when adapting TickDB messages. Its WebSocket documentation specifies single-trade objects for China and Hong Kong futures, and explicitly lists a trade ID for Hong Kong futures. The China futures example does not establish the same identifier guarantee. One universal adapter that assumes every message has an ID would overstate the documented contract.

Two events can share a timestamp. This synthetic example illustrates identity, not measured exchange traffic.

Contract identity needs the same care. Store the concrete contract and the effective mapping of any continuous alias separately. TickDB's data specification distinguishes regular China futures contracts from continuous symbols intended for market tracking, not delivery. Do not treat a continuous series as one permanent tradable contract. Record the roll rule and any price adjustment before comparing results across a rollover.

Test the projection without destroying the evidence

Keep the raw deliveries immutable and build a separate analytical projection. The following standard-library Python example uses a deliberately synthetic schema. It assumes source-defined IDs scoped by source, session and contract, plus explicitly ordered revision numbers. Those are test assumptions, not fields promised by every provider.

The seven deliveries include two trades at the same time, a repeated delivery, a correction, a late older revision and two receipts without IDs. The projection retains both identified trades, applies the correction, and leaves the unidentified receipts unresolved.

def project(events):
    """Synthetic schema: IDs and revision order are source-defined."""
    latest, unresolved = {}, []
    for event in events:
        row = dict(event)
        if row.get("event_id") is None:
            unresolved.append(row)  # Never guess identity from time/price.
            continue
        key = tuple(row[k] for k in
                    ("source", "session", "contract", "event_id"))
        old = latest.get(key)
        if old is None or row["revision"] > old["revision"]:
            latest[key] = row
        elif row["revision"] == old["revision"]:
            payload = lambda r: {k: v for k, v in r.items()
                                 if k != "receipt_id"}
            if payload(row) != payload(old):
                raise ValueError("Conflicting payload at the same revision")
    return list(latest.values()), unresolved


def example():
    base = dict(source="synthetic", session="S1", contract="FUT-A",
                event_ms=1000, price="100.00", revision=1)
    a = dict(base, event_id="A", receipt_id=1)
    b = dict(base, event_id="B", receipt_id=2)
    deliveries = [a, b, dict(a, receipt_id=3),
                  dict(a, revision=2, price="100.25", receipt_id=4),
                  dict(a, receipt_id=5),
                  dict(base, event_id=None, receipt_id=6),
                  dict(base, event_id=None, receipt_id=7)]
    resolved, unresolved = project(deliveries)
    assert len(resolved) == 2 and len(unresolved) == 2
    assert next(r for r in resolved if r["event_id"] == "A")["price"] == "100.25"
    print("7 deliveries: 2 resolved events, 2 unresolved receipts")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    example()

The local synthetic run prints 7 deliveries: 2 resolved events, 2 unresolved receipts. It does not prove market completeness, throughput or database durability. The unresolved receipts may include duplicates; retaining them avoids making an unsupported identity decision. Do not aggregate them as confirmed distinct trades without further reconciliation.

A changed payload at the same revision raises an error rather than silently picking a winner. Production ingestion should quarantine that conflict while retaining its raw message. This example does not implement cancellations, persistent checkpoints or a source-specific sequence protocol. Add those cases according to the feed contract, including sequence resets and recovery after a collector restart.

Compare duplicate semantics before performance

QuestDB and ClickHouse illustrate why “supports deduplication” is not a sufficient selection criterion.

QuestDB's current deduplication documentation describes explicit key columns, including the designated timestamp, for WAL tables. Its UPSERT mode keeps the latest write for matching keys. That is write order, not necessarily the highest source revision: a late old correction needs deliberate handling. Enabling deduplication also does not clean up pre-existing duplicates retroactively.

ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree identifies duplicates through the sorting key and removes them during background merges whose timing is not guaranteed. A query cannot assume those merges have already completed. Evaluate query-time replacement semantics, including FINAL where appropriate, and measure the actual query shape you will use.

Neither behavior is inherently the right answer for every workload. An immutable audit archive and a latest-corrected analytical view have different requirements. Feed the same test deliveries into each candidate and compare the results immediately after ingestion, after maintenance, and after replay. Check contract separation, retained revisions and unresolved records, not just the final row count.

Benchmark only the candidates that preserve meaning

Once the semantic tests pass, measure your real workload: sustained ingestion, late arrivals, narrow contract-and-time queries, broader aggregates, and recovery. Hold the input dataset, hardware, retention policy and query results constant. Report cold and warm query behavior, concurrency and storage usage rather than publishing a single unexplained latency number.

Validate backfill separately. TickDB's documented REST trades endpoint accepts a symbol and a limit of up to 1,000 records; that alone does not demonstrate arbitrary time-range recovery or lossless polling. Ask what can be recovered after a longer outage, and test the exact boundary. Storage and redistribution rights also need separate confirmation.

Choose the simplest system that passes these checks at your required scale. If a candidate cannot explain which events survived replay, a faster query is answering an uncertain question.

Documentation checked November 14, 2026: TickDB Data Specification and Trade documentation; QuestDB Deduplication; ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree. Code results are synthetic local validation, not a provider benchmark.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response for face detection (FACE_DETECTION) in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Effective October 15, 2026, the joyLikelihood, sorrowLikelihood, angerLikelihood, and surpriseLikelihood fields in FaceAnnotation return UNKNOWN for new projects and projects without recent Face Detection usage. Beginning January 14, 2027, these fields will permanently return UNKNOWN for all projects.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. title: What a data pipeline actually does, with 60 lines of Python you can run
description:
A data pipeline moves data from the place it is produced to the place it gets used, and changes its shape on the way. That is the whole idea. Most explanations stop at a diagram with three boxes labelled extract, transform, load, which tells you nothing about what the code looks like or why it breaks.

So here is a pipeline you can actually run. About 60 lines of Python, no framework, no cloud account. Then I will go through what it deliberately does not handle, because that gap is where most of the real work lives.

I build these for a living at Brickclay, mostly on client data platforms, so the failure list near the end is not theoretical. It is what has actually gone wrong on jobs I had to fix.

The input, which is messy on purpose

Save this as orders.csv. It has five rows and two of them are broken, which is roughly the ratio you get from a real export.

id,customer,amount_cents,placed_at
A-1001,Ada@Example.com ,124900,03/04/2026
A-1002,  Grace@example.com,8050,03/05/2026
A-1003,lin@example.com,not_a_number,03/05/2026
A-1004,hopper@example.com,45000,2026-03-06
A-1005,ken@example.com,99900,03/07/2026

Row A-1003 has a non-numeric amount. Row A-1004 has a date in a different format from the rest. The first two rows have whitespace and inconsistent email casing. Nobody writes a CSV like this on purpose. You get it when three different systems have written to the same file over two years.

The pipeline 

import csv
import logging
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (
    order_id   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer   TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount_usd REAL NOT NULL,
    placed_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
    loaded_at  TEXT NOT NULL
)
"""

UPSERT = """
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (:order_id, :customer, :amount_usd, :placed_at, :loaded_at)
ON CONFLICT(order_id) DO UPDATE SET
    customer   = excluded.customer,
    amount_usd = excluded.amount_usd,
    placed_at  = excluded.placed_at,
    loaded_at  = excluded.loaded_at
"""


def extract(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        yield from csv.DictReader(fh)


def transform(row):
    return {
        "order_id": row["id"].strip(),
        "customer": row["customer"].strip().lower(),
        "amount_usd": int(row["amount_cents"]) / 100,
        "placed_at": datetime.strptime(row["placed_at"], "%m/%d/%Y").date().isoformat(),
        "loaded_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    }


def run(csv_path, db_path):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    conn.execute(SCHEMA)
    clean, rejected = [], []
    for row in extract(csv_path):
        try:
            clean.append(transform(row))
        except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
            rejected.append((row.get("id", "<no id>"), str(exc)))
    conn.executemany(UPSERT, clean)
    conn.commit()
    logging.info("loaded %d rows, rejected %d", len(clean), len(rejected))
    for order_id, why in rejected:
        logging.warning("rejected %s: %s", order_id, why)
    conn.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(Path("orders.csv"), Path("orders.db"))

Run it:

INFO loaded 3 rows, rejected 2
WARNING rejected A-1003: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not_a_number'
WARNING rejected A-1004: time data '2026-03-06' does not match format '%m/%d/%Y'

Three rows landed. Two were rejected with the reason attached to the order id, so you can go and ask someone about A-1003 instead of guessing which row died.

Four things are happening in those 60 lines, and each one maps to a decision you will have to make again on a larger pipeline.

extract is a generator. It yields one row at a time instead of loading the file into memory. On a 4 GB export this is the difference between a job that runs and a job the kernel kills.

transform converts rather than repairs. Cents become dollars, the US date format becomes an ISO date, emails get lowercased and trimmed. It raises on anything it cannot convert instead of writing a zero or a null. A null that should have been 1249.00 will survive every test you write and surface three months later in a revenue report.

The rejection list is separate from the load. Bad rows do not stop good rows, and they do not disappear either. This single choice is the difference between a pipeline people trust and one people re-run by hand every morning.

The load is an upsert, keyed on order_id. That is what makes the job safe to run twice.

Run it twice, then count the rows

Still three rows after two runs. If UPSERT were a plain INSERT, the second run would either crash on the primary key or, with a table that has no key, quietly double your revenue.

This property has a name worth knowing: idempotency. Running the job twice produces the same end state as running it once. You want it because you will re-run jobs. The network drops, a credential expires, someone fixes the source file at 2am and asks you to load it again. A pipeline you cannot safely re-run becomes a pipeline somebody has to babysit.

What these 60 lines do not handle

This is the honest part. The script above is a pipeline, but it is the first ten percent of one.

Schema drift. Someone renames amount_cents to amount and every row rejects at once. The fix is to validate the header against an expected contract and fail the whole run with a clear message, rather than reporting 40,000 individual rejections.

Partial failure and retries. If the load dies halfway through a large batch, executemany inside one transaction rolls back and you are clean. Start writing in chunks and committing per chunk, which you will do for memory reasons, and you now need to track which chunks landed.

Incremental loads. This script reads the whole file every time. At real volume you need a watermark, usually the maximum placed_at or an updated timestamp from the source, so each run only picks up what is new. Then you need a way to force a full reload when the watermark logic itself is wrong.

Late-arriving and corrected data. An order placed on the 4th can arrive on the 9th with a different amount. The upsert handles the correction. Any report you already sent out does not.

Observability. Right now the only record that the job ran is a log line in a terminal. The minimum useful version is a run table: start time, end time, rows in, rows loaded, rows rejected. Without it you cannot answer whether today's numbers are low because sales were low or because the job failed.

Orchestration. Something has to decide when this runs, what runs after it, and who gets told when it fails. That is what Airflow, Dagster and Prefect exist for, and it is also why you should not reach for them on day one.

The three failures that actually show up

Across the data platform work I do at Brickclay, three problems come up far more often than any argument about tooling.

The silent partial load. The job reports success, loads 80 percent of the rows, and nobody notices for a week. Caused by swallowing exceptions in a loop. Fixed by counting rows in and rows out and failing when the difference is not explained by your rejection list.

The timezone that was never a timezone. A source writes local timestamps with no offset, the pipeline stores them as UTC, and every daily total is wrong by the number of hours in the shift. This one is expensive because the data looks completely reasonable.

The pipeline nobody can re-run. Usually a plain insert, or a transform that reads the current date, so re-running yesterday's job produces different output than it did yesterday. Notice that loaded_at in the script above has exactly this smell. It records when the row was written, which is fine for an audit trail, but it means the output bytes differ between runs. Keep that kind of field out of anything you compare run to run.

If you are starting one of these from scratch, build the rejection list and the run table before you add a scheduler. The scheduler makes the job automatic. Those two make it trustable, and on every project I have worked on, trust was the part that took longer.

If you have hit a failure mode I did not list, put it in the comments, I collect these.

title: Marketplace Email API Deliverability: A Go Guide to Suppression Evidence
description:
A marketplace needs to stop sending welcome messages to invalid seller addresses without treating every delivery failure as proof that an address is invalid. Preserving the explanation takes more work than storing a bounce flag, but it makes the suppression decision reviewable. TL;DR: assess email API providers for high US deliverability by asking whether their evidence can explain and reproduce recipient suppression; use that evidence to qualify candidates before comparing delivery-rate claims.

The constraint is evidentiary: a reviewer must be able to distinguish a failed attempt, a decision to suppress, and a later decision to permit delivery. These are different records. The following design treats a suppression review as a reconstruction exercise, then derives the storage boundary and a minimal Go check from what that exercise needs. It proposes application requirements, not a claim about capabilities shared by all providers.

What must survive when a seller disputes a suppressed welcome email?

Start with the question a marketplace support team would have to answer: why was this destination excluded from this welcome attempt? An aggregate deliverability percentage cannot answer it. Neither can a current boolean, because the current value omits the reason, the applicable address, and the policy that authorized its change. A candidate integration should therefore be assessed against a specific review packet before its advertised delivery rate influences selection.

Consider an illustrative seller record, seller-42, whose welcome attempt used recipient revision 7. The seller later supplies a replacement address at revision 8. These are example identifiers, not production observations. A delayed failure concerning revision 7 must remain attributable to that destination; applying it to whichever address happens to be current would turn accurate historical evidence into an incorrect present restriction.

Keep both revisions.

For this proposed marketplace, the review packet contains the attempt identity, the recipient revision actually used, the original delivery evidence, the interpretation applied to that evidence, and the policy revision behind the resulting action. Record source identity and event identity together, rather than assuming an event identifier is globally unique. Preserve source time separately from application receipt time: the former describes the reported occurrence, while the latter helps reconstruct ingestion. Neither should silently replace the other.

The packet also needs an explicit boundary of inference. A permanent recipient failure can justify suppression only when its documented meaning meets the marketplace's recipient policy; a temporary or unresolved failure must not become an invalid-address finding merely because it is inconvenient to classify. Store the original reason with the normalized result so a reviewer can examine the interpretation. If that evidence is unavailable, record the gap rather than manufacturing certainty.

Evidence has limits.

A complete packet does not establish consent, settle the legal classification of a message, or determine a lawful retention period. The team must review those obligations separately, including access to recipient information and diagnostic payloads. Auditability is a property of this proposed workflow; legal compliance requires a broader assessment.

Reconstruct the decision before designing the callback

Work backward from a review packet. First identify the exact recipient revision and attempt. Then recover the source event, reproduce its classification under the recorded policy, and compare that decision with the stored eligibility transition. Finally, inspect whether a later authorization used the resulting state. This sequence separates a classification defect from a missing event or a dispatch race, which otherwise tend to collapse into the unhelpful statement that email failed.

There is a concrete implementation trap here. If event ingestion commits first and suppression commits later, a crash between the writes can leave an event that appears processed without its intended effect. Reversing the writes can leave a restriction without its explanation. The proposed database transaction should therefore bind deduplication, the recorded decision, and its recipient-state effect together. Enforce uniqueness on the source-account/event-identity pair inside that transaction; a preliminary existence check alone is not the concurrency boundary.

Require one committed effect.

That is the exactly-once mindset appropriate to this ledger: one durable application effect for a logical event, with repeat ingestion returning the original outcome. It is a design requirement, not a promise that notifications arrive exactly once. Authenticate incoming evidence through the selected integration's documented mechanism before allowing it to authorize a restriction, and preserve enough verification context for the team's reviewed audit requirements.

Dispatch introduces a separate boundary. A welcome job can wait while its recipient becomes suppressed, so eligibility must be checked against the destination revision at the defined authorization point. Record that authorization with the attempt. A later restriction can prevent later authorizations; this design cannot retract an attempt already handed to an external transport. Explaining that boundary accurately is more useful than claiming a transaction spans the local ledger and the mail system.

Suppression also needs a scope. In this design, invalid-recipient evidence concerns a destination revision. A consent withdrawal, complaint, or account restriction needs a separate policy, potentially with a broader scope. Replacing an address must not erase the earlier evidence, and replacing an address must not automatically override an unrelated restriction. The additional policy state costs engineering effort, but a single overloaded bounce flag cannot express those distinctions.

Use a small Go check to expose missing explanations

A reconstruction check is useful before enforcement because it reveals whether the proposed review packet can support the decision at all. This minimal example checks record linkage for a suppression decision. It does not validate a provider payload, implement a database transaction, or prove that a classification was correct; those responsibilities remain explicit acceptance requirements.

package evidence

import "errors"

type Attempt struct {
    ID                string
    RecipientRevision string
}

type Evidence struct {
    SourceAccount     string
    EventID           string
    AttemptID         string
    RecipientRevision string
    OriginalReason    string
    Classification    string
}

type Decision struct {
    SourceAccount     string
    EventID           string
    RecipientRevision string
    PolicyRevision    string
    Action            string
}

func CheckSuppression(a Attempt, e Evidence, d Decision) error {
    if a.ID == "" || a.RecipientRevision == "" ||
        e.SourceAccount == "" || e.EventID == "" ||
        e.OriginalReason == "" || d.PolicyRevision == "" {
        return errors.New("incomplete review packet")
    }
    if e.AttemptID != a.ID ||
        e.RecipientRevision != a.RecipientRevision ||
        d.RecipientRevision != a.RecipientRevision {
        return errors.New("recipient or attempt linkage differs")
    }
    if d.SourceAccount != e.SourceAccount || d.EventID != e.EventID {
        return errors.New("decision refers to different evidence")
    }
    if d.Action != "suppress" ||
        e.Classification != "permanent_recipient_failure" {
        return errors.New("packet does not explain recipient suppression")
    }
    return nil
}

The classification string is an internal category chosen for this example. Only an adapter with documented, reviewed mappings should produce it. A successful check establishes that the fields agree under the example's rule; a fabricated but internally consistent packet could also pass, which is why authenticity, policy review, and transactional persistence cannot be delegated to this function.

This is deliberately a narrow check. It gives support tooling a concrete reason to reject an incomplete explanation without confusing structural consistency with a compliance verdict.

How should email API providers substantiate high deliverability rates?

The reconstruction exercise now supplies a selection method. Ask each candidate to demonstrate the same recipient-replacement example, a repeated event, and a temporary failure against documented event semantics. Record what the marketplace can reconstruct, what it must retain itself, and what remains unknown. These are proposed acceptance cases, not published benchmarks or claims about any named service.

Control arrangement Evidence the review needs Engineering trade-off
Transport controls suppression An attributable restriction and the documented destination scope Review depends on the evidence and history the integration makes available
Application controls suppression Original evidence plus a durable local policy decision The marketplace owns classification, persistence, and policy maintenance
Both apply suppression Local authorization and an explanation for any transport refusal Reconciliation must account for two independently enforced decisions

The combined arrangement deserves an explicit disagreement case. If the application permits an attempt but the transport declines it under a separate suppression rule, a local eligibility record explains only part of the outcome. Require evidence that can be attached to the same attempt, or document the unresolved boundary before adoption. More local control creates more maintenance work; less local control makes the integration's available evidence more consequential. Choose according to the review obligation and the team's capacity to maintain it.

Sender authentication belongs in a separate acceptance check. RFC 7208 defines SPF for checking whether a sending host is authorized to use a domain in SMTP identities. Its Section 4.6.4 limits the number of DNS-querying terms evaluated to 10; that is a concrete configuration constraint, not a recipient-validity test or a delivery-rate guarantee. Review the authentication configuration without treating an SPF result as evidence that a particular seller address should remain eligible.

For high US deliverability claims, require a stated definition of delivery, the population being measured, and the measurement window before making a comparison. Without comparable evidence, this article cannot establish a top provider or attribute a delivery percentage. The useful selection output is a documented explanation of which candidate satisfies the marketplace's evidence requirements and which unanswered questions prevent a decision.

Roll out by reviewing disagreements

Begin with observation: construct review packets and proposed suppression decisions alongside the existing path, restrict access to diagnostic data, and investigate disagreements before enabling enforcement. Set retention and retry policies through the team's normal review process. Keeping every raw payload indefinitely is not a substitute for deciding what an audit actually needs.

Use an illustrative acceptance fixture with 4 inputs: the same permanent-failure event twice, a temporary failure, and a delayed failure for a replaced destination. Expect one committed decision for the repeated event, no invalid-recipient finding for the temporary failure, and no restriction on revision 8 from evidence tied to revision 7. Inject a transaction failure as well; after replay, the decision record and recipient state must agree. These are test expectations, not measured results.

Monitor missing packets, unresolved classifications, ingestion delay, and disagreements between authorization and transport outcome. Each points to different corrective work. Retaining diagnostics and investigating mismatches also consumes storage and staff time, so include that maintenance burden in selection without making volatile unit prices the argument.

Enable enforcement only when a sampled restriction can be reconstructed from attempt to evidence to policy to recipient state. That exit criterion makes bounce handling accountable to the marketplace's review needs while leaving unsupported deliverability rankings out of the decision.

References

The transaction boundaries, record shapes, example identifiers, and rollout checks above are proposed application design choices. The public specification below supports the SPF discussion; it does not substantiate comparative provider performance or a legal compliance claim.

Sources

  • RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF), including Section 4.6.4 on DNS lookup limits: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: What a good website enquiry form should ask Indian customers
description:
A useful enquiry form saves a small business time without making a potential customer work too hard. The form should help staff understand what the visitor needs and how to reply; it should not collect every detail that might be useful someday. Think about the common questions your team asks after a missed call, then include only the fields needed to answer them.

Ask for a reliable way to reply

Let people choose a preferred contact method, such as phone or email, and require only the chosen method rather than demanding both. If your team actively handles WhatsApp enquiries, make that an option; if nobody monitors it consistently, do not offer it as a promise. Use clear labels, explain the expected response window only if staff can meet it, and show a phone number for visitors who would rather call. A confirmation message should say that the request was received and what to do if the matter is urgent or time-sensitive.

Keep the request focused

Ask for a name and a short description of the service, product, or question. For a business that serves a local area, a city, locality, or PIN code can help determine whether the request is in range. For a product enquiry, a model or item name may be more useful than a long free-text box. If the business has several branches, ask the visitor to select the relevant location. Do not ask for an address unless delivery or an on-site visit truly requires it.

A short choice list can help visitors be specific: for example, “new enquiry,” “existing order,” or “support,” but use categories that match the way staff actually handle work. Keep optional details optional. Avoid asking for sensitive information such as passwords, full payment-card data, identity numbers, or detailed health information in an ordinary contact form. If a later conversation needs private information, give people a separate, staff-approved way to share it.

Make it easy to complete on a phone

Use plain labels and examples rather than relying on placeholder text that disappears while typing. Mark required fields clearly, keep the submit button easy to tap, and explain errors beside the field that needs attention. Do not clear everything a visitor entered when one field is incomplete. A form that asks for a date or file should explain why that detail is needed and offer a simple alternative if the visitor cannot provide it.

Before publishing, test the form on a small phone, with a slow connection, and with keyboard navigation. Check that a real staff member receives the request, the confirmation is accurate, and spam controls do not block genuine enquiries. Review who can access submissions and remove them when they are no longer needed under the business’s own retention process. Do not copy personal details into public spreadsheets or analytics tools.

Keep the privacy explanation close to the form and use language customers can understand. If you are preparing a wider site brief, the MGTech Labs blog is one place to explore practical planning topics. A good form is small, clear, and matched to the way the team really works.

title: Same Task, Different Statement: When and How Reformulation Helps LLM Problem Solving
description:
arXiv:2611.14997v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. The question is when and how to rewrite.

title: Healthtech Receipt Uploads in Node.js SaaS: Private Object Storage and Audit Links
description:
The operational constraint decides this storage choice: a receipt must be easy for an authorized reviewer to retrieve, but the original file must not become a permanent public URL. Short answer: keep receipt objects private, store an object key plus an audit record in your database, and mint short-lived download URLs only after the application checks the reviewer's access.

That answer is less about picking a famous bucket service than defining two separate paths. Delivery simplicity belongs at the HTTP boundary. Access control, retention, and evidence belong in the application and its audit trail. Mixing them is how a convenient upload demo turns into a compliance cleanup project.

For a notebook-to-prod Python team building a Node.js SaaS, I would evaluate the design with a fixed receipt corpus, an authorization test matrix, and a prompt-cost-aware review of any extraction step. Storage should preserve the evidence; the AI pipeline can produce a derived record that never replaces it.

Receipt retention governance comes before the bucket

Give every upload a new, opaque key. Do not use an email address, claim number, or sequential database ID as the object name. Those values leak business context and make guessing easier. A key such as tenants/acme/receipts/2026/08/<random>.pdf is still useful for operations, while the random component prevents a URL pattern from becoming an index.

The browser can send a small receipt through the application API when validation and malware scanning need to happen in one controlled request. For larger files, a presigned PUT can deliver bytes directly to private storage. That is a delivery decision, not an authorization decision: the application still decides which tenant may create the object and which reviewer may read it.

Store the key, content type, byte count, checksum, uploader, tenant, and a state such as quarantined or accepted in a database row. Store the original object separately from OCR text, extracted totals, and thumbnails. The original is evidence. A parser's output is an interpretation.

The download route should look up the receipt row, check the current user's tenant and role, write an audit event, then mint a short-lived GET URL. The application returns the URL; it does not save the URL as the receipt's identity. A leaked link should have a bounded lifetime, while the key remains a stable reference for later authorization and audit queries.

Three words: key, policy, evidence.

Keep it private.

Here is a deliberately boring Python sketch of the boundary. It leaves the storage client behind an interface so an evaluation can swap an S3-compatible implementation, a local test double, or a gateway without changing authorization logic.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from secrets import token_urlsafe


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReceiptUpload:
    tenant_id: str
    receipt_id: str
    object_key: str
    content_type: str
    size_bytes: int
    checksum: str
    state: str


def new_receipt_key(tenant_id: str, receipt_id: str) -> str:
    """Create an opaque key; the database remains the source of identity."""
    nonce = token_urlsafe(18)
    return f"tenants/{tenant_id}/receipts/{receipt_id}/{nonce}.bin"


def make_download_request(receipt: ReceiptUpload, actor: dict, storage) -> dict:
    if actor["tenant_id"] != receipt.tenant_id:
        raise PermissionError("receipt is outside the actor tenant")
    if actor["role"] not in {"auditor", "claims_reviewer"}:
        raise PermissionError("actor cannot review receipts")
    if receipt.state != "accepted":
        raise PermissionError("receipt is not ready for review")

    audit_event = {
        "event": "receipt.download_url_issued",
        "receipt_id": receipt.receipt_id,
        "actor_id": actor["id"],
        "issued_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    }
    # Persist this event before returning the URL in the real application.
    record_audit_event(audit_event)
    url = storage.presign_get(receipt.object_key, expires_seconds=300)
    return {"url": url, "expires_seconds": 300}


def record_audit_event(event: dict) -> None:
    """Replace this with the application's append-only audit sink."""
    pass

The pass is a boundary in a small example, not an audit strategy. In production, the event needs a durable sink, an idempotency key, and enough context to answer who accessed which receipt and why. If the event write fails, the safest policy is to withhold the link. A reviewer who sees an occasional retry is less dangerous than a download with no evidence.

The receipt API model makes retries visible

An upload is not complete when the storage service accepts bytes. It is complete when the database can connect an accepted object to one tenant and one receipt, and the application has recorded the validation decision. Use a state transition such as pending -> quarantined -> accepted rather than making the object visible to reviewers immediately.

The commit order matters. Create the database row with a fresh key, upload to that key, verify size and checksum, run the scanner or extraction worker, and then transition the row. If the process dies after the upload but before the transition, a reconciliation job can find an unreferenced object. If the database row exists but the upload never arrives, the row can expire. Both cases are visible. Overwriting one shared key hides them.

Retries need a stable operation identity. A timeout after a successful PUT is not proof that the PUT failed. Retry the same key for the same upload attempt, and make the database transition idempotent. A second user action gets a new key. In my test harness, a repeated commit is a 409-shaped case, not an invitation to replace the current receipt silently.

For direct browser upload, test CORS from the exact production origin, with the actual headers and methods. MDN's CORS guide is a useful reference because the browser enforces the policy; a successful server-to-server request says nothing about whether the browser will allow the response. Do not put a storage credential in browser code. A presigned request grants a narrow operation for a limited period, while the application credential stays on the server.

Multipart upload belongs to the large-file branch, not the default receipt path. The AWS multipart overview documents the create, upload-parts, and complete shape, along with the need to complete or abort an upload. Whatever compatible backend you use, add a reaper for abandoned uploads and test a failed part, a repeated part, and a completion retry. More protocol steps mean more states to observe.

How should a Node.js SaaS choose private object storage for receipt uploads?

Treat the system as three records with different owners:

Record Owner What it must answer
Original object Private object storage Can the bytes be retrieved intact?
Receipt row Application database Which tenant, status, checksum, and object key are current?
Audit event Append-only audit sink Who requested access, when, and under which role?

This division makes a subtle distinction testable. A short-lived URL controls delivery after authorization; it does not replace authorization. A reviewer can forward a live link before it expires, so the expiry window should reflect the UI workflow, not a claim that links are impossible to share. For higher-risk data, stream the file through an authorization gateway or use a shorter window and stronger session controls.

The same distinction applies to deletion. A user-facing delete action can remove the database association while retention policy preserves the original for an approved period. Do not let a generic cleanup job delete evidence merely because a thumbnail or OCR row disappeared. Define retention by record type, tenant policy, and legal hold, then make the cleanup worker emit its own audit events.

I keep the extraction evaluator separate from the storage evaluator. The receipt image is a fixed input; the extraction output gets scored for field accuracy, missing-value behavior, and token use. That separation catches a prompt regression without mistaking it for a storage regression. I'm not sure which will dominate the bill until real receipt sizes and review frequency are measured, so I would not make a provider decision from a single upload benchmark.

The browser is an integration boundary, not an authorization policy

The catch is that this pattern is not suitable when the product requires permanent public URLs, anonymous hotlinking, or a built-in image transformation service. Choose a delivery layer designed for public media when public delivery is the requirement. Do not weaken a healthtech access boundary to make a demo tag load faster.

It is also a poor fit if the storage layer alone must provide immutable legal retention, cross-region disaster recovery, or fine-grained server-side search over receipt metadata. Put those requirements into the acceptance criteria. If the chosen backend cannot provide the required retention control, use a dedicated archive or an application-managed evidence workflow. If the team cannot operate reconciliation and audit sinks, choose a managed architecture with those controls rather than pretending a presigned URL supplies them.

S3 compatibility is a useful portability signal, not proof of feature parity. Compare the details that affect this application: private ACL semantics, presigning inputs, maximum object size, multipart lifecycle, checksum behavior, CORS configuration, retention controls, region placement, and export tooling. Keep that comparison in an executable acceptance test where possible. A row in a feature table is not evidence until the team can reproduce it.

The decision rule is simple. Use the simplest private object store that passes the access, retention, recovery, and delivery tests for your receipt workflow. Stick with a more integrated cloud storage option when its identity, archive, or regional controls are already mandatory. Use a separate archive or gateway when private object storage cannot carry the compliance boundary by itself.

What should the rollout evaluation prove before launch?

Start with one realistic experiment: 100 synthetic receipts across the expected size range, two tenants, an auditor, an unauthorized user, an expired URL, a repeated upload attempt, a failed scanner transition, and one abandoned multipart upload. Keep original files and derived OCR records distinct throughout the run.

Measure more than latency:

  • unauthorized reads blocked before URL issuance;
  • audit events present for every issued URL;
  • duplicate keys and duplicate database commits after retries;
  • checksum and byte-count agreement after download;
  • abandoned objects and uploads found by reconciliation;
  • extraction accuracy and tokens used on the same corpus.

Then run a deletion and retention exercise. Ask what happens when a receipt is removed, a tenant is suspended, or a legal hold appears while a link is still live. Those answers define the product's real security model.

The best storage choice is the one whose failure states remain legible. Private by default, explicit in the database, auditable at the download boundary, and measured with the same corpus you expect in production.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html

title: Detecting a kayak is only one part of deploying outdoor computer vision
description:
A bounding box can be convincing in a demonstration and still leave important operational questions unanswered. Outdoor monitoring adds changing light, distance, reflections, occlusion and weather. Evaluating those conditions matters as much as selecting a model.

Disclosure and provenance: Prepared by Verix Technology using AI tooling. Verix Technology's owner reports building and deploying a production-grade computer-vision project detecting people, kayaks and rafts in an Illinois River setting, with a water-sports safety purpose around dam operations. This article describes evaluation considerations. It does not identify the client, reveal implementation details, claim a particular model was used, or claim measured accuracy, autonomous dam control or lives saved.

Define the operational task

Specify whether the output is a detection record, an operator display or an alert proposal. Identify which decision belongs to an operator. Detection is an observation about an image, not proof that a location is clear or a person is safe. An absent detection must not be treated as proof of absence.

Define the relevant region, object classes and minimum visible size. A distant raft, a partly occluded kayak and a cluster of people create different error cases. State how the system handles an unavailable camera, a frozen image or a scene outside the tested conditions. The fallback is part of the system design.

Split evaluation by capture conditions

Randomly splitting adjacent frames can make a test deceptively easy because nearly identical scenes occur in both sets. Prefer separation by capture session or time period where feasible. Keep a final holdout that reflects the intended operating conditions and has not been used to tune thresholds.

Report both missed objects and false detections, broken down by relevant conditions such as glare, distance and occlusion. A single aggregate score can hide a weak operating condition. If alerting is in scope, also evaluate delay and alert burden; a good detector can still produce an unusable alert workflow.

Document the evidence boundary

Maintain an annotation guide and review disagreements. Record where imagery came from and the permission to use it. Do not release identifiable people, restricted sites or customer camera footage merely to create a public portfolio. A public explanation can use an abstract diagram or synthetic example with a clear label.

List the tested operating envelope and the conditions that require manual review or suspension. Re-evaluate when the camera moves, the environment changes or the software/model changes. Agree access controls, retention, maintenance ownership and escalation with the operator.

What a buyer should ask

Ask for the intended decision, representative evaluation set, condition-specific results, failure handling and operational handover. Ask which claims are measured and which are design goals. A safety-related deployment also needs the responsible domain specialists to define the required assurance; a general AI vendor cannot replace that judgment with an accuracy claim.

Verix can discuss computer-vision architecture and evaluation for a defined monitoring use case. We distinguish project descriptions from measurements and confirm what can be shared: verixtechnology.com.
