title: Read your AWS Cost Explorer CSV in 19 lines of Node
description:
Cost Explorer's charts answer "which service". The CSV answers the better question, "which line item, and when did it change". You can read it with a script short enough to paste into a terminal, and no AWS credentials are involved: you only read a file you already downloaded.

Get the file

In Cost Explorer, set the date range to the last 30 to 90 days, granularity Daily, Group by: Usage type, then Download CSV. The file has one row per usage type, one column per day, and a final column with the total.

Here is a tiny made-up file (synthetic, not from a real account), saved as sample.csv:

"Usage type","2026-10-01","2026-10-02","2026-10-03","Total costs($)"
"USE1-BoxUsage:m5.large",36.86,36.86,36.86,110.58
"USE1-NatGateway-Bytes",8.00,8.00,31.00,47.00
"USE1-NatGateway-Hours",2.16,2.16,2.16,6.48
"USE1-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes",12.00,12.00,12.00,36.00
"USE1-PublicIPv4:InUseAddress",0.48,0.48,0.48,1.44
"Total costs",59.50,59.50,82.50,201.50

The script

Save as top.mjs. It needs Node 18 or newer and nothing from npm:

import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

// Split one CSV line; commas inside "quotes" stay in the field.
const cells = (line) => line.match(/("([^"]|"")*"|[^,]*)(,|$)/g)
  .map((c) => c.replace(/,$/, '').replace(/^"|"$/g, '').replace(/""/g, '"'))
  .slice(0, -1);

const [head, ...rows] = readFileSync(process.argv[2], 'utf8').replace(/^\uFEFF/, '').trim().split(/[\u000d\u000a]+/);
const days = cells(head).slice(1, -1);                        // the date columns
const items = rows.map(cells)
  .filter((r) => !/^Total costs/.test(r[0]))
  .map((r) => ({ type: r[0], first: +r[1], last: +r[r.length - 2], total: +r[r.length - 1] }))
  .sort((a, b) => b.total - a.total);

console.log(`${days[0]} to ${days.at(-1)}`);
for (const i of items.slice(0, 10)) {
  const jump = i.first > 0 && i.last / i.first >= 2 ? `  <- ${(i.last / i.first).toFixed(1)}x since day 1` : '';
  console.log(`${i.type.padEnd(34)} $${i.total.toFixed(2).padStart(8)}${jump}`);
}

Run node top.mjs sample.csv and you get:

2026-10-01 to 2026-10-03
USE1-BoxUsage:m5.large             $  110.58
USE1-NatGateway-Bytes              $   47.00  <- 3.9x since day 1
USE1-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes   $   36.00
USE1-NatGateway-Hours              $    6.48
USE1-PublicIPv4:InUseAddress       $    1.44

That output was produced by running the script on the file above. It handles a byte-order mark, Windows line endings and quoted names that contain commas.

What to look at in the output

  1. The biggest line is rarely the interesting one. Compute is large and expected. The lines worth a question are the ones you cannot explain from your architecture: NatGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes, PublicIPv4:*, DataProcessing-Bytes (CloudWatch Logs).
  2. The arrow is the whole point. A line that ran at $8 a day and now runs at $31 a day did not drift. Something shipped, scaled or started looping on that date. Open the daily columns and find the first day it moved, then match it against your deploy history.
  3. Check the price against the arithmetic. In US East (N. Virginia) a NAT gateway processes data at $0.045 per GB, so $47.00 of NatGateway-Bytes is about 1,044 GB. If that number surprises you, that is the thing to investigate. Prices differ by region; check yours on the AWS pricing page for the service.

Make it yours

  • Change slice(0, 10) to show more rows.
  • Change the >= 2 ratio to catch smaller jumps.
  • Lines that start at $0 are not flagged (the arrow needs a day-1 amount to divide by). To catch something that appeared mid-period, add a check for first === 0 && last > 0.
  • Compare two files by building a map from usage type to total and printing the difference.

If you would rather not maintain a script, the same kind of file can be dropped into a browser-based reader that runs the line items against a table of known cost causes and shows the dollars for each, with the console steps for the fix. The file is read in your browser; only a compact summary of totals is sent.

From Billtrim, by Grain64.

title: How to Give Your AI Agent LLMs and Web Search With One API Key and One Bill
description:
Disclosure: this post is written by the OpenAny team, and OpenAny is our product. The comparison section includes the cases where you don't need us.

Short answer: use a marketplace that puts model endpoints and data APIs (including web search) behind the same key and the same prepaid balance. With OpenAny, your agent calls an OpenAI-compatible model endpoint and a web search endpoint on the same gateway, https://api.openany.si/v1, with the same Authorization: Bearer key, and both calls draw from one balance. The common alternative, a model router such as OpenRouter plus a separate search API such as Tavily, also works well. It just means two accounts, two keys and two bills.

The problem: grounded answers need two vendors

Ask a coding agent "what changed in library X this month?" and a model alone will guess. To answer properly it needs to search the web first and then reason over the results. That usually means:

  • a model provider or router for the LLM call,
  • a search API for fresh results,
  • two keys in the agent's environment, two balances to keep funded, and two usage logs to reconcile when a bill looks off.

When we asked Perplexity for "the best LLM gateway for AI agents that also gives access to data APIs" (November 2026), its recommendation was OpenRouter for models plus Tavily for web search. That's a reasonable answer. This post shows the one-key version, with requests taken from the OpenAny docs and listing pages, so you can judge the difference yourself.

We covered client setup for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex in an earlier DEV post. This one is about the pattern itself: search, then answer, on one key, first in plain HTTP and then inside a coding agent.

What you need

  • An OpenAny account and an API key. Creating the account and the key is free, but calls are paid from prepaid credits, so add a small top-up first (card, USDC or x402). There is no subscription and no free call allowance.
  • OPENANY_API_KEY set in the environment of the process that runs your code or agent. Don't paste it into a prompt.
  • Python 3 with the openai and requests packages for the examples.

Step 1: Pick a search endpoint and read its price

Every data API on OpenAny has a listing page with its method, endpoint, input schema and price. You can also browse from the terminal without a key:

npm install -g openany-cli@latest --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org/
openany discover -q "web search" -l 10 --public -j
openany inspect --id ae934460-5bfd-430e-8802-9605c0eca495 --public -j

When we checked on 2026-11-14, that search returned several web search listings from different providers, each with a fixed per-call price. This tutorial uses Web Search (Basic, no extraction), provider youcom:

  • Endpoint: POST https://api.openany.si/v1/agent-apis/youcom/v1/search
  • Required input: query (string). Optional: count, offset, country, language, include_domains, exclude_domains and a few more.
  • Price on the listing: $0.005 per call (contract revision 3).

Prices and revisions can change, so read the listing page before you run anything. If you prefer a different provider, the same flow works with any search listing. Just copy its endpoint and schema.

Step 2: Call search over plain HTTP

This is the request shown on the listing page, trimmed to two fields:

curl 'https://api.openany.si/v1/agent-apis/youcom/v1/search' \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENANY_API_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"query": "Node.js 24 release notes", "count": 5}'

When we ran this on 2026-11-14 it returned HTTP 200 in about two seconds. The body looks like this (trimmed):

{
  "metadata": {"query": "Node.js 24 release notes", "search_uuid": "...", "latency": 0.51},
  "openany_cost": 5000,
  "results": {
    "web": [
      {
        "title": "Node.js — Node.js 24.0.0 (Current)",
        "url": "https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v24.0.0",
        "description": "...",
        "snippets": ["We're excited to announce the release of Node.js 24! ..."],
        "favicon_url": "...",
        "thumbnail_url": "..."
      }
    ]
  }
}

Three things to notice:

  • results.web holds the hits. Each has title, url, a short description and a snippets array with longer extracts, which is the better text to ground a model on. The listing's sample also shows a results.news array; our queries only came back with web, so treat news as optional.
  • openany_cost is the charge for this call in micro-USD: 5000 means $0.005, matching the listing. The response headers also carry an x-request-id you can match against your usage records.
  • Errors come back as JSON too. A request without a valid Authorization header returned HTTP 401 with "code": "openany_authentication_invalid", a readable message and "openany_cost": 0. Your agent can branch on code instead of parsing prose.

Step 3: Let the model choose the searches, on the same key

The model endpoint is OpenAI-compatible, so the official openai package works with a changed base_url. Model IDs are route-specific, so copy one from the model catalog. We tested with deepseek-v4-flash, which supported tool calling through OpenAny when we ran this on 2026-11-14. Check the listing for the model you pick.

The flow has two model calls. First the model gets a web_search tool and decides what to search for. Then it answers from numbered sources, with no tools offered:

import json
import os

import requests
from openai import OpenAI

KEY = os.environ["OPENANY_API_KEY"]
BASE = "https://api.openany.si/v1"
MODEL = os.environ.get("OPENANY_MODEL", "deepseek-v4-flash")  # copy a current ID from the catalog
client = OpenAI(api_key=KEY, base_url=BASE)

def web_search(query: str, count: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    r = requests.post(
        f"{BASE}/agent-apis/youcom/v1/search",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"},
        json={"query": query, "count": count},
        timeout=30,
    )
    body = r.json()
    if r.status_code != 200:
        raise RuntimeError(f"search failed: {r.status_code} {body.get('code')} {body.get('message')}")
    print(f"search {query!r}: openany_cost={body.get('openany_cost')} micro-USD")
    return [
        {"title": w["title"], "url": w["url"], "text": " ".join(w.get("snippets") or [w.get("description", "")])}
        for w in body["results"].get("web", [])
    ]

TOOLS = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "web_search",
        "description": "Search the web. Returns titles, URLs and text snippets.",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["query"],
        },
    },
}]

def ask(question: str, max_searches: int = 2) -> str:
    # Round 1: let the model decide what to search for.
    first = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        tools=TOOLS,
        max_tokens=1000,  # reasoning tokens count against this limit
    )
    msg = first.choices[0].message
    if not msg.tool_calls:
        return msg.content  # the model answered without searching

    # Run at most max_searches of the requested searches.
    sources = []
    for tc in msg.tool_calls[:max_searches]:
        query = json.loads(tc.function.arguments or "{}").get("query")
        if query:
            sources += web_search(query)

    # Round 2: answer from the numbered sources, with no tools offered.
    numbered = "\n\n".join(f"[{i+1}] {s['title']} ({s['url']})\n{s['text']}" for i, s in enumerate(sources))
    final = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Answer only from the numbered sources and cite them like [1]. If they don't cover something, say so."},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"{question}\n\nSources:\n{numbered}"},
        ],
        max_tokens=4000,  # leave headroom: reasoning tokens count too
    )
    print("model usage:", final.usage)
    return final.choices[0].message.content

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(ask("What are the headline changes in Node.js 24?"))

On our run the model asked for two searches in parallel ("Node.js 24 headline changes release" and "Node.js 24 new features announcement"). The script ran both and the model answered with a cited list: the V8 13.6 and npm 11 upgrades, global URLPattern, Undici 7, the --permission flag and more, each tagged with source numbers.

Some things we learned while getting this to work:

  • Reasoning tokens count against max_tokens. This model reasons before it answers. With max_tokens=500 the final answer came back empty with finish_reason: "length", and on a longer prompt even 2,000 tokens all went to reasoning. The script leaves 4,000 for the answering call.
  • Keep the answering call free of tools. In a multi-round loop, the model kept asking for more searches, and tool_choice: "none" didn't stop it on the route we hit. Offering tools once and then answering from a plain sources message was the reliable pattern.
  • Cap the searches yourself. max_searches limits paid calls no matter how many the model asks for.

Every call draws from one balance. The searches are billed at the listing's per-call price and the model calls at the route's token rates, and all of them show up in the same usage records. openany calls list listed both kinds of rows side by side, each with a chargedCostMicroUsd.

Step 4: Let Claude Code, Cursor or Codex do it

In a coding agent you usually don't write this loop yourself. The OpenAny skill plus CLI gives the agent the same two capabilities through its terminal, and it leaves the agent's own main model alone.

  1. Save the skill where your client looks for it: .claude/skills/openany/SKILL.md (Claude Code), .cursor/skills/openany/SKILL.md (Cursor) or .agents/skills/openany/SKILL.md (Codex). The file is at https://openany.si/SKILL.md. Read it before installing.
  2. Install the CLI (Node.js 22+) and run openany setup --scenario call in your own terminal to store the key.
  3. Give the agent a bounded task:

Use the openany skill. Search the web for the Node.js 24 release notes with one search API, show me the price before calling, then summarize the top results with links. Budget: $0.05.

The skill tells the agent to check the balance, discover a search API, inspect its schema and price, then run it, and to report the request ID and cost. You can audit afterwards with openany calls list --limit 20 -j.

If you also want the editor's chat model billed through OpenAny, that's a separate, optional step: Cursor's Override OpenAI Base URL set to https://api.openany.si/v1, or a custom model_providers.openany block in ~/.codex/config.toml with wire_api = "responses". Check that the chosen model route supports the protocol your client needs first; Chat Completions support alone doesn't guarantee Codex's Responses API works.

OpenRouter + Tavily vs one balance: an honest comparison

OpenRouter alone is fine when your agent only needs models. It's a mature router with a large model catalog and a long track record. If you never call a data API, adding OpenAny gives you nothing.

OpenRouter plus a separate search API is fine when you only need one or two data sources and you're happy managing them. Tavily, Exa and others are built specifically for agent search, with their own docs and SDKs. Two keys and two bills is a small cost if the setup doesn't change.

One balance helps when:

  • your agent keeps reaching for new data sources (search today, GitHub or finance data next week) and you don't want a new account for each,
  • you want one usage log that answers "what did this agent spend, and on what?" across models and APIs,
  • you want to fund agents with USDC or x402 top-ups as well as cards,
  • you want prices visible before the call, so the agent can show the cost and ask first.

Where OpenAny is weaker:

  • It's young. We launched in October 2026. Listings are not uptime guarantees, so test the endpoints you depend on.
  • It's hosted only. You can't self-host the gateway.
  • Protocol coverage varies by route. Responses API and tool calling depend on the model route.
  • x402 here is for funding your balance. Direct per-request x402 payment applies only to endpoints that explicitly support it.
  • Data APIs come from many providers. Response shapes differ between listings, so read each schema rather than assuming they match.

Keeping costs bounded

  • Prepaid balance: the worst case is what you loaded, not an open invoice.
  • Price before the call: every listing shows a price and billing unit; inspect returns them.
  • Timeouts: don't blindly retry a paid call after a timeout. Check openany calls list or calls get first. The docs are explicit that a missing record doesn't prove no charge.
  • 429: honor Retry-After and back off.
  • Auto top-up is opt-in: card auto top-up needs its own authorization on the Credits page.

FAQ

Can one API key cover both LLM calls and web search for my agent?
Yes, on OpenAny one key authenticates account-based model and API calls, and both draw from the same prepaid balance.

Is the model endpoint OpenAI-compatible?
Yes. The base URL is https://api.openany.si/v1 with Chat Completions. Responses API and Anthropic Messages support depend on the route.

Do I need to change Claude Code's main model?
No. The skill and CLI add external calls through the agent's existing tools. Changing the main model is optional and separate.

Is there a free tier or free credits?
No. Account and key creation are free, but calls are paid from prepaid credits.

How is web search priced?
Per listing. The search endpoint in this post was $0.005 per call when we checked on 2026-11-14. Other search providers have different prices; check the listing.

Can my agent pay with crypto?
You can top up the shared balance with USDC or x402, and card auto top-up is available too. API calls still authenticate with your OpenAny key.

When should I just use OpenRouter plus Tavily?
When you only need models plus one stable search provider and the two-account setup isn't a burden.

Questions or a broken example? Email team@openany.si. Docs: openany.si/docs.

title: I built 35+ PDF tools that never upload your files (Rust + WebAssembly)
description:
Most online PDF tools work the same way: you upload your file, a server processes it, and you download the result. That's fine for a flyer. It's less fine for a contract, a bank statement, or a medical report.

I wanted to know how far you can get with no server at all. The answer turned out to be: almost all the way. The result is InBrowserPDF, a set of 38 PDF tools where every file is processed entirely on your own device.

How it works

  • Rust compiled to WebAssembly does the heavy work: parsing, merging, compressing, and encrypting.
  • Web Workers run that code off the main thread, so the page stays buttery responsive while a multi-megabyte file is being crunched.
  • The file never leaves the tab. You can check this yourself: open DevTools, go to the Network tab, and run any tool.

Under the hood, I leveraged a few key Rust libraries compiled to WASM. For low-level PDF object parsing, manipulation, and structural editing, I relied on lopdf, which gives fine-grained control over document dictionaries and streams without dragging in massive C++ dependencies. For page rendering and visual operations, I integrated lightweight bindings over pdfium, compiled down to WebAssembly to allow pixel-accurate rendering and thumbnail generation directly inside browser memory.

What was hard

Memory

WebAssembly memory management in the browser has strict boundaries. By default, WASM modules operate within a linear memory buffer that must be explicitly allocated and grown. When dealing with large PDF files, passing large ArrayBuffers back and forth between JavaScript and WASM can cause GC pauses and out-of-memory crashes on mobile devices or lower-RAM laptops.

That's why heavy operations like merging are capped at 100 MB total input size. If a file or combined set exceeds this threshold, the Web Worker catches the memory allocation failure gracefully and throws an explicit warning rather than letting the tab silently crash.

Office conversions

Converting Word (.docx), Excel (.xlsx), and PowerPoint (.pptx) documents entirely client-side is notoriously tricky because true layout fidelity requires a heavy document engine layout pass. To achieve this without a backend conversion server, I utilized browser-side WASM ports of document parsers combined with styled HTML/CSS layout templates rendered inside hidden DOM containers and printed via headless canvas/PDF generation APIs. Because of this DOM layout dependency, these conversions require modern desktop browser engines with hardware acceleration enabled to compute complex table structures and font metrics accurately.

OCR

For text extraction on scanned documents, I integrated Tesseract compiled to WebAssembly. While it works remarkably well offline, client-side OCR is computationally expensive. To keep memory footprints reasonable and processing times under a few seconds per page, the current WASM build is restricted to lightweight data packs optimized strictly for printed English text rather than heavy multilingual neural nets.

What I'd do differently

If I could rewrite one part of the architecture, I would have decoupled the larger WASM worker tasks earlier. Initially, I tried bundling too many disparate utility functions into a single monolithic Web Worker script, which bloated the initial worker initialization chunk and complicated error propagation. Splitting them into isolated, single-responsibility worker modules loaded on-demand via dynamic imports saved me days of debugging data-clone serialization bottlenecks.

What it can do today

  • Merge, split, organize, extract, and remove pages
  • Compress, repair, and OCR
  • Convert Word, Excel, PowerPoint, JPG, and HTML to PDF, and back
  • Edit, sign, fill forms, watermark, crop, and add page numbers
  • Protect with AES-256, unlock, redact, compare, and remove metadata
  • Convert PDF to Markdown and summarize

It's free and needs no account.

Known limits

  • Merge handles up to 100 MB in total
  • Compare handles up to 20 pages
  • Batch handles up to 20 files
  • OCR is printed English only

I'd like your feedback

If you try it, I'd like to know:

  1. Did anything fail or slow down on a large or unusual file?
  2. How did the Office conversions handle your real documents?
  3. What would you want next?

Try it at inbrowserpdf.app, and tell me what breaks.

title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.15515v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.

title: Goodbye... Pico.
description:
Lucas Larroche declared on Oct 4, 2026 that he was archiving PicoCSS and it really upset me. Here was a library that I promoted, used in several websites, and really saw as the future of minimalistic web development.

This was basically me after the news:

Starting last month sometime, I decided that I would rewrite the library to not only address some of the issues Lucas outlind such as using OKLCH colors, cascade layers, and the Popover API, but to also make some architectural decisions that I didn't agree. And guess what? Today's the day I finally pushed everything up on GitHub. There is a full demo on jsfiddle too: https://jsfiddle.net/mvsq4wbg/

The name I decided to go with is T'Pico, which is a double entendre not only representing the minimalistic nature of Pico's original vision but also as a play on the Cajun norm of putting "T" in front of people's names (like father "Bob" and son "T'Bob"); in a sense T'Pico is a child born out of PicoCSS.

I think one of the best new features that I added was the offcanvas component. This takes the existing paradigm of using an <aside> element to transform existing component, in this case it turns a normal dialog into an offcanvas that comes in and out of view from the "start" side of the viewport. An example of a basic offcanvas looks like this:

<dialog id="example-offcanvas" closedby="any" aria-labelledby="offcanvas-title">
  <aside>
    <article>
      <header>
        <button type="button" command="request-close" commandfor="example-offcanvas" aria-label="Hide offcanvas"></button>
        <h2 id="offcanvas-title">T'Pico Offcanvas</h2>
      </header>

      <p>
        Let slide into your view baby.
      </p>

      <footer>
        <button type="button" command="request-close" commandfor="example-offcanvas">
          Close
        </button>
      </footer>
    </article>
  </aside>
</dialog>

Another feature that existed in Pico as part of the class-based version that I ported over without using classes is the dropdown component. This takes a button and a list then leverages the native Popover attribute to display dropdowns:

<button type="button" popovertarget="example-dropdown">
  Settings
</button>
<ul id="example-dropdown" popover>
  <li><a href="#profile">Profile</a></li>
  <li><a href="#settings">Settings</a></li>
  <li><a href="#help">Help</a></li>
</ul>

Outside of implementing new things, I think more importantly is that there were some questionable practices that weren't carried over. For example, the RTL attribute in Pico was used to dictate the direction of components when in reality, MDN defines it as:

A locale property indicating that text is written from right to left.

Rather than hijacking this attribute to manage visual appearances of components, I felt like it was better left out entirely.

Full disclaimer if you decide to check out the repository: I basically gave ChatGPT my source code for T'Pico and told it to write the documentation for me. This saved me hours in building out the documentation. I know some will poo-poo on that, but it really helped me with the tedious stuff that I'm not really good at. In case you can't tell by this post, I cant spel are grammur goodly.

I look forward to hearing y'all's feedback and let's keep the move to more minimalistic web development going!

title: Which Enterprise Platforms Unify Identity, Billing, and Deployment Across Multiple Clouds? A Three-Layer Coverage Matrix (2026)
description:
Few platforms unify identity, billing, and deployment natively across multiple clouds. Most enterprises combine an identity provider, a FinOps tool, and a deployment layer, and the real question is which layer each product owns versus integrates. Control Plane (a platform that runs production workloads across clouds) unifies all three for workloads it runs: one definition deploys to every cloud, one identity model reaches cloud services, and one invoice covers that compute on every cloud.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Almost no single product covers identity, billing, and deployment across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) without relying on other tools.

  • Identity splits into two problems: human access (SSO, RBAC, groups) and workload identity (how running code gets credentials for cloud services without long-lived keys). Most multi-cloud identity products solve only the first.
  • Billing splits into visibility over separate cloud bills versus one actual invoice from one payer. Most FinOps tools give visibility. They do not consolidate the invoice.
  • Deployment splits into one definition deployed to several clouds versus a catalog that provisions per-cloud resources. Terraform modules and Kubernetes fleet managers both abstract provisioning, but the abstraction depth varies.
  • Few products unify all three. Cloud management platforms (CMPs) typically cover deployment and billing visibility but rely on an external identity provider. FinOps tools cover billing visibility only. Identity providers cover human access only.
  • Four stack patterns dominate: CMP-led, Kubernetes-led, hyperscaler-led, and best-of-breed. Each requires two to four products.
  • Control Plane is the platform-led alternative. It provides one workload definition across clouds, Universal Cloud Identity (Control Plane’s single workload identity for AWS, GCP, and Azure), and one invoice covering compute Control Plane provides.
  • In a demo , ask to see one workload getting credentials in two clouds without stored keys, one invoice versus three bills, one definition deployed to two clouds, cost broken down by team across clouds, and what happens to access when an employee leaves.

Which enterprise platforms unify identity, billing, and deployment across multiple clouds?

No widely adopted platform unifies all three layers with full depth across every major cloud. The market is segmented by origin: cloud management platforms like CloudBolt and HPE Morpheus Enterprise started from provisioning and added cost visibility, Flexera One centers on FinOps and asset management, and Nutanix Cloud Manager centers on provisioning with on-premises cost governance. All of them rely on external identity providers for SSO and have no native workload identity across clouds. FinOps tools like Vantage and Apptio Cloudability focus exclusively on cost visibility and optimization. Identity providers like Okta Workforce Identity and Microsoft Entra ID solve human access and federation but do not deploy workloads or consolidate billing.

Kubernetes-centric platforms such as Red Hat OpenShift with Advanced Cluster Management deploy containerized workloads across clusters in multiple clouds, but billing and identity remain largely external concerns. Azure Arc with Microsoft Entra ID comes closest within the hyperscaler ecosystem by combining human identity, Azure management for servers and Kubernetes clusters in other environments, and Azure Cost Management, but Azure Cost Management does not report AWS or Google Cloud spend, and workload identity across non-Azure clouds requires additional configuration.

The result is that enterprises assemble stacks of two to four products, each owning one layer. The top multi-cloud management platforms in 2026 compares the CMP landscape in more depth.

What does unifying each layer actually mean?

Each layer has two meanings that vendors often blur.

Identity: human access and workload identity

Human access is who can sign in and what they can change. This includes SSO, RBAC, groups, and lifecycle management. Enterprise identity providers like Okta and Microsoft Entra ID solve this well. They federate a single directory to AWS, Azure, GCP, and SaaS applications, giving security teams one place to grant and revoke access.

Workload identity is how running code gets credentials for cloud services without long-lived keys. Each cloud has its own mechanism: AWS uses IAM roles with OIDC federation, Google Cloud uses workload identity federation, and Azure uses managed identities. Each mechanism can trust tokens from outside its cloud, but each needs its own trust configuration. Getting a single workload to authenticate to services in two or three clouds without storing any cloud keys is a harder problem, and most “multi-cloud identity” products do not address it. Enterprises typically solve workload identity per cloud, which means each cloud has its own credential chain, its own trust configuration, and its own blast radius.

The guide to one identity model for multiple clouds covers the workload side in depth.

Billing: visibility versus one invoice

Visibility and allocation means one dashboard that normalizes cost data from AWS, Azure, and GCP, maps it to teams or business units, and supports chargeback. FinOps tools like Vantage, Apptio Cloudability, and Flexera do this. They ingest billing exports from each cloud, normalize discount structures (Savings Plans, Committed Use Discounts, Reserved Instances), and present unified reports. This is valuable, but you still receive and pay three separate cloud bills.

One invoice means a single payer issues one bill that covers compute across multiple clouds. This is rare. Apart from narrow partnerships such as Oracle Database@Azure, the hyperscalers do not offer it for each other’s services. A platform that runs your workloads across clouds and bills you directly can provide it, but only for the resources it manages.

The comparison of cloud cost optimization tools covers the visibility side.

Deployment: one definition versus a provisioning catalog

One definition deployed to several clouds means you write a workload specification once and the platform runs it in AWS, Azure, GCP, or OCI regions without separate per-cloud configuration. The abstraction can come from Kubernetes (same pod spec, different clusters), from IaC (shared module patterns, one provider block per cloud), or from a platform that maps one workload definition to multiple cloud regions.

A provisioning catalog means the platform can create resources in multiple clouds, but each resource type has its own cloud-specific definition. You still author and maintain per-cloud templates. Many CMPs work this way: they reduce portal-hopping without removing per-cloud configuration.

Which layers does each platform unify?

Eleven platforms, mapped against the three layers. “Native” means the platform provides the capability itself, “Integrates” means it relies on another product, and “Partial” means it covers part of the layer.

Platform Category Human identity Workload identity across clouds Billing (visibility or one invoice) Deployment across clouds What you still stitch together
Flexera One FinOps and IT asset management Integrates (SSO via external IdP) No Native (visibility, no consolidated invoice) Partial (policy automation; no current provisioning catalog) Identity provider, deployment tool, workload identity per cloud, invoice consolidation
CloudBolt CMP Integrates (SSO via external IdP) No Native (FinOps visibility and optimization, no consolidated invoice) Native (provisioning catalog) Identity provider, workload identity, invoice consolidation
HPE Morpheus Enterprise CMP Integrates (LDAP/SAML via external IdP) No Native (visibility across clouds) Native (provisioning catalog with blueprints) Identity provider, workload identity, invoice consolidation
Nutanix Cloud Manager CMP Integrates (SSO via external IdP) No Partial (Cost Governance covers on-premises Nutanix only) Native (provisioning and governance) Identity provider, workload identity, FinOps tool for public cloud
Red Hat OpenShift (with Advanced Cluster Management) Kubernetes platform Integrates (OAuth/OIDC via external IdP) Partial (per-cluster service accounts; no unified cross-cloud identity) Partial (Red Hat cost management for OpenShift and cloud spend visibility, no consolidated invoice) Native (Kubernetes fleet deployment across clusters) Identity provider, FinOps tool, workload identity across clouds
Azure Arc with Microsoft Entra ID Hyperscaler extension Native (Entra ID for human access) Partial (managed identities for Arc-enabled resources, limited outside Azure) Partial (Azure Cost Management covers Azure only; its AWS connector was retired in 2025) Native (Arc-enabled Kubernetes and servers) FinOps tool for non-Azure cost, workload identity for non-Azure services
Vantage FinOps No No Native (visibility across clouds, no consolidated invoice) No Identity provider, deployment tool, workload identity, invoice consolidation
Apptio Cloudability FinOps No No Native (visibility across clouds, no consolidated invoice) No Identity provider, deployment tool, workload identity, invoice consolidation
Okta Workforce Identity Identity provider Native (SSO, RBAC, lifecycle) No (human identity only) No No Deployment tool, FinOps tool, workload identity per cloud
HashiCorp Terraform (HCP Terraform) IaC Integrates (SSO via external IdP) No (dynamic provider credentials cover Terraform runs only; deployed workloads need their own) No Native (IaC modules for multiple providers, per-provider config) Identity provider, FinOps tool, workload identity, Vault for secrets
Control Plane Application platform Partial (native policies, groups, and service accounts; SSO via Google, GitHub, Microsoft, or SAML) Native (Universal Cloud Identity for AWS, GCP, Azure) Native (one invoice per billing account; Cost & Usage per org and per resource; billing API by GVC, workload, and location) Native (one workload definition deployed across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions via Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC)) SSO identity provider for console sign-in, cloud bills for non-Control Plane services

This table reflects each vendor’s public documentation as of November 2026.

What does each platform do best?

Each platform has a different center of gravity.

Flexera One

Flexera One normalizes cost data across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud and adds IT asset management, SaaS management, and policy automation. Best fit: enterprises that want FinOps governance and software asset management in one product and already run an identity provider.

CloudBolt

CloudBolt offers self-service provisioning with approval workflows and cost reporting. Best fit: IT teams that want a governed service catalog across clouds.

HPE Morpheus Enterprise

Morpheus provisions across clouds, bare metal, and virtualization platforms from one catalog with blueprints, and aggregates spend across those environments. Best fit: hybrid estates that mix VMware, bare metal, and public clouds.

Nutanix Cloud Manager

Nutanix Cloud Manager combines self-service provisioning with blueprints, on-premises cost governance, and Security Central compliance. Best fit: Nutanix-centric enterprises extending into AWS and Azure that run a separate FinOps tool for public cloud.

Red Hat OpenShift with Advanced Cluster Management

OpenShift with Advanced Cluster Management manages Kubernetes clusters across clouds from one hub, with fleet-wide policy and placement. Best fit: enterprises standardized on Kubernetes that already run a FinOps tool and an identity provider.

Azure Arc with Microsoft Entra ID

Azure Arc brings servers and Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure under Azure management, and Entra ID handles human access. Best fit: Azure-primary enterprises with some workloads in AWS or Google Cloud.

Vantage

Vantage reports cost across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and other providers. Best fit: FinOps teams that need a dedicated cost platform on top of existing identity and deployment tooling.

Apptio Cloudability

Cloudability, part of IBM since its acquisition of Apptio, provides cost normalization, showback, chargeback, and optimization recommendations across clouds. Best fit: large enterprises with mature FinOps practices.

Okta Workforce Identity

Okta federates single sign-on and manages user lifecycle across clouds and SaaS applications. Best fit: one directory and access policy for every human user, whatever clouds they touch.

HashiCorp Terraform (HCP Terraform)

Terraform defines infrastructure as code for any cloud through provider plugins, and HCP Terraform adds remote state, policy as code, and team workflows. Best fit: platform teams comfortable maintaining per-provider modules.

Control Plane

Control Plane runs the workloads themselves, so it covers all three layers for those workloads: one definition deployed across clouds, one workload identity for AWS, GCP, and Azure, and one invoice for the compute it provides. It relies on your SSO provider for console sign-in, and services you run directly in your cloud accounts stay on those bills. Best fit: teams that want one platform to deploy, secure, and pay for workloads across clouds.

The guide to consolidating multiple clouds on one platform walks through a migration.

What stacks do enterprises actually assemble?

Most enterprises land on one of four patterns, each with a different product count, number of identity models, and owner for the glue between layers.

Stack Identity Billing Deployment Number of products to operate
CMP-led Entra ID or Okta CloudBolt or Morpheus (visibility) CloudBolt or Morpheus (provisioning catalog) + cloud-native IaC 3 to 4
Kubernetes-led Okta Vantage or Cloudability OpenShift ACM or Rancher 3 to 4
Hyperscaler-led Entra ID Azure Cost Management (Azure only) Azure Arc 2 to 3 (but limited outside Azure)
Best-of-breed Okta Vantage Terraform 3 to 4
Platform-led Your existing SSO provider (for console sign-in) Control Plane (one invoice for Control Plane-provided compute) Control Plane (one workload definition via GVC) 1 platform (plus your existing SSO provider)

The CMP-led stack gives broad provisioning coverage and cost visibility but requires a separate identity provider and per-cloud workload identity configuration. The Kubernetes-led stack standardizes on containers and fleet management but adds a FinOps tool and an identity provider. The hyperscaler-led stack minimizes product count for Azure-primary shops but loses depth outside Azure. The best-of-breed stack gives each layer a best-in-class tool but creates the most integration work and the most identity models to maintain.

The trade-off in every stack is who owns the glue. In a CMP-led or best-of-breed stack, your platform engineering team writes and maintains the integrations between the identity provider, the FinOps tool, and the deployment layer. In the platform-led stack, the platform owns the integration because it provides deployment, workload identity, and billing for the workloads it runs.

Whichever stack you choose, avoiding cloud vendor lock-in depends on keeping each layer replaceable.

How do you evaluate a multi-cloud platform’s identity, billing, and deployment claims?

Ask for each of these in a demo or proof of concept. Each one separates a layer the platform owns from one it integrates.

Identity

  • Show one workload getting credentials in two clouds without stored keys. Ask to see the credential flow end to end, from workload startup to authenticated API call in AWS and then GCP.
  • Show what happens to access when an employee leaves. Disable a user in the identity provider and verify that console access, API tokens, and the user’s service account keys are revoked within minutes.
  • Show how workload identity is scoped. Can you limit a workload to specific cloud accounts and services, or does it get broad access?

Billing

  • Show one invoice versus three bills. Ask whether the invoice covers compute in multiple clouds or is just a dashboard over separate cloud bills.
  • Show cost by team across clouds. Ask how cost is attributed when one team’s workloads run in AWS and GCP simultaneously.
  • Show what happens when a discount or commitment changes. Does the platform reflect updated pricing automatically, or does it require manual reconfiguration?

Deployment

  • Show one definition deployed to two clouds. Ask to see the same workload specification running in an AWS region and a GCP region without separate per-cloud configuration files.
  • Show a rollback across clouds. If a deployment fails in one region, how does the platform handle the other regions?
  • Show how cloud-specific services are consumed. Can a workload deployed across clouds call an AWS service in one region and a GCP service in another, using the same identity?

The guide to using services from multiple clouds in one application covers the last question in detail.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane unifies identity, billing, and deployment for the workloads it runs. It does not replace your identity provider for human SSO or a FinOps tool for your existing cloud accounts.

Deployment. Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. A Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) is Control Plane’s named set of locations; a workload deployed to a GVC runs in every location of that GVC from one definition. Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and OCI, VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API.

Workload identity. Universal Cloud Identity lets workloads reach AWS, GCP, and Azure services through one identity, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. An identity holds at most one AWS, one GCP, and one Azure cloud account. One workload can call Amazon S3, BigQuery, and Azure Cosmos DB through that one identity.

Human identity and access. Console sign-in supports Google, GitHub, Microsoft, and SAML single sign-on. Access inside an org comes from policies that bind users, groups, service accounts, and workload identities to permissions on specific resources.

Billing. A Control Plane billing account pays for one or more orgs on a single invoice, itemized per org. Cost and Usage breaks spend down per org and per resource, and the billing API can break cost down by GVC, workload, and location, and returns invoices as JSON or PDF. A monthly spend alert emails billing admins. The single invoice covers compute Control Plane provides in AWS, GCP, Azure, and OCI regions. Your other cloud services stay on your cloud bills. Control Plane customers typically see 30 to 50 percent lower compute costs compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

Scope. Workloads on Kubernetes clusters you bring or your own machines still run on infrastructure you pay for. Universal Cloud Identity covers AWS, GCP, and Azure; Oracle Cloud is a deployment target only. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

FAQ

Each answer covers one question buyers ask when comparing these platforms.

Which enterprise platforms unify identity, billing, and deployment across multiple clouds?

Most enterprises combine separate products for each layer. Cloud management platforms like CloudBolt and HPE Morpheus unify deployment and cost visibility but rely on external identity providers. FinOps tools like Vantage, Apptio Cloudability, and Flexera One handle billing visibility. Identity providers like Okta and Microsoft Entra ID handle human access only. Control Plane unifies all three for the workloads it runs.

What is a multi-cloud management platform?

A multi-cloud management platform is software that provides visibility, governance, and operational control over resources running in two or more public clouds. Capabilities typically include provisioning, cost reporting, policy enforcement, and compliance monitoring. Most CMPs do not include native identity management or consolidated billing.

Can one identity provider cover AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud?

For human access, yes. Providers like Okta and Microsoft Entra ID federate SSO across all three clouds, giving users one login and centralized lifecycle management. For workload identity, no. Each cloud has its own workload identity mechanism (IAM roles, workload identity federation, managed identities), and a single identity provider for human access does not automatically provide cross-cloud workload credentials. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives each workload on the platform one identity for AWS, GCP, and Azure services.

How do workloads authenticate to multiple clouds without long-lived keys?

Each cloud supports short-lived token exchange through its own federation mechanism. AWS supports OIDC federation with IAM roles, GCP supports workload identity federation, and Azure supports workload identity federation through federated credentials on managed identities or app registrations. The hard part is coordinating three separate trust setups for one workload. On Control Plane, one Universal Cloud Identity spans AWS, GCP, and Azure.

Can I get one bill for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud?

Not from the hyperscalers themselves. Each cloud issues its own invoice. FinOps tools aggregate and normalize billing data into unified dashboards, but you still pay three separate bills. A platform that runs your workloads across clouds and bills you directly can provide a single invoice for the compute it manages. Control Plane does this for the compute it provides in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions. Databases and storage you manage directly in your cloud accounts are billed by those clouds.

What is the difference between FinOps visibility and consolidated billing?

FinOps visibility means a tool ingests billing data from multiple clouds, normalizes it, and presents unified reports for cost allocation, chargeback, and optimization. You still receive and pay separate cloud bills. Consolidated billing means one payer issues one invoice that covers resources across multiple clouds. Most products in the market provide visibility. Few provide a consolidated invoice.

Do I need Kubernetes to deploy the same app to multiple clouds?

No. Kubernetes is one route to deployment portability. IaC tools like Terraform and Pulumi can provision infrastructure across clouds, though each provider requires its own configuration. Control Plane deploys workloads to a GVC that spans AWS, GCP, Azure, and OCI regions from one definition, without requiring you to manage Kubernetes clusters yourself.

How does Control Plane unify identity, billing, and deployment?

One workload definition deploys to every location of a GVC across AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions; Universal Cloud Identity gives those workloads one identity for AWS, GCP, and Azure services; and one billing account invoice covers the compute Control Plane provides, with cost by GVC, workload, and location through the billing API. Console sign-in uses your existing SSO provider.

Run every cloud’s workloads under one identity model and one invoice. Talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Converting a brand palette from hex to OKLCH, and what the numbers do and don't tell you
description:
Tailwind v4's default colors and shadcn/ui's theme variables are written in oklch(). If your brand palette lives in hex, at some point you convert it. Online converters work, but I wanted to see the math and check the numbers against a palette I know well, so here's a small converter and what the output taught me.

The palette is from Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop site I use for demos: cream background, terracotta primary, sage green accent, dark brown text.

The converter

OKLCH is OKLab in polar form, and OKLab comes from Björn Ottosson's published matrices. From hex: undo the sRGB gamma, go to an LMS-like space, take cube roots, go to Lab, then turn a/b into chroma and hue.

const lin = (c) => (c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4);

function hexToOklch(hex) {
  const [r, g, b] = [1, 3, 5].map((i) => lin(parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255));
  const l = Math.cbrt(0.4122214708 * r + 0.5363325363 * g + 0.0514459929 * b);
  const m = Math.cbrt(0.2119034982 * r + 0.6806995451 * g + 0.1073969566 * b);
  const s = Math.cbrt(0.0883024619 * r + 0.2817188376 * g + 0.6299787005 * b);
  const L = 0.2104542553 * l + 0.793617785 * m - 0.0040720468 * s;
  const A = 1.9779984951 * l - 2.428592205 * m + 0.4505937099 * s;
  const B = 0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.808675766 * s;
  const C = Math.hypot(A, B);
  const H = C < 0.0005 ? 0 : (Math.atan2(B, A) * 180 / Math.PI + 360) % 360;
  return `oklch(${(L * 100).toFixed(1)}% ${C.toFixed(3)} ${H.toFixed(1)})`;
}

The C < 0.0005 check is for greys and white: with no chroma the hue is meaningless, and atan2 would return noise.

Output for the palette:

Role Hex OKLCH
background #fffaf3 oklch(98.7% 0.011 76.6)
surface #f6eadb oklch(94.2% 0.024 73.6)
border #ead8c3 oklch(89.1% 0.035 71.6)
muted text #7a6656 oklch(52.5% 0.035 60.6)
primary #c2410c oklch(55.3% 0.174 38.4)
accent #4d7c5a oklch(54.3% 0.074 152.1)
text #2b1d14 oklch(24.5% 0.027 53.8)

oklch(55.3% ...) and oklch(0.553 ...) are the same color; CSS accepts lightness either way.

You can read the palette from this table in a way you can't from hex: all the neutrals sit around hue 54 to 77 (warm), their chroma stays under 0.04 (barely tinted), and they step down in lightness from 98.7 to 24.5. The primary has five times the chroma of any neutral and more than twice that of the green accent.

1. Lightness is not contrast

Primary and accent are almost the same OKLCH lightness, 55.3% and 54.3%. So I expected the accent, being slightly darker, to have slightly more contrast on the cream background. It's the other way round:

Color OKLCH L WCAG contrast on #fffaf3
primary #c2410c 55.3% 4.99:1
accent #4d7c5a 54.3% 4.65:1
muted #7a6656 52.5% 5.24:1

WCAG 2 contrast is built on relative luminance, a weighted sum of the linear sRGB channels in which green counts for about 72%. OKLCH lightness is designed to match how light a color looks, which is a different model. They usually agree in direction, but between two colors a point apart they can disagree, as here. OKLCH is great for building scales; still run the actual contrast check on the pairs you ship.

2. Lowering L alone falls out of gamut

The obvious way to make a hover shade in OKLCH is to keep chroma and hue and lower the lightness. Converting back to sRGB shows what happens with a saturated color:

oklch(55.3% 0.174 38.4)  -> #c2410b, in sRGB
oklch(50%   0.174 38.4)  -> blue channel -0.076, outside sRGB
oklch(47%   0.174 38.4)  -> blue channel -0.119, outside sRGB

A negative channel means there's no sRGB color with that lightness, chroma and hue. CSS lets you write it anyway, and the browser has to map it to something the screen can show, so you don't get exactly what you wrote, and a wide-gamut screen may show something different from an sRGB one.

The site's real hover color is #9a3412, which is oklch(47.0% 0.143 37.3): the designer dropped the chroma from 0.174 to 0.143 while darkening. That's the pattern for saturated colors: lower L and C together. A quick way to check is to convert back and look for channels below 0 or above 1.

It goes the other direction too. At the same lightness and hue, the primary's chroma can only go up to about 0.179 before the blue channel goes negative, so 0.174 is already close to the most saturated terracotta sRGB has at that lightness.

3. Rounding costs one step, and that's fine

With three decimals, converting the primary back gives #c2410b, not #c2410c: the blue channel is off by one out of 255. That's invisible, but it means a round trip through the rounded oklch() string won't give you byte-identical hex. If a test compares the colors exactly, compare before rounding or allow a difference of one.

Using it for shadcn/ui

With the values converted, the shadcn/ui mapping is: background to --background and --popover, surface to --card, --secondary and --muted, text to --foreground and the -foreground variables, primary to --primary and --ring, border to --border and --input. White on the primary is 5.18:1, so --primary-foreground can stay white.

One thing to avoid: shadcn's --accent is the background of a hovered menu item, not a brand color. Put the sage green there and every hover turns green. I keep it as a separate --brand-accent and set --accent to a faint tint of the text color.

Short version

  1. The conversion is 15 lines of math; check it against a known value before trusting it.
  2. Read the OKLCH table for structure: hue family, how tinted the neutrals are, the lightness steps.
  3. Don't use OKLCH lightness as a contrast check. Compute WCAG contrast.
  4. Darken saturated colors by lowering L and C together, then convert back to make sure you're still in sRGB.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that reads a site's palette with roles and writes this kind of shadcn/ui theme in oklch(); its values for this demo site match the converter above to the last digit. There's a guide here: turn any website into a shadcn/ui theme. If you already have your hex values, the converter is all you need.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every value above comes from running the code shown on the demo palette.

title: Does a Tiny Desk AI Clip Keep the Reference's Cuts and Camera Moves? Measuring Shot Timing With NumPy Phase Correlation (Tested)
description:
"Does the AI version keep the same camera moves as the original?" is one of the first things people ask about photo-to-video meme generators. The Tiny Desk Outstanding studio makes a strong claim here. Its about page says a photo "does not change the length, the camera, or the song already in the clip", and every scene page calls the source "a 15-second vertical clip with the original soundtrack".

That's a testable claim. The home page has eight public sample files: the "Whole Band reference video" and seven generated or alternate cuts. So I measured two things in each one: where the hard cuts are and how much the whole picture moves between frames. I used NumPy and ffmpeg only, no OpenCV. Everything below was run on the box on November 14, 2026 (Asia/Shanghai), and the outputs are pasted as they came out.

Why phase correlation

When a camera pans, most of the frame shifts by the same amount. When you shift an image, its Fourier transform keeps the same magnitude and only the phase changes. If you divide the cross-power spectrum of two frames by its own magnitude and take the inverse FFT, you get one sharp peak at the shift. That peak's height also tells you something useful:

  • high peak (0.2 to 0.98): same shot, and the peak's location is the global shift in pixels
  • very low peak (about 0.03): the two frames don't share structure, which means it's a hard cut

So the same 10 lines give you a pan/tilt estimate and a cut detector.

The script

camera_motion.py decodes the clip at 12 fps, 144×256 grayscale (aspect forced to 9:16 so clips of different sizes compare), and runs phase correlation between consecutive frames:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Global camera motion + cut map for a short vertical clip (NumPy + ffmpeg only).

usage: python3 camera_motion.py clip.mp4 [more.mp4 ...] [--fps 12] [--csv out.csv]
"""
import argparse, csv, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np

W, H = 144, 256  # analysis size (9:16); small is enough for global motion

def frames(path, fps):
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path, "-vf",
           f"fps={fps},scale={W}:{H}:force_original_aspect_ratio=disable,format=gray",
           "-f", "rawvideo", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, H, W).astype(np.float32)

WIN = np.outer(np.hanning(H), np.hanning(W)).astype(np.float32)

def phase_corr(a, b):
    """Return (dx, dy, peak) so that b is roughly a shifted by (dx, dy)."""
    A = np.fft.fft2((a - a.mean()) * WIN)
    B = np.fft.fft2((b - b.mean()) * WIN)
    R = np.conj(A) * B
    R /= np.abs(R) + 1e-9
    r = np.fft.ifft2(R).real
    y, x = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(r), r.shape)
    if y > H // 2: y -= H
    if x > W // 2: x -= W
    return float(x), float(y), float(r.max())

def analyse(path, fps, cut_peak=0.06):
    f = frames(path, fps)
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, len(f)):
        dx, dy, peak = phase_corr(f[i - 1], f[i])
        rows.append({"t": round(i / fps, 3), "dx": dx, "dy": dy,
                     "peak": round(peak, 3), "cut": peak < cut_peak})
    return rows

def summary(rows):
    cuts = [r["t"] for r in rows if r["cut"]]
    # merge cut flags closer than 0.25 s (one cut can flag two pairs)
    merged = []
    for t in cuts:
        if not merged or t - merged[-1] > 0.25:
            merged.append(t)
    still = [r for r in rows if not r["cut"]]
    pan = sum(abs(r["dx"]) for r in still)
    tilt = sum(abs(r["dy"]) for r in still)
    moving = sum(1 for r in still if abs(r["dx"]) + abs(r["dy"]) >= 1) / max(len(still), 1)
    return merged, pan, tilt, moving

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("clips", nargs="+")
    ap.add_argument("--fps", type=float, default=12)
    ap.add_argument("--csv")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    out = []
    print(f"{'clip':<14}{'cuts (s)':<34}{'pan px':>8}{'tilt px':>8}{'moving':>8}")
    for c in a.clips:
        rows = analyse(c, a.fps)
        cuts, pan, tilt, moving = summary(rows)
        name = c.rsplit("/", 1)[-1][:12]
        print(f"{name:<14}{', '.join(f'{t:.2f}' for t in cuts):<34}{pan:>8.0f}{tilt:>8.0f}{moving:>8.0%}")
        out += [{"clip": name, **r} for r in rows]
    if a.csv:
        with open(a.csv, "w", newline="") as fh:
            w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(out[0]))
            w.writeheader(); w.writerows(out)

Does it measure what it says? A self-test

Before pointing it at real clips, I cut two windows out of the same blurred noise texture with a known offset, and also compared the frame with unrelated noise:

import numpy as np, camera_motion as cm
# smooth random texture, then cut two windows offset by a known shift
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
big = rng.random((cm.H + 40, cm.W + 40)).astype(np.float32)
for _ in range(3):  # cheap blur so it looks like an image, not noise
    big = (big + np.roll(big, 1, 0) + np.roll(big, 1, 1) + np.roll(big, -1, 0) + np.roll(big, -1, 1)) / 5
a = big[20:20 + cm.H, 20:20 + cm.W]
for dx, dy in [(3, 0), (-2, 5), (7, -4)]:
    b = big[20 - dy:20 - dy + cm.H, 20 - dx:20 - dx + cm.W]
    x, y, peak = cm.phase_corr(a, b)
    print("true", (dx, dy), "measured", (x, y), "peak", round(peak, 3))
other = rng.random((cm.H, cm.W)).astype(np.float32)
print("unrelated frame peak", round(cm.phase_corr(a, other)[2], 3))

true (3, 0) measured (3.0, 0.0) peak 0.977
true (-2, 5) measured (-2.0, 5.0) peak 0.972
true (7, -4) measured (7.0, -4.0) peak 0.936
unrelated frame peak 0.03

The shift comes back exactly, matching frames peak at 0.94 to 0.98, and unrelated frames peak at 0.03. In the real clips, cuts landed at 0.027 to 0.045 and ordinary frames had a median peak of 0.23 to 0.31, so a 0.06 threshold sits in the gap.

Results on the eight public samples 

python3 camera_motion.py samples/*.mp4 --csv motion.csv

clip          cuts (s)                            pan px tilt px  moving
0299078c3f43  5.33, 11.67, 15.00                     152     160     57%
632c0129d45a  5.33, 11.67, 15.00                     248     212     71%
8256cd873b7e  5.25, 11.42, 14.75                     225     203     60%
875d2458181e                                         102      60     94%
947f5eb2a447  1.50, 7.00, 13.67, 17.33               257     258     59%
db033545db00  1.58, 4.75, 7.83                       160     145     64%
db09b1c54359  5.17, 11.17                            260     164     74%
f7ff52686113  1.50, 6.92, 10.08, 13.17, 16.50        273     274     62%

(pan px / tilt px add up the absolute per-frame shift at 144×256 within shots, and moving is the share of frame pairs that shifted by at least 1 px.) db09b1c54359 is the reference. 0299…, 632c… and 8256… are the three full recasts (632c… is the cat version the home page also shows). The others are alternate or partial cuts the site labels as such (a 10-second take, a longer cut, a 4-second close-up).

To line the recasts up against the reference shot by shot, shot_compare.py splits each clip at its cuts and reports the mean shift per frame in each shot:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compare each clip's shot list and per-shot camera motion with a reference.

usage: python3 shot_compare.py reference.mp4 clip.mp4 [clip.mp4 ...]
"""
import sys
import numpy as np
from camera_motion import analyse, summary

FPS = 12

def shots(path):
    rows = analyse(path, FPS)
    cuts, *_ = summary(rows)
    end = round((len(rows) + 1) / FPS, 2)
    edges = [0.0] + cuts + [end]
    out = []
    for a, b in zip(edges, edges[1:]):
        seg = [r for r in rows if a < r["t"] < b and not r["cut"]]
        mag = np.mean([np.hypot(r["dx"], r["dy"]) for r in seg]) if seg else 0.0
        out.append((a, b, mag))
    return out

def fmt(s):
    return " | ".join(f"{a:5.2f}-{b:5.2f}s {m:4.2f}px/f" for a, b, m in s)

ref = shots(sys.argv[1])
print("reference ", fmt(ref))
for clip in sys.argv[2:]:
    s = shots(clip)
    name = clip.rsplit("/", 1)[-1][:10]
    print(f"{name:<10} ", fmt(s))
    n = min(len(ref), len(s))
    drift = [s[i][1] - ref[i][1] for i in range(n - 1)]  # cut-time differences
    print(f"{'':<11} shots {len(s)} vs {len(ref)}; cut drift vs reference: "
          + ", ".join(f"{d:+.2f}s" for d in drift))

python3 shot_compare.py samples/db09b1c5…mp4 samples/0299078c…mp4 samples/632c0129…mp4 samples/8256cd87…mp4

reference   0.00- 5.17s 0.94px/f |  5.17-11.17s 2.59px/f | 11.17-14.50s 2.58px/f
0299078c3f   0.00- 5.33s 0.22px/f |  5.33-11.67s 2.36px/f | 11.67-15.00s 1.42px/f | 15.00-17.58s 0.41px/f
            shots 4 vs 3; cut drift vs reference: +0.17s, +0.50s
632c0129d4   0.00- 5.33s 0.68px/f |  5.33-11.67s 2.91px/f | 11.67-15.00s 2.50px/f | 15.00-17.67s 0.74px/f
            shots 4 vs 3; cut drift vs reference: +0.17s, +0.50s
8256cd873b   0.00- 5.25s 0.13px/f |  5.25-11.42s 3.37px/f | 11.42-14.75s 1.87px/f | 14.75-17.42s 0.66px/f
            shots 4 vs 3; cut drift vs reference: +0.08s, +0.25s

What the numbers say

  1. The shot list is kept. The reference has three shots: the desk trio around the red keyboard (0 to 5.17 s), the lead singer's laughing close-up (to 11.17 s) and the sax solo (to 14.5 s). Each full recast has the same three shots in the same order, and the cuts land within +0.08 to +0.50 s of the reference's.
  2. But the recasts run longer and add a fourth shot. All three full recasts cut back to the desk at 14.75 to 15.0 s and keep going for another 2.6 s, ending at 17.4 to 17.7 s. I checked a frame strip to confirm: it really is a return to the desk trio. So "15 seconds" is the reference, not a promise about every output file.
  3. The camera's motion profile is similar, not identical. The close-up is the busiest shot everywhere (2.36 to 3.37 px/frame vs 2.59 in the reference), and the desk shot is the calmest. The opening shot is steadier in the recasts (0.13 to 0.68 vs 0.94 px/frame). That fits how reference-video models work: the reference drives the camera path and timing, and the model re-renders each frame, so small handheld wobble isn't copied pixel for pixel.

Caveats: phase correlation measures the single dominant shift, so a laughing head in a close-up counts as "motion" even if the camera is still. It doesn't detect zoom or rotation. Use it to compare clips against each other, not as an absolute camera tracker. A 12 fps analysis can't place a cut more precisely than about 0.08 s.

Why it matters if you edit the clip

If you plan to cut your own clip on the beat, add a slow-motion replay, or line up captions with the laugh, don't hard-code the reference's timestamps. Run camera_motion.py on your file and use its cut list. The shots are in the same order, but a recast can be up to half a second late and about 3 seconds longer.

The scene choices (Just Me for the close-up, Back Row for the two standing singers in the opening shot, Whole Band for all five seats) are compared on the scenes page. Every scene uses the same reference, so these shot timings apply to all three.

title: Store generated images in user folders: object lifecycle deletes for Express
description:
Short answer: give each generated image an immutable object key, record that key in a database at write time, and use a scheduled retention policy plus a storage lifecycle rule to remove old data. The visible "per-user folder" is a key prefix, not a database index or a deletion receipt.

This matters most when an AI feature moves from a notebook into an Express API. A single request can create several candidates; an evaluation run can create many more. If the gallery is built by listing a bucket prefix and retention is judged from a successful job log, the system has no durable account of which image belongs to which run, user, or policy decision.

I would treat the experiment as failed until it can answer two questions from independent data: which objects should exist now, and which objects were actually deleted. Fast uploads are not enough.

What does a per-user folder mean in object storage?

Object storage does not require a real directory for each user. A name such as images/u_8f12/run_20260807/a31c.webp is an object key; the slashes make a useful prefix for people and tools, but the application should not depend on directory semantics. In particular, a prefix is a poor substitute for a gallery query: listing is paginated and ordered by key, while a gallery needs filters, stable pagination, and a record of soft-deleted images.

Use opaque internal identifiers in the key. Email addresses and display names change, and putting them in names can spread personal data into logs and operational tooling. A run identifier earns its place too. It lets a model evaluation retain the exact image set used for a comparison without confusing it with a user's normal gallery.

Here is the small data model I want before adding cleanup code:

Field Why it exists
user_id scopes authorization and per-user retention
run_id groups candidates from one request or evaluation
object_key the immutable name used for reads and deletes
created_at and deleted_at makes age and deletion state queryable
byte_size and content_type supports quotas, cost review, and safe responses

Keep the delivery URL out of this table as the source of truth. A URL can change with a CDN hostname, a signing policy, or a route rewrite. The exact key is the value that the storage API operates on. Small distinction. Expensive consequence.

How should Express store AI-generated images in per-user object storage and delete old images?

The HTTP handler should validate the authenticated user, construct the key on the server, write the bytes, and persist the exact key and metadata. In a production system, make the database write retryable and reconcile incomplete pairs later: an object without a row is an orphan, and a live row without an object is a missing asset. Neither state should silently become a successful gallery entry.

The following Python is deliberately provider-neutral. It shows the boundary an Express route or a Python worker needs: the route passes bytes and trusted IDs into an application service; the application service owns key construction and writes one ledger row. It does not construct a key from a client-supplied filename.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from hashlib import sha256


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GeneratedImage:
    user_id: str
    run_id: str
    object_key: str
    byte_size: int
    created_at: datetime


def make_object_key(user_id: str, run_id: str, payload: bytes) -> str:
    digest = sha256(payload).hexdigest()
    return f"images/{user_id}/{run_id}/{digest}.webp"


def save_generated_image(store, images, user_id: str, run_id: str, payload: bytes) -> GeneratedImage:
    key = make_object_key(user_id, run_id, payload)
    store.put(key=key, body=payload, content_type="image/webp")
    image = GeneratedImage(
        user_id=user_id,
        run_id=run_id,
        object_key=key,
        byte_size=len(payload),
        created_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    )
    images.insert(image)
    return image

For large uploads, use a multipart-upload protocol rather than treating a whole file as one request. Multipart upload divides an object into parts that can be uploaded independently, then completes as one object; incomplete multipart uploads need their own cleanup policy. That detail is easy to miss in an image pipeline because individual generations start small, then a higher-resolution model or a batch export changes the input size without changing the handler.

Secrets belong outside source code, notebooks, prompts, and request logs. Inject short-lived or scoped credentials through the deployment environment or a dedicated secret-management system, and make storage permissions narrow enough that one user-facing process cannot enumerate unrelated prefixes. OWASP's guidance is useful here because a storage credential has a much larger blast radius than an image-processing failure.

The retention policy needs two layers

Use the database for rules that understand product state. "Keep the newest 30 images for this user," "retain evaluation runs for 14 days," and "hold images attached to an active review" all require ordering and metadata that an object name alone cannot provide. A scheduled worker can select the rows beyond the rule, attempt deletion using their stored object_key, and mark only the confirmed outcomes according to the API's documented response semantics.

Then add a lifecycle rule in the storage system as a coarse backstop for the images/ prefix. Lifecycle policies are good at age-based expiry and at aborting incomplete multipart uploads. They are not suitable when the business rule depends on the newest N objects per user, a legal hold, or a review state; keep those decisions in the ledger.

The catch is that lifecycle expiry is usually an asynchronous storage operation, so it is not a deletion acknowledgement suitable for a user-facing "erase now" promise. For a deletion requirement that must be demonstrable per object, keep an explicit audit trail and confirm the storage-side outcome. For a low-risk thumbnail cache, an age-based lifecycle policy may be the entire answer. Your retention window should be driven by reproducibility and product expectations, not by an assumed storage bargain.

There is a useful ordering to these decisions. First decide what the user is allowed to see and for how long; that is an application policy, so it belongs in a queryable record. Next decide how a background worker identifies candidates without racing a fresh upload: a row state, an eligibility timestamp, and an idempotent attempt record make that decision inspectable. Then decide how long untracked or abandoned bytes may remain before lifecycle expiry clears them. The three layers serve different failure modes, which is why compressing them into one prefix convention is tempting but wrong. A prefix can scope a broad rule. It cannot explain why one image was retained while its neighbor was erased, nor can it reconstruct the image set that produced an evaluation result after the fact. Those answers come from application metadata.

Measure the cleanup path before trusting it

Start with a small reconciliation job. Select a sample of active users, compare ledger keys with keys observed under each prefix, and publish counts for orphaned objects, missing objects, bytes by retention class, and the age of the oldest eligible object. An evaluation-driven image workflow benefits from one more metric: how long an evaluation artifact remains reproducible after the test result was recorded.

One short run is enough to reveal a lot.

def reconcile_prefix(images, store, user_id: str) -> dict[str, int]:
    expected = set(images.active_keys_for_user(user_id))
    observed = set(store.list_keys(prefix=f"images/{user_id}/"))
    return {
        "orphan_count": len(observed - expected),
        "missing_count": len(expected - observed),
        "expected_count": len(expected),
        "observed_count": len(observed),
    }

Don't alert only on worker exceptions. A worker can run on schedule while deleting the wrong keys, while a lifecycle rule can remove objects the ledger still considers live, or while a failed database transaction leaves a newly uploaded object untracked. The reconciliation numbers expose those mismatches directly. Tune the sample size, retention windows, and retry behavior after observing real request volume; the correct threshold depends on image size, generation rate, and the cost of losing a reproducible evaluation artifact.

The practical design is modest: immutable keys, a ledger, explicit policy, and a backstop. It leaves room for an Express API today and batch-oriented Python evaluation work tomorrow without making bucket listings carry product semantics they do not have.

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
