title: Spring Boot in a 512 MB container: JVM flags, a layered image, and honest start-up numbers
description:
TL;DR: By default the JVM takes only a quarter of a container's memory limit for the heap, and a small Boot app can take half a minute to start on a quarter of a CPU. Telling the JVM how much it may use, trimming what Boot starts, and building a layered image on Java 21 fixes most of it. Measured start-up figures, database connection sizing, health checks and the three log failures we see most, tested on our own Spring Boot app.

Spring Boot has a reputation for being heavy, and on a 512 MB container with a quarter of a CPU the reputation is partly earned: with default settings a small Boot app can take half a minute to start and hold more memory than it needs. SnapDeploy itself is a Spring Boot application, so this is not theory. Here is what it takes to make a Boot 3 service start, fit and stay up on a free container tier.

Why 512 MB is tight for the JVM by default

Since JDK 10 the JVM reads the container's memory limit, but its default maximum heap is only 25% of that limit: 128 MB in a 512 MB container. Everything else (metaspace, thread stacks, the JIT's code cache, direct buffers) lives outside the heap.

A Boot app with Spring Data and a web server usually wants 150 to 250 MB of heap and another 100 to 150 MB of non-heap. Left to its defaults it either runs out of heap or the JIT and GC threads fight the single quarter-core for CPU during start-up.

1. Tell the JVM how much it may use 

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xss512k -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=48m
  • MaxRAMPercentage=65 gives the heap about 330 MB and leaves the rest for non-heap memory. Do not go above 75 or the container will be killed on the first spike.
  • UseSerialGC is the right collector for one CPU: G1 spends threads you do not have.
  • Xss512k halves the default thread stack. Tomcat's request threads add up.
  • ReservedCodeCacheSize=48m caps the JIT's code cache; the default reserve is far larger than a small service needs.

Set it as an environment variable in the container settings, or bake it into the Dockerfile with ENV. The JVM prints "Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS" on start, which is how you confirm it took effect.

2. Trim what Boot starts 

# application.properties
server.tomcat.threads.max=20
server.tomcat.threads.min-spare=2
spring.jmx.enabled=false
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health

Twenty request threads is plenty for a service that gets a few requests a second; the default 200 is sized for a real server. Lazy initialization defers bean creation until first use, which cuts start-up time noticeably on a slow CPU at the cost of a slower first request. If you use Spring Boot Actuator, keep only the health endpoint exposed; it is the one thing you want reachable at /actuator/health.

3. Build a layered image

SnapDeploy's generated Dockerfile builds a Maven or Gradle project on Java 17 and runs the jar on a JRE 17 image, which is fine for a first deploy. If your project needs Java 21, or you want faster rebuilds, bring this Dockerfile instead. It uses Boot's layer tools so that dependency layers are cached between builds and only your classes change:

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/*.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/application/ ./
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65 -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xss512k -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=48m"
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]

-Djarmode=tools is Spring Boot 3.3 and later; on 3.0 to 3.2 use -Djarmode=layertools with the same extract command. Gradle projects swap the build line for ./gradlew -q bootJar and the jar path for build/libs/*.jar.

4. Start-up time, honestly

On a quarter vCPU, expect a small Boot 3 service to start in roughly 15 to 40 seconds depending on how much auto-configuration it triggers. On a free SnapDeploy container that matters twice: on deploy, and on every wake after 15 minutes without traffic, where the wake itself takes about 60 seconds and the app's own start-up adds to it. Things that help, in order of payoff:

  • Lazy initialization (above).
  • Remove starters you do not use. Every starter on the classpath runs its auto-configuration.
  • Class data sharing: Boot 3.3+ can produce a CDS archive with a training run (-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit), typically 20 to 30% off start-up. Worth it once the service is stable.
  • If the app must answer instantly at any hour, that is what Always-On is for ($12/month for the same 512 MB, $25 for 2 GB), not a keep-alive ping.

5. Database connections

HikariCP defaults to a pool of 10 connections. A SnapDeploy PostgreSQL Mini allows 50, so one small service is fine, but if you run three services against one Mini, set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=5 in each. When the container sleeps, the pool goes with it; that is normal, and the first request after a wake pays for a new connection.

Deploying it

  1. Push to GitHub with the Dockerfile above (or without one, to use the generated Java 17 build).
  2. Containers → Deploy from GitHub → pick the repository. The port is 8080 unless server.port says otherwise.
  3. Add environment variables: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod, the database URL, and JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS if it is not in the Dockerfile.
  4. Deploy, then open the logs and look for two lines: "Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS" and "Started ... in N seconds". If N is over 60, go back to section 2.

6. Health checks and the wake page

Expose one cheap endpoint that returns 200 as soon as the application context is up: Actuator's /actuator/health if you use it, or a two-line controller if you do not. Two reasons.

First, it is what you curl after a deploy to know the app is alive rather than merely started. Second, on a free container the platform's wake page polls the container until it answers, then redirects the visitor; the sooner the app answers, the shorter the visible wait.

A health endpoint that touches the database is fine, but keep the query trivial: on a sleeping database connection the first check can take longer than the request timeout, and a health check that fails during start-up looks like a crash.

7. Reading the logs: three failures and their fixes

What the log shows What happened Fix
The container exits with code 137, often with no Java stack trace The kernel killed the process for exceeding 512 MB. Usually the heap percentage is too high or the code cache and threads pushed non-heap memory over the limit. Lower MaxRAMPercentage to 60, keep Xss512k and the code cache cap, cut Tomcat threads.
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space The opposite problem: the heap is too small for what the app holds, often a large result set or an in-memory cache. Page the query, bound the cache, or move to Always-On Medium (2 GB).
"Started … in 12 seconds" but the URL times out Boot is listening on a port the platform is not routing to, or bound to localhost. Match server.port to the container's port setting (8080 by default) and do not set server.address.

One more line worth knowing: Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is printed by the JVM itself before any Boot logging. If it is missing, the environment variable never reached the process and every flag in section 1 is inactive.

Numbers to keep: free container 512 MB and 0.25 vCPU, sleeps after 15 minutes, wakes in about 60 seconds; Always-On Small $12/month (512 MB), Medium $25 (2 GB), Large $45 (4 GB); PostgreSQL Mini $29/month with 50 connections. All on the pricing page and the free tier docs.

title: Go Pricing-Flag Alerts for Property SaaS (Uptime Monitoring API Selection)
description:
Choose a reliable uptime monitoring API by checking whether its page tells the on-call engineer to pause the new property-pricing rule. Start with a managed HTTP/HTTPS monitor if an external request can establish that decision; add a scheduled business assertion when a successful response can still contain the wrong rent calculation. A green endpoint alone cannot authorize a rollout.

TL;DR: Choose a reliable uptime monitoring API for SaaS apps by testing its evidence and notification path on the free plan: periodic checks, enough endpoints, a useful interval, and an alert that reaches the person who can act. Require explicit SLA terms for the service level you will buy. For a pricing rule behind a flag, judge signal quality by whether the page identifies a failing workflow and supports a pause decision.

Consider this design exercise for a Go service used by a property-management application. The hypothetical page reads: pricing preview failed for the new-rule test fixture; the control fixture passed; rollout expansion is paused. Those are acceptance requirements, not an account of an actual incident or a vendor's default alert payload. The on-call engineer needs the check time, fixture identifier, flag state, expected result, observed result, and a link to the response evidence. Keep resident information out of the notification.

Pause expansion first.

How do you choose an uptime monitoring API for a pricing rollout?

Work backward from that page. A public availability check answers whether the service can be reached, while a pricing assertion answers whether a known input still produces its approved output; both matter, but collapsing them into one healthy/unhealthy label creates a dangerous ambiguity for the person deciding whether to expand the rollout. A response can satisfy the availability check while violating the business assertion. Define those as separate signals.

Use a synthetic property fixture whose inputs and approved output are controlled by the test. Run it once with the existing rule and once with the proposed rule, recording which rule was selected for each request. Don't assume that the rollout percentage proves which rule a particular check evaluated. The useful earlier signal is a failed assertion associated with the selected rule, before expansion exposes more traffic to it.

For this exercise, use 2 fixtures and a proposed 60-second interval. Neither number is a vendor limit or a production recommendation. They make a capacity question concrete: 2 fixtures checked every minute produce 2,880 executions per day, before retries, confirmation checks, additional locations, or a separate availability monitor. A free plan that cannot sustain that experiment cannot validate the design at that resolution. Increase the interval deliberately or narrow the trial, and document what detection delay that choice introduces.

The arithmetic matters.

Instrument the decision, then choose the delivery path

The instrumentation change belongs at the point where the pricing rule is selected and its output can be checked. Record an observation connecting the fixture, selected rule, assertion outcome, and request identifier. These are proposed application fields, not a vendor API schema. Decide which aggregate dimensions the rollout decision actually needs, and keep detailed evidence in the corresponding application record.

An uptime page should distinguish an unreachable service from a rejected pricing assertion. It should also make the next action explicit: pause expansion, inspect the fixture, or investigate shared availability. An alert saying only that a request failed transfers the classification work to the on-call engineer at the least convenient time.

OpenTelemetry's logs documentation is useful when deciding how to represent the evidence associated with an observation. A log record can support investigation; it doesn't establish that a scheduler ran, an alert was delivered, or a business calculation was correct. Verify each transition separately during the trial, including the case where the expected observation never arrives. Use a heartbeat-oriented tool such as Healthchecks for that missing-run requirement.

Infrai is worth considering for the supporting backend layer when one key and one bill across services would reduce credential administration and invoice reconciliation, while one REST API covering 295 routes across 20 modules gives the team a consistent interface for adjacent backend work. No SDK is required: the Go query worker below uses plain HTTP through the standard library, which keeps a separate vendor client out of the rollout job's dependencies. Public, self-describing discovery lets the team inspect the integration contract before implementation. Keep scheduled probing, heartbeat supervision, and notification ownership explicit in the design, and assess those responsibilities separately from the queryable evidence layer.

For the query component, the following standalone Go program retrieves the metrics response without inventing filter parameters or interpreting an undocumented response shape. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's HTTPS API base ending in /v1, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your key; save this as main.go and run it with go run main.go. The environment configuration keeps vendor URLs out of this independent comparison. This is evidence retrieval, not a pricing assertion or a complete uptime monitor.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    u, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.User != nil || u.Path != "/v1" || u.RawQuery != "" ||
        u.Fragment != "" || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set an HTTPS API base ending in /v1 and an API key")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+"/metrics/query", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if at, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if wait := time.Until(at); wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("query returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The request explicitly uses GET and sends no filters. Retries are bounded, with exponential backoff that respects a longer Retry-After value. The code performs no writes. Its timeout bounds each HTTP attempt; a server-requested backoff can extend the total run, which matters if this component is scheduled frequently. A query returning evidence still leaves the platform team responsible for identifying who operates every other component in the path to an actionable page.

Compare the operating responsibility, not the product labels

Put UptimeRobot, Checkly, and Better Stack through the same trial. Their official documentation is linked below; the table assigns each a concrete evaluation role, rather than asserting an unverified free-plan entitlement. A product earns its place only after its current plan, API, and delivery behavior satisfy the role.

Candidate or approach Role to test in this rollout Buy-versus-build decision and limitation
UptimeRobot Baseline external HTTP/HTTPS availability Prefer this candidate if its current API, interval, endpoint allowance, and notification options meet the simple probe requirement; test pricing correctness separately when reachability cannot establish it.
Checkly A check that validates the pricing workflow Prefer this candidate if the trial can express the approved fixture assertion and return useful failure evidence; include assertion maintenance in the operating cost.
Better Stack The path from a failed check to an owned notification Prefer this candidate if its current configuration gets the right evidence to the responsible responder; verify the required channels and their plan eligibility.
Healthchecks plus an application-owned job Detection that an expected pricing-validation run did not report Use for the missing-run requirement; retain a separate assertion for correctness and an external check for public availability.
Application-owned checks and alert worker Full control over fixtures and decision logic Build when that control justifies owning scheduling, retries, state, delivery, and capacity; include maintenance and on-call responsibility in the roadmap.

These aren't rankings.

A team with a simple public endpoint may finish the trial at the first row, whereas a team whose new rule changes the pricing workflow needs evidence from the second kind of test, and a team with unclear incident ownership should resolve the delivery path before adding more probes. Buying more capabilities doesn't resolve an unspecified acceptance criterion.

For each candidate, verify whether email, webhook, or SMS delivery is available for the intended plan, and test the channel you will actually use. Do the same for programmatic monitor creation, configuration changes, and reading check results. The word API on a product page is insufficient evidence that the operations your rollout requires are available under the trial's limits.

Treat the free plan as an experiment budget. Record its allowed endpoint count, check frequency, execution allowance, and relevant notification restrictions from current documentation. This article makes no vendor-specific allowance claim; copying an old number into the design review would conceal the very constraint the trial is meant to expose.

Put the SLO and check budget on the same page

A supplier SLA and the application's SLO answer different questions. Review the supplier's coverage, exclusions, support commitments, and remedy before relying on its promise, then define the application's acceptable availability and correctness behavior independently. A monitoring service's contractual commitment doesn't certify the pricing rule.

For a trial threshold, suppose the team requires 2 consecutive assertion failures before paging. At a proposed 60-second cadence, an error arising just after a successful check could wait nearly 120 seconds for the second failed scheduled check, before adding execution time and notification delay. This is a timing model under stated assumptions, not measured detection latency. Decide whether that delay fits the rollout's exposure budget before accepting the threshold.

Longer confirmation reduces sensitivity to an isolated bad check but delays action on a persistent error. Shorter confirmation buys speed at the cost of more interruptions. The right choice depends on how quickly the flag expands exposure and how much incorrect pricing the team is willing to tolerate during detection and response.

Budget retries too.

If every fixture immediately retries after the primary signal fails, a monitoring design can multiply work precisely when the target is least able to absorb it. Cap confirmation attempts, avoid synchronized schedules, and include confirmation load in capacity planning. Verify that the chosen service can express the intended behavior rather than assuming its default retry policy matches the rollout.

A threshold is also a claim on the on-call team's attention

Close the trial by exercising four proposed cases: an unreachable service, a reachable service with an incorrect pricing result, an isolated failed observation followed by success, and a scheduled run that never reports. These are test cases to execute, not outcomes already observed. Save detection and delivery evidence for each, including which component owns the response.

Then count interruptions that offered no useful action. A threshold that pages for every isolated observation may look responsive while consuming the attention needed to investigate a persistent pricing error; a threshold that requires excessive confirmation can leave the rollout expanding while the evidence accumulates. False positives have an operating cost even when the monitoring trial itself is free.

Choose the least complex design that passes those tests within the agreed detection budget. Expand the flag only when the correctness assertion, external availability signal, and notification path provide enough evidence for the next decision. The result should be a page the on-call engineer can use, with a known cost in checks and interruptions.

References

The OpenTelemetry source supports the log-signal discussion. The product documentation supports checking each candidate's current integration and plan boundaries; no vendor-specific quota or SLA is assumed here.

  • OpenTelemetry log signal concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/
  • UptimeRobot official API documentation: https://uptimerobot.com/api/
  • Checkly official documentation: https://www.checklyhq.com/docs/
  • Better Stack uptime documentation: https://betterstack.com/docs/uptime/
  • Healthchecks official documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/

Further reading

For the missing-run test, start with the heartbeat model at https://healthchecks.io/docs/ and compare its role with the log-signal model at https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/logs/.

title: Rollback Needs a Network Plan Too: Reversing a Cross-Cloud Cutover Without Stranding Traffic
description:
Most cutover plans describe how traffic moves to the new cloud in careful steps. The rollback section is usually one line: revert if something goes wrong. That line hides the hardest part. By the time a cutover starts, DNS records have changed, routes have been withdrawn in one place and announced in another, connections are open on paths that did not exist an hour earlier, and some data has already been written on the new side. Reversing a cutover is not the forward plan played backwards. It is its own network design, and it needs to be written, timed, and tested before the window opens.

1. Name the point of no return before you start

Every cutover has a moment after which a simple rollback stops being possible. It might be the first write accepted only on the new side, the moment an old queue is drained and deleted, or the step where a shared database changes format. Write that moment down as a specific, observable event, not a feeling.

Before that moment, rollback means restoring the previous routing and DNS state. After it, rollback means a second migration, with its own data reconciliation. Teams get into trouble when they treat a post point of no return failure as if the first kind of rollback still applied. The runbook should have two separate sections, with different owners, different time estimates, and a clear rule for who declares which situation the team is in.

A useful test: if the decision maker cannot say, in one sentence, what has already changed irreversibly, the cutover is not ready to start.

2. Lower TTLs early, and raise them back on purpose

DNS is often the steering wheel for a cutover, and also the slowest part to reverse. If records still carry a one hour TTL when the window opens, a rollback decision taken at minute ten may not reach every resolver for most of an hour. Some clients will keep arriving at the new side long after the team believes traffic has returned.

Lower the TTLs for every record involved at least one full old TTL period before the window, and verify the shorter value is actually being served from public resolvers, not just present in the zone file. Record the original values in the runbook so the rollback restores the record and, later, the original TTL. Leaving production records at a five minute TTL for weeks after a cutover is a quiet cost: more query traffic, more dependence on DNS availability, and a resolver behaviour change nobody chose deliberately.

Also plan for the clients that ignore TTLs altogether. A small share of resolvers and pinned clients will keep using the old answer past its expiry. Rollback is complete only when connection counts on the new path fall to near zero, not when the record change returns a success message.

3. Reverse routes in the opposite order to data

Forward cutovers usually move data first, then shift read traffic, then shift write traffic, then withdraw the old routes. Rollback tempts teams to withdraw the new routes first, because that feels like undoing the change. That order can strand traffic: clients still steered to the new side arrive to find no return path, and stateful firewalls drop the replies even when a forward path exists.

A safer rollback order is:

  1. Stop new work starting on the new side, while keeping its paths up.
  2. Steer clients back with DNS or load balancer changes, and watch connection counts move.
  3. Drain and reconcile writes made on the new side since the cutover began.
  4. Confirm the old side is serving normally under real traffic, not just health checks.
  5. Withdraw the new routes and close the temporary firewall openings last.

Keeping the new path alive during the return is counterintuitive and essential. The path you are abandoning is still carrying the sessions you need to bring home.

4. Track every temporary opening as rollback debt

Cutovers accumulate temporary state: a firewall rule opened for a migration tool, a route added for one subnet, a security group widened for a single night, an exception in an egress policy. In a forward success those items are cleaned up in a calm follow up. In a rollback they are confusing. Nobody is sure which openings the old configuration still needs, so everything is left in place, and the estate ends the night less secure than it started.

Keep a single rollback ledger from the first change: each temporary item, why it exists, what depends on it, and the exact step that removes it in both the success and the rollback path. Assign the ledger to one person whose only job in the window is that list. If an item is not in the ledger, it does not get created during the window.

5. Decide the rollback triggers in advance, in numbers

In the middle of a failing cutover, every signal looks ambiguous. Error rates are up, but perhaps they are settling. Latency is worse, but perhaps the caches are cold. Without pre agreed triggers, the rollback decision becomes a debate held at the worst possible time, and teams press on past the point where returning was cheap.

Set triggers while everyone is calm: for example, a defined error rate sustained for a defined number of minutes, a data replication lag above a set threshold, or a failure of a named critical transaction tested from a named location. Also set a latest decision time. If the cutover has not reached a named milestone by that time, rollback starts automatically, because the remaining window is too short to finish and still leave room to return.

Writing the triggers down also protects the person who calls the rollback. Returning on a pre agreed trigger is following the plan, not giving up.

6. Rehearse the return, not just the arrival

Game days for migrations usually rehearse the forward path. Add a rehearsal where the team stops halfway and comes back. That exercise finds the missing pieces quickly: the old side certificate that expired during the project, the route that was already withdrawn in preparation, the dashboard that only shows the new path, the access that was moved and not duplicated. Each of those is a small fix in rehearsal and a long delay at 2 a.m.

A rollback that has been practised once is a procedure. A rollback that exists only as a paragraph is a hope.

Teams that design private multi-cloud connectivity as a managed estate, rather than as a set of one off cutover fixes, work through patterns like these as part of the platform itself. That is the approach taken by CloudVerg, where VergMesh handles multi-cloud networking and VergRail and VergShield cover the connectivity and zero trust side, so the return path is planned with the same care as the arrival.

title: Host a Discord bot 24/7 for $1/month on a NAT VPS
description:
A Discord bot never waits for incoming connections. It opens a connection to Discord and keeps it alive. That means it doesn't need its own IPv4 address. A NAT VPS, which shares one IPv4 address between customers and gives each server a block of ports, runs a bot just as well as a full VPS for a fraction of the price. Free bot hosts tend to sleep or restart your bot; a small VPS keeps it running and gives you root.

In this guide I use natbox.io's Nano plan ($1/month: 512 MB RAM, 5 GB SSD, 10 ports). Disclosure: I run natbox. The manual steps work on any Debian or Ubuntu server.

1. Create the bot in Discord

  1. Open the Discord Developer Portal and create a new application.
  2. Under Bot, reset and copy the token. Treat it like a password.
  3. If your bot reads message text, turn on Message Content Intent.
  4. Under OAuth2 → URL Generator, tick bot, choose permissions, and open the link to invite the bot to your server.

2. Get a server

Order a Nano plan with Debian or Ubuntu. It's ready in under a minute. New customers can use the free one-month trial instead (256 MB RAM, 3 GB SSD, 5 ports, no payment details needed), which is enough for a small bot.

3a. The quick way: one-click Discord bot

natbox has a one-click Discord bot app. It installs a ready Python bot; you paste your bot token in the client area and it stays online 24/7. Use it if you want a running bot in two minutes and plan to edit the code afterwards.

3b. The manual way: your own code

Connect over SSH. Your login and port are in the client area; SSH listens on the first port of your block:

ssh root@natbox.io -p <your-first-port>

Install Python and create a project:

apt update && apt install -y python3 python3-venv
mkdir -p /opt/bot && cd /opt/bot
python3 -m venv venv
./venv/bin/pip install -U discord.py

Create /opt/bot/bot.py:

import os, discord
from discord.ext import commands

intents = discord.Intents.default()
intents.message_content = True
bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix="!", intents=intents)

@bot.command()
async def ping(ctx):
    await ctx.send("pong")

bot.run(os.environ["DISCORD_TOKEN"])

Store the token outside the code:

echo 'DISCORD_TOKEN=paste-your-token-here' > /opt/bot/.env
chmod 600 /opt/bot/.env

4. Keep it running with systemd

Create /etc/systemd/system/discord-bot.service:

[Unit]
Description=Discord bot
After=network-online.target

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/opt/bot
EnvironmentFile=/opt/bot/.env
ExecStart=/opt/bot/venv/bin/python bot.py
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then start it and enable it at boot:

systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now discord-bot
journalctl -u discord-bot -f

Type !ping in your server. The bot should answer pong. If it crashes, systemd restarts it within five seconds.

5. Lock it down

Every natbox server gets its own routed /80 of IPv6, which is reachable on every port and isn't filtered. A bot needs no inbound ports, so allow SSH and nothing else:

apt install -y ufw
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow <your-ssh-port>/tcp
ufw enable

Good to know

  • Outbound mail on ports 25, 465 and 587 is blocked. If your bot sends email, use an email API over HTTPS.
  • Docker isn't supported (servers are LXC containers), so run the bot directly as shown.
  • When you outgrow Nano, upgrade in place from the client area. Your data, IPs and ports stay the same.
