title: The FBI’s ARTEX Flash: When Noise Stopped Meaning Unsophisticated
description:
The FBI issued a flash on ARTEX-class AI attack frameworks. It doesn’t describe a new vulnerability or a specific victim set. It describes a shift in who can run known techniques, and how fast those techniques run when a language model is executing them.

The number: GitGuardian tested an ARTEX build that shipped no secret-scanning code. Prompt was neutral — assess the repo’s security posture, nothing about secrets. The agent found 8 of 9 planted credentials. First hunting command ran 6–13 seconds into the task.

The broken assumption: for two decades, SOC triage has relied on a correlation: noisy, broad, high-volume traffic signals an unsophisticated actor. Sophisticated actors move quietly. AI tooling breaks the correlation without breaking the noise — the agent fires API calls at inference-loop speed and doesn’t know it’s supposed to be quiet.

What changed: AntiFox (ARTEX 0.1.1 fork, v2.0) generated hundreds of AWS API calls in ~30 minutes in confirmed intrusions. Most returned AccessDenied. The successful GetSecretValue against a production secret was embedded in that burst. A triage analyst who closed the ticket on the denial count missed the intrusion.

What didn’t change: least privilege, IMDSv2, CloudTrail data events, OIDC instead of long-lived keys, MFA on privileged accounts — every one of those controls still stops it. What changes is which signal you treat as the incident.

A wall of denials with one success is the search. The success is the intrusion.

Full article with hunt guidance and mitigation checklist at the link above.

title: One Bad Day: The Cloud Concentration Tax
description:
One Bad Day: The Cloud Concentration Tax

At 1:26 PM Eastern on November 12, 2026, Microsoft 365 went dark. Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune — one by one, the services that 430 million monthly active users depend on stopped responding. Downdetector lit up with over 129,500 reports for Outlook alone by 1:28 PM. The outage would stretch past 20 hours, spanning two business days across three continents, with Microsoft's own engineers watching their recovery attempts fail in real time.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

View original article on BleepingComputer →

View original post on X →

This was not a cyberattack. It was not a natural disaster. It was a health check — an automated process designed to protect systems — that cascaded into a global failure. And it exposed something that every organization running on cloud SaaS already knows but refuses to budget for: the cloud concentration tax.

The same week, Claude.ai went down — Anthropic's entire product surface, from chat to API to Claude Code and Claude Cowork, disappeared at once because it all runs on the same infrastructure. Different vendor. Same architecture. Same lesson.

The Anatomy of a Cascading Health Check Failure

The technical postmortem from Control Plane reveals a failure mode that should terrify every cloud architect: the system's own safety mechanisms triggered the collapse.

Here is what happened, step by step:

  1. Servers fail health checks and drop out of rotation. Microsoft's monitoring detected servers not meeting automated health thresholds. Standard procedure: remove them.
  2. Load redistributes to survivors. The remaining servers absorb the orphaned traffic. Demand did not increase — Microsoft confirmed this explicitly.
  3. Survivors become overwhelmed. A core process responsible for establishing secure connections gets saturated. The surviving servers stop responding.
  4. The cascade accelerates. More servers fail their health checks, more traffic shifts, more servers buckle. A self-reinforcing loop.
  5. Recovery attempts flap. Engineers restart servers and return them to service — but they fail again the moment they receive traffic. Microsoft admitted: "The servers we returned to service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic."

View full analysis on Control Plane →

Then came the second blow: some virtual machines got stuck in a bad state, blocking configuration changes from syncing. The recovery plane depended on the same infrastructure that was broken. Microsoft's own status update, hours into the incident, conceded: "Actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief."

ℹ️ The health check paradox: a system designed to remove unhealthy servers removed too many too fast, with no circuit breaker on the removal rate. The cure became the disease.

This is not a novel failure mode. Google's SRE handbook documents it explicitly: thread starvation under load can make health endpoints unable to respond in time, triggering the very cascade that health checks are supposed to prevent. AWS Builder Center has warned that systems which overreact to health check failures "can turn small problems into complete outages."

The Scale Nobody Talks About

The numbers tell a story that "service degradation" — Microsoft's official classification — does not.

Reports came from 74 countries and territories. The UK's National Health Service was affected, with hospitals warning patients of long wait times on calls. Richemont delayed its earnings release. Workhorse Group moved its Q3 results from November 12 to November 16. Air India temporarily rerouted its entire email infrastructure. U.S. Representative Josh Gottheimer requested a briefing, questioning whether the incident's scale and timing suggested something more serious than a technical failure.

View original article on CybersecurityNews →

Microsoft's EVP for Copilot, Agents and Platform, Charles Lamanna, told BleepingComputer that Microsoft "regret[s] the impact these outages had on those who depend on us." The apology came roughly 24 hours after the problems began.

But here is the number that matters most: approximately 15 other hosted services beyond email, Teams, and Copilot lost full access. When Exchange Online is the dependency root for authentication flows, calendar access, security alerts, and compliance tooling, one service's failure becomes every service's failure.

The $600 Billion Tax You Are Already Paying

Splunk's 2026 report, "The Hidden Costs of Downtime" — produced with Oxford Economics — puts the aggregate cost of unplanned downtime for Global 2000 companies at $600 billion annually. That is a 50% increase over two years. The average company faces about 60 downtime incidents per year, at an average cost of $300 million each.

View original article on Help Net Security →

The most important data point in the report is not the headline number. It is this: downtime caused by third parties — SaaS platforms, APIs, and cloud providers — increased from 24% in 2024 to 63% in 2026. In two years, external dependencies went from a quarter of your downtime risk to nearly two-thirds.

ℹ️ Splunk Field CTO Peter Sprenger: "When an issue originates from a SaaS or third-party application, security teams must navigate a complex web of cloud dependencies. The problem is intensified by siloed ownership and a lack of visibility into critical dependencies."

Stock markets have noticed. Companies now see an average 3.4% stock decline following downtime events, up from 2.5% in 2024. For a Fortune 500 company, that translates to billions in market cap evaporating because a health check went sideways.

ThousandEyes' Internet Report found that localized failures routinely go global. Their analysis of an April 2026 Microsoft 365 outage concluded: "The impact was global in practice, even if the cause was geographically specific." They counted between 199 and 386 global network outage events per week in Q1 2026 alone.

Pattern Recognition: This Keeps Happening

The November 12 outage was not an isolated event. It is the latest in a pattern that is accelerating:

  • January 22-23, 2026: Microsoft 365 down for approximately 9 hours. North American infrastructure "not processing traffic as expected." Over 15,000 Downdetector reports at peak.
  • July 23, 2026: Microsoft 365 disrupted after a West US network failure affecting Teams, SharePoint, and Azure services.
  • October 12, 2026: Azure Rights Management failures hit SharePoint, Purview, and Power BI.
  • August 31, 2026: Authentication configuration error took down multiple services.

And it is not just Microsoft. The February 2026 YouTube outage hit hundreds of thousands of users. The May 2026 Google Cloud outage disrupted 50+ services globally — an outage that nearly shut down banking operations across Europe. AWS's October 2025 DynamoDB incident took down 2,500+ companies for 15 hours because of a DNS management race condition.

View discussion on Hacker News →

View discussion on Hacker News →

The common thread: cascading failures through shared dependencies. Not individual bugs, but architectural concentration risk.

On the same day the MS365 outage was raging, the top post trending on Hacker News was "Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud" — 495 points, 140 comments. The anti-cloud-dependency sentiment is not a fringe position anymore. It is a practitioner movement.

View discussion on Hacker News →

The "Is It Down" Economy

Here is something nobody in enterprise IT wants to admit: the first thing most organizations do during a cloud outage is check Downdetector.

Not their monitoring dashboards. Not their runbooks. Not their DR procedures. They search "is Outlook down" and wait for confirmation that the problem is not on their end.

This behavior — the "is it down" reflex — is the clearest signal that organizations have outsourced their situational awareness along with their infrastructure. When your monitoring cannot tell you whether your service is down or your provider's service is down, you have a visibility gap that no amount of spending on observability tools will fix, because the problem is architectural.

Backblaze's analysis nails the structural issue: "Most organizations spread their compute across providers while consolidating authentication, orchestration, and monitoring with a single vendor." The compute layer is diversified. The control plane is not. And the control plane is where the single points of failure actually live.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Multi-cloud is the wrong prescription. It trades one set of concentration risks for integration complexity and operational overhead. You do not need two clouds. You need to know exactly which workflows die when your one cloud goes dark — and have a manual workaround for each. The organizations that weathered November 12 best were not running multi-cloud. They were running clear-eyed dependency maps with tested fallbacks.

What This Means for You

The cloud concentration tax is not going away. It is going up. Here is what practitioners should do about it:

1. Map your SaaS dependency chain — all of it. Not just your cloud provider. Every SaaS tool, every identity provider, every API. Cloud concentration risk analysis makes clear: "Unlike technical single points of failure, concentration risk describes correlated failure modes across your entire technology stack." You cannot manage what you have not mapped.

2. Distinguish "broken" from "busy" in your own health checks. The November 12 outage was caused by health checks that could not tell the difference between a dead server and a stressed server. If your own systems use binary health checks, you have the same vulnerability. Implement graduated health signals: healthy, degraded, overloaded, and dead are four different states requiring four different responses.

3. Rate-limit your safety mechanisms. Health checks should have a circuit breaker on how much capacity they can remove per time window. If your automated systems can drain your entire fleet in minutes, they are a risk, not a safeguard.

4. Keep your recovery plane independent of your data plane. Microsoft's stuck VMs blocked the fix from reaching the fleet. If your management infrastructure shares failure domains with your production infrastructure, your recovery plan has the same single point of failure as your production system.

5. Test your "cloud is down" playbook quarterly. Not a tabletop exercise — an actual drill. Turn off your email provider for an hour and see what breaks. The organizations that handled November 12 calmly had done this before. The ones that panicked had not.

💡 For organizations invested in cloud-native AI tooling, this is especially critical. When your development workflow, code review, and deployment pipeline all depend on a single AI provider, a Claude-style outage does not just slow you down — it stops you entirely. The same single-point-of-failure risk that applies to cloud infrastructure applies to AI infrastructure.

For more on how AI platform outages create cascading failures, see our earlier analysis: Every AI Model Crashed at Once. It Wasn't the AI. The lesson from the Cloudflare-Deno acquisition is also relevant here: infrastructure consolidation creates efficiency but also creates blast radius.

The Bottom Line

The MS365 outage of November 12 was not a black swan. It was the entirely predictable consequence of an industry that has concentrated critical business infrastructure onto a small number of providers, without investing proportionally in resilience.

The cloud concentration tax is real. Every organization pays it — in lost productivity during outages, in unbudgeted recovery costs, in the slow erosion of operational independence. The November 12 outage just made the invoice visible.

Microsoft will publish a postmortem. They will identify the specific configuration change or code path that triggered the initial health check failures. They will implement safeguards. And in three to six months, something similar will happen again — at Microsoft, or Google, or AWS, or Anthropic — because the systemic risk is architectural, not operational.

The question is not whether your cloud provider will have a bad day. The question is whether you will have a plan for when they do.

The cloud concentration tax: everybody pays it. Almost nobody budgets for it. The organizations that survive are the ones that stopped pretending it would not come due.

Originally published at ComputeLeap

title: One framework, few dependencies: stack discipline that compounds
description:
---
title: "One framework, few dependencies: stack discipline that compounds"
published: true
description: "Fewer dependencies is not zero dependencies. How one framework ecosystem and the web platform, with a few earned exceptions, keep a codebase cohesive."
tags: nextjs, react, security, webdev
canonical_url: https://brokeinprod.dev/full-stack/one-framework-few-dependencies-stack-discipline
---

The most consequential decisions in this build were not the things I added. They were the things I declined to add.

Start here: Pick one framework ecosystem and lean on the web platform (native fetch, FormData with server actions, crypto.randomUUID, Intl, Tailwind utilities) before reaching for a library. Then allow a few deliberate exceptions that close a real gap you would otherwise implement worse: image processing, MDX, an email SDK, accessible drag-and-drop. The goal is not zero dependencies, which is its own failure mode. The goal is that every dependency earned its place. Cohesion compounds: one mental model, fewer version conflicts, smaller bundles.

The setup

By the time this build had a blog engine, an admin panel, image processing, email, and rate limiting, the package.json could have ballooned. It did not, and that was not an accident. It was a rule applied at every "should I install something for this?" moment. The rule has two halves: commit to one framework ecosystem, and make every dependency earn its weight.

Half one: one ecosystem

Next.js is React's meta-framework, so "React or Next" is not a choice between two ecosystems. It is one. The discipline is not bolting a second UI paradigm onto that: no adding Vue for one widget, no Svelte for a chart. Not because those tools are bad, they are excellent, but because cohesion is a feature. One set of idioms, one mental model, one rendering story, one set of version constraints. Every additional paradigm multiplies the surface area a future maintainer (often you) has to hold in mind.

Half two: lean on the platform first

A surprising amount of what people install, the platform now does natively. In this build:

  • fetch + FormData instead of an HTTP client and a form library. Server actions take a FormData straight from the request.
  • crypto.randomUUID() instead of a UUID package.
  • Intl for date and number formatting instead of a date library.
  • Tailwind utilities instead of a component-styling runtime.

None of these needed a dependency. Reaching for the platform first is the cheapest way to keep the tree small without writing anything clever.

The exceptions that earned their weight

"Few dependencies" is not "no dependencies." That is the opposite failure, where you reimplement crypto, image processing, or accessible drag-and-drop yourself and do it worse. The test is whether a library closes a real, hard, well-solved gap. The ones that passed:

  • Sharp. Image resizing and format conversion wrap libvips. You do not hand-roll this.
  • next-mdx-remote. Compiling and rendering MDX with embedded components is involved.
  • The Resend SDK. Thin, but it makes the email API ergonomic and typed.
  • The drag-and-drop library. Accessible reordering (pointer, keyboard, and screen-reader semantics) is deceptively hard and easy to get wrong.

Each one replaced something I would have built badly. That is the bar.

The rule earned its keep at the install prompt, not in a design review. The moment that tests it is the one where the package is two keystrokes away and the platform version is two hours away.

The honest counterpoint: Astro islands

There is a real, deliberate case for mixing frameworks, and it is worth being fair about it. Astro's islands architecture lets you run React, Vue, Svelte, and others on the same page, each as an isolated island, so you can pick the best tool per component, migrate a site incrementally, or avoid lock-in. Notice how: the mixing is intentional and isolated, with a performance model that makes it cheap, and Astro's own docs note that most developers still stick to one framework anyway. That is the distinction. Deliberate, isolated islands are not the same as mixing paradigms by default inside a single SPA. The discipline is not "never combine." It is "combine on purpose, never by drift."

Why it compounds

A cohesive stack pays off slowly and then all at once: faster onboarding, fewer "why are there two ways to do this" moments, fewer transitive-dependency security advisories, fewer version-conflict afternoons, smaller bundles. None of it shows up in a demo. All of it shows up six months later.

Pick one ecosystem and go deep. Add a dependency only when it closes a gap you would otherwise fill worse.

FAQ

Isn't "fewer dependencies" reinventing the wheel?
No. The rule is justified dependencies, not zero. Reimplementing crypto, date math, or accessible drag-and-drop yourself is the opposite failure. Use the platform where it is capable, and use a library where it closes a real, hard gap.

Doesn't Astro prove that mixing frameworks is fine?
Astro deliberately supports it via isolated islands: best tool per component, incremental migration, no lock-in. It isolates them on purpose, and even its docs note that most developers stick to one. Mixing by default inside a single SPA is the anti-pattern. Intentional, isolated islands are not.

How do I decide if a dependency earns its weight?
Ask what it replaces (a real, well-solved hard problem versus a few lines of platform code), the maintenance and security surface it adds, and whether it locks you in. Sharp wrapping libvips earns it. A date library for one format string usually does not.

Further reading

  • Astro — Islands architecture (the deliberate, isolated multi-framework model): https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/
  • MDN — Fetch API (how much the platform now does natively): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API
  • Next.js — Server Actions and Mutations (FormData straight from the request): https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/updating-data

Originally published at brokeinprod.dev — field notes from production: the error, the cause, the one-line fix.

title: Built a Free Tool to Track AI Tokens and API Costs
description:
I’ve been spending a lot of time exploring AI tools and working with prompts recently.

One thing I noticed is that it’s not always easy to understand how much a prompt actually costs when using AI APIs.

You write a prompt, send it to a model, get a response, and move on.

But what if you’re testing multiple prompts or comparing different AI models? Keeping track of token usage and API costs can become confusing.

Why I Built It

I wanted a simple place where I could:

  • Count the tokens in a prompt.
  • Estimate API costs before sending requests.
  • Compare the costs of different AI models.
  • Make prompts shorter and more efficient.

Instead of constantly switching between different tools, I decided to build a small project that brings these features together.

Introducing PromptBurn

PromptBurn is a free tool designed for people who work with AI prompts and APIs.

It currently includes:

  1. Token Counter

Check how many tokens your prompt contains.

  1. API Cost Calculator

Estimate potential API costs based on token usage and model pricing.

  1. Model Comparison

Compare costs across supported AI models.

  1. Prompt Compression

Experiment with making prompts shorter while keeping their meaning.

Privacy Was Important to Me

I also wanted to keep the experience simple and privacy-conscious.

PromptBurn is designed to process prompt text directly in the browser, rather than sending it to a server.

What’s Next?

This is still a work in progress.

I’d like to improve the accuracy, add useful features, and make the experience better for developers working with AI APIs.

You can check it out here:

https://prompt-burn.com

I’d genuinely appreciate feedback from other developers.

A few questions:

  • What would you improve first?
  • What feature is missing?
  • How do you currently track token usage and API costs?

Thanks for reading!

title: Browser Report Downloads: 4 Object Storage Export Race and Wrong-Key Prefix Checks
description:
Short answer: keep customer-support exports private, and expose a browser download link only after the export job has recorded both a completed upload and the exact object key; a 404 at this boundary usually indicates a race condition or a wrong key prefix, not a missing public ACL.

The decision is therefore to treat link delivery as a state transition, not as string construction. The application database owns the export state and exact key, object storage confirms existence with HEAD, and presigning happens only after both agree. This preserves a useful invariant: no authenticated customer sees a download action for an object that the export worker has not finished publishing.

For a team that wants this storage boundary to remain stable while the provider behind it changes, I recommend trying Infrai for the object check and private-link path: its REST contract stays fixed across its supported storage vendors, so changing the vendor does not require changing application code. The service exposes this capability through one REST API: it is pure HTTP, needs no SDK installation, and works from any language or runtime.

The second advantage is operational: Infrai uses a single API key across all 295 routes in 20 backend modules and consolidates their usage on one bill. A support platform can therefore add email delivery to the export worker without maintaining a separate service key or reconciling a separate provider invoice. Its public, keyless discovery surface also publishes the request schema and runnable examples, which lets a team audit the storage contract before customer data crosses it. The underlying storage specialist still holds the bytes, however, and its region and contractual terms remain part of the trust decision.

How can access control prevent a browser download link 404 after an export job?

Four checks belong on the commit path, in this order: the job has finished generating the report; the upload has completed; the database contains the exact bucket and object key used by that upload; and a HEAD request confirms that object before the application enables the button or sends email. This ordering matters because report.pdf, customers/482/report.pdf, and jobs/0193/report.pdf are three different keys even when they describe the same business report. Reconstructing one of them later from a display name quietly creates the classic wrong-prefix 404.

Do not guess.

The durable row should contain an opaque export ID, authenticated customer ID, status, bucket, exact object key, created timestamp, completion timestamp, and any deletion timestamp your policy requires. Metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix listing in this storage surface, so the database is the index and audit trail. A prefix such as customers/{customer_id}/exports/{export_id}/report.pdf is useful for human inspection and scoped listing, but the stored full key — not the naming formula — is authoritative.

This is an exactly-once decision even if the worker and HTTP calls are at-least-once. A retry may upload the same deterministic key again, but only one guarded database transition should move uploading to ready; the transition records the key that was actually written. Since conditional If-Match writes are unavailable at this layer, strict concurrent ownership belongs in a queue or database transaction. That separation is easy to overlook when an export normally completes in two seconds and the button is rendered immediately, yet it is the difference between an auditable publication event and a timing assumption.

Reliability ledger: define release before retry

The primary invariant is ready => database key recorded AND object HEAD succeeds. The second is authorization: the customer identity checked by the application must own the export row before any private link is minted. The third is temporal: links are delivery credentials, not records of retention, so expiration of a link neither proves nor causes deletion of the underlying report.

There are two expected failure boundaries. If the row is still generating or uploading, the UI says the export is processing and retries later. If the row says ready but HEAD reports 404, the system records a reconciliation event with export ID, customer ID, bucket, exact key, job attempt, and request ID, then offers retry or export-again rather than weakening access control. That event is valuable because it distinguishes a premature publication transition from a deterministic key mismatch without putting customer data into logs.

No row, no link.

I'm not sure what retention period is appropriate for a particular support organization; contracts, legal holds, and the sensitivity of report contents resolve that question. The architecture can still enforce the answer mechanically: store the chosen deletion deadline, run deletion from that record, and retain an audit event proving which export ID and object key were targeted. The lifecycle granularity starts at one day, so hour-level expiry needs application scheduling, and object versioning or object lock is unavailable. A financial-grade WORM record therefore belongs in a system designed for immutable retention, not in this export bucket. Region is equally concrete. The API boundary can normalize calls and expose vendor readiness through public discovery, but it cannot turn an underlying processor's storage region into a different contractual guarantee. Record the selected provider and region beside the export policy, verify the provider agreement, and keep support-report content out of any route whose processor boundary has not passed review. The specialist storage provider remains responsible for byte persistence; the API layer handles the stable routing contract. This allocation must appear in the data-processing inventory as two boundaries, because a stable integration contract is useful engineering but does not collapse the legal identity of the processor that persists the report.

Governance and migration: inventory every processor boundary

Option Best fit Access and trust trade-off Decision here
Infrai over R2, S3, OSS, or COS A small backend team that wants one REST storage contract while retaining provider choice Private delivery fits; the team must still validate the selected specialist's region, retention, and processor terms Good fit for HEAD and presigned-link orchestration
Amazon S3 directly Teams that need direct control of specialist features and account policy More provider-specific integration, but the direct relationship is preferable for requirements such as versioning or object lock Choose for immutable retention or deeper S3 controls
Cloudflare R2 directly Teams already standardized on R2 account controls and direct operations Tighter coupling to R2, with fewer abstraction boundaries to investigate during an incident Choose when direct R2 ownership matters more than portability
Alibaba Cloud OSS or Tencent Cloud COS directly Workloads whose approved region and processor contract already point to one of these providers Direct SDK and policy ownership increase integration specificity Choose when regional governance dictates the provider
Google Cloud Storage directly Organizations standardized on Google Cloud governance It is outside the abstraction's listed storage-vendor coverage, so the stable storage route does not apply Keep GCS when organizational controls require it

The catch is that Infrai is not suitable for static website hosting, permanent public image links, or any design that depends on public-read; public URLs remain null. It also is not the right abstraction when browser-direct upload requires self-service CORS changes, when cross-region replication is mandatory, or when a migration program needs cross-cloud bulk tooling. Stick with the relevant direct specialist in those cases. Private customer downloads are narrower, which is why the abstraction fits this decision without pretending to solve every storage problem.

The byte custodian remains.

Implementation: compile the ready predicate into Go

This small command performs the readiness probe that belongs between the database transition and link exposure. It reads the API key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, honors Retry-After on 429, and returns the response body for the caller's audit record. Run it with a bucket and the exact database key; a successful check permits the separate presigning step, while 404 returns a reconciliation outcome rather than a public-ACL change.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if at, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil && time.Until(at) > 0 {
        return time.Until(at)
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func headObject(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey, bucket, key string) ([]byte, int, error) {
    const route = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key}"
    path := strings.ReplaceAll(route, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket))
    path = strings.ReplaceAll(path, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key))
    endpoint := path

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, 0, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, 0, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, resp.StatusCode, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, 0, ctx.Err()
            }
        }
        return body, resp.StatusCode, nil
    }
    return nil, 0, fmt.Errorf("rate-limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=... go run . <bucket> <exact-object-key>")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, status, err := headObject(ctx, http.DefaultClient, os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Args[1], os.Args[2])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if status == http.StatusNotFound {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "object not ready: reconcile the export status and exact key")
        os.Exit(3)
    }
    if status < 200 || status >= 300 {
        fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "object check failed with status %d: %s\n", status, body)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The code deliberately does not derive a key, list a prefix hoping to find a match, or parse undocumented response fields. The application still has one more authorization check before presigning: compare the authenticated customer ID with the export row, then ask the storage adapter for a short-lived private link. Audit both the authorization decision and link issuance, but never log the signed URL itself because it is a temporary bearer credential.

Security rejection: public ACLs do not repair missing objects

Making the bucket public was rejected. It would trade away the access-control requirement while leaving both causal faults intact: an upload that has not completed still has no object to serve, and a wrong prefix still addresses the wrong key. A public ACL can be valid for a deliberately public asset host, but it doesn't repair either fault; this storage surface does not provide public or public-read ACLs, and authenticated customer-support reports are the wrong material for that design anyway.

The practical troubleshooting rule is short: inspect the export row before the bucket. Confirm job state, compare the stored key byte-for-byte with the worker's upload key, issue HEAD, and only then investigate link issuance. Prefix listing can help an operator inspect a known customer or job namespace, but it must not become production lookup logic because metadata is not server-searchable beyond that prefix filter.

This boundary also makes deletion testable. A deletion worker consumes the stored key, records its attempt, and changes the row only according to the resulting policy decision; retries are coordinated through the database or queue because the storage layer has no conditional write primitive. Reports requiring recovery from accidental overwrite, legal hold, or automatic cross-region copies should move to a specialist configuration that explicitly supplies those controls. No abstraction can infer them after the fact.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage troubleshooting guide and verify the live schema and provider readiness before implementing the adapter.

References

  • AWS S3 Multipart Upload overview
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation

title: Evaluating Staged Retrieval for E-commerce Search with Go and Freshness Gates
description:
For e-commerce product search, the useful boundary is between retrieval and the answer layer: retrieve a bounded, fresh set of products with tenant metadata and source IDs, then let the answer or ranking service operate on that traceable context. An evaluation set should measure that boundary explicitly. I would use staged retrieval with named collections, strict query limits, and evidence attached to every result; a single HTTP surface can simplify swapping the provider behind that contract, but it does not remove the need to test freshness or access control.

I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat search pipelines the same way I treat queues: every handoff needs a visible contract, a timeout, and an idempotent replay story. The incident lesson is simple. A plausible top result is not proof that the pipeline is healthy.

What should an evaluation set prove in product search?

Start with queries that represent the storefront, not the embedding model. Each row should contain the query, tenant, access policy, expected product or document identifiers, and a freshness cutoff. Add hard negatives: products with the right color but wrong size, an old listing with a perfect title match, and an item from another tenant. Keep the expected evidence ID or URL beside the relevance label so a reviewer can inspect why a result was accepted.

The set becomes a contract when you can state the checks in operational language:

  • Recall@k asks whether an eligible product appears in the bounded candidate set.
  • Freshness checks reject a result whose indexed timestamp is past the query's cutoff.
  • Isolation checks fail if a result carries a tenant or access-control value that does not belong to the request.
  • Traceability checks require a source URL or document identifier on returned context.

Do not collapse these into one score. A high relevance score with a stale or unauthorized item is a production failure, not a small metric regression. Your mileage may vary on the exact k and cutoff; those values depend on catalog size and how quickly inventory changes, and the evaluation set should record the decision rather than hide it.

Infrai fits at this boundary when you want the retrieval contract to survive a provider change. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, and its live catalog spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so the web-context and vector stages can be documented and operated through one consistent HTTP convention.

For Infrai, the practical second advantage is one key, one bill for those capabilities. That removes a credential rotation and reconciliation step from the runbook when the same evaluation job touches web context, vector retrieval, and later backend services.

How do chunking, freshness, and bounded queries interact?

Chunking controls what a retriever can see. For a product catalog, one chunk per product variant often preserves the fields a shopper needs: SKU, title, attributes, availability, and policy text. Long manuals or seller pages need smaller chunks, but splitting a product's price from its stock status creates a misleading candidate. Put a stable product or document ID in each chunk and carry tenant metadata with it.

Freshness is a second clock. At ingest, store the source update time and the time the chunk entered the collection. At query time, pass a cutoff into the retrieval contract and filter the candidate set before reranking. If the backend cannot enforce that filter, enforce it in the boundary service and count how many candidates were discarded. That count belongs in your trace.

Bound the work. Set a deadline for web enrichment, cap the number of candidates handed to the reranker, and retry only within the remaining budget. A slow source should reduce optional context, not block checkout search. A 429 response deserves exponential backoff and the server's Retry-After value; a retry without a stable request identity can duplicate writes or distort your evaluation logs.

Here is a small Go client for the vector stage plus an evaluator for the contract. The client uses the documented base URL and route; the assertions remain provider-neutral.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func queryVector(ctx context.Context, payload map[string]any) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    body, err := json.Marshal(payload)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: status %s: %s", resp.Status, string(data))
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: rate limit persisted after retries")
}

type Candidate struct {
    ID          string
    Tenant      string
    UpdatedAt   time.Time
    Source      string
    AccessClass string
}

type Case struct {
    Query        string
    Tenant       string
    FreshAfter   time.Time
    ExpectedIDs  map[string]bool
    AllowedClass string
}

func valid(c Candidate, tc Case) bool {
    return c.Tenant == tc.Tenant &&
        !c.UpdatedAt.Before(tc.FreshAfter) &&
        c.Source != "" &&
        c.AccessClass == tc.AllowedClass
}

func recallAtK(candidates []Candidate, tc Case, k int) float64 {
    if k > len(candidates) {
        k = len(candidates)
    }
    seen := 0
    for _, c := range candidates[:k] {
        if valid(c, tc) && tc.ExpectedIDs[c.ID] {
            seen++
        }
    }
    if len(tc.ExpectedIDs) == 0 {
        return 0
    }
    return float64(seen) / float64(len(tc.ExpectedIDs))
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 3*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    _, _ = queryVector(ctx, map[string]any{"collection": "catalog", "query": "waterproof hiking boot", "limit": 20})
    case1 := Case{
        Query:        "waterproof hiking boot",
        Tenant:       "shop-42",
        FreshAfter:   time.Date(2026, 9, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
        ExpectedIDs:  map[string]bool{"sku-17": true, "sku-22": true},
        AllowedClass: "storefront",
    }
    candidates := []Candidate{
        {ID: "sku-17", Tenant: "shop-42", UpdatedAt: time.Date(2026, 9, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), Source: "catalog/sku-17", AccessClass: "storefront"},
        {ID: "sku-old", Tenant: "shop-42", UpdatedAt: time.Date(2026, 8, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), Source: "catalog/sku-old", AccessClass: "storefront"},
    }
    fmt.Printf("recall@2=%.2f\n", recallAtK(candidates, case1, 2))
}

The point is not the metric implementation. It is that a provider swap cannot silently change what "eligible" means. Keep these assertions in CI and in a replayable sample of production traces.

Keep it boring.

Where do the main retrieval options fit?

The provider is one component in this contract. I compare options by control at the boundary, not by a demo's top answer.

Option Strength for product retrieval Trade-off to test
Elasticsearch Mature lexical filters, facets, and operational tooling Vector and freshness policies often require more components and tuning
OpenSearch Open ecosystem with hybrid search and familiar query concepts Managed feature and version differences can complicate repeatable evaluation
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused retrieval API You still own catalog filtering, evidence plumbing, and a separate lexical path
Weaviate Vector plus schema-oriented filtering in one product Schema and module choices add another lifecycle to operate
A unified HTTP gateway One authentication and request contract across retrieval capabilities You must verify provider readiness, limits, and the exact collection semantics

For the last row, Infrai is a reasonable fit when the team wants the contract to stay put while the backend capability changes. Its public discovery surface describes available capabilities, and one REST API uses the same bearer-key pattern across them; that can remove SDK and credential handoffs around a retrieval boundary. The supporting benefit here is breadth with a consistent interface, which makes it practical to keep web enrichment and vector querying in the same runbook without turning this article into an endpoint catalog.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the handoff between web-backed context and vector candidates when a plain HTTP integration and one provider contract matter more than owning every index detail. Keep Elasticsearch or OpenSearch when facets, analyzers, and low-level shard controls are the product. Choose Pinecone or Weaviate when a managed vector specialist is the simpler operational boundary for your team.

A replayable handoff with explicit evidence

The retrieval flow should leave a record that another engineer can replay: query text, collection name, tenant, cutoff, candidate limit, request ID, and source identifiers. Web search can supply current seller or policy context; vector query can retrieve catalog chunks. These are separate stages, and the second stage should not accept context that lacks an evidence ID.

In production, I make the deadline visible in the trace and return a partial answer when optional enrichment times out. Then I alert on the rate of partials and on freshness or isolation failures, rather than hiding them behind a generic "search failed" counter. Short logs are easier to page on.

The long tail is where the handoff earns its keep: imagine a seller policy page arriving six minutes after a catalog update, a tenant filter applied in the wrong process, and a retry fired just as the original request completes. A useful trace shows the cutoff, both collection names, the discarded stale chunk, the source identifier, and the request ID. Without those fields, an evaluator can report a green recall number while a shopper sees an item they cannot buy. I am not sure any vendor-specific dashboard will preserve all of that context for you, so keep the record in your own boundary service and replay it during every index or provider change.

The catch is that a unified surface cannot decide your relevance labels, chunk boundaries, or tenant policy. It also does not make a specialist index unnecessary. If those controls are your differentiator, the extra component is justified. If the boundary itself is the expensive part to maintain, a single HTTP contract is the useful trade.

If this boundary matches your system, start by checking the vector capability and its request schema at the retrieval documentation.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/search-plugins/knn/index/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/understanding-indexes
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/concepts/search

This simplifies migrations of legacy workloads while maintaining an active security posture.

title: Marginal-Preserving Coupled Diffusion Composition for Long-Horizon Planning
description:
arXiv:2611.15585v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.

title: OpenAI Python SDK errors, retries and timeouts: what it retries for you and what it can't
description:
Network calls fail. Rate limits get hit, servers have bad minutes, requests are malformed, keys expire.

The OpenAI Python SDK already retries the retryable errors for you (connection problems, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx) with exponential backoff. Your job is three things: set sensible timeouts, handle the errors that retrying cannot fix, and log the request id so a failure can be traced later.

1. The exception hierarchy 

openai.APIError
├── APIConnectionError          -> retried automatically
│   └── APITimeoutError         -> retried automatically
└── APIStatusError
    ├── 400 BadRequestError          -> fix the request
    ├── 401 AuthenticationError      -> fix the config
    ├── 403 PermissionDeniedError    -> fix the config
    ├── 404 NotFoundError            -> fix the request
    ├── 422 UnprocessableEntityError -> fix the request
    ├── 429 RateLimitError           -> retried automatically
    └── 5xx InternalServerError      -> retried automatically

2. Automatic retries, observed

fake_client below is a small stub that scripts HTTP responses, so you can watch the retry logic without spending tokens or waiting for a real outage.

import openai
from fake_openai import fake_client

# a 429 then a 500, then success: the SDK retries with backoff and you never see the errors
client = fake_client(script=[{"status": 429}, {"status": 500}, "Recovered."], max_retries=2)
r = client.responses.create(model="gpt-5.6-luna", input="hello")
print(r.output_text, "| HTTP requests made:", len(client.fake.requests))

# more failures than retries: the error reaches your code
client = fake_client(script=[{"status": 429, "message": "Rate limit reached for requests"}] * 5, max_retries=2)
try:
    client.responses.create(model="gpt-5.6-luna", input="hello")
except openai.RateLimitError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e.status_code, "| request id:", e.request_id,
          "| requests made:", len(client.fake.requests))

# a 400 is NOT retried: sending the same bad request again would fail again
client = fake_client(script=[{"status": 400, "message": "Invalid value for 'model'"}], max_retries=2)
try:
    client.responses.create(model="gpt-5.6-luna", input="hello")
except openai.BadRequestError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e.status_code, e.message, "| requests made:", len(client.fake.requests))

Output:

Recovered. | HTTP requests made: 3
RateLimitError 429 | request id: req_fake_8 | requests made: 3
BadRequestError 400 Error code: 400 - {'error': {'message': "Invalid value for 'model'", 'type': 'fake_error', 'code': None}} | requests made: 1

Three requests for one call in the first case, and the 400 went out exactly once.

3. Timeouts 

import openai
from fake_openai import fake_client

client = fake_client(script=[{"delay": 2.0}, "too late"], timeout=0.5, max_retries=0)
try:
    client.responses.create(model="gpt-5.6-luna", input="summarise this long report")
except openai.APITimeoutError as e:
    print("timed out:", type(e).__name__)

# per-call override for a known-slow request (e.g. high reasoning effort)
client = fake_client(script=[{"delay": 0.8}, "done"], timeout=0.5, max_retries=0)
r = client.with_options(timeout=2.0).responses.create(model="gpt-5.6-luna", input="hard question")
print("with a longer timeout:", r.output_text)

Output:

timed out: APITimeoutError
with a longer timeout: done

The default timeout is 10 minutes. That suits long reasoning calls, not a web request where a user is waiting. Set a timeout per use case (interactive: 30-60 s; background: longer), stream interactive responses so users see progress, and remember a retried timeout multiplies the wait: worst case = timeout × (retries + 1).

4. A handling pattern for applications 

import logging
import openai

log = logging.getLogger("assistant")

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    try:
        r = client.responses.create(model=MODEL, input=question, max_output_tokens=800)
    except openai.RateLimitError:
        return "We're busy right now. Please try again in a minute."      # already retried by the SDK
    except openai.APITimeoutError:
        return "That took too long. Try a shorter question."
    except openai.APIConnectionError:
        log.exception("network problem reaching OpenAI")
        return "Temporary connection problem."
    except openai.BadRequestError as e:
        log.error("bad request %s: %s", e.request_id, e.message)          # a bug in OUR code
        return "Sorry, something went wrong."
    except (openai.AuthenticationError, openai.PermissionDeniedError):
        log.critical("OpenAI credentials rejected")                        # page someone
        raise
    if r.status == "incomplete":
        log.warning("incomplete response %s: %s", r.id, r.incomplete_details)
    return r.output_text

Order matters: APITimeoutError is a subclass of APIConnectionError, so catch it first.

Error Meaning Action
401 / 403 bad, revoked or under-privileged key alert; never retry in a loop
400 / 422 your request is invalid (parameters, schema, too long) fix the code; log the request id
404 unknown model, file or response id check names and ids (models get retired)
429 rate limit or quota exceeded retried automatically; if it persists, cut concurrency or raise limits; check billing
5xx, connection, timeout transient server or network trouble retried automatically; degrade gracefully if it persists

Recap

  • The SDK retries connection errors and 408/409/429/5xx (max_retries, default 2) with backoff.
  • Other 4xx errors mean fix your request; retrying won't help.
  • Set timeouts per use case; the default is long.
  • Log request_id and check status == "incomplete".

This is part 12 of a free 20-part OpenAI Python SDK guide. The full series (streaming, structured outputs, function calling, evals, cost) is at recallrun.dev/guides/openai-sdk.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them in Production
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Them in Production

Understanding ACH Return Codes

When a bank rejects an ACH transaction, it sends back a standardized return code. These codes—defined by Nacha (the National Automated Clearing House Association)—tell you exactly why a transfer failed. Unlike generic "declined" messages, ACH returns are deterministic: the same code always means the same thing, and your handling logic should reflect that.

As a developer building payment systems, you need to decode these codes and route them to the right recovery path: retry, notify the user, switch payment rails, or escalate to compliance.

The Major ACH Return Codes

Here are the codes you'll encounter most often in production:

Code Meaning Recovery Path
R01 Insufficient funds Retry later or ask user to top up
R03 No account / account closed Mark account invalid; use alternate
R04 Invalid account number Verify routing + account; flag as bad
R05 Account frozen Contact user; escalate to support
R07 Authorization revoked User must re-authorize or use new account
R10 Customer advises not authorized Fraud signal; escalate immediately
R11 Check digit error Verify routing/account format
R20 Non-transaction account Account type incompatible with ACH
R29 Corporate account closed Mark account closed; notify user
R31 Permissible return entry (CCD only) Retry with different entry code

The full Nacha ruleset defines R01–R85. Focus on R01, R03, R04, R05, R07, R10, R11, R20, and R29 first; they cover ~85% of real-world returns.

Handling Returns Programmatically

When your ACH processor (Stripe, Plaid, FedNow, or your bank's API) notifies you of a return, capture the code and timestamp. ACH returns typically arrive 1–5 business days after the original debit.

def handle_ach_return(return_event):
    code = return_event['return_code']  # e.g., 'R01'
    payout_id = return_event['payout_id']
    timestamp = return_event['returned_at']

    if code in ['R01']:  # Insufficient funds
        # Retry in 2–3 days or notify user
        schedule_retry(payout_id, delay_days=3)
        notify_user(f"Payout failed due to low balance. Retrying {delay_days} days.")

    elif code in ['R03', 'R04', 'R20', 'R29']:  # Account invalid/closed
        # Mark account as unusable; offer alternate
        mark_account_invalid(payout_id)
        notify_user("Your bank account is no longer valid. Add a new one.")

    elif code in ['R05', 'R07']:  # Frozen or revoked
        # Require user action
        escalate_to_support(payout_id)
        notify_user("Your account requires manual review.")

    elif code == 'R10':  # Unauthorized
        # Fraud signal; investigate
        log_fraud_alert(payout_id)
        freeze_account(payout_id)

    else:
        # Fallback: log and notify ops
        log_unknown_return(code, payout_id)

Retry Logic and Timing

  • R01 (insufficient funds): Safe to retry after 2–3 business days. The user may have deposited funds.
  • R03, R04, R20, R29 (invalid/closed account): Do not retry. Route to an alternate payment method (another bank account, card, or wire).
  • R05, R07 (frozen/revoked): Require user intervention. Do not auto-retry.
  • R10 (unauthorized): Treat as fraud. Freeze the account and escalate.

Switching Rails on Return

If ACH fails and you have a fallback, consider RTP (Real-Time Payments) or Visa Direct:

  • RTP: Settles in seconds, no returns (immediate confirmation or decline). Cost: $0.10–$0.50 per transaction. Best for time-sensitive payouts.
  • Visa Direct: Settles in minutes, reversible within 120 days. Cost: $0.50–$2.00. Best for high-value or recurring payouts.
  • ACH: Settles in 1–2 days, returnable for 5 days. Cost: $0.01–$0.25. Best for bulk, low-cost payouts.

When an ACH return fires, log it, notify the user, and offer to retry via RTP or

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: A physics-constrained deep reinforcement learning method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes
description:
arXiv:2611.15389v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.

title: Why My Friend Just Walked Away From Microsoft AI After 14 Years
description:
A few weeks ago, someone I deeply respect resigned from Microsoft. Not quietly — they published a statement. "Innovation has no clear path to application," they wrote. "Cost-reduction research isn't taken seriously." Fourteen years. Co-founder of a lab. Someone who literally helped define the field.
I've been thinking about this daily since. Because this isn't just a personnel change. It's a signal.

The Person Behind the Headline

John Langford spent over a decade at Microsoft leading the AI Frontiers lab. If you're not familiar with his work, Contextual Bandits should ring a bell — it's foundational to everything we now call intelligent decision-making systems. Offline policy evaluation? That's Langford territory. Exploration algorithms? Again, him.
This is someone who didn't just ride the ML wave. They mapped its currents.
His team — roughly 50 people — got folded into Mustafa Suleyman's new Microsoft AI division this past September. The merger created friction around research direction, innovation channels, and how teams get reorganized. Langford chose to leave.

What He's Actually Saying (And Why It Matters)

Langford isn't anti-scaling. He openly acknowledged that bigger models improve prediction performance and offer clearer ROI for enterprises. Fair. Obvious, even.
What he objects to is singular focus. When scaling becomes the only narrative, everything else gets starved — including the slower, harder problems that actually determine whether AI systems work in production versus paper.
Let me translate what happened here into terms every engineer should hear:
You can spend three years developing a more efficient approach to learn from incomplete feedback — an approach that could reduce compute requirements significantly — and when you bring it up, the answer comes back as "just make the model bigger instead."
That's not a resource allocation problem. That's a cultural one.

The Real Tragedy Isn't That He Left

It's that the departure reveals something most organizations won't admit: large-scale AI research and practical, efficient AI research are increasingly seen as competing rather than complementary.
Scaling laws gave us something remarkable — a predictable relationship between model size and performance. Predictability is valuable when you need to justify spending to executives. But predictability is also dangerous when it becomes dogma.
Contextual bandits research is precisely the kind of work that makes AI cheaper to deploy, not more expensive. It asks: how do we make better decisions with less data? How do we learn safely from historical logs without costly online experimentation? These aren't academic questions. Every company running AI at production scale wrestles with them daily.
When your organization signals that the answer to every efficiency problem is "use more compute," you don't have a strategy. You have a spending habit.

Lessons for Anyone Building AI Systems

From observing this unfold, here's what stays with me:
Signal your values through resource allocation. Research direction isn't what you write in mission statements. It's which projects get staffed, which get compute credits, and which get promoted. Organizations mean what they fund.
The biggest risk isn't missing the next scaling breakthrough. It's arriving at a future where only one approach exists and everyone depends on it. Diversity of method is a risk management strategy.
**If you're doing meaningful technical work and nobody inside your org seems to care, the problem might not be your work. Sometimes it's the ladder. Knowing when to climb off is a skill engineers rarely discuss.

A Question Worth Discussing

Every engineering organization I know is facing this tension right now — between chasing the biggest model and building the smartest system. What have you observed in your own experience? Have you seen innovation stall because the preferred solution was always "scale up"? And more importantly: what did you do about it?
I'd genuinely like to hear different perspectives in the comments. This isn't theoretical for anyone still working in this space.

title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
description:
arXiv:2611.14910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: Japanese Text Breaks Your App in 7 Quiet Ways (With Code)
description:
Your app passes every test in English. Then a Japanese user types their name, presses Enter, and the form submits half a word.

Japanese text breaks a lot of quiet assumptions: that words have spaces, that length counts characters, that Enter means "send", that sorting by string sorts by sound. None of these show up as errors. They just make the app feel slightly broken to Japanese users.

I'm a native Japanese developer. Here are the seven I see most, with code you can copy. (In part 1 I covered checkout forms: names, furigana, addresses and prices.)

1. Enter during IME input is not "send"

Japanese is typed through an IME (input method). You type kaigi, see かいぎ, press Space to convert it to 会議, then press Enter to confirm the conversion. If your chat box or search field sends on Enter, it sends the half-finished text.

This is the most common bug I see in chat apps, comment boxes and to-do apps built outside Japan.

input.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
  if (e.key !== 'Enter') return;
  // Enter while converting Japanese text: let the IME handle it
  if (e.isComposing || e.keyCode === 229) return;
  e.preventDefault();
  send(input.value);
});

isComposing is true while the IME is converting. The keyCode === 229 check covers older Safari, which fires the confirming Enter after composition has already ended.

React users: check e.nativeEvent.isComposing.

2. length doesn't count characters 

'𠮷野家'.length;        // 4  (𠮷 is outside the BMP: 2 UTF-16 units)
[...'𠮷野家'].length;   // 3  (code points)

Code points still aren't what a user calls "one character". Emoji with joiners are several code points:

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('ja', { granularity: 'grapheme' });

[...'👨‍👩‍👧家族'].length;               // 7
[...seg.segment('👨‍👩‍👧家族')].length;   // 3  ← what the user sees

So when you cut text to fit ("max 20 characters", previews, notifications), cut by graphemes, or you'll slice a character in half and show a broken symbol:

const truncate = (text, max) => {
  const chars = [...seg.segment(text)].map((s) => s.segment);
  return chars.length > max ? chars.slice(0, max).join('') + '…' : text;
};

truncate('𠮷野家の牛丼👨‍👩‍👧をみんなで', 8); // "𠮷野家の牛丼👨‍👩‍👧を…"

Also: Japanese is dense. 20 Japanese characters say roughly what 40–60 English characters say. A limit that's fine in English can be roomy in Japanese — but each character is about twice as wide, so the pixel width often grows. Don't give buttons a fixed width tuned for English.

3. Line breaks: no spaces, and some characters can't start a line

Japanese has no spaces between words, so browsers may break a line between any two characters — including in the middle of a word.

Two CSS properties help:

:lang(ja) {
  line-break: strict;        /* never start a line with 。、ー or small kana like ゃ */
  word-break: auto-phrase;   /* break between phrases, not inside words (Chrome/Edge 119+) */
}

.title, .button-label {
  text-wrap: balance;        /* evens out short headings */
}

auto-phrase only works when the element is marked lang="ja", and browsers that don't support it simply keep the normal behaviour, so it's safe to add.

For headings, the most reliable fix is still to keep them short enough to fit on one line on a phone.

4. Don't build sentences by joining strings

Word order is different. English puts the verb first; Japanese puts it last:

English Japanese
Delete 3 files? 3件のファイルを削除しますか？
Sent to Yamada 山田様に送信しました

So this can't be translated:

// ❌ the translator only sees fragments
t('delete') + ' ' + count + ' ' + t('files') + '?'

Give the translator the whole sentence with a placeholder:

// ✅
const messages = {
  en: { confirmDelete: 'Delete {count} files?' },
  ja: { confirmDelete: '{count}件のファイルを削除しますか？' },
};

Plurals are simpler in Japanese — there's only one form:

new Intl.PluralRules('en').select(1); // "one"
new Intl.PluralRules('ja').select(1); // "other"
new Intl.PluralRules('ja').select(2); // "other"

But Japanese uses counters instead: 3*件* (items, results), 3*個* (objects), 3*人* (people), 3*枚* (flat things like tickets). The counter belongs to the noun, so keep it inside the translated string, not in your code.

Lists, too:

new Intl.ListFormat('ja', { type: 'conjunction' })
  .format(['りんご', 'みかん', 'ぶどう']); // "りんご、みかん、ぶどう"

5. Sorting names by string doesn't sort by sound

Intl.Collator('ja') sorts hiragana and katakana together in あいうえお order:

['リンゴ', 'あめ', 'かさ', 'イチゴ', 'ばなな', 'さくら']
  .sort(new Intl.Collator('ja').compare);
// ["あめ", "イチゴ", "かさ", "さくら", "ばなな", "リンゴ"]  ✅

But kanji don't carry their reading. Sorting kanji names gives an order no Japanese person would expect:

['山田', '佐藤', '鈴木', '田中'].sort(new Intl.Collator('ja').compare);
// ["佐藤", "山田", "田中", "鈴木"]
// expected (by reading): 佐藤 (さとう), 鈴木 (すずき), 田中 (たなか), 山田 (やまだ)

This is why Japanese forms ask for the name's reading (furigana). If you list people or customers, sort by the reading field, not the name.

6. Search: make hiragana, katakana and half-width match

The same word can be typed in several ways: やまだ, ヤマダ, ﾔﾏﾀﾞ (half-width). Users expect search to find all of them. Normalize both the query and the data the same way:

const toKatakana = (s) =>
  s.replace(/[ぁ-ゖ]/g, (c) => String.fromCharCode(c.charCodeAt(0) + 0x60));

const fold = (s) => toKatakana(s.normalize('NFKC').toLowerCase());

fold('ﾔﾏﾀﾞ') === fold('やまだ'); // true  (both become "ヤマダ")
fold('ＡＢＣ１２３');             // "abc123"

NFKC turns half-width katakana and full-width letters into their normal forms; the second step folds hiragana into katakana.

For splitting text into words (search indexing, highlighting), Intl.Segmenter works for Japanese too:

const words = new Intl.Segmenter('ja', { granularity: 'word' });
[...words.segment('今日は東京で会議があります')]
  .filter((s) => s.isWordLike)
  .map((s) => s.segment);
// ["今日", "は", "東京", "で", "会議", "が", "あり", "ます"]

It's not as good as a real Japanese tokenizer, but it's built in and much better than splitting on spaces (there are none).

7. The same character can look Chinese

Chinese and Japanese share many characters with the same Unicode code point, but the shapes differ slightly (直, 骨, 角, 写 are classic examples). If the font is chosen for Chinese, Japanese readers notice — it looks like a typo.

The fix is to tell the system the text is Japanese:

<html lang="ja">

:lang(ja) {
  font-family: "Hiragino Sans", "Noto Sans JP", "Yu Gothic UI", "Yu Gothic", sans-serif;
}

On mobile, the same idea: set the app or view's locale to Japanese when showing Japanese, and in games, make sure the font you ship is a Japanese font (Noto Sans JP is free), not a Chinese one.

Mixed content is the tricky case — for example, a Chinese user's comment shown inside a Japanese page. Mark it with its own lang attribute if you know it.

Checklist

  • [ ] Enter during IME conversion doesn't send (isComposing)
  • [ ] Character limits and truncation count graphemes (Intl.Segmenter)
  • [ ] line-break: strict and word-break: auto-phrase on Japanese text; no fixed-width buttons
  • [ ] Whole sentences with placeholders; counters inside the translation
  • [ ] People sorted by reading, not by kanji
  • [ ] Search folds hiragana / katakana / half-width (NFKC)
  • [ ] lang="ja" and a Japanese font

None of this is translation. Your Japanese text can be perfect and the app can still feel "not made for here" because of these seven. The good news is they're all small fixes.

If you want the full list, there's a free printable Japan-Ready Checklist (31 points across language, names, addresses, checkout, layout and store pages). And if you'd like a native Japanese developer to go through your actual screens, I do Japan-ready reviews on Fiverr.
