title: Your leaderboard is ranking luck: 3,736 models, 46,284 graded calls, and a split-half correlation of 0.04
description:
We run a population of model instances that publish pre-event probability calls on football fixtures. Every call is written to ai_predictions at creation, graded exactly once after the event, and stored as a boolean. As of this audit: 46,884 rows, 46,284 with a non-null grade, 26,415 hits — a global rate of 57.07%.

Our public leaderboard reads ai_models.hit_rate, sorts descending, renders the top. Standard design, structurally broken. The failure is not the sort comparator; it is a property of sorting point estimates computed from wildly unequal denominators.

Here is the board as it renders today:

rank model_id n hit_rate
1 36959 7 100.0
2 38833 7 100.0
3 34115 7 100.0
4 43282 6 100.0

Four rows, four perfect records, none above seven graded calls. Across the table, 327 models sit at exactly 100.0%, and 204 of those have a single graded call. Of the 584 models with at least 20 graded calls, zero are at 100%. The first hundred rows of the board contain no model with ten or more calls.

A leaderboard topped by 204 coin flips is not a leaderboard. It is a sampling artifact rendered as a ranking.

Two populations, one table

The first thing an audit has to separate is how many models exist versus how many have enough evidence to be compared.

-- population split: board cache vs. the fact table
SELECT count(*)                                        AS board_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE total_predictions > 0)   AS with_evidence,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_predictions) AS median_n
FROM ai_models;

WITH t AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND model_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT count(*)                                        AS models,
       sum(n) AS rows, sum(h) AS hits,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE n >= 20)                 AS n20,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE n >= 50)                 AS n50,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE n >= 200)                AS n200,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY n)  AS median_n,
       max(n)                                          AS max_n
FROM t;

Output, unedited:

board_rows 8942 | with_evidence 3229 | median_n 7.0
models 3736 | rows 46284 | hits 26415 | n20 661 | n50 171 | n200 7 | median_n 6.0 | max_n 381

Three numbers matter. The median model has six graded calls, 171 models clear fifty, seven clear two hundred. Sorting 3,229 estimates where the median sample is 7 is not ranking models — it is ranking the draws.

The test: split each model's history in half

If a hit rate reflects a durable property of the model, the rate on the first half of its own history must predict the rate on the second half. If it reflects noise, the halves are independent and the ranking carries no forward information.

The split is by sequence position, not calendar time, so a model that started last week is treated like one that started in June. Both halves need at least ten graded calls, restricting the test to the 661 models with n ≥ 20.

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT model_id, hit,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY model_id ORDER BY id) AS rn,
         count(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY model_id)             AS n
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE hit IS NOT NULL AND model_id IS NOT NULL
),
halves AS (
  SELECT model_id, max(n) AS n,
         avg(CASE WHEN rn <= n/2 THEN hit::int END) AS h1,
         avg(CASE WHEN rn >  n/2 THEN hit::int END) AS h2,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE rn <= n/2 AND hit)  AS k1,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE rn <= n/2)          AS n1
  FROM ordered WHERE n >= 20 GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT count(*) AS models, corr(h1, h2) AS pearson,
       avg(h1) AS mean_h1, stddev_samp(h1) AS sd_h1,
       avg(h2) AS mean_h2, stddev_samp(h2) AS sd_h2
FROM halves;

Result over 661 models:

models 661 | pearson 0.0443 | mean_h1 0.6291 | sd_h1 0.0991 | mean_h2 0.5656 | sd_h2 0.1135

A correlation of 0.0443. Spearman on the same pairs is 0.0261. For practical purposes these are zero — the first half of a model's record tells you almost nothing about its second half.

Note the drift, not just the flatness: first half averages 62.91%, second half 56.56%. Instances are not stationary across their own lifetime. One tuned against recent fixtures starts hot and mean-reverts, and a board built on the early record is systematically reading the hot streak.

What the top of the board is worth

Take the 661 pairs, sort by first-half rate, cut the top 66, look at what that group did next.

slice models first half second half decay
top decile 66 80.85% 60.36% −20.5 pp
everyone else 595 — 56.13% —
bottom decile 66 46.14% 56.29% +10.2 pp

The top decile displays 80.85% and delivers 60.36%. The surviving edge over the rest of the population is 3.8 points, not the 24.7 the display implies. The bottom decile displays 46.14% and delivers 56.29% — the global rate within noise. Both tails converge on 56–57% because that is where the population lives; the spread at the tails was estimation error, not skill.

This is what rewarding luck means numerically. A 100.0% display on seven calls is not a stronger signal than a 60% display on 380 calls — it is a weaker one wearing a better font.

The multiplicity check

Under the null that every model draws from the same 57.07% process, the probability of a clean sweep at n calls is 0.5707^n:

n=5   6.05e-02
n=7   1.97e-02
n=10  3.67e-03
n=20  1.34e-05

At n=7 a perfect record happens once in fifty-one. With 3,229 board rows and thousands of small-n models, dozens of perfect records are expected, not remarkable. Summing 0.5707^n over every model's actual n gives an expected 661.75 perfect records. We observe 401.

Observed is below expected, and the reason is informative: the smallest buckets underperform. Models with 1–9 graded calls hit 49.02% across 8,606 rows; the 100–199 bucket hits 61.01%. Fresh instances start worse than the population they are compared against, so perfect records are not over-represented relative to chance — they are the surviving right tail of many short, slow-starting records.

Correct for multiplicity and the picture gets worse. With 3,229 candidates at α = 0.05 the per-test threshold is 1.55e-5, which requires n ≥ 20 with a clean sweep. We have 584 models at n ≥ 20 and none is perfect. No defensible 100% exists on this board.

Trying to fix the ranking function

The obvious next move is replacing the point estimate with something that penalises small samples — a Wilson lower bound, or a Beta posterior shrunk toward the population rate. Implement both, then re-run the same split-half evaluation at the same 66-model cut.

import math

P0 = 0.570716        # 26,415 hits / 46,284 graded rows
STRENGTH = 20.0      # pseudo-count mass pulling toward P0

def wilson_lb(k, n, z=1.96):
    if n == 0:
        return 0.0
    p = k / n
    denom  = 1 + z * z / n
    centre = p + z * z / (2 * n)
    margin = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n))
    return (centre - margin) / denom

def shrunk(k, n, prior=P0, strength=STRENGTH):
    return (k + prior * strength) / (n + strength)

def top_slice(rows, key, k):
    """rows: dicts with h1, k1, n1, n, h2"""
    chosen = sorted(rows, key=key, reverse=True)[:k]
    return {"second_half": round(sum(r["h2"] for r in chosen) / len(chosen), 4),
            "mean_n":      round(sum(r["n"]  for r in chosen) / len(chosen), 1)}

Run over the same 661 pairs, k = 66:

ranking function mean n second-half rate
raw first-half rate 34.1 0.6036
Wilson lower bound (95%) 55.8 0.5936
Beta posterior, strength 20 44.5 0.5858
raw rate, gate n ≥ 30 46.0 0.5777
no ranking (all 661) — 0.5656

The honest result: none of them fixes the forward rate. Every variant lands within 3.8 points of the population mean, and the raw sort is nominally best — not because raw sorting is good, but because the top decile of a positively-correlated noisy signal still concentrates some genuine signal, and shrinkage trades that sliver for conservatism.

The problem is not the ranking function. It is the object being ranked. With a median of six graded calls, no monotone transform of (k, n) can recover forward skill, because there is no forward skill in the estimator to recover.

What actually works

Never render a point estimate without its denominator and interval. 60.4% (n=62, 95% CI 47.9–71.7) is honest. 100.0% is a lie of omission when n=4. The interval is one line of Python; the bare number has no excuse.

Freeze the board as a historical artifact. A live query whose ordering reshuffles as rows arrive can be gamed by waiting. Materialise a weekly snapshot of (as_of, model_id, k, n, rank) and publish that. A model falling from rank 1 to rank 90 then becomes a visible fact instead of a silent overwrite.

Report the panel, not the total. The 171 models at n ≥ 50 average 59.66% with a standard deviation of 6.17 points. That spread is the real content: the credible population sits in a band roughly ±12 points wide at two sigma. A ranked list of 3,229 rows destroys that information; a distribution preserves it.

Set the threshold by what the estimate can support. At n = 50 the standard error of a 0.6 estimate is 0.069, so a 95% interval spans ~27 points. Nobody should compare two models across a 27-point interval. Either label the board as a discovery surface below fifty calls, or restrict ranking to the 171 models where the interval is narrower than the effect being claimed.

The generalisable lesson

Any system ranking entities by a ratio of two counters fails this way once the denominators vary by more than an order of magnitude — recommender A/B tests, creative scoring, per-shard error rates, per-endpoint latency percentiles, analyst dashboards. The tell is always the same: the top of the list is held by the smallest denominators, and the list collapses into ties at the boundary value (100%, 0%, perfect).

The diagnostic is cheap: split each entity's own history in half, correlate the halves, and check what the top decile delivers next. Near-zero correlation plus a twenty-point mean reversion means the ranking is measuring sample size, not the entity.

We still show the board. We now show it with n, with intervals, with a weekly frozen snapshot, and with a hard label that below fifty graded calls the ordering is not a comparison. The models did not get worse. The display stopped flattering the ones that had barely played.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: Reddit Reviews: the internet's favorite shopping hack is getting an AI layer
description:
For about ten years my process for buying anything has been the same. I type the product name, then add "reddit" at the end, and I skip every result that looks like it was written to rank.

I'm not alone. That little suffix turned into a quiet protest against SEO-stuffed review sites. Reddit noticed.

What Reddit launched

On November 10, 2026, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, as reported by TechCrunch. AI organizes the conversations people already have about products into dedicated review pages. It starts with about 10,000 products.

You reach a page by searching a product or category, or by tapping a highlighted product name inside someone's comment. A page shows:

  • a "what people are saying" summary of the important conversations
  • a breakdown of how many comments are positive, negative or mixed
  • what people liked and disliked
  • comments you can filter by topic
  • links back to the original threads, where you can ask your own question
  • a way to jump to the whole category and compare similar products

It's rolling out to all US users on iOS, Android and the web. Reddit has been testing since February: first in Electronics, Video Games and Health & Beauty, then Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel from September. More countries are promised "over time", with no dates.

Why this is genuinely useful

I'll be fair first. Reading Reddit to make a decision is a lot of work. One thread about an espresso machine can run to hundreds of comments: half of them jokes, a quarter about a different model, and one gem buried at the bottom saying the steam wand breaks after a year.

As a developer, I like the design. Sentiment counts plus topic filters is the right shape. It's basically what I do by hand anyway: "show me only the comments about noise" or "only the ones about durability". If the summary links back to real comments, and it does, it works more like a table of contents than a verdict.

Why it makes me a bit nervous

Reddit worked as a review source because it was never meant to be one. Nobody was summarizing it, so nobody had much reason to game the summary. People argued, someone got grumpy, someone else posted a photo of their broken unit, and you made up your own mind.

Once a thread feeds a tidy page with a sentiment bar, the math changes. Every comment about a product becomes a vote in a score that shoppers will see. Both TechCrunch and Inc. point out the obvious risk: astroturfing. Reddit's answer is its existing rules, its tools against automated abuse and spam, and community moderators. Reports also say brands can't pay for placement in Reddit Reviews. That matters, but a paid slot was never the real worry. The fake "honest stranger" is.

I've been on the founder side long enough to know the temptation. The week before a launch, "let's just get a few helpful comments out there" sounds very reasonable at 1 AM. Reddit has fought this forever. Now there's simply more at stake.

The ad that pretends to be a random stranger just got a promotion.

What I'd do as a buyer

Nothing dramatic. A few habits:

  1. Treat the summary as a map, not the answer. Use it to find which topics matter (noise, battery, returns), then read those comments yourself.
  2. Check the commenters. A two-week-old account with a glowing paragraph is a different signal from a five-year regular in a hobby subreddit who complains about everything.
  3. Look for specifics. Real owners mention annoying details: the cable is too short, the app needs an account, the lid squeaks. Fake praise tends to be smooth and generic.
  4. Sort by negative. The "mixed" and "negative" buckets are where you learn whether a problem is a dealbreaker for you.

What I'd do as a founder

If your product could end up on one of these pages, the lesson is old and boring: be present honestly. Answer questions under your real name, own the bugs people mention, and don't buy comments. Moderators on Reddit have long memories, and an AI that summarizes "people feel this brand is shady" will be far worse for you than a few honest complaints.

My overall take

I think Reddit Reviews will be useful for most people most of the time, especially for boring purchases where you just want the consensus. Whether it stays useful depends on whether Reddit can keep the raw conversations human now that they matter more. I'm cautiously optimistic, and I'll keep clicking through to the comments.

So here's my question: when you research a purchase, do you trust an AI summary of the crowd, or do you still read the raw threads yourself? Why?

title: Hello, I'm Shahbaz, and this is what I'm building
description:
Hi everyone, I'm Shahbaz. This is my first post here, so I'll say who I am
and what I'm working on.

What I build

I'm the developer behind Nusk, a project management
tool I've been building for a while. The idea is simple: most teams run
one project across four or five tools. Tasks in Jira, the schedule in MS
Project or Smartsheet, documentation in Confluence, risks in a
spreadsheet. Each tool is fine alone. Together they drift apart, and
someone ends up copying updates between them.

Nusk puts these in one workspace:

  • Work items, boards and sprints, with child items and custom fields
  • Gantt scheduling with dependencies and critical path
  • A spreadsheet-style grid with formulas
  • A wiki, plus RAID logs (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies)
  • Meeting minutes, timesheets, and portfolio-level reports
  • Importers for Jira, Smartsheet and MS Project files
  • Support for SAFe planning

It runs as a hosted service, and there is a self-hosted option for teams
that need it on their own servers.

The part that surprised me

Nusk has a built-in MCP server. You can point Claude Code, Cursor or
Codex at it, and the agent can read and update your real project data:
list your open work, create a task, check a sprint, read a risk log.
Changes made this way are labeled in the revision history and can be
reverted. I'll write a full walkthrough of the setup in a later post.

What I'll write about here

I'll mostly cover things I run into while building it:

  • Designing permissions that hold up on every endpoint
  • Importing messy data from other tools
  • Building a scheduling engine
  • Giving AI agents access to a real system safely

I'll include what went wrong, since that's usually more useful than what
went right.

Try it

There's a demo that needs no signup: nusk.dev/demo
creates a sample workspace that lasts an hour. If you try it, I'd like to
hear what's confusing or missing. Comments here work, and so do direct
messages.

Looking forward to reading what you all are building.

title: Next.js ~API Routes~
description:
With API Routes(or Route Handlers) of Next.js, you can build the API endpoint in the application directly without an extra server.

There are two ways: App Router and Pages Router. Each of them has a different implementation.

1 . Implementation for App Router

You have to create the api folder under the app/ directory, and place router.ts in the api folder. This method is recommended in Next.js

Structure of directories

text

app/
└── api/
    └── user/
        └── route.ts  #This is the URL: /api/user

Example (app/api/user/route.ts)

HTTP methods such as GET and POST can be exported as the name of a function.

typescript

import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

// GET request
export async function GET() {
  const data = { message: 'Hello from App Router!' };
  return NextResponse.json(data);
}

// POST request
export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const body = await request.json();
  return NextResponse.json({ received: body }, { status: 201 });
}

2 . Implementation for Pages Rpouter

You have to place a file under pages/api/ directory. This is the conventional method.

Structure of directories

text

pages/
└── api/
    └── user.ts  # /api/user

title: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.15835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In pre-deployment testing of AI systems such as AI agents, a developer can often deal with known failure modes (e.g., leaking API keys, deleting important databases, or installing a malicious package) by implementing fixes or making contingency plans for when the same issue might occur again. What is more challenging are the unknown unknowns: the unseen failure modes that haven't surfaced during testing. The decision to stop testing and deploy therefore faces an inherent tradeoff: continue testing to observe more behaviors, at the cost of time and resources, or stop testing and deploy, at the risk of failure modes remaining undiscovered. How then does the developer decide when they have tested enough? To answer this, we develop an algorithm that certifies when the probability of observing an unseen failure mode is sufficiently small. The algorithm constructs an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence on this quantity, so the developer can repeatedly test a system, inspect the bound, and decide to stop when it falls below a chosen threshold without invalidating the statistical guarantee. Our problem can be interpreted as a sequential variant of the missing-mass estimation problem which gave rise to the classic Good-Turing estimator (Good, 1953). On SWE-Chat, a dataset of real-world coding agent traces (Baumann et al., 2026), we implement our procedure and show that it achieves tighter upper bounds than a simple multiple-testing corrected Good-Turing baseline, and even dominates a fixed-horizon (non-multiple-testing-corrected) Good-Turing upper confidence bound, which is not anytime valid. Additionally, to better match realistic evaluation pipelines, we extend our method to handle sampling from a different task distribution and imperfect automated failure labeling.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

UPM

1000

1000

Cap height

710

710

x-height

530

530

Ascender

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
description:
arXiv:2611.14949v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

title: RAG Evaluation Metrics: How to Test a RAG Chatbot Before You Ship It
description:
A RAG chatbot fails quietly. It still answers, in confident prose, even when retrieval has returned the wrong passage or the model has ignored the context. Without a way to measure that, every change to chunk size, embedding model, prompt or provider is a guess. This guide covers how to build an evaluation you can repeat, and how to describe its results without overstating them.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately

A wrong answer has two possible causes, and they need different fixes. Either the right passage never reached the model (a retrieval problem), or it did and the model used it badly (a generation problem). If you only score the final answer you cannot tell which, so measure both stages.

Retrieval metrics

  • Hit rate or context recall. For a question with a known source passage, did that passage appear in the top results? This is the first number to look at, because nothing downstream can recover a passage that was never retrieved.
  • Precision. How much of what was retrieved is relevant? Low precision floods the model with noise, which raises cost and tempts it to blend unrelated facts.
  • Ranking quality. Measures such as mean reciprocal rank reward putting the right passage first, which matters when you pass only a few passages to the model.

Tune the number of passages and any similarity cut-off against these numbers rather than by feel, and remember that a cut-off that is too strict produces confident refusals, while one that is too loose produces confident nonsense.

Generation metrics

  • Groundedness (faithfulness). Is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved passages? This is the closest measurable proxy for hallucination.
  • Answer relevance and completeness. Does the answer address the question that was asked, and does it include the parts that matter?
  • Citation correctness. A citation that points at a real retrieved passage is not the same as a citation that supports the sentence it follows. Checking that the reference exists is easy and worth doing, but it only proves the format, not the truth.
  • Refusals. When the documents do not contain the answer, the bot should say so. Include questions that cannot be answered and check that it declines.
  • Forbidden claims. List statements the bot must never make, such as promising a refund the policy does not allow, and check that they never appear.

Build a test set that earns its name

Thirty to one hundred questions is a useful starting size. Draw them from real sources: support tickets, search logs, questions the client's staff actually ask. Avoid questions you wrote by copying a sentence from a document, because they are trivially easy. For each question record the passage or passages that should be retrieved, and where it helps, the key facts a correct answer must contain. Add unanswerable questions and tricky ones: negations, numbers, questions that span two documents, and wording that does not match the document's vocabulary.

Keep the test set stable. Changing questions after a failure so the numbers recover is the quickest way to make an evaluation meaningless.

Choose checks you can repeat

Two families of check complement each other.

  • Deterministic checks are cheap and stable: the expected source was retrieved, a forbidden phrase is absent, every citation tag refers to a retrieved passage, the answer arrived within a time limit. They run on every change and never disagree with themselves.
  • Model-graded checks use a second language model as a judge of groundedness or relevance. They catch nuance a string match cannot, but a judge has its own biases and varies between runs. Calibrate it by comparing its verdicts with human labels on a sample, and record which judge model and prompt you used.

Whichever you use, add periodic human review of a random sample. It is the only check that can catch what both automated methods miss.

Make it a regression test

The real value of an evaluation is comparing runs. Freeze and record the whole configuration with each run: chunk size and overlap, embedding model, number of passages, similarity cut-off, system prompt, generation model and its settings. A short fingerprint of that configuration lets you see at a glance whether two results are comparable. Then make a rule that a change to any of those settings does not ship until the suite has run and the differences are understood.

Measure latency and cost per question

Record the time each question took and report percentiles, not just an average. For cost, use the token counts that the provider returns with each response, multiplied by the provider's current prices. A flat per-answer estimate looks tidy in a report but hides the expensive cases.

Reporting results to a client

A pass rate is only meaningful with its definition beside it. A useful report states the test set size and where the questions came from, the configuration that was tested, what each check means, which cases failed and why, and the date. It also states limits. A passing score means the bot did well on those questions with those documents. It does not guarantee behavior on questions nobody wrote, and a citation check shows that an answer cites a source, not that the answer is correct.

Common mistakes

  • A tiny test set where a single case moves the score by several points.
  • Only easy, document-derived questions, and no unanswerable ones.
  • Scoring the final answer alone, so retrieval and generation faults cannot be told apart.
  • Treating a model judge as ground truth without calibrating it.
  • Re-running until the numbers look good, or editing the test set after a failure.

Where to go next

If you are choosing a starting point for a RAG project, the RAG boilerplates category lists the options, and this comparison explains how two of them differ. Whatever you choose, build your own test set first and judge any starter by how it performs on it.

The idea in short

A fixed test set of questions runs through the same pipeline as live traffic. For each question the run records which passages were retrieved, the answer produced and the time taken, then applies retrieval checks, answer checks and a configuration fingerprint, so two runs can be compared after any change.

Originally published at boilershelf.com.

title: Fix: ChatGPT Work Mode HTTP 500 Error
description:
Originally published on DebugRadar.

ChatGPT Work Mode is returning HTTP 500 on every message, including brand-new conversations — and as of November 12, 2026, it has been broken for over 38 hours with no improvement. OpenAI Support confirmed the failure is server-side and escalated it for technical investigation. Then Support went quiet for 36 hours. Regular Chat works fine on the same account. This is not a problem you can fix from your side — but you can confirm that in two minutes and keep working today.

Quick Fix Summary

  • Problem: ChatGPT Work Mode returns HTTP 500 on POST /backend-api/f/conversation for every message, including brand-new conversations, while regular Chat works normally.
  • Fix: There is no user-side fix. OpenAI Support confirmed a server-side failure and escalated it, with no timeline and no reply in 36 hours.
  • Workaround: Use regular Chat or Codex Work for the same tasks, and send OpenAI Support your request IDs, timestamps, and a HAR file.

Technical Root Cause

Error Code Affected Version Root Cause Current Status
HTTP 500 on POST /backend-api/f/conversation ChatGPT Plus, Work Mode, model GPT-6.1 Sol (Low), all devices (iPhone, Safari, desktop Chrome on Windows) Server-side failure during Work's internal preparation, before the response begins — confirmed by OpenAI Support from internal logs Still broken as of November 12, 2026 — 38+ hours; OpenAI's status page shows Work as Operational; no fix or timeline; Support has not replied in 36 hours

Step-by-Step: Confirm It and Keep Working

Step 1 — Confirm the Failure Is on OpenAI's Side

  1. Open status.openai.com and check the ChatGPT components. The status page shows Work as Operational, which matches what users see: this hits specific accounts and workspaces, not every user at once.
  2. Send a message in a brand-new Work conversation. If it fails with "Network Error" or "Something went wrong", the problem is not your chat history.
  3. Send the same message in regular Chat. If regular Chat answers and Work fails on the same account, the failure is not your browser, network, or plan.
  4. Try another device or network — Incognito mode, another browser, mobile data. Users who tried all of these got the same HTTP 500. If Work fails everywhere and regular Chat works everywhere, it is server-side.

Step 2 — Capture Evidence for OpenAI Support

If you have not contacted Support yet, send them what they ask for — it is the only thing that moves a case like this:

  1. Open Chrome DevTools (F12 → Network tab) and reproduce the failure in Work Mode.
  2. Find the failed request: POST /backend-api/f/conversation → HTTP 500. Copy its request ID.
  3. Export a HAR file: in the Network tab, right-click and choose Save all as HAR with content. Remove any personal data from it before sending.
  4. Send Support the request IDs, the timestamps of the failed attempts, the conversation URLs, and the sanitized HAR file.

The user who reported this on November 10 sent all of it 24 hours ago and has heard nothing back since — set your expectations there.

While Work Mode is down, keep working
A broken Work Mode should not stop your workday. Claude Pro gives you a full AI workspace to keep going in — projects, files, and long tasks — while OpenAI sorts out Work Mode. Gemini Advanced is the other fallback worth having open in a second tab. (Affiliate link — DebugRadar earns a commission if you sign up through it.)

Step 3 — Work Around It Today

Use regular Chat or Codex Work for the same tasks. Both run normally on the same account while Work Mode fails. Move the files and context you need into a regular chat or a Codex session and carry on — do not wait on Work Mode to come back before doing the work.

Step 4 — What NOT to Do

  • Do not clear all your browser data, reinstall the app, or reset your account hoping for a fix. Users tried all of it across devices and networks. The failure is server-side.
  • Do not pay for a third-party "fix" tool. No tool can fix an HTTP 500 that comes from OpenAI's servers.
  • Do not hammer the retry button. Retrying hard during a backend failure can trigger rate-limit messages on top of the 500s.

FAQ

Is ChatGPT Work Mode down for everyone?
No. OpenAI's status page shows Work as Operational. The failure hits specific accounts and workspaces — regular Chat works on the same account. That is why it persists while no global outage is declared.

Will clearing my cache or reinstalling the app fix it?
No. Users tried Incognito mode, other browsers, other devices, and mobile data — same HTTP 500. The failure happens during Work's preparation step on OpenAI's servers.

When will OpenAI fix it?
No timeline exists. Support confirmed the server-side failure and escalated it, then went quiet for 36 hours. Keep working in regular Chat or Codex Work, and check the community thread for updates from other affected users.

Sources: OpenAI Developer Community thread, updated November 12, 2026 — "It's now November 12, and the problem has persisted for over 38 hours without any improvement." (https://community.openai.com/t/chatgpt-work-mode-completely-stopped-working-http-500-across-all-devices-anyone-else-experiencing-this/1415391). Related thread: "ChatGPT Work broken for over 48 hours — server-side failure confirmed, but OpenAI Support has stopped responding" (https://community.openai.com/t/chatgpt-work-broken-for-over-48-hours-server-side-failure-confirmed-but-openai-support-has-stopped-responding/1412217).

title: How Shopify Killed Third-Party Cookies (And How to Build Embedded Apps with App Bridge 4.0 in 2026)
description:
If you’ve tried building an embedded Shopify app recently using older Express or cookie-based session tutorials, you probably ran into the dreaded blank white screen on Safari, iOS, or modern Chrome.

Here is why that happens—and how the modern 2026 Shopify stack completely solves it with App Bridge 4.0 and Header-Based JWTs.

The Death of Third-Party Cookies in Iframes

Historically, Shopify apps ran inside an <iframe> on admin.shopify.com. Developers set traditional HTTP cookies to maintain merchant sessions:

[Merchant Browser] ──(loads iframe)──> [admin.shopify.com] ──(embeds)──> [YourApp.com with Session Cookie]

However:

  1. Apple Safari ITP (Intelligent Tracking Prevention) blocks all cross-site cookies inside iframes by default.
  2. Google Chrome Privacy Sandbox has systematically phased out third-party cookie access.
  3. If your app attempts to read document.cookie or expects session cookies in an embedded iframe, the request fails silently, leaving merchants with a broken spinner or white screen.

The Modern Solution: App Bridge 4.0 & Cryptographic Session Tokens

In modern Shopify architecture, we never use cookies. Instead, authentication relies on short-lived, cryptographically signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) generated directly by Shopify's frontend client.

Step 1: Client-Side Token Injection

With Shopify App Bridge 4.0, you don't even need bulky npm packages on the frontend. A single script tag in your root document handles everything:

<script 
  src="https://cdn.shopify.com/shopifycloud/app-bridge.js" 
  data-api-key="YOUR_SHOPIFY_API_KEY">
</script>

App Bridge automatically intercepts all native window.fetch requests and injects a 60-second signed JWT in the request headers:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

Step 2: Backend JWT Verification

On your backend (React Router / Remix or Node), you verify the token using your SHOPIFY_API_SECRET and extract the authenticated shop domain:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export async function verifyShopifySessionToken(request: Request) {
  const authHeader = request.headers.get("Authorization");
  if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
    throw new Response("Unauthorized: Missing Bearer Token", { status: 401 });
  }

  const token = authHeader.split(" ")[1];
  const [headerB64, payloadB64, signatureB64] = token.split(".");

  // Verify HMAC SHA-256 signature against your App Secret
  const calculatedSig = crypto
    .createHmac("sha256", process.env.SHOPIFY_API_SECRET!)
    .update(`${headerB64}.${payloadB64}`)
    .digest("base64url");

  if (calculatedSig !== signatureB64) {
    throw new Response("Forbidden: Invalid Token Signature", { status: 403 });
  }

  const payload = JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payloadB64, "base64url").toString("utf-8"));

  // Extract authenticated merchant domain
  const destUrl = new URL(payload.dest);
  return { shop: destUrl.hostname };
}

No cookies. No Safari ITP blocks. 100% reliable across every modern browser.

Open-Source Starter Code on GitHub

I've made the core architectural boilerplate and JWT verification snippets completely open-source:

⭐ View the Companion Starter Repository on GitHub

Want the Complete Zero-to-Production Guide?

Building a production-ready Shopify app in 2026 involves more than just auth. You need:

  • GraphQL Admin API Leaky Bucket rate-limit handling & cursor pagination
  • Webhook HMAC verification with Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ)
  • Prisma Multi-Tenant Database modeling
  • Shopify Billing API for recurring SaaS subscriptions
  • Multi-stage Docker & Fly.io zero-cost cloud deployment

I compiled everything into a comprehensive 59-page engineering handbook:

👉 Get The Modern Shopify App Development Blueprint on Gumroad ($29)

👉 Also available on Leanpub ($19 - $29)

It includes complete starter code, architectural blueprints, and a 25-point App Store pre-flight checklist.

Drop any questions below about App Bridge 4.0 or the GraphQL migration—happy to help!

title: Science Prediction Universe
description:
arXiv:2611.15049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humanity has long sought to explain natural phenomena. Reliable prediction of experimental outcomes is a central test of our understanding of the processes that produce them. If artificial general intelligence (AGI) is to surpass human scientific capabilities, it must also predict experimental outcomes more reliably than humans. Such capabilities could accelerate scientific discovery across disciplines, help address humanity's most pressing challenges, and improve human well-being. We introduce Science Prediction Universe (SPU), a benchmark of hidden experimental outcomes with 100 public verified tasks from chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine, and 16 private tasks from unpublished wet-lab experiments. Given an experimental setup and candidate conditions, an agent works with any resources it needs to rank the candidates by a measured outcome.
  We evaluate thirteen agent configurations spanning twelve frontier models across two harnesses (Codex and Claude Code). Current agents remain far from saturating wet-lab outcome prediction, with substantial performance disparities across models: on the public benchmark, configurations separate into two distinct tiers, with task-adjusted Spearman correlations ranging from 0.227 for the lowest-performing configuration to 0.478 for the best. Analysis of 1,155 scored public trajectories (227,103 tool calls) suggests that the bottleneck lies in scientific judgment rather than tool execution: agents rely on shared monotone priors, agreeing far more with one another than with experimental reality (0.52 vs. 0.33), and frequently compute trivial physical or chemical proxies that do not influence the final outcome.

title: Initialize Once, Hydrate Deliberately: Choosing a FeatureCell's Starting State
description:
A FeatureCell does not start with "whatever was in the constructor." Calling initialize() activates the runtime pipeline, and the value it begins with depends on a resolved decision between a declared default, a previously persisted value, and a deliberate hydrate() factory. Knowing which source wins — and why — is what separates an accidental starting value from an intentional one.

This post walks through what initialize() actually activates, when hydrate() overrides everything else, and how to choose between a static default, Persist behaviors, and an explicit factory when your FeatureCell comes online.

Key takeaway: Initialization is not a direct mutation. Whatever value is selected — hydrated, persisted, or declared — is enqueued as a replaceState operation and processed through the same pipeline as any other update.

Initialization Is a Runtime Boundary

A FeatureCell is not operational the moment it is declared. It becomes a runtime participant only after initialize() is called — once, and exactly once. Reading state, issuing updates, or interacting with a FeatureCell before initialization results in a runtime error, and calling initialize() a second time does the same.

That boundary matters because initialization is where configuration becomes behavior. Filters, reducers, taps, error handlers, and emit configuration all have to be declared on the fluent builder before initialize() runs. Once initialization completes, the pipeline is fixed for the lifetime of that FeatureCell.

What initialize() Actually Activates

Calling initialize() transitions a FeatureCell from a configured definition into an active runtime participant. In order, it validates the declared configuration and behaviors, registers the FeatureCell with the Vault runtime, activates the Conductor execution surface, evaluates whichever initialization source was declared, and — if that source produced a value — enqueues it as the first replaceState operation.

If no initialization mechanism is declared at all, the FeatureCell still becomes active, but with value: undefined, waiting for an explicit replaceState() call. Declaring a default is optional; becoming active is not.

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell<Employee[]>({
  key: 'employees',
  // Initial state is declared directly in the descriptor
  initialState: [
    { id: 1, name: 'Alice' },
    { id: 2, name: 'Bob' }
  ]
});

employeeCell.initialize();

Here, descriptor.initialState is the only declared source, so that array becomes the first candidate through Resolve, Filters, Reducers, and Emit — the same pipeline any later update travels through.

When hydrate() Wins

During initialization, Vault evaluates exactly one initialization source, in strict precedence order:

  1. hydrate() — highest precedence
  2. Persist behaviors
  3. descriptor.initialState
  4. No source declared — manual initialization

These are not fallback layers. Vault does not try hydrate(), fail, and then fall back to Persist or the descriptor. Only the single highest-precedence declared source is evaluated at all.

hydrate(factory) registers a deferred factory that does not run when it is called — it runs only when initialize() runs. The factory may return a value synchronously, return a Promise, resolve to undefined, or throw. When declared, it overrides both Persist behaviors and descriptor.initialState outright, because declaring hydrate() is an explicit statement that persisted or static data should not be treated as authoritative for this initialization cycle.

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell<Employee[]>(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    // ignored
    initialState: []
  }
);

employeeCell.hydrate(() => Promise.resolve(...)).initialize();

⚠️ Warning: That descriptor still declares initialState: [], but once hydrate() is registered, it is never evaluated. Declaring both is not a layering strategy — only one source wins.

Choosing Between Defaults, Persistence, and Hydration

The practical question at startup is simple: should this FeatureCell begin with a declared default, a persisted value, or an explicit factory? Each source answers a different need.

Source Nature Choose it when
descriptor.initialState Static, declared at configuration time The starting value is fixed and known in advance, with no runtime dependency
Persist behaviors Previously committed state, restored from storage Continuity across reloads or sessions matters more than a guaranteed-fresh value
hydrate() Deferred factory, evaluated only during initialize() Startup state must be computed or fetched, and stale persisted data or a static default would be wrong

Persisted storage can go stale the moment the underlying data changes elsewhere, and a static descriptor is static by definition. hydrate() exists for the case where neither of those should be treated as authoritative — if dynamic resolution is not actually needed, do not declare it, and Vault evaluates storage or the descriptor according to precedence instead.

Handling Missing Values and Failures

A deferred factory does not always resolve the way you expect, and hydrate() treats "no value" very differently from "something went wrong."

Factory result What happens
Returns a value Enqueued as replaceState and processed through Resolve, Operators, Filters, Reducers, and Emit
Resolves to undefined No write occurs; the FeatureCell remains with value: undefined and hasValue: false
Throws or rejects Initialization fails; no fallback source is evaluated; the error is emitted

An undefined result is not treated as a failure — it just means nothing committed. A thrown error or rejected Promise is treated as a failure, because the declared authoritative source did not resolve the way the application promised it would.

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'employees'
});

employeeCell.hydrate(() => fetch('/api/employees').then((res) => res.json())).initialize();

If that fetch rejects, initialization fails: hasValue stays false, value stays undefined, and error is populated. The pipeline keeps running — it does not crash the application — but nothing committed as declared. Recovery, if you want it, has to be explicit, using reset() and replaceState() to put the FeatureCell into a known state on your own terms.

⚠️ Warning: If hydrate() throws, Vault does not quietly drop down to Persist behaviors or descriptor.initialState. The FeatureCell does not activate partially, and the failure is visible instead of masked.

A live, interactive StackBlitz demo of hydrate() overriding a descriptor default is available on the original article if you want to try the sequence yourself.

Deeper Dive

Read the full method contracts for initialize() and hydrate() in the FeatureCell API reference, including the full precedence rules, diagrams, and resolution outcome tables this post draws from.

title: Report Attachments: Transactional Email Template Preview With Signup Status Polling
description:
A generated health report changes the acceptance test for a transactional welcome email. Rendering the message is only one step; the integration must establish how the report becomes an attachment and what evidence remains after sending. A template preview cannot prove that the intended file reached the intended recipient.

Short answer: Create and preview the HTML/text template before production, send after successful signup or account activation once the report is ready, and retain the returned message identifier for delivery-status and event polling. Make documented attachment support an acceptance requirement. Keep report contents out of telemetry.

For a Node.js backend, the useful boundary is an application-owned delivery record connecting the signup event, generated report, and provider message identifier. Integration effort depends on the assumptions that record must absorb. Attachment representation, template rendering, send acceptance, and subsequent delivery evidence require separate checks.

How should a transactional email welcome flow preview its report template?

Start with the report.

The concrete job is to send a generated report as an email attachment in a healthtech welcome flow. Establish which business event authorizes sending, which artifact belongs to that event, and which recipient the application resolved. Successful signup can trigger a welcome message; a report-bearing message also needs a completed report. Keeping these conditions explicit prevents an account-created callback from becoming an accidental promise that every downstream artifact already exists. This is a proposed application design, rather than a claim about a provider's workflow engine.

Use a synthetic report for the acceptance test. Preview the welcome template with representative variables and check both HTML and text. Then test the actual attachment through the candidate integration. Inspect its filename, content type, and contents at the receiving mailbox. Obtain the required request fields from current documentation; these checks do not establish which fields a particular API accepts.

That distinction matters. Template creation, preview, send, and message retrieval establish a transactional sequence, but their existence does not establish an attachment schema. Do not infer a file parameter from a send operation. An adapter qualifies for this job only after demonstrating the attachment requirement.

Use one activated account, one generated report, and one intended message as the initial test. Add a second attempt for the same business event to examine duplicate handling. A preview would miss that problem.

Read the contract before writing the adapter

Infrai provides a single API key and unified billing through one REST API, with no SDK required; its public, self-describing discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the team can read a capability contract before building an adapter. Its per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata offers a separate advantage for the bounded telemetry record described below. These strengths support evaluation; they do not establish the report-attachment requirement.

Read the public capability contract before constructing a send payload. After an approved test send, this minimal curl example retrieves its message details. Set EMAIL_API_ORIGIN to the documented API origin without a trailing slash or version prefix, INFRAI_API_KEY to your credential, and EMAIL_MESSAGE_ID to the returned identifier. The command performs an explicit read, surfaces HTTP errors, and bounds retries. Curl's retry behavior uses exponential delays and honors Retry-After for supported transient responses, including HTTP 429.

curl --request GET \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 4 \
  --retry-max-time 60 \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set your API key}" \
  --url "${EMAIL_API_ORIGIN:?Set the documented API origin}/v1/email/get/${EMAIL_MESSAGE_ID:?Set the returned message identifier}"

This retrieves one message. It does not send a report. Inspect the send contract's request schema and runnable example before preparing a payload, and require documented attachment support before proceeding. Inventing attachment fields would make a short example look complete while leaving the central requirement untested.

Once qualified, prebuild the template and approve its preview. Connect the send to the successful business event, retain its returned message identifier, and monitor later status and event history. Do not make the monitoring job reconstruct business intent from log lines.

Writes need a separate retry decision. A timed-out request does not establish whether the write was applied. Verify the selected operation's idempotency contract before enabling retries, and bind the retry identity to the same business intent. Generating a fresh identity on every attempt defeats that objective. Rate-limit retries should honor Retry-After when present and use exponential backoff.

Separate delivery evidence from polling noise

The workflow considered here exposes events through pull operations. A small scheduled poller therefore belongs in the application. Its observation interval creates a deliberate delay between an event becoming available and the application retrieving it. Standard welcome-message monitoring can accommodate that interval when the product requirements permit it. Complex real-time cross-channel orchestration calls for a different evaluation.

Avoid inventing certainty.

Retain the provider's documented status meaning. Send acceptance does not establish that a report was read. Record what was observed, when it was retrieved, and the message identifier needed for investigation. Keep the business intent separate from these observations so a monitoring retry cannot become another send attempt.

Consider a planning example, not a measured workload: 10,000 report emails daily and six checks per message produce 60,000 polling observations per day. At an assumed 500 bytes per observation, the raw payload is 30,000,000 bytes daily and 900,000,000 bytes over 30 days. Indexing, replication, and storage overhead are excluded. Change either retention or polling frequency and the result changes directly. These assumptions make the calculation useful without pretending to predict a monitoring invoice.

Repeated unchanged observations need not become separate application log records. Keep the latest observation in the delivery record and emit a transition record when the observed state changes. This retains a useful sequence while reducing repeated evidence. The trade-off is precise: a transition log cannot reconstruct every polling request.

Cardinality needs its own budget. With 10,000 new messages daily and 30 days of retention, a metric label containing message identifiers can introduce 300,000 distinct identifier values. That assumes one new identifier per message; it is not a prediction of a particular backend's series count. Recipient and report identifiers add further dimensions. Keep identifiers in access-controlled records for deliberate lookup and use a bounded vocabulary for aggregate metrics.

Do not sample the only record connecting a report-send intent to its returned message identifier. Sampling is more defensible for repetitive diagnostics. A proposed policy could retain every observed state transition and a sample of unchanged checks, while maintaining aggregate counts for all checks. Its limitation is explicit: sampled diagnostics cannot reconstruct every request. Report contents, rendered bodies, and attachment bytes add nothing to these aggregate counters, so exclude them from telemetry.

Compare candidates against the same report

The comparison should start with the same synthetic attachment and delivery-record requirements. Otherwise, a candidate can appear easier merely because its evaluation stopped at send acceptance. The table gives distinct review priorities, not a completed attachment certification or an assertion of feature parity.

Candidate First documentation review Acceptance boundary
Amazon SES Review the send operation against the generated report and the application's request-construction needs. Advance it if the documented attachment representation produces an acceptable application adapter.
Twilio SendGrid Review attachment handling alongside the team's template ownership and release process. Advance it if the report and approved template can be tested together with clear ownership.
Mailgun Review message sending against the application's file handoff and subsequent investigation needs. Advance it if the report handoff and delivery evidence satisfy the same test.

These are real alternatives with different documentation entry points. Their current contracts should determine the wire-level implementation. This comparison does not establish their attachment limits, event guarantees, or approval for regulated data. A product name cannot substitute for deployment-specific review.

Integration effort remains the decision axis. Count the work required to construct the attachment, release the template, preserve retry identity, and investigate delivery. SDK installation is only one component. A team already committed to an SMTP relay, managed email OTP, or pushed events should explicitly qualify those requirements before choosing an adapter. They are separate requirements from a standard transactional welcome message.

The report test is decisive. A readable schema helps a team evaluate an API, but a successful attachment test and interpretable delivery evidence establish whether it fits this job.

Roll out with a bounded evidence record

Begin with the synthetic account and report. Approve the template preview, demonstrate the attachment at a receiving mailbox, retain the returned message identifier, and verify that polling records later observations without resending. Exercise the duplicate-attempt case before expanding the rollout.

Then choose an observation interval, polling stopping rule, and record-retention period. Treat these as operational decisions. Compare actual retained bytes with the planning calculation and inspect metric label cardinality before increasing volume.

Keep the initial rollout small. A working report attachment with useful evidence is a better acceptance result than a preview followed by a large pile of logs.

Sources

References for contract review and the standards checks adjacent to this workflow:

  • Amazon SES SendEmail API reference
  • Twilio SendGrid attachment documentation
  • Mailgun sending documentation
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework
  • NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines

title: Node.js SMS OTP API Cutovers — Release Gates for SaaS Login Templates
description:
A supplier cutover is unsafe if the platform team can roll back its adapter but cannot restore the instructions customers received. Short answer: for a Node.js SaaS login serving US/EU users, start with managed SMS OTP generation and code verification, while keeping template approvals and contact-form routing under application ownership. Release the approved message and its support policy together. Treat provider replacement as a controlled release, with evidence that rollback preserves that pairing.

Consider a production rehearsal for a fintech service handling event ticket verification. A customer cannot complete login, follows the message's support instructions, and selects a contact-form reason. During a supplier change, the replacement message uses different instructions; the form now sends an account-access request to ticket review. This is a hypothetical failure exercise, not a reported incident or a delivery benchmark. A successful OTP verification test would miss it.

The lesson is about change authority: the owner who approves customer instructions must also approve their routing consequences. A transport migration should not silently acquire that authority.

Fintech platform teams should try Infrai for managed SMS OTP when a plain REST API keeps the Node.js integration small enough to replace without maintaining a provider SDK. Its public discovery schemas provide a second useful advantage: reviewers can inspect request and response contracts before changing the adapter, reducing contract-reconstruction work during migration. That does not make SMS payloads interchangeable with another supplier's API.

Infrai also uses one key and one bill across its backend capabilities. For a team already using that platform for operational evidence, this avoids adding a separate credential rotation and invoice reconciliation task for SMS, although the shared credential makes access review more consequential.

Keep the evidence.

What must an SMS OTP API cutover prove for SaaS login?

The release artifact should contain the approved wording, locale, business revision, provider mapping, and expected contact-form destination. These are proposed application records, not provider request fields. For this scenario, separate “I cannot sign in” from “I signed in but my ticket is wrong,” and preserve that distinction across the old and replacement messages. An SMS delivery observation is useful troubleshooting context; only the verification result establishes that a code check succeeded, and neither result decides ticket entitlement.

Approval is the invariant. Provider identifiers are replaceable mappings.

That difference determines the rollback procedure. An outstanding challenge retains its original provider reference and approved business revision until it expires or finishes; new traffic can use the replacement adapter, but an adapter switch must not rewrite the history needed to explain an older customer's support request. Do not assume a challenge created by one provider can be verified by another. The application contract promises continuity of routing and evidence, not transfer of a provider's authentication state.

Before release, compare rendered messages with their approved wording, submit the corresponding form reasons, and inspect the resulting support destinations. Include an unresolved challenge, a successfully verified challenge, an unknown revision, and a rollback to the previous mapping. Unknown revisions belong in a review queue rather than a guessed business queue. That choice trades a visible manual review for a quiet misroute, which is usually the more defensible failure mode for a fintech support workflow.

The acceptance record should distinguish three observations: message delivery, successful code verification, and correct form routing. Collapsing them into one green “notification succeeded” counter makes a migration look healthy while hiding the very regression the approval process exists to catch.

Make the release gate executable

The following Go program combines contract inspection with a runnable policy example for the support boundary of a Node.js service. Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with Go. It retrieves the SMS transport discovery schema and sends no SMS; the provider adapter supplies the verification result separately. Discovery is public, so authentication is optional there; the example uses an environment-based Bearer header to demonstrate credential handling. Every routing field below belongs to the application. The fixture checks both the old and new provider mappings against the same approved routing policy, then refuses an unapproved template revision.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 2 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                delay = wait
            }
        } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
            if wait := time.Until(date); wait > delay {
                delay = wait
            }
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-timer.C:
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

type Revision struct {
    Approved bool
    LoginQueue string
    TicketQueue string
}

type Contact struct {
    Revision string
    Provider string
    Reason string
    Verified bool
}

func destination(c Contact, revisions map[string]Revision) string {
    r, ok := revisions[c.Revision]
    if !ok || !r.Approved {
        return "template-review"
    }
    switch c.Reason {
    case "cannot-sign-in":
        return r.LoginQueue
    case "ticket-is-wrong":
        if c.Verified {
            return r.TicketQueue
        }
        return r.LoginQueue
    default:
        return "support-triage"
    }
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal("set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := inspect(ctx, key); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    revisions := map[string]Revision{
        "access-r7": {true, "account-access", "ticket-review"},
    }
    fixtures := []struct {
        Contact Contact
        Want string
    }{
        {Contact{"access-r7", "old", "cannot-sign-in", false}, "account-access"},
        {Contact{"access-r7", "new", "cannot-sign-in", false}, "account-access"},
        {Contact{"access-r7", "old", "ticket-is-wrong", true}, "ticket-review"},
        {Contact{"access-r7", "new", "ticket-is-wrong", true}, "ticket-review"},
        {Contact{"access-r7", "new", "ticket-is-wrong", false}, "account-access"},
        {Contact{"access-r8", "new", "ticket-is-wrong", true}, "template-review"},
    }
    for i, f := range fixtures {
        got := destination(f.Contact, revisions)
        if got != f.Want {
            log.Fatalf("fixture %d: got %q, want %q", i, got, f.Want)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s %s: %s\n", f.Contact.Provider, f.Contact.Revision, got)
    }
}

The provider field deliberately has no authority over destination selection. It remains available for investigation, while the approved business revision controls routing. This is the concrete replaceability contract: the same business inputs produce the same support destination before and after supplier replacement. It says nothing about transport compatibility or delivery performance.

The small program also has a deliberate limit. It verifies routing logic, not rendered messages, template approval at a supplier, or a full authentication lifecycle. Those acceptance checks remain release requirements; six passing fixtures cannot substitute for them.

Budget the overlap before buying the replacement

Capacity planning changes during migration because old challenges and new challenges coexist. Suppose, purely as a sizing exercise, 600 challenges need delivery observations and each is polled every 10 seconds: that creates roughly 60 status requests per second before retries or new sends. Halving the polling interval doubles that load. The numbers are assumptions, not a vendor quota or measured throughput.

Budget the overlap.

For Infrai, plan delivery and event observation through polling. Put geographic admission rules, per-country spend cutoffs, and anti-abuse throttling before challenge creation in the application, and give polling a bounded lifetime so abandoned login attempts do not leave permanent background work. Keep authentication-attempt limits separate from transport retries: a delayed response is not permission to issue another customer-visible code.

Define an SLO for time from contact-form submission to the correct queue, and track unknown-revision reviews separately. Delivery latency and verification completion deserve their own indicators. Choose targets from the support team's requirements and destination acceptance tests; an API description is not an uptime or latency measurement. On HTTP 429, use bounded exponential backoff, honor Retry-After, and stop at the caller's deadline. For write retries, retain the same operation identity and verify the selected capability's idempotency contract before enabling automatic replay.

The staffing decision belongs beside that request budget. Buying code generation and verification removes work from the authentication implementation, but template review, queue semantics, abuse policy, and the migration approval record still need named owners. An application-owned email-code fallback adds another authentication lifecycle to maintain. A multi-channel requirement should therefore be evaluated as a separate operating commitment rather than a checkbox attached to SMS.

Buy versus build follows the release obligations

The comparison below concerns responsibility, not a claim that one supplier delivers faster or supports every US/EU destination. Check destination eligibility and template controls directly before approving a rollout.

Option Buy Build or retain Appropriate decision boundary
Infrai managed SMS OTP Code generation and verification through plain REST; inspectable discovery schemas Approval ledger, provider mappings, polling, abuse rules, routing gate Try it when a small HTTP adapter and contract inspection make replacement review practical
Twilio Verify A dedicated verification product Business wording approval and routing acceptance; review its template contract Evaluate it when verification-specific requirements dominate the purchase
Vonage Verify A dedicated verification alternative The same business approval evidence, against a different provider contract Include it in a specialist comparison rather than assuming one verification API fits all template requirements
Amazon SNS plus application verification SMS transport Challenge generation, expiry, verification attempts, replay policy, and support approvals Choose this build when control of the entire challenge lifecycle justifies the on-call responsibility
Amazon SES for an email fallback Email transport rather than managed SMS verification Email-code lifecycle, approved wording, and fallback routing Evaluate separately when email recovery is required; it does not replace the SMS OTP purchase

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify are candidates for buying the verification lifecycle; Amazon SNS illustrates buying transport while retaining that lifecycle. Their contracts require separate acceptance work. A familiar cloud account is a weak reason to take ownership of security-sensitive challenge state, just as a general REST interface is a weak reason to ignore a specialist requirement.

The limitation of the Infrai fit is operational: delivery observation is a polling responsibility, and an email-code fallback is application-owned. If push-driven orchestration, SMTP relay, or voice, WhatsApp, or RCS is mandatory, evaluate a specialist contract that explicitly meets that requirement. Do not generalize a US/EU SMS acceptance result into an unrelated regional email compliance conclusion.

The release decision should be narrow: buy managed OTP for the beginner-friendly login path, retain authority over customer instructions, and approve a replacement only when the routing evidence survives rollback. A successful send is one observation. It is not release approval.

References

The verification specialists' documentation and the SMS transport documentation establish what is being purchased. NIST's authenticator guidance provides security context; none of these references establishes a measured delivery SLO for this application.

Sources

  • Twilio Verify
  • Vonage Verify
  • Amazon SNS SMS
  • Amazon SES
  • NIST authenticator guidance

If this release boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation index and inspect the selected capability's contract before approving the adapter.
