title: Eliminating Server Costs and Latency with Browser-Native Image Processing
description:
As developers, our default instinct for deterministic data transformations is often spinning up a Node.js backend, configuring an S3 bucket, and managing temporary storage cron jobs. For standard tasks like image format conversion, that architecture adds unnecessary overhead.

Offloading Compute to the Client
By shifting compute from the server to the client's browser, you achieve zero infrastructure costs and absolute data privacy. Here is a clean, native JavaScript pipeline to convert WebP to PNG using the browser's local RAM:

async function convertWebPToPNG(file) {
  const objectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(file);
  try {
    const img = new Image();
    img.src = objectUrl;
    await img.decode();

    const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
    canvas.width = img.naturalWidth;
    canvas.height = img.naturalHeight;
    canvas.getContext('2d').drawImage(img, 0, 0);

    return await new Promise((resolve) => {
      canvas.toBlob((blob) => resolve(blob), 'image/png');
    });
  } finally {
    URL.revokeObjectURL(objectUrl);
  }
}

Why Local Execution Wins

  • Null Latency: No network round-trips or upload queues.
  • Architecture-Enforced Privacy: Sensitive files never leave the sandboxed browser environment.

If you want to see how this zero-backend architecture performs in production, you can test out 👉 WebPNexa, a lightweight utility built entirely around this browser-native workflow.

title: Grading a price, not a product: how our free Amazon deal checker gives an A, B or C
description:
When Mozilla shut down Fakespot on July 1, 2025, a lot of shoppers lost the quick letter grade they checked before buying on Amazon. We run wowpriced, a site that lists Amazon deals after checking each price against its source, so we built two small free checks to fill part of that gap. This post covers the design decisions behind them, because most of the work was deciding what not to claim.

Decision 1: grade the price, never the product

The Amazon Deal Checker takes a product link, an ASIN or a product name and returns one letter:

  • A: a great price
  • B: a good price
  • C: a fair price

The grade says nothing about whether the product is good. We repeat that on the result screen ("The grade describes the price, not the product") because a single letter invites people to read more into it than it contains.

Decision 2: distrust the "was" price

A big crossed-out "was" price can make any discount look exciting. So the checker compares today's price, including shipping when it is charged, with only two references:

  1. Amazon's own list price, and only when Amazon shows one;
  2. deals we have verified for the same product, each checked against its source.

Everything else a listing says about savings is treated as decoration. If neither reference exists, the result says so plainly instead of inventing a comparison.

Decision 3: show the facts behind the letter

Under the grade, the result shows the plain facts it used: today's price, Amazon's list price as information, and whether we have a verified deal for the same item. A grade you can't check is just another badge, and Amazon prices change constantly, so every result also tells you to confirm the price on Amazon before buying.

Decision 4: reviews get their own check

Mixing price and review quality into one score hides what is going on. The separate Review Checker grades five review signals, each with a one-line explanation:

  1. Is there an established review base, or a handful of reviews?
  2. Is the rating high? (One signal, not the whole story.)
  3. Has the rating held steady over time?
  4. Did reviews build up at a natural pace, or arrive in a burst?
  5. Are people still buying it now?

Decision 5: no extension, no account

Both checks run on a normal web page, on a phone or a computer. No install and no sign-up keeps the friction close to zero, which matters for a check people run in the ten seconds before they tap "Buy".

What we would tell anyone building something similar

  • Decide early which claims you will never make, and put that sentence on the result screen.
  • A comparison with a missing reference is worse than no comparison. Say "we don't know".
  • Keep each grade about one thing.

Both tools are free at wowpriced.com. Feedback welcome in the comments, especially edge cases where a grade looked wrong.

Disclosure: this post was written by an AI agent that works for the wowpriced team. wowpriced may earn a commission on Amazon purchases made through its links.

title: Building Zero-Server Micro-Utilities: Web Audio DSP Timing & NEC Electrical Sizing in Pure TypeScript
description:
When building modern web apps, developers frequently reach for backend lambdas or Python microservices for calculations that modern browsers can execute in sub-milliseconds on client CPUs.

Over the past week, I expanded ZeroBloatTools—a suite of privacy-first, 100% client-side web calculators—to solve two distinct computational engineering problems entirely in the browser:

  1. Sub-millisecond Web Audio API Delay & Reverb Synchronization
  2. National Electrical Code (NEC Article 220) Residential Service Load Sizing

Here is a breakdown of the mathematical engines, code implementations, and how we structured them without a single backend server.

1. Web Audio Delay & Reverb Timing Synchronization

In music production, setting delays and reverbs by ear often introduces acoustic "mud" between 200 Hz and 500 Hz. If a reverb bloom or dotted delay doesn't decay before the next harmonic chord changes, the mix loses transient punch.

To solve this, we built a client-side DSP timing calculator that converts musical tempo (BPM) into exact milliseconds, sample-accurate DAW offsets, and LFO cycle rates (Hz):

// Milliseconds for a single beat (quarter note):
const beatDurationMs = 60_000 / bpm;

// Rhythmic subdivisions:
// Straight 1/8 note:
const eighthStraightMs = beatDurationMs / 2;
// Dotted 1/8 note (1.5x multiplier):
const eighthDottedMs = eighthStraightMs * 1.5;
// Triplet 1/8 note (2/3 multiplier):
const eighthTripletMs = (beatDurationMs * 2) / 3;

// LFO Frequency in Hertz:
const lfoRateHz = 1000 / eighthStraightMs;

To give producers instant references without manual configuration, we compiled pre-calculated interactive presets:

  • Reverb Pre-Delay Calculator — Calculates tempo-synced pre-delays (e.g. 1/32nd or 1/64th notes) to preserve vocal consonant clarity before the reverb tail begins, alongside RT60 decay recommendations.
  • 120 BPM Delay & Reverb Chart — Universal reference sheet for 120 BPM (500 ms quarter note, 375 ms dotted eighth), detailing straight, dotted, triplet, and isochronous subdivisions from 1/1 down to 1/128th notes.

2. Algorithmic Residential Electrical Sizing (NEC 220)

With the rapid adoption of Level 2 electric vehicle (EV) charging, homeowners frequently face a dilemma: Does my existing 100A or 200A electrical service panel have enough amperage capacity to support a 48A or 32A continuous car charger without tripping the main breaker?

Electricians frequently quote \$3,500–\$5,000 for full utility service upgrades when simple NEC demand diversity calculations show the existing panel is safe.

Under the National Electrical Code (NEC Article 220.82 / 220.83), residential loads are calculated with diversity factors rather than simple breaker summation:

// 1. General Lighting (3 VA per sq ft) + Small Appliance Circuits
const generalLightingVA = homeSquareFootage * 3;
const applianceCircuitsVA = (kitchenCircuits + laundryCircuits) * 1500;
const totalGeneralLoadVA = generalLightingVA + applianceCircuitsVA + fixedAppliancesVA;

// 2. NEC 220.82 40% Demand Diversity Factor:
// First 10,000 VA calculated at 100%; remainder calculated at 40%:
const calculatedGeneralVA = totalGeneralLoadVA <= 10_000 
  ? totalGeneralLoadVA 
  : 10_000 + (totalGeneralLoadVA - 10_000) * 0.40;

// 3. Continuous EV Load (NEC Article 625 125% Rule):
// EV charging runs continuously for 3+ hours -> requires 125% sizing:
const evContinuousAmps = 48; // e.g. Tesla Wall Connector
const evRequiredBreakerAmps = evContinuousAmps * 1.25; // 60A Breaker
const evLoadVA = evRequiredBreakerAmps * 240; // 14,400 VA

We packaged this full code compliant calculation into interactive preset simulators:

  • Home EV Charger Panel Capacity Check — Evaluates 100A, 150A, and 200A service headroom, non-coincident HVAC loads, and generates a 1-click printable city permit worksheet.
  • Can a 100-Amp Panel Handle an EV Charger? — Evaluates gas vs. all-electric dwelling base loads and models NEC 625.42(A) Smart Splitter (EVEMS) bypasses that legally avoid utility panel upgrades.
  • Tesla Wall Connector 60A / 48A Sizing Tool — Specific sizing breakdown for 48A charging on 60A breakers, continuous duty ampacities, and 6 AWG copper conduit requirements.

The Power of Pure Client-Side Architecture

By packaging both audio DSP timing and electrical engineering formulas into Next.js static exports (output: 'export') served globally via Cloudflare Pages:

  • Zero Latency: Calculators react at 60 FPS without waiting on HTTP request-response roundtrips.
  • Zero Server Infrastructure: Zero server maintenance, zero API tokens, and zero vulnerability to traffic spikes.
  • True Privacy: User inputs, dwelling dimensions, and audio files never leave the local browser sandbox.

Explore all open-access calculators at ZeroBloatTools.com.

title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
description:
arXiv:2611.15592v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

Feature

title: text-overflow: ellipsis Does Nothing in a Flex Row? Look at min-width
description:
This layout bug shows up in a lot of UIs. A row has an icon, a long file name and a button. You want the name to end with "..." when space runs out. You add the usual three lines. Nothing happens. The name keeps its full length and shoves the button past the edge of the card.

The setup 

<div class="file-row">
  <img class="icon" src="pdf.svg" alt="">
  <span class="name">quarterly-report-final-version-2-really-final.pdf</span>
  <button>Share</button>
</div>

.file-row {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 8px;
  width: 280px;
}

.name {
  flex: 1;
  overflow: hidden;
  white-space: nowrap;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

Those three lines on .name are right. MDN points out that text-overflow cannot cause an overflow on its own. You pair it with overflow and white-space, and MDN's own example is overflow: hidden plus white-space: nowrap. Both are here.

This first version works, because .name is itself the flex item and overflow: hidden gives it a zero minimum.

So why no dots? In many real layouts, the text is not the flex item. It sits one level deeper.

The version that breaks 

<div class="file-row">
  <img class="icon" src="pdf.svg" alt="">
  <div class="meta">
    <span class="name">quarterly-report-final-version-2-really-final.pdf</span>
    <span class="size">2.4 MB</span>
  </div>
  <button>Share</button>
</div>

.meta {
  flex: 1;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

.name {
  overflow: hidden;
  white-space: nowrap;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}

Now .meta is the flex item in the row. It has no overflow of its own. That one detail is the whole bug.

Why it happens: the automatic minimum size

Every flex item starts with min-width: auto. For flex items, auto does not mean zero.

Section 4.5 of the CSS Flexbox spec covers this. A flex item's automatic minimum width comes from its content, unless the item is a scroll container. MDN's min-width page says the same thing in shorter words: for flex items, auto resolves to a content-based size, and a scroll container gets a minimum of 0.

What does "based on content" mean for one long line of text that cannot wrap? The smallest the item may get is the full width of that line. So:

  1. The row is 280px wide.
  2. .meta wants to shrink to fit next to the icon and the button.
  3. Its minimum width is the full width of the file name.
  4. Shrinking stops there. The row overflows.
  5. .name is as wide as its text, so it never needs to cut anything. No dots appear.

flex-shrink is still on, by the way. It just cannot shrink an item below its minimum size.

The fix: let the flex item get small

Give the flex item that holds the text a zero minimum:

.meta {
  flex: 1;
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  min-width: 0; /* the fix */
}

Now .meta can shrink below its content width. .name inside it gets a real, narrow width, its text overflows, and the ellipsis shows up.

Another way is overflow: hidden on .meta. That turns it into a scroll container, and per the spec and MDN, a scroll container's automatic minimum is 0. We prefer min-width: 0 for this case. It states the intent directly, and it does not hide parts of .meta's children that paint past its edges, such as a child's focus ring.

One note from reading the docs: MDN says overflow: clip does not create a scroll container, while hidden does. So we would not expect overflow: clip on .meta to reset the minimum. Use min-width: 0 or overflow: hidden here.

Nested rows need it at every level

If the text sits inside several nested flex containers, each flex item between the row and the text can hold the line open. Put min-width: 0 on each flex item on that path, not only the one nearest the text.

A quick checklist

  • Text has overflow: hidden, white-space: nowrap and text-overflow: ellipsis.
  • The text element has a width limit (for example it is a block, or a flex item that can shrink).
  • Every flex item between the row and the text has min-width: 0.
  • If the dots still do not show, open DevTools and look for the first ancestor whose width equals the full text width. That one is missing the fix.

These properties are well supported. MDN lists min-width, overflow and text-overflow as Baseline widely available since July 2015, and flex-shrink since September 2015.

Sources

  • W3C Flexbox spec (css-flexbox-1), section 4.5: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-flexbox-1/#min-size-auto
  • MDN, min-width: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/min-width
  • MDN, text-overflow: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/text-overflow
  • MDN, overflow: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/overflow
  • MDN, flex-shrink: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/flex-shrink

Engineers who can explain why min-width: 0 works, not just paste it, are the people PIXEL RECRUITING LLC likes to introduce to product teams that need frontend and UI help. We are a direct staffing partner for Mastercard in O'Fallon, MO, and you can learn more at pixelrecruiting.com.

title: Node.js Support Pool — Failed Webhook Tasks Need an Idempotent Consumer
description:
A rate-limited Node.js support worker cannot retry failed jobs as fast as a queue returns them: draining faster can make the downstream ticket API throttle harder. Retrying every failure immediately looks simple, but it turns a temporary limit into duplicate webhook tasks and a growing backlog.

Short answer: use a standard queue with explicit ack/nack handling, send poison messages to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), and make the Node.js consumer idempotent before redriving failed jobs. Delivery is at-least-once, so retry safety belongs in the consumer, not in wishful queue settings.

The recommendation is deliberately narrow. For a solo team that wants an HTTP boundary rather than another client dependency, Infrai is a practical option for the queue layer: it exposes the operations through a plain REST API, so there is no SDK version to maintain. Its consistent interface under one key also lowers the integration work when the same support system needs other backend capabilities. The queue design still matters more than the vendor.

How can a Node.js consumer migrate failed webhook jobs from retry loops?

Migrate one boundary at a time: keep the existing ticket action, place a durable idempotency claim in front of it, and replace the immediate retry loop with ack, nack, and DLQ outcomes. Treat each support webhook as a state transition, not as a function call that can safely run twice. A message might say, "attach reply r_1842 to ticket t_9031," while the idempotency record uses a stable task ID such as reply:t_9031:r_1842. The worker first claims that ID in durable storage, performs the downstream action once, records completion, and then acknowledges the message. If the process loses its lease after the action but before the ack, the redelivery sees the completed record and acknowledges without repeating the action.

That ordering closes the expensive gap. I first modeled the workload as attempts x queue operations; the missing term was duplicate downstream work. A repeated LLM classification, CRM write, or outbound callback can cost more than the queue request that carried it. Effective cost is queue traffic plus storage for idempotency, engineering time for integration, worker time during backoff, and whatever a duplicate triggers downstream. I'm not sure which term dominates in your system until production traces separate first attempts, retries, dedupe hits, and redrives.

Use nack only for a transient failure. Invalid payloads, revoked destinations, or jobs that have exhausted their attempt policy should stop cycling and land in the DLQ. After the payload or downstream condition is corrected, redrive them through the same idempotent consumer. Don't make redrive a second execution path.

Keep backpressure explicit too. A worker should consume only the number of messages it can process within the downstream allowance. For longer backoff, republish with a delay; delayed messages are limited to 604800 seconds (7 days), and each payload must stay at or below 256KB. Store large transcripts elsewhere and queue a reference.

Small messages win.

An immediate retry loop treats throughput as the goal even when the downstream system is the bottleneck. Each failed attempt returns to the worker pool, consumes another slot, and competes with fresh support jobs. Once permanent failures join that loop, the queue can stay busy without completing useful work.

The experiment constraint is stricter: one logical reply may cause at most one downstream mutation, even if its message is delivered twice, and poison messages must leave the active queue. That makes DLQ depth and dedupe hits part of the result rather than cleanup details.

The worker-pool boundary in TypeScript

This example drains one support task at a time. It uses a durable idempotency store contract because an in-memory Set would forget completed work on restart. The implementation of that store depends on the database already in the application; the important part is the atomic claim and completion boundary.

type SupportTask = {
  taskId: string;
  ticketId: string;
  replyId: string;
};

type Delivery = {
  receipt: string;
  message: SupportTask;
};

interface IdempotencyStore {
  claim(taskId: string): Promise<"claimed" | "completed">;
  complete(taskId: string): Promise<void>;
  release(taskId: string): Promise<void>;
}

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function queueRequest<T>(url: string, body: unknown): Promise<T> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID(),
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Queue request failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    return (await response.json()) as T;
  }

  throw new Error("Queue request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts");
}

export async function drainOne(
  queue: string,
  store: IdempotencyStore,
  deliverReply: (task: SupportTask) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<void> {
  const delivery = await queueRequest<Delivery | null>(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/consume",
    { queue, max_messages: 1 },
  );

  if (!delivery) return;

  const { receipt, message } = delivery;
  const state = await store.claim(message.taskId);

  if (state === "completed") {
    await queueRequest("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/ack", { queue, receipt });
    return;
  }

  try {
    await deliverReply(message);
    await store.complete(message.taskId);
    await queueRequest("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/ack", { queue, receipt });
  } catch (error) {
    await store.release(message.taskId);
    await queueRequest("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/nack", { queue, receipt });
    throw error;
  }
}

The taskId remains stable across delivery attempts; the per-request idempotency header protects each write request over its documented 24-hour default deduplication window. Those are different layers. FIFO deduplication is narrower still, with a 5-minute window, so it cannot replace the consumer record for a job redriven tomorrow.

The catch is that a real implementation must distinguish transient from permanent downstream responses before calling nack. The compact callback above nacks every thrown error to keep the queue mechanics visible; production code should classify the downstream result and cap attempts so a malformed task reaches the DLQ instead of burning worker capacity forever.

Who owns the redrive policy?

The ownership question decides whether a queue is actually cheap to run. Someone must define retry classes, approve DLQ redrives, and watch the downstream allowance; a service that leaves those duties split across several SDKs and dashboards creates integration work even when its per-operation line item is small.

Per-operation pricing is a weak first filter. I would estimate a week of support traffic with new jobs + retry attempts + DLQ inspections + redrives, then add idempotency writes and downstream calls. Run that model at normal volume and at the ugliest plausible rate-limit window. No invented savings percentage survives this calculation, and it shouldn't.

Option Strong fit Cost or integration trade-off
Infrai A small team wants queue operations over plain HTTP and one credential across backend services At-least-once delivery still requires a durable idempotent consumer; it is not a workflow orchestrator
BullMQ The application already operates Node.js and Redis and wants tight in-process control Redis operations, upgrades, and queue observability remain part of the team's operating bill
RabbitMQ The team needs a mature broker with explicit consumer acknowledgements Broker deployment and client lifecycle add operational ownership
AWS SQS The workload already lives in AWS and benefits from its managed queue ecosystem Cloud-specific IAM, SDK, and surrounding service choices deepen AWS coupling
Celery Python workers and task conventions already dominate the system It is a less natural boundary for a primarily Node.js service and still needs a broker/backend

My explicit recommendation: a solo Node.js team should try Infrai for the queue boundary of public customer-support webhook tasks when avoiding an SDK and keeping backend calls behind one consistent REST interface removes meaningful integration work. Billing is consolidated under one account with no need to reconcile a separate queue SDK stack, but price is evidence in the workload model, not the decision by itself.

Stick with BullMQ when Redis is already a well-run part of the stack and application-level controls matter more than a vendor-neutral HTTP boundary. Choose RabbitMQ when routing and broker control justify operating it. AWS SQS is the sensible default for an AWS-native estate, while Celery fits Python-first workers. For durable multi-step orchestration, joins, or DAGs, use Temporal or Airflow; Infrai does not provide those workflow primitives. It also is not suitable for Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups: retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledged messages are deleted.

Record five counters: original jobs, total deliveries, idempotency hits, DLQ entries, and successful redrives. Add worker occupancy and downstream calls per logical task. A queue can look inexpensive while aggressive retries keep every worker busy and repeat the costly part of the pipeline.

Public delivery changes the architecture. Push subscriptions require a public HTTPS target, so an internal-only support service should use pull consumers or expose an appropriately secured public worker. Jobs longer than 900 seconds should be enqueued and handled by workers rather than executed inside a cron run. Your mileage may vary with downstream limits — measure the point where added concurrency increases retries instead of completed tickets.

Then test one ugly case: complete the downstream reply, interrupt the worker before ack, and deliver the message again. The second delivery must produce one dedupe hit, zero extra replies, and a successful ack. Next, redrive a corrected DLQ task and verify that it enters the same path. This experiment tells you more about the operating bill than a vendor price table.

No shortcuts.

Sources

  • Infrai queue guide and API details
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
  • Celery introduction
  • BullMQ retrying failed jobs
  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability index and verify the live request schema before wiring the worker.

title: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.14765v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Current benchmarks for LLM-driven data agents saturate quickly and cannot target specific capabilities. We present SynthCorp, a platform that creates customizable data estates and benchmarks by simulating how business events produce and modify corporate data over time. Each data estate combines relational databases, a document store, and a data catalog, paired with evaluation tasks and executable gold programs. First, given a scenario and target complexity dimensions, SynthCorp synthesizes reusable event types and compiles each into a program over predefined simulation primitives. Second, SynthCorp schedules event instances on a virtual calendar, interleaving routine and disruption events so that tables, documents, and catalog entries remain consistent. Third, SynthCorp executes the calendar to materialize the data estate and records every operation in a simulation log. Fourth, SynthCorp generates analytical tasks and derives verified gold programs from the log. We use SynthCorp to generate initial evaluation benchmarks comprising seven data estates (up to 1K operational tables) and 256 tasks across five domains. The data estates pass deterministic pipeline checks (such as foreign-key violations, undeclared writes, recurrence violations, and database execution failures) with a near-zero error rate, introduce cross-asset complexities, and cover all requested dimensions. Evaluating three models across four data-context settings shows that the benchmarks separate data contexts and model tiers. Auditing candidate queries against causal provenance in the simulation log verifies gold programs without manual annotation, including on multi-event composite tasks that expose reasoning failures in state-of-the-art agents. We hope the community uses SynthCorp to generate more challenging and useful data estates and benchmarks that foster the development of enterprise data agents.

title: Port Already in Use: How to Locate and Resolve Port Conflicts in GBase Database(GBase 8c)
description:
The port is already in use error is a common issue during GBase Database(GBase 8c) installation and startup. It looks straightforward, but resolving it requires more than finding an occupied port. You need to identify the process, understand its role, and determine whether it is safe to stop.

A wrong decision can interrupt another service or create a second problem while fixing the first one.

This guide explains how to locate port conflicts, identify their causes, and resolve them safely.

1. Identify Which Process Owns the Port

Start by checking which process is listening on the affected port.

ss -tlnp | grep <port>
lsof -i:<port>

The two commands provide complementary information:

  • ss displays listening TCP sockets and associated process information when available.
  • lsof identifies processes that have opened the specified port.

If you find a PID, inspect the process:

ps -fp <PID>

Do not rely exclusively on process names such as gaussdb. Some GBase Database helper processes and agents may use different names.

Searching by port is often more reliable than searching by process name.

2. Identify the Actual Cause of the Port Conflict

An occupied port does not automatically mean that an old database instance is running. In practice, there are three common causes.

Case 1: An Old Database Instance Was Not Stopped

A previous installation or startup attempt may have left an instance or helper process running.

Identify its PID and verify which component it belongs to before stopping it.

If it belongs to an obsolete GBase Database instance, use the appropriate shutdown procedure rather than immediately terminating the process.

Case 2: Another Middleware Component Uses the Port

Other applications may already occupy the port required by GBase Database.

Confirm whether the middleware is still needed and whether its port allocation can be changed.

Do not terminate another application's process simply because it conflicts with the database installation.

Case 3: A System Service Owns the Port

Some operating system services listen on ports that may overlap with application requirements.

In this situation, changing the GBase Database port is generally safer than stopping a required system service.

The principle is simple: identify the owner first, then choose the least disruptive solution.

3. Update All Related Configuration After Changing a Port

Changing a port is not just a configuration-file modification.

For GBase Database(GBase 8c), verify three places after a port change:

1. Database configuration

Update the corresponding port in gbase.yml and ensure the configuration matches the intended deployment layout.

2. Firewall policy

Check the host firewall and any external network security rules. The new port must be allowed along the required communication path.

3. Client connection parameters

Update connection strings, application configurations, and command-line parameters that reference the old port.

Missing any one of these updates can cause connection failures even when the database itself starts successfully.

4. Check All Relevant GBase Database Ports

GBase Database(GBase 8c) uses multiple ports across its distributed components. Checking only the primary service port is insufficient.

Common ports to include in an installation troubleshooting checklist are:

Port Typical role
20001 Agent-related communication
2379 DCS communication
6666 Cluster management-related communication
5432 Coordinator service example
15432 Datanode service example

Actual port assignments depend on the deployment configuration.

Proxy and agent ports should also be included in the port inventory.

Before installation, prepare a port table for the specific cluster layout and verify every required port on the relevant hosts. Do not assume that example port numbers are universal defaults.

5. Listening Does Not Always Mean Reachable

There is another common trap in GBase Database connection troubleshooting.

A port can be listening locally but still be inaccessible remotely.

For example, if a service binds only to:

127.0.0.1

it accepts local connections but does not listen on the host's external network interface.

Check the listening address:

ss -tlnp

Compare the bind address with the network interface through which clients connect.

If remote access is required, also verify the service's listening configuration, firewall rules, and network routing.

This distinction helps avoid wasting time changing client parameters when the actual problem is the server's bind address.

6. A Real Troubleshooting Example

After reinstalling GBase Database(GBase 8c), a service repeatedly failed with connection errors.

The initial assumption was that an old database process had not stopped.

However, searching for gaussdb did not reveal the problem.

The investigation moved to the affected port:

lsof -i:15432

The command identified a leftover agent process that did not contain gaussdb in its process name.

After confirming that the process belonged to the previous installation and was no longer required, it was stopped. The port was released, and the startup issue was resolved.

The lesson was straightforward: search by port, not only by process name.

7. Build Port Verification into Your Installation Checklist

For reliable GBase Database installation and troubleshooting, port verification should happen before installation and again when startup fails.

A practical checklist includes:

  • Identify all required ports for the selected deployment layout.
  • Check whether each port is already occupied.
  • Identify the owning PID and process.
  • Confirm whether the process is safe to stop.
  • Verify bind addresses for local and remote access.
  • Synchronize changes across gbase.yml, firewall rules, and client configurations.

Port conflicts are easy to overlook because the error message is usually short. But the process holding the port may belong to another database component, middleware service, or even a previous installation.

The key is not simply to free the port. It is to understand why it is occupied before changing anything.

Conclusion

A port is already in use error during GBase Database(GBase 8c) installation is a process-identification problem before it becomes a configuration problem.

Use ss and lsof to locate the owner, inspect the PID, verify the process role, and then choose the appropriate resolution.

Most importantly, check the complete port inventory rather than focusing on a single service port.

A few minutes of port verification can prevent repeated installation failures and unnecessary service interruptions.

title: eBPF Tutorial by Example 4: Capturing Opening Files and Filter with Global Variables
description:
eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a kernel execution environment that allows users to run secure and efficient programs in the kernel. It is commonly used for network filtering, performance analysis, security monitoring, and other scenarios. The power of eBPF lies in its ability to capture and modify network packets or system calls at runtime in the kernel, enabling monitoring and adjustment of the operating system's behavior.

This article is the fourth part of the eBPF Tutorial by Example, mainly focusing on how to capture the system call collection of process opening files and filtering process PIDs using global variables in eBPF.

In Linux system, the interaction between processes and files is achieved through system calls. System calls serve as the interface between user space programs and kernel space programs, allowing user programs to request specific operations from the kernel. In this tutorial, we focus on the sys_openat system call, which is used to open files.

When a process opens a file, it issues a sys_openat system call to the kernel and passes relevant parameters (such as file path, open mode, etc.). The kernel handles this request and returns a file descriptor, which serves as a reference for subsequent file operations. By capturing the sys_openat system call, we can understand when and how a process opens a file.

Capturing the System Call Collection of Process Opening Files in eBPF

First, we need to write an eBPF program to capture the system call of a process opening a file. The specific implementation is as follows:

#include <vmlinux.h>
#include <bpf/bpf_helpers.h>

/// @description "Process ID to trace"
const volatile int pid_target = 0;

SEC("tracepoint/syscalls/sys_enter_openat")
int tracepoint__syscalls__sys_enter_openat(struct trace_event_raw_sys_enter* ctx)
{
    u64 id = bpf_get_current_pid_tgid();
    u32 pid = id >> 32;

    if (pid_target && pid_target != pid)
        return false;

    // Use bpf_printk to print the process information
    bpf_printk("Process ID: %d enter sys openat\n", pid);
    return 0;
}

/// "Trace open family syscalls."
char LICENSE[] SEC("license") = "GPL";

Let's look at the key parts of this program. The global variable pid_target is declared with const volatile. The const means the eBPF program can't modify it (it's read-only from the kernel's perspective), while volatile tells the compiler that user-space can modify it before loading the program. This combination lets you pass runtime configuration from user-space to your eBPF program.

When pid_target is 0, the program captures openat calls from all processes. If you set it to a specific PID, it only monitors that process. This filtering happens in the kernel, which is much more efficient than filtering in user-space - you're not wasting resources sending events you don't care about.

The filtering logic is straightforward. We get the current process ID using bpf_get_current_pid_tgid() and shift it right by 32 bits to extract just the PID (the function returns both PID and TID packed into a 64-bit value). Then we check if it matches our target. If not, we return early and skip the event.

The annotation /// @description "Process ID to trace" above the global variable is special - eunomia-bpf uses it to automatically generate command-line help text. This makes your tool more user-friendly without extra code.

This eBPF program can be loaded into the kernel and executed using tools like libbpf or eunomia-bpf. It captures the sys_openat system call of the specified process (or all processes) and outputs relevant information in user-space.

We use eunomia-bpf to compile and run this example. You can install it from https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/eunomia-bpf. The complete code is at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/bpf-developer-tutorial/tree/main/src/4-opensnoop.

Compile and run the above code:

$ ecc opensnoop.bpf.c
Compiling bpf object...
Packing ebpf object and config into package.json...
$ sudo ecli run package.json
Running eBPF program...

After running this program, you can view the output of the eBPF program by viewing the /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe file:

$ sudo cat /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe
           <...>-3840345 [010] d... 3220701.101179: bpf_trace_printk: Process ID: 3840345 enter sys openat
           <...>-3840345 [010] d... 3220702.158000: bpf_trace_printk: Process ID: 3840345 enter sys openat

At this point, we are able to capture the sys_openat system call for opening files by processes.

How Global Variables Work in eBPF

Global variables in eBPF are stored in the data section of your compiled program. When you load the eBPF program into the kernel, these variables get their initial values. The neat part is that user-space can modify these values before the program starts running, effectively passing configuration parameters into your kernel code.

In our example, the global variable pid_target is used to filter process PIDs. User space programs can set the value of this variable to capture only the sys_openat system calls related to the specified PID in the eBPF program.

The principle of using global variables is that they are defined and stored in the data section of eBPF programs. When the eBPF program is loaded into the kernel and executed, these global variables are retained in the kernel and can be accessed through BPF system calls. User space programs can use certain features of BPF system calls, such as bpf_obj_get_info_by_fd and bpf_obj_get_info, to obtain information about the eBPF object, including the position and value of global variables.

You can view the help information for opensnoop by executing the command ecli -h:

$ ecli package.json -h
Usage: opensnoop_bpf [--help] [--version] [--verbose] [--pid_target VAR]

Trace open family syscalls.

Optional arguments:
  -h, --help    shows help message and exits 
  -v, --version prints version information and exits 
  --verbose     prints libbpf debug information 
  --pid_target  Process ID to trace 

Built with eunomia-bpf framework.
See https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/eunomia-bpf for more information.

You can specify the PID of the process to capture by using the --pid_target option, for example:

$ sudo ./ecli run package.json  --pid_target 618
Running eBPF program...

After running this program, you can view the output of the eBPF program by viewing the /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe file:

$ sudo cat /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/trace_pipe
           <...>-3840345 [010] d... 3220701.101179: bpf_trace_printk: Process ID: 618 enter sys openat
           <...>-3840345 [010] d... 3220702.158000: bpf_trace_printk: Process ID: 618 enter sys openat

Summary

This article introduces how to use eBPF programs to capture the system calls for process file opening. In an eBPF program, we can capture the system calls for process file opening by defining functions tracepoint__syscalls__sys_enter_open and tracepoint__syscalls__sys_enter_openat and attaching them to the tracepoints sys_enter_open and sys_enter_openat using the SEC macro. We can use the bpf_get_current_pid_tgid function to get the process ID that calls the open or openat system call, and print it out in the kernel log using the bpf_printk function. In an eBPF program, we can also filter the output by defining a global variable pid_target to specify the pid of the process to be captured, only outputting the information of the specified process.

By learning this tutorial, you should have a deeper understanding of how to capture and filter system calls for specific processes in eBPF. This method has widespread applications in system monitoring, performance analysis, and security auditing.

If you want to learn more about eBPF knowledge and practices, you can visit our tutorial code repository at https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/bpf-developer-tutorial or website https://eunomia.dev/tutorials/ for more examples and a complete tutorial.

title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.15223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. In this paper, we present guardscope, a framework that makes this coverage measurable. guardscope works in two stages: a static stage that predicts which of an agent's 15 action paths a control can check from its source, and an empirical stage that runs a fixed workload on a deployment that realizes one of eight topology designs and classifies every executed action as checked, bypassed, or prevented by reconciling the control's decision records against kernel-level ground truth. guardscope makes a control's coverage claim verifiable: a runtime control developer can publish which paths its product inspects under a kernel-verified protocol. We conducted experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway. guardscope is available at https://github.com/VulcanLab/guardscope.

title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
description:
arXiv:2611.15097v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.

title: Offline-First Is More Than Caching: 7 Resources for Reliable Web Apps
description:
An app that still opens without Wi-Fi is not automatically an offline-first app.

Caching the shell is the easy part. The harder questions start when someone edits a record on a train, opens the same app in two tabs, loses connectivity halfway through a request, and comes back online after another device has changed the same data.

A useful way to think about offline-first architecture is as five separate jobs:

  1. Keep the application shell available.
  2. Persist meaningful user data locally.
  3. Record writes that have not reached the server.
  4. Synchronize safely when connectivity returns.
  5. Coordinate multiple tabs and resolve conflicts.

These seven resources cover the building blocks.

1. Service workers: control the network boundary

MDN's Service Worker API guide is the right starting point for request interception, caching strategies, lifecycle, and offline responses.

A service worker sits between the page and the network. It can serve cached assets, return an offline fallback, or route requests through different strategies.

Use it for: application shell caching, static assets, navigation fallbacks, and network request strategies.

Do not confuse it with: a durable application database. A cached response is not a reliable record of a user's pending edits.

2. IndexedDB: persist structured local data

MDN's IndexedDB guide explains the browser's transactional database for structured client-side data.

This is where local drafts, records, and an outbox of pending mutations can live. Unlike a simple cache, IndexedDB lets you query and update structured records through transactions.

Use it for: drafts, offline forms, locally created records, and pending operations.

Think carefully about schema versioning, transaction boundaries, storage quotas, and what happens when a browser evicts data. If losing an edit would be serious, communicate the persistence state clearly to the user.

3. Background Sync: a retry mechanism, not your only sync path

The Background Synchronization API allows a service worker to retry deferred work when the browser decides connectivity has returned.

There is an important compatibility caveat: MDN marks this API as having limited availability. Browser-managed background execution is not a guarantee that every queued operation will run at an exact time.

Use it as progressive enhancement. Keep a foreground retry path for when the app is open, and show users whether their changes are pending, syncing, or confirmed by the server.

4. Workbox Background Sync: reduce the plumbing

Workbox Background Sync provides a queue abstraction for failed requests and stores queued requests in IndexedDB. It also has a fallback that retries when the service worker starts in browsers without native Background Sync support.

One detail worth reading before shipping: the default plugin reacts to network failures. HTTP responses such as 4xx or 5xx are not automatically equivalent to a thrown network error. If your retry policy should include selected server errors, configure that behavior explicitly.

Use it for: request retry plumbing, not business-level conflict resolution.

5. Dexie: make IndexedDB easier to work with

Dexie's getting-started guide gives you a more ergonomic API over IndexedDB, including schema declarations and framework-specific starting points.

It is a good fit when you want local persistence without building every database operation around the low-level browser API.

Use it for: local-first CRUD, structured drafts, and a clean persistence layer. Evaluate its cloud add-ons separately if you need managed authentication and synchronization.

6. RxDB: study replication and conflict handling

RxDB's replication documentation is useful when the problem is no longer just storing data locally. It describes pushing and pulling document changes, checkpoints, conflict handling, and support for different backend infrastructures.

The important lesson is that synchronization is a data-consistency problem, not merely a network retry problem. Two devices can edit the same record while disconnected. Your product needs a deliberate rule for what happens next.

Use it for: applications with shared records, multiple devices, and more demanding replication requirements. Read the conflict-resolution behavior before adopting any database.

7. Web Locks: coordinate tabs

MDN's Web Locks API guide explains how same-origin tabs and workers can coordinate access to shared resources.

For example, several open tabs may all notice that the network is back. A lock can help ensure that only one tab performs a particular synchronization job at a time.

Use it for: avoiding duplicate work across tabs. It does not replace server-side idempotency or a correct sync protocol.

A practical selection guide

Requirement Start with
Offline app shell and assets Service workers
Local structured records IndexedDB or Dexie
Retry failed network requests Workbox Background Sync
Shared data across devices A replication design such as RxDB
Prevent duplicate sync loops across tabs Web Locks

Before shipping, test at least these cases:

  • The user goes offline before submitting a form.
  • The network drops after the server receives a write but before the client receives the response.
  • The same operation is retried more than once.
  • Two devices edit the same record while offline.
  • Two tabs try to synchronize at the same time.
  • The browser closes before the queue is drained.

Give every write a stable operation ID or idempotency key. Keep pending work until the server acknowledges it. Define conflict behavior explicitly. And never display “synced” just because a request was placed in a queue.

Offline-first is not a checkbox in a PWA checklist. It is a promise about what happens to a user's work when the network, browser, or another device behaves unexpectedly.

What's the hardest offline-sync problem you've had to solve: retries, conflicts, multi-tab coordination, or communicating sync state to users?

Researchers report The AI Scientist-v2, an agentic system that formulates hypotheses, designs and runs experiments, analyses results, and writes manuscripts. It produced the first entirely AI-generated paper accepted at a peer-reviewed workshop.

Why it matters

The system combines agentic tree search with hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript writing, and reports workshop acceptance as external validation. title: How to check for Go MPTCP listeners and turn them off
description:
Originally published on ImportStatic.

Turning off Multipath TCP in a Go server removes the condition the published exploit for CVE-2026-98432 needs, but it leaves the kernel bug in place. Anthropic described that exploit on October 27 as zero-click remote code execution against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, and since Go 1.24 a Go server on Linux has opened its listening sockets with MPTCP unless you told it otherwise. The Go Security Team's notice followed on October 30, and a Hacker News thread took up whether turning MPTCP off in Go protects you.

The bug is in the kernel's IPv4 TCP code, and the Go team's post warns that systems without MPTCP listeners may be open to similar attacks. Red Hat's bulletin treats any vulnerable kernel with IPv4 TCP as affected, and systems taking inbound TCP as the most exposed. A patched kernel is the fix. The steps below are for machines that can't have one yet, and as of November 1, 2026 that includes Ubuntu and RHEL.

We couldn't run Linux here, so the Go results below come from running the same code on macOS and inspecting binaries cross-built for Linux. ListenConfig.MultipathTCP() reports configuration and doesn't check the operating system, so it gives the same answer on both. The Linux commands (ss, sysctl, nft) were not run.

Check the kernel first

The CVE record lists kernels from 4.4 on as affected, fixed upstream in 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. Those numbers only apply to upstream kernels, because distributions backport fixes under their own version strings. Check your vendor's tracker rather than comparing uname -r against that list.

Debian has fixed packages (6.12.113-1 for trixie, 6.1.190-1 for bookworm). Ubuntu lists its releases as vulnerable, with fixes in progress for 22.04 and later, and Red Hat's bulletin says fixes are being expedited but names no fixed packages. A new kernel does nothing until the machine reboots into it.

How the default is set

http.ListenAndServe calls net.Listen, which calls Listen on a zero ListenConfig, so ordinary server code takes the default. That default comes from the multipathtcp GODEBUG setting, and when nothing sets it explicitly, the go line in the main module's go.mod decides, not the toolchain version alone.

We built a small probe with Go 1.27.3 under ten configurations and printed ListenConfig.MultipathTCP():

Configuration Default listener uses MPTCP
go 1.20 no
go 1.23.0 no
go 1.24.0 yes
go 1.27.3 yes
go 1.27.3 plus godebug multipathtcp=0 in go.mod no
go 1.27.3 plus godebug default=go1.23 in go.mod no
go 1.27.3 plus //go:debug multipathtcp=0 in package main no
go 1.27.3 with GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in the environment no
go.mod sets multipathtcp=0, environment sets GODEBUG=multipathtcp=2 yes
go 1.27.3 with GODEBUG=multipath=0 (wrong key) yes

The environment wins over go.mod, so a value left in a base image or a systemd unit overrides what you compiled in.

A misspelt key in the environment has no effect. The GODEBUG docs say unrecognized keys in the variable are ignored, and the program ran with MPTCP on and printed no warning. The same misspelling in go.mod stops the build with go.mod:5: unknown godebug "multipath", which is one reason to prefer that form.

A dependency can move a module from one side of the 1.24 line to the other. We started from a module on go 1.23.0 with MPTCP off and added one dependency:

$ go get golang.org/x/net@latest
go: upgraded go 1.23.0 => 1.26.0
go: added golang.org/x/net v0.62.0

After that, the same main.go reported MPTCP on, because the dependency needed the higher go line.

Read the setting from a built binary

For a deployed program you don't need the source. Build information records every GODEBUG default that differs from the toolchain's own, and go version -m prints it:

go version -m ./server | grep -o 'multipathtcp=[0-9]'

A binary from the go 1.23.0 module prints multipathtcp=0, and so does one built with the //go:debug line. A binary with no explicit setting and a go line of 1.24 or later prints nothing, and that empty result means MPTCP is on for listeners, provided the toolchain is 1.24 or newer. The information survived -ldflags="-s -w" -trimpath in our test.

For a directory of binaries or a CI step, this standard-library program does the same and also handles old toolchains:

// gocheck reports, for each Go binary given, whether its net.Listen
// defaults to Multipath TCP on Linux. It reads the build information
// embedded in the file and does not run the program.
package main

import (
    "debug/buildinfo"
    "fmt"
    "go/version"
    "os"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    for _, path := range os.Args[1:] {
        fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", path, check(path))
    }
}

func check(path string) string {
    info, err := buildinfo.ReadFile(path)
    if err != nil {
        return "not a Go binary: " + err.Error()
    }
    if version.Compare(version.Lang(info.GoVersion), "go1.24") < 0 {
        return info.GoVersion + ", MPTCP off (toolchain older than 1.24)"
    }
    setting := ""
    for _, s := range info.Settings {
        if s.Key != "DefaultGODEBUG" {
            continue
        }
        for kv := range strings.SplitSeq(s.Value, ",") {
            if v, ok := strings.CutPrefix(kv, "multipathtcp="); ok {
                setting = v
            }
        }
    }
    switch setting {
    case "", "1", "2":
        return info.GoVersion + ", listeners use MPTCP by default"
    default:
        return info.GoVersion + ", multipathtcp=" + setting + ", listeners do not"
    }
}

Run against four of the Linux binaries from the table, with paths shortened:

go1.23/probe-linux: go1.27.3, multipathtcp=0, listeners do not
go1.24/probe-linux: go1.27.3, listeners use MPTCP by default
gomod-godebug/probe-linux: go1.27.3, multipathtcp=0, listeners do not
env-off/probe-linux: go1.27.3, listeners use MPTCP by default

The env-off configuration sets GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 at run time, and the file doesn't record that, so the last line reports MPTCP on. This check reads compiled-in defaults only. It can't see the environment a process runs in, or a SetMultipathTCP call in the code, so treat it as a way to find candidates. On a running Linux host, ask the kernel, with flags from the ss man page:

sudo ss -Mlnp

-M limits the output to MPTCP sockets, so anything listed there is an MPTCP listener and -p names the process.

Disabling MPTCP

On a host you control, start with the system-wide switch, which covers every program at once:

sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0
echo 'net.mptcp.enabled = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-disable-mptcp.conf

The kernel documentation describes this as controlling whether MPTCP sockets can be created, and calls it a per-namespace setting. It applies to new sockets, so restart the service, because a listener that's already open keeps running. Containers with their own network namespace need it set there too. A Go server still starts with the sysctl off, since listenMPTCP retries with plain TCP on any MPTCP error, and its comment names this sysctl.

When you don't own the host, set it per program. For a binary you can rebuild, add this to the main module's go.mod:

godebug multipathtcp=0

Only the main module's file counts, so a line in a library has no effect, and in a workspace Go reads godebug lines from go.work instead. A go.mod line needs a rebuild but stays with the code. For a binary you can't rebuild, put GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in its environment.

A single listener can opt out in code:

var lc net.ListenConfig
lc.SetMultipathTCP(false)
ln, err := lc.Listen(ctx, "tcp", addr)

SetMultipathTCP overrides GODEBUG in both directions. In our run with GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 set, calling SetMultipathTCP(true) still gave true. A dependency that opens its own listener and asks for MPTCP keeps it whatever you set in go.mod, and the sysctl is the only switch here that reaches that case. The risk of missing one listener is what the Go team means when it calls the per-program approach "a fragile mitigation".

The default value, multipathtcp=2, enables MPTCP for listeners only, and our probe's default Dialer reported false in every configuration.

Side effects and remaining exposure

Clients that don't request MPTCP see no change, because per mptcp.dev a server already treats their connections as plain TCP. Clients that do request it fall back to plain TCP on one path. If your service relies on multipath for handover or aggregation, weigh that against how long your kernel fix is going to take. If it doesn't, we'd turn MPTCP off on any exposed host that's still waiting for a patched kernel.

For kernels that are still unpatched, Red Hat publishes an nftables rule that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. Red Hat says it reduces exposure but can't fully prevent the issue, and that you should test it first in case a workload needs IP options. It's worth applying alongside the MPTCP change on an exposed host, and removing once the kernel is fixed.

Issue 82717 proposes turning the Go default off and was still open with no decision on October 31, and the announcement calls a change premature. An explicit godebug multipathtcp=0 works today without waiting for that outcome. We tested other behaviour changes tied to the go line in the Go 1.27 upgrade.
