title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: Feature Flags Service: Safe Notification Toggles and Rollback Explained
description:
Use a feature flag to return a failing notification service to its previous delivery path, and verify delivery outcomes before declaring the rollback complete. Changing a stored Boolean is only the start: workers must refresh their decisions, and notifications already in flight may still finish on the candidate path.

TL;DR: To build a simple feature flags service in Node.js, store flag states in an object or database and expose Express handlers for reading and toggling them. For a B2B SaaS notification service, keep false mapped to the previous delivery path, make control retries idempotent, and judge rollback success against delivery failures and the delivery SLO.

Protect the old path.

Infrai offers a unified API with a single key and a single bill: 295 routes across 20 modules use one REST API, without separate SDKs for each capability. This broad backend coverage through a simple interface is useful when flags are one part of a larger integration; its public, self-describing discovery API supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, helping review the next capability before wiring it into the application. The rollback acceptance test still decides suitability.

How should a feature flags service handle a toggle?

Start with one application flag, notification_delivery_v2, defaulting to false. True selects the candidate delivery behavior. Keep that interpretation stable across application versions; a rollback instruction becomes dangerous if different workers interpret the same Boolean differently.

The failure mode is an increase in notification delivery failures after enabling the candidate. Record the value actually used for each attempt, its outcome, the notification identifier, tenant identifier, and application version. These are proposed application log fields, not a provider's ingestion schema. Compare outcomes against attempted-delivery volume and inspect the mix of notifications in each cohort. A quieter queue can make the failure count drop even while the failure rate gets worse, and a flag read from the control service cannot tell you which path a worker actually used. Define the delivery SLI, measurement window, and error-budget condition before the release, then test that the outcome signal distinguishes the two paths. Do not invent a universal rollback percentage.

Count attempts first.

A flag affects future decisions. It cannot recall a message an external delivery provider has accepted or reverse an existing side effect. Delivery deduplication and control-request deduplication solve different problems.

Choose the operational boundary before buying

An object-backed Express service is a reasonable single-process starting point. Shared storage becomes relevant when instances must agree, but a database does not choose refresh intervals, authorize operators, or settle conflicting writes. The team owns those decisions.

The buy-versus-build table distinguishes evaluation priorities. Treat each acceptance test as a requirement to verify in the selected deployment and plan, rather than assuming every product supplies the same controls.

Option Useful evaluation priority Trade-off and rollback acceptance test
Build an Express service A small control surface with application-specific semantics. The team owns persistence, access control, and recovery; prove retry safety and restart behavior.
LaunchDarkly Evaluate a dedicated flag product for the release-control workflow. Confirm the worker refresh and operator disable workflow before accepting an external control dependency.
Unleash Make deployment ownership a central selection question. Confirm the selected deployment model and assign responsibility for recovery and capacity.
Flagsmith Review flag operations alongside application configuration. Verify environment and credential separation, including the migration work required by the chosen setup.

The control plane also needs an evidence plane. Sentry, Datadog, and Grafana are real candidates to evaluate here, alongside OpenTelemetry's log concepts; they should not be treated as interchangeable replacements for the flag store. For Sentry, make investigation of individual delivery failures the acceptance test. For Datadog, test whether the selected setup supports the delivery SLO workflow your operators need. For Grafana, test how the chosen data sources connect attempted-delivery volume to the release decision. These are distinct evaluation tasks, not promises about bundled features. Reject a setup that can show a configuration change but cannot explain its effect on deliveries.

Keep a separate release record.

For this workflow, use client polling and application decision logs. A stored flag value is not a change audit trail, evaluation statistics, or a dependency graph. Assign alerting and heartbeat monitoring separately, including the case where scheduled work never produces a delivery attempt. Log correlation identifiers also do not establish a distributed trace view. Avoid deleting a flag while either delivery path still needs it.

Implement a read boundary without guessing the response

In Node.js, an object can hold the initial state and Express can expose read and toggle handlers. Validate the flag name, authorize control access, and reject unknown keys. An atomic update must include both the state change and the record that deduplicates its operation identifier; putting those writes in separate steps creates an ambiguous retry window.

A blind toggle can undo itself.

For the managed alternative, the Go program below performs one read using the verified value route. Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain after setting INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_API_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS API origin, without a version suffix. The origin is deployment configuration, so no vendor URL is embedded in this article. The program prints the successful JSON response intact instead of inventing an envelope field. Use the published response schema when wiring the result into an Express handler.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    origin := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_ORIGIN"), "/")
    base, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || base.Scheme != "https" || base.Host == "" ||
        base.Path != "" || base.RawQuery != "" || base.Fragment != "" ||
        base.User != nil || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set the API key and an HTTPS API origin")
    }
    endpoint := origin + "/v1/flags/get_value/notification_delivery_v2"
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<uint(attempt))
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 45 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry scheduled beyond this run's deadline")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(date)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is a read-only diagnostic, so retrying it cannot toggle the flag. It uses an explicit method, bounded requests, response-status checks, and exponential backoff for HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. It deliberately does not provide a write payload whose schema has not been established.

For a toggle implementation, use one operation identifier for one intended change and reuse it on retries. Prefer an explicit desired state for rollback where the implementation supports it. If two operators can race, add conflict control rather than assuming a retry key establishes ordering. In-memory state is insufficient once restart survival or multiple instances matter; retain both state and deduplication history durably, and bound history retention.

Verify propagation before trusting the switch

Start with false and verify a read. Apply one authorized toggle with a new operation identifier, repeat the same operation, and confirm the second request does not reverse the first. Submit a distinct operation to return to false. Check unknown keys and unauthorized writes as well.

Then inspect a real worker decision.

In an isolated test, introduce a controlled delivery failure and confirm that attempt logs identify the selected path. Disable the candidate, allow workers to refresh, and verify that subsequent attempts select the previous behavior. Keep the test isolated from customer delivery effects.

Polling deserves a capacity estimate: 120 workers polling every 15 seconds generate about 8 reads per second on average, before retries and startup bursts. This is illustrative arithmetic, not a measured capacity claim. Add jitter so refreshes do not synchronize; shorter polling intervals improve refresh speed at the cost of more reads.

Budget for bursts.

The rollback deadline must account for refresh interval, cache behavior, request timeout, and in-flight attempt duration. Measure the combined effect in the actual deployment. A last-known value can protect continuity during a failed refresh but can preserve the candidate behavior longer; defaulting to the previous path can favor rollback speed but changes behavior during a control-plane interruption. Choose deliberately.

Disable the candidate, then verify delivery outcomes

During a suspected regression, read the current value and record the desired target. Serialize operator changes, preserve the operation identifier for retries, and read back the state if a control request times out. A fresh identifier for the same intended toggle can reverse a successful first operation.

Wait for worker evidence.

New attempts should select the previous path; older attempts may finish on the candidate. Compare failures and attempted-delivery volume against the same delivery SLO used before rollout. Investigate remaining candidate decisions for stale configuration. If there are no attempts at all, use the separate heartbeat signal to distinguish silence from healthy delivery.

Keep the previous code path and the release record until the incident is understood. A Boolean is a useful rollback control only while its interpretation, propagation, and effect remain inspectable.

References

  • OpenTelemetry logs concepts
  • Express routing
  • Go HTTP standard library
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • Flagsmith documentation
  • Sentry documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Grafana documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation

title: Build 'Find My Photos' for Event Galleries with Amazon Rekognition and Node.js
description:
After a wedding, a conference or a marathon, the photographer uploads three thousand photos and every guest asks the same question: which ones am I in? Scrolling through a gallery that size is miserable. Uploading one selfie and getting back only your photos is a feature people actually remember.

This tutorial builds that feature with Amazon Rekognition's face collections, S3 and a small Node.js service. By the end you will have three pieces: indexing every face in a gallery, searching that index with a selfie, and the cost and privacy decisions you need to make before shipping it.

You will need an AWS account, Node.js 18 or later, and the AWS SDK for JavaScript v3.

npm install @aws-sdk/client-rekognition @aws-sdk/client-s3

How Rekognition face search works

Rekognition does not store your photos. When you index an image, it detects each face, turns it into a face vector, and stores that vector in a collection along with an id you choose. Later, you send a new image and ask, "which stored faces match this one?" It returns matching face ids with a similarity score.

So the design is simple:

  1. One collection per event.
  2. Index every gallery photo into it, tagging each face with the photo's key.
  3. Search the collection with the guest's selfie and return the photo keys that matched.

Step 1: Create a collection per event 

import {
  RekognitionClient,
  CreateCollectionCommand,
} from "@aws-sdk/client-rekognition";

const rek = new RekognitionClient({ region: "ap-south-1" });

export async function createEventCollection(eventId) {
  await rek.send(new CreateCollectionCommand({
    CollectionId: `event-${eventId}`,
  }));
}

A collection per event keeps searches fast and accurate, because a guest's selfie is only compared against faces from that event. It also makes deletion clean: when the event's retention period ends, you delete one collection.

Step 2: Index the gallery

Photos live in S3, so Rekognition can read them directly without you downloading anything.

import { IndexFacesCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-rekognition";

export async function indexPhoto(eventId, bucket, key) {
  const res = await rek.send(new IndexFacesCommand({
    CollectionId: `event-${eventId}`,
    Image: { S3Object: { Bucket: bucket, Name: key } },
    ExternalImageId: key.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_.\-:]/g, "_"),
    MaxFaces: 15,
    QualityFilter: "AUTO",
    DetectionAttributes: [],
  }));

  return res.FaceRecords.length;
}

A few choices here matter:

  • ExternalImageId is how you get from a matched face back to a photo. It only accepts a restricted character set, so sanitize the S3 key, or store a short id and keep a lookup table in your database.
  • MaxFaces caps how many faces are indexed per photo. Group shots can contain dozens of tiny background faces that are useless for search and cost money to store. Rekognition keeps the largest faces first.
  • QualityFilter: "AUTO" skips faces that are too blurry, dark or small to match reliably. Leave it on.

For a gallery of thousands of photos, do not index them in a loop inside a web request. Trigger indexing from an S3 upload event (S3 to SQS to a worker, or straight to Lambda), and keep concurrency modest to stay inside your account's Rekognition transactions-per-second limit.

Step 3: Search with a selfie

The guest's selfie never needs to touch S3. Send the bytes directly:

import { SearchFacesByImageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-rekognition";

export async function findMyPhotos(eventId, selfieBuffer) {
  const res = await rek.send(new SearchFacesByImageCommand({
    CollectionId: `event-${eventId}`,
    Image: { Bytes: selfieBuffer },
    FaceMatchThreshold: 90,
    MaxFaces: 500,
  }));

  const keys = new Set(
    res.FaceMatches.map((m) => m.Face.ExternalImageId)
  );
  return [...keys];
}

SearchFacesByImage finds the largest face in the selfie and compares it against the collection. One person can appear in many photos, so expect many matches and de-duplicate by photo.

Choosing the threshold. FaceMatchThreshold is the minimum similarity to return. At 80 you will catch more photos but start showing guests their cousin. At 95 you will miss profile shots and photos taken in poor light. For event galleries, 90 is a good starting point. Tune it against a real event before launch: take ten volunteers, count the photos each one should get, and compare.

Step 4: Handle the edge cases users will hit on day one

  • No face in the selfie. Rekognition throws an InvalidParameterException. Catch it and ask for a clearer, front-facing photo instead of returning an empty gallery.
  • Several people in the selfie. Only the largest face is searched. Say so in the upload screen.
  • Sunglasses, masks, heavy makeup. Matching drops sharply. Telling guests "best results with a clear, front-facing selfie" saves support messages.
  • Children's faces change fast and match less reliably across ages, which matters for school events.

Step 5: Cost

Rekognition charges per image processed for IndexFaces and SearchFacesByImage, plus a small monthly fee per thousand face vectors stored. Check the current price for your region, then estimate with real numbers:

  • A 3,000-photo event costs 3,000 index calls once.
  • Each guest search costs 1 call. 400 guests searching twice is 800 calls.
  • Storage is charged on the number of faces stored, which is why MaxFaces and the quality filter keep the bill down.

The biggest avoidable cost is re-indexing. Store which photos you have indexed so a retry or a redeploy does not process the whole gallery again.

Step 6: Privacy is part of the feature

Face vectors are biometric data, and in many places, including under India's DPDP Act and the EU's GDPR, that comes with real obligations. Build these in from the start:

  • Consent. Tell guests clearly that their selfie is used only to find their photos, and get an explicit yes before upload.
  • Do not keep selfies. Search with the bytes and discard them. Never index a guest's selfie into the collection.
  • Retention. Delete the event's collection when the gallery expires: 
import { DeleteCollectionCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-rekognition";

await rek.send(new DeleteCollectionCommand({
  CollectionId: `event-${eventId}`,
}));
  • Opt-out. Let a guest remove their face from the index. Search with their selfie, then call DeleteFacesCommand with the matched face ids.

What you have built

An indexing pipeline that turns a gallery into a searchable face collection, a single endpoint that turns a selfie into a personal gallery, and the threshold, cost and privacy decisions that make it safe to ship. The whole feature is under 100 lines of application code. Most of the work is in the decisions around it, which is exactly where it should be.

title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
description:
arXiv:2611.15215v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

Announcement

Starting November 1, 2026, at 02:00 a.m. local time, unpatched Cloud SQL for MySQL instances that evaluate certain local Canadian time zones (across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories) will lag by one hour because the instances still follow the autumn fall back schedule. Stored timestamp data isn't modified.

What should I do?

Before November 1, 2026, do one of the following fixes:

  • Apply self-service maintenance (Recommended): If your applications rely on database functions to calculate, schedule, or display times in these Canadian time zones (such as Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver, or Winnipeg), then update your instances to the latest maintenance release using the Google Cloud console or the gcloud CLI.

    Updated time zone rules that reflect permanent standard daylight offsets across Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Northwest Territories are supported in Cloud SQL for MySQL maintenance release *.R20260726.00_36 or later.

    For more information, see Perform self-service maintenance.

  • Database configuration stopgap: If your organization can't restart instances before November 1, 2026, then you can set the time zone for your database session without causing downtime for your instance. Set the default_time_zone flag for the database session to your target fixed numeric offset (for example, '-06:00' for Alberta, '-07:00' for British Columbia, or '-05:00' for Manitoba).

    For more information about configuring database flags, see Configure database flags.

title: Scale Is Safe. Innovation Shouldn't Be.
description:
Last November, I saw a departure note from someone who'd spent 14 years at Microsoft. The reason wasn't salary or location. It was silence. The researcher said new ideas rarely made it past internal review, and cost‑cutting initiatives were dismissed rather than examined. The news came from a routine report by IT Home, but the detail stuck: John Langford, co‑founder of AI Frontiers, left because his team’s work on contextual bandits and offline policy evaluation felt adrift from any product path.
Langford’s group had been folded into Mustafa Suleyman’s broader AI division that September. The merger was supposed to align research with deployment. Instead, it highlighted a tension many of us feel: scaling models delivers predictable gains, while exploring alternatives demands patience and risk capital that budgets rarely allocate. Langford acknowledged that bigger models improve accuracy. He worried that treating size as the only lever crowds out genuinely different approaches.
I’ve seen this pattern elsewhere. When I led an internal hackathon, three teams proposed lightweight, interpretable models for a specific domain. Two were shelved because they didn’t promise a tenfold speedup. One shipped after six months of guerrilla prototyping. The winning metric was “used by nobody.” The losing ones sat in a shared drive, still cited internally. It wasn’t malice. It was alignment: investors and leadership reward trajectories they can forecast. Novelty doesn’t fit neatly into quarterly OKRs.
This isn’t an argument against scale. Scaling has delivered remarkable results. But it also creates a filter. Experiments that can’t demonstrate immediate ROI get deprioritized. Researchers who thrive on open‑ended problems find themselves writing grant proposals disguised as product tickets. The result is a quiet attrition of talent—not because people hate their companies, but because the feedback loop between curiosity and impact grows thin.
Langford’s departure mirrors a broader shift. Companies now treat AI research like feature development: ship fast, measure downstream metrics, iterate. There’s value in discipline. Yet when the bridge between basic insight and applied work erodes, the people best equipped to cross it walk away. They take methodological heuristics with them. They stop mentoring junior engineers who could have learned the trade‑off between depth and pragmatism on the job.
What should we do? One answer is to protect “blue‑sky” slots inside corporate labs—time where failure is allowed and success isn’t measured by revenue per engineer. Another is to celebrate small wins publicly, even when they don’t move the needle on benchmarks. A third, more uncomfortable option: let researchers leave without guilt, and build external networks that let knowledge circulate anyway.
I’m not advocating escape. I’m asking how we keep good ideas alive when the institution that spawns them cannot sustain them. If you’ve watched promising work gather dust, what kept you there? And when does staying become its own compromise?

title: Why a2ui's JSON-Driven Layout Schema Breaks Down in Production Modal Stacks
description:
The Promise: Agent-Streamed UI Without Manual DOM Wrangling

When evaluating a2ui-project/a2ui for a conversational dashboard rebuild, the pitch was clean: backend agents stream JSON layout descriptors, and the React adapter hydrates them into live components. No manual createElement chains, no brittle template strings. The repository ships adapters for React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—universal generative UI.

The reality hit during our first modal implementation. a2ui's layout schema handles flat component trees elegantly, but once you introduce nested modals with focus trapping and portal rendering, the abstraction starts bleeding through the seams.

The Failure Surface: Portal Boundaries and TailwindCSS Context Loss

Test Case: Agent-Driven Confirmation Dialog

Our agent streams this layout descriptor:

{
  "type": "modal",
  "id": "confirm-delete",
  "backdrop": true,
  "children": [
    {
      "type": "box",
      "className": "bg-white rounded-lg shadow-xl p-6 max-w-md",
      "children": [
        { "type": "text", "content": "Delete 47 items?" },
        {
          "type": "button",
          "variant": "danger",
          "label": "Confirm"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

The React adapter wraps this in a Radix Dialog.Root. Problem: TailwindCSS utility classes don't cascade into React portals unless you explicitly configure tailwind.config.js to scan portal roots. The modal renders, but bg-white and shadow-xl vanish—the dialog appears as unstyled gray blocks.

Hardening Configuration

Force Tailwind to scan portal containers:

// tailwind.config.js
module.exports = {
  content: [
    './src/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx}',
    './node_modules/@a2ui/react-adapter/**/*.js',
    // Critical: scan React portal mount points
    './public/index.html'
  ],
  theme: {
    extend: {}
  }
};

But now you've coupled your build pipeline to a2ui's internal DOM structure. When the adapter changes its portal strategy (observed between v0.8.3 and v0.9.1), styles break silently in production.

The Focus Trap Deadlock

Scenario: Nested Confirmation Flows

Agent streams a second modal ("Are you sure?") while the first is still open. a2ui's React adapter chains Dialog.Root components, but focus management collapses:

  1. User presses Tab inside the second modal.
  2. Focus escapes to the first modal's backdrop.
  3. Screen reader announces the wrong dialog title.
  4. Keyboard navigation enters a deadlock—Escape key dismisses both modals simultaneously.

Root cause: a2ui's layout schema has no explicit focus scope boundaries. The JSON descriptor treats modals as generic containers, delegating focus control entirely to the component library (Radix, in this case). When you nest portals, Radix's FocusScope gets confused by React's reconciliation order.

Manual Override

We patched the adapter to inject data-focus-scope attributes:

// Custom React adapter override
import { Dialog } from '@radix-ui/react-dialog';
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

function A2UIModal({ descriptor, children }) {
  const scopeRef = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (scopeRef.current) {
      scopeRef.current.focus();
    }
  }, []);

  return (
    <Dialog.Root open={true}>
      <Dialog.Portal>
        <Dialog.Overlay className="fixed inset-0 bg-black/50" />
        <Dialog.Content
          ref={scopeRef}
          data-focus-scope={descriptor.id}
          className="fixed top-1/2 left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2"
        >
          {children}
        </Dialog.Content>
      </Dialog.Portal>
    </Dialog.Root>
  );
}

This works, but now we're maintaining a fork of the adapter. Every upstream change requires manual merge conflict resolution.

Operational Trade-Off: Schema Rigidity vs. Escape Hatches

The core tension: a2ui's JSON schema optimizes for agent-side simplicity (LLMs generate clean, validated layouts), but sacrifices client-side flexibility. When you hit edge cases—stacked z-index conflicts, viewport-aware positioning, touch gesture cancellation—you're forced to either:

  1. Extend the schema with custom properties (breaks cross-platform compatibility).
  2. Eject to raw component libraries (defeats the purpose of a2ui).

Example: We tried adding a trapFocus: "strict" flag to the modal descriptor. The React adapter honored it, but the Flutter adapter ignored it (no equivalent in Flutter's showDialog). Cross-platform consistency collapsed.

When This Matters

If your generative UI flows are linear and non-overlapping (form wizards, chatbot threads), a2ui's abstraction holds. But production apps demand:

  • Toast notifications overlaying modals
  • Popovers inside dropdown menus inside sidebars
  • Drag-and-drop interactions across portal boundaries

These patterns expose a2ui's unresolved question: should the layout schema stay minimal (forcing platform-specific hacks), or should it expand into a full declarative accessibility DSL (risking bloat and divergence from native primitives)?

No clean answer yet. The repository's issue tracker shows 14 open threads on focus management alone.

title: What to put in the footer of an Indian small business website
description:
A website footer is easy to treat as leftover space, but visitors often look there for reassurance and a way to get unstuck. For a small Indian business, a useful footer is less about filling every column and more about giving people accurate details in a predictable place. Keep it short enough to scan, and make sure every item has an owner who can keep it current.

Start with identity and contact

Show the business name as customers know it, along with a location or service area when that information helps them decide whether the business is relevant. Include a working phone number, email address or other contact route the team actually monitors. On mobile, make phone numbers tappable and avoid presenting an image of contact details that cannot be copied. If the business has a physical shop, add clear directions or a link to a map only if the destination is correct.

Add useful navigation, not a second menu

A few links can help visitors reach high-value pages without scrolling back to the header: services, products, booking, FAQs, delivery or returns, and contact. Choose links based on real customer tasks. A long list of every page makes the footer harder to use and may bury the important details. Group related links under plain headings and use descriptive text rather than vague labels such as “click here.”

Make policies easy to find

If the business sells online or collects enquiries, provide the relevant privacy information and explain how customers can request a correction or ask a question. A shop may need clear delivery, cancellation, refund and exchange information; a service provider may need appointment, rescheduling or scope terms. Include only policies that apply, and have the business verify legal and tax wording with a qualified adviser. A footer link does not make a confusing or outdated policy adequate.

Include trust details carefully

A registration detail, professional credential or social profile can be useful when it is accurate and relevant. Do not add awards, certifications, review scores or claims that the business cannot substantiate. Social icons should lead to active accounts, not empty or unrelated profiles. If a copyright line is used, keep the year current rather than hard-coding a stale date.

Check the footer like a customer

Test each link, phone number and email address on a phone and desktop. Confirm the footer does not overlap the page, that text has readable contrast, and that keyboard users can reach every item. Open the site in a private browsing window or on another device to catch links that only work for a logged-in editor. Ask a colleague to find the address, return policy or contact method without hints.

When a footer needs a redesign, define the visitor tasks and content first, then discuss layout and accessibility with a web development firm in India. The goal is not to make the footer impressive; it is to make the next useful action and the business’s essential information easy to find. Revisit it whenever contact details, services, locations or customer policies change.

title: My PDF parser failed on the first two calls of every fresh process. My error dashboard showed zero.
description:
I run a resume builder for Indian job seekers. The first thing a new account does is upload the resume it already has. Last month 21 people signed up, 9 saved a resume, and none came back a second day. My usage table showed no failed call in two weeks, so I assumed uploads were fine. They were not.

The symptom

I made a throwaway account and uploaded a small text PDF. The toast said "We couldn't read that file". I uploaded the same file again and it worked. Same bytes, different answer.

Reproducing it outside the app

The upload route uses pdf-parse, which bundles pdf.js v1.10.100 from 2018. I took the route out of the picture and called the library 80 times in a row on the same 2.4 KB file, printing X for a throw and . for a result:

XX..............................................................................

The first two calls throw bad XRef entry. Every call after that succeeds. Six fresh processes gave the same picture, whether the first call came 0 ms or 1.5 s after the module loaded, so it is a count, not a timer. The file is not broken: it was written by ReportLab, and its startxref points exactly at the xref table. A PDF produced by my own templates never failed.

On a laptop that is a curiosity. On serverless it is the normal case: a cold function is a fresh process, so a person whose upload lands on one gets the failure.

Why nothing showed it

Simplified, the route did this:

try {
  text = await extractText(buffer, file.type);
} catch (e) {
  return json({ error: "We couldn't read that file." }, 400);
}
const parsed = await parseResumeText(text, user.id); // the first logged call

Only model calls were written to the usage table, and the failure happens one line before the first of them. "Zero errors" was true and meant nothing. Three of those 21 accounts had a resume parsed and never got one saved, and I cannot tell how many never got that far.

What I changed

  1. Retry the local parser. In a plain Node process the third call works, so four tries cover it.
  2. When it still fails, hand the file itself to a model that reads PDFs and images and ask for a plain transcription. That also covers scans and photos of a resume, which have no text layer at all and had always ended in the same error.
  3. Log every such read with its reason (pdf_unreadable: bad XRef entry, pdf_no_text_layer, image), success or not.
  4. Detect the type from the first bytes. Phones hand over PDFs as application/octet-stream or with no type, and those were being rejected as unsupported.

Then I checked production, and step 1 turned out to be worth less than I thought. On the deployed function the same file failed all four tries and was read by the fallback in two seconds. The retry that fixes a local process does not fix a serverless one, and I only know that because step 3 wrote a row saying so. Eight fallback reads cost about a third of a cent in total by my own price table.

One place does not get the fallback: the ATS checker. Its job is to report what a parser finds in the file, and for a scan the true answer is "nothing". Transcribing the picture there would turn that finding into a pass.

What I took from it

  • A dashboard that only counts the calls you log shows zero errors for everything that fails before them. Log the step in front of the first "real" call.
  • Test a parser in a fresh process, not in a warm REPL or a test runner that has already called it.
  • A fix measured locally is a guess until production writes down what it did.

The site is ResumeBanao, a resume builder for India; the same upload sits behind the free ATS checker. Written by an AI assistant from my own build notes and usage logs.

title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
description:
arXiv:2611.15475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.

title: Frontend system design for enterprise apps: 8 decisions
description:
This is the overview of the free series Frontend system design for enterprise applications, first published on tt-tech.io.

An enterprise frontend outlives its framework, its first team and usually its first architect. That changes which concepts matter. The concepts were never the hard part. Knowing which ones to ignore was.

Most frontend system design content prepares you for an interview: design a news feed in 45 minutes, on a whiteboard, for nobody. Enterprise frontends fail in a different way. They do not fail on day one. They fail in year seven, when the decision nobody made on purpose is now in four hundred files.

I have spent more than twenty years in software, building enterprise applications. This series is what I would tell a team starting one, or inheriting one.

What makes a frontend "enterprise"

It is not the size of the bundle. It is five things that small apps rarely have at the same time.

Time. The code lives longer than the framework. AngularJS support ended in January 2022.[1] The apps built on it did not end with it. I have been part of several migrations from AngularJS to Angular, in different teams and roles. The lesson every time: the boundaries you draw in year one decide what you can delete in year ten.

Teams. Many teams in one codebase, often one monorepo. The lines between their code are the architecture, whether anyone drew them or not.

Rules. Banking and healthcare come with rules the frontend cannot wave away. Access control is "only effective when implemented in trusted server-side code or serverless APIs", and broken access control keeps the top spot in the OWASP Top 10:2025.[2] In the EU, the European Accessibility Act covers consumer banking services provided to consumers after 28 June 2025.[3] For banks in scope, accessibility is a requirement there, not a nice-to-have.

Roles. The same screen looks different for a customer, an advisor and an auditor. Somebody has to decide where that logic lives.

Languages. For Morocco and the Gulf, Arabic is right to left, French text often runs longer than English, and Moroccan money is MAD with its own format. A layout built with left and right breaks the day Arabic arrives. CSS logical properties describe directions "relative to the content's writing direction, rather than a physical direction",[4] and that one choice decides whether RTL is a small task or a rewrite.

In enterprise, the decision outlives the people who made it. Design for the next team.

The eight parts

Eight areas, and in each only the five to seven concepts that change a decision.

  1. Architecture. Layers, enforced boundaries, monorepo or not, micro-frontends mostly not, and the legacy corner you keep deletable.
  2. State. Who owns each piece of state and how long it lives. Server data, UI, forms, the URL.
  3. Networking and caching. One question, so one part: where does this data live, and when is it wrong?
  4. Rendering. Many logged-in enterprise apps do not need server rendering. When they do, and what it costs.
  5. Performance. Budgets that fail the build, measured on the devices your users really have.
  6. Security. The frontend is the untrusted part. What the client can protect, and what it only shows.
  7. Accessibility. A legal requirement, and the design system is where it is won or lost.
  8. Languages, RTL and money. Arabic, French and MAD from the first component, not as a later project.

Caching sits with networking because a cache without an owner is a bug with a delay. RTL gets its own part because for readers in Morocco and the Gulf it is not a sub-bullet of accessibility.

How each part works

Every part has the same shape:

  • The few concepts that matter, each with one line on why.
  • When to choose what. Signals or RxJS, CSR or SSR, monorepo or polyrepo. The trade-off in plain words, Angular first, React next to it where the choice differs.
  • What I left out, and why. A concept that sounds important but rarely changes a decision in an enterprise app.
  • An example on Atlas Bank, the open demo app of the AI with Angular series: an imaginary Moroccan bank, built as an Nx monorepo, with module boundaries that npm run lint:arch enforces and two legacy corners (an NgModule transfer screen and an AngularJS beneficiaries screen). The repo is public. Never client code.

A glossary tells you what a word means. Production tells you which words you can ignore.

On Monday

  • Take the oldest screen in your app. For each of the eight areas, ask: was this decided on purpose, or did it happen by default?
  • Write down the one you cannot answer. That is your first architecture decision record.
  • Start with Atlas Bank's architecture page: it shows the dependency contract the first part builds on.

For your coding agent

The rules of all eight parts in one file, written for an agent. Paste them into your AGENTS.md, save them as a skill, or point your agent at the file. Each part also has its own file at the end of the article.

The file: https://tt-tech.io/agents/frontend-system-design.md

Sources

  1. AngularJS, Version Support Status, docs
  2. OWASP, A01 Broken Access Control - OWASP Top 10:2025, 2025
  3. EUR-Lex, Directive (EU) 2019/882 on the accessibility requirements for products and services, 2019
  4. MDN, CSS logical properties and values

The overview of the free series Frontend system design for enterprise applications on tt-tech.io, also in French and Arabic.

title: The GitHub API rate limit broke my self-updater for 20 minutes: falling back to the releases/latest redirect without trusting it any more
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of Relaymote, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote is an open-source (MIT) companion that mirrors Claude Code sessions from a PC to a phone browser. Its Windows install keeps itself current from GitHub Releases: every few hours the daemon asks which release is the latest, and if it is newer, downloads the installer, verifies it and runs it when nothing is busy.

"Asks which release is the latest" meant one call to api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest. Unauthenticated, that API allows 60 requests an hour per IP address, and that budget is shared with every other script on the machine that talks to the API without a token. One evening another tool on the same PC polled it in a loop, spent the hour's budget, and for about twenty minutes the update check got HTTP 403 and did nothing.

The fix is small, and the interesting part is not the fallback itself but what it is allowed to change.

Where the latest tag is available without the API

https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest is an ordinary web page, and it answers with a redirect to the newest release's tag page:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/tag/v0.2.182

You do not need the body, only the Location header. So the fallback is one request that is never followed:

function latestFromPage(repo) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = https.get(`https://github.com/${repo}/releases/latest`,
      { headers: { 'User-Agent': 'my-updater/' + current() }, timeout: 30000 }, res => {
        res.resume(); // discard the body; we only want the header
        const m = /\/releases\/tag\/v?([0-9][0-9A-Za-z.\-]*)$/.exec(String(res.headers.location || ''));
        if ([301, 302, 303, 307, 308].includes(res.statusCode) && m) return resolve(m[1]);
        reject(new Error(`no release redirect (HTTP ${res.statusCode})`));
      });
    req.on('timeout', () => req.destroy(new Error('timed out')));
    req.on('error', reject);
  });
}

Three details matter:

  • res.resume() drains the response so the socket is released, even though nothing reads it.
  • The regex is anchored to the end of the redirect and requires a digit first. A redirect somewhere else (a login page, a changed URL scheme) is an error, not a version.
  • Any status that is not a redirect is an error. If GitHub ever serves the page directly instead, the updater reports it rather than guessing.

Building the asset URLs from the tag

The API response also listed each asset's download URL. Without it, the URLs have to be constructed, which works because release downloads follow a fixed pattern:

https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/v<version>/<file>

The updater already knew which file it wants for each kind of install, so it builds exactly three URLs: the installer, SHA256SUMS.txt and SHA256SUMS.txt.sig.

} catch (e) {
  out.error = e.message;
  if (/^HTTP (403|429)\b/.test(e.message)) {          // rate limited, nothing else
    try {
      const latest = await latestFromPage(s.repo);
      const base = `https://github.com/${s.repo}/releases/download/v${latest}/`;
      const names = [assetName(kind, latest), 'SHA256SUMS.txt', 'SHA256SUMS.txt.sig'].filter(Boolean);
      Object.assign(out, {
        ok: true, latest, newer: cmpVersion(latest, out.current) > 0,
        assets: Object.fromEntries(names.map(n => [n, base + n])),
        via: 'release page (API limited)',
      });
      delete out.error;
    } catch (e2) { out.error += '; release page: ' + e2.message; }
  }
}

Only 403 and 429 trigger it. A 404 (wrong repository), a DNS failure or a timeout still fail the check, because those are not "the API said no for now", and hiding them would make a broken configuration look healthy.

When both routes fail, the error keeps both reasons (HTTP 403; release page: no release redirect (HTTP 200)), so a log line explains the whole story.

Why the fallback does not weaken anything

The tempting worry is: the API is the "proper" source, and now the version comes from scraping a redirect. Is that less trustworthy?

It is not, because neither source was ever trusted with the installer's integrity. The download step does the same thing whichever route found the version:

  1. Fetch SHA256SUMS.txt and SHA256SUMS.txt.sig.
  2. Verify the signature with an Ed25519 public key that is compiled into the app. The release workflow signs with the matching private key, held as a CI secret. No valid signature, no install.
  3. Find the installer's line in that signed file. Not listed, no install.
  4. Download the installer and compare its SHA-256 with the signed line. Mismatch, delete the partial file, no install. 
if (!verifySums(sums, sig, key)) return { ok: false, error: 'SHA256SUMS.txt signature does not verify with the release key: refused' };
const want = listedHash(sums, name);
if (!want) return { ok: false, error: `${name} is not listed in the signed SHA256SUMS.txt: refused` };

So the worst a wrong version number can do is point at a release whose files fail those checks, and the update is refused. The redirect only answers "which version should I look at?", never "is this file safe to run?". That separation is what made the fallback a ten-line change rather than a security review.

If your updater trusts the API response for anything more than discovery (an asset URL from a third-party mirror, a hash from the same JSON), a fallback like this would be a downgrade. Put the trust in a signature first; then the discovery step can be as simple as you like.

Tests

Four checks were added, with https.get stubbed:

  • API returns 403, the page redirects to v9.9.9: the check succeeds, reports 9.9.9 as newer and records via: 'release page (API limited)'.
  • In the same case, the checksum and signature URLs point at /releases/download/v9.9.9/, and the release page was actually requested.
  • API returns 500: the check fails exactly as before, with no fallback.
  • API returns 403, the page returns 200 with no redirect: the check fails, and the error names both reasons.

What I would do differently from the start

  • Cache the last answer. An update check every few hours does not need a fresh API call when the last one was minutes ago; the budget belongs to the whole machine, not to your process.
  • Treat a shared rate limit as an expected state, not an error. It is not your bug, but it is your outage if the only route is the API.
  • Keep discovery and verification in separate functions. Here, that is why the fallback could not touch the part that matters.

The code is lib/updater.js (check, latestFromPage, fetchVerified) and test/updater.js in the repository; the change shipped in 0.2.182.

Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2611.14769v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Arena-style rankings of language models are a widely used evaluation framework in online leaderboards, research papers, and model evaluation in production. These rankings aim to realistically assess model performance using pairwise comparisons of anonymous models on user prompts, aggregating votes via the Bradley-Terry model to produce the final ranking. However, we find that these leaderboards are highly vulnerable to several manipulation strategies that unscrupulous providers could use to boost a model's rank: strategic voting (individual votes that boost a model's rank, including votes on irrelevant models), strategic prompting (choosing prompts that favor a model), and strategic nomination (boosting the rank of a model by inserting irrelevant models). We demonstrate these effects on public leaderboard data, analyze the circumstances that cause these vulnerabilities, and describe approaches to safeguard against each attack. Notably, these issues hold for any preference-based evaluation using the Bradley-Terry model that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission. These manipulations boost the rank of nearly every tested model; each attack can boost a model by up to 15-20 places in a ranking and, combined, they can boost a model by up to 45 places.

title: Tax Rounding in POS Receipts: Why Line-Level and Invoice-Level GST Totals Differ by a Few Paise
description:
A point-of-sale system can calculate the correct GST rate and still produce a receipt whose tax total differs by a few paise from the amount expected by the cashier or customer. This usually happens because tax calculations involve decimal precision, rounding rules, discounts, and the level at which the final amount is rounded.

For retailers, restaurants, supermarkets, and multi-outlet businesses, even a small difference can create reconciliation issues. The problem becomes more noticeable when a POS application calculates tax separately for each product line but the accounting system calculates tax on the invoice subtotal.

The solution is not simply to round every number to two decimal places. A reliable POS application needs a consistent tax calculation policy that defines precision, rounding mode, tax grouping, and the point at which rounding occurs.

Why GST Totals Differ

Consider a receipt with several taxable items. The POS calculates GST on each line, rounds each tax amount, and then adds the rounded values.

An alternative method is to add the taxable values first, calculate GST on the combined amount, and round the final tax.

These methods can produce different totals because rounding is not distributive.

For example, assume three taxable line amounts of ₹10.05 each, with an illustrative GST rate of 5%.

The unrounded tax for each line is:

10.05 × 0.05 = ₹0.5025

If each line is rounded to ₹0.50, the total line-level GST becomes ₹1.50.

If the taxable amounts are first combined:

(10.05 + 10.05 + 10.05) × 0.05 = ₹1.5075

The invoice-level result rounds to ₹1.51.

The difference is ₹0.01. With more lines, different rates, and discounts, the difference can become more noticeable.

The important point is that both calculations may be mathematically consistent, but the POS must follow the applicable tax and accounting policy rather than switching methods unpredictably.

Line-Level Versus Invoice-Level Tax Calculation

A POS application should define whether it calculates tax at the individual item level or at the grouped invoice level.

Calculation method How it works Common consideration
Line-level Tax is calculated and rounded for each item Small differences can accumulate
Invoice-level Tax is calculated on aggregated taxable values Requires grouping by tax treatment
Tax-category level Taxable values are grouped by rate or category Different rates must remain separate
Component-level CGST, SGST, IGST, or other components are calculated separately Component rounding must be consistent

The correct approach depends on applicable regulations, accounting policy, and the business's invoicing requirements. A POS should not assume that one calculation method is appropriate for every jurisdiction.

Use Decimal Arithmetic Instead of Floating-Point Calculations

One common technical cause of unexpected totals is the use of binary floating-point numbers for financial calculations.

Values such as 0.1 cannot always be represented exactly in binary floating-point. Repeated calculations can therefore introduce tiny precision differences.

For financial amounts, developers should use decimal arithmetic or integer minor-unit calculations where appropriate.

A simplified example using decimal arithmetic:

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

amount = Decimal("10.05")
rate = Decimal("0.05")
tax = amount * rate
rounded_tax = tax.quantize(
    Decimal("0.01"),
    rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP
)
print(rounded_tax)

This makes the intended precision and rounding mode explicit. The selected rounding mode must still match the applicable business and tax requirements.

Define the Rounding Policy Before Development

A POS application should not allow individual modules to make independent rounding decisions.

The tax engine should centrally define:

  • Calculation precision before rounding.
  • Final currency precision.
  • Rounding mode.
  • Whether rounding happens per line or per tax group.
  • Treatment of discounts and promotions.
  • Handling of returns and partial refunds.
  • Whether tax components are rounded separately.
  • Treatment of cash rounding, where legally and operationally applicable.

For example, a product module, receipt generator, refund service, and accounting integration should all use the same approved calculation policy.

If the receipt rounds line-level tax but the refund module recalculates invoice-level tax, the refund amount may not match the original transaction.

How Discounts Affect GST Rounding

Discounts can make tax calculations more complicated because the taxable base may change before GST is calculated.

A POS system should distinguish between:

  1. Item-level discounts.
  2. Order-level discounts.
  3. Promotional discounts.
  4. Coupons and loyalty adjustments.
  5. Post-sale discounts or credit notes.

The system must apply the correct discount treatment before calculating tax, based on the relevant tax rules.

For an order-level discount distributed across multiple items, the application needs a consistent allocation method. It could allocate the discount proportionally across eligible lines, while retaining the original values and allocated discount amounts for audit purposes.

The receipt should show enough detail to explain how the taxable amount was derived.

A Better Data Model for POS Tax Calculations

A reliable POS database should preserve both source values and calculated results.

A practical structure may include:

Table Purpose
orders Stores transaction-level details
order_items Stores product quantity, unit price, and line amount
tax_categories Defines tax classifications
tax_rates Stores applicable tax rates and effective periods
discount_allocations Records discounts applied to each line
tax_calculation_lines Stores taxable base and calculated tax
payment_transactions Records payments and adjustments
refund_lines Preserves original transaction references

Each tax calculation record should retain the applicable rate, taxable base, tax amount before rounding, rounded tax amount, and calculation policy version.

This makes it easier to investigate a receipt discrepancy without recalculating the transaction using current tax settings.

Testing Tax Rounding in a POS Application

Testing should cover more than ordinary product purchases.

Important scenarios include:

  • Several low-value items with the same tax rate.
  • Products with different GST rates.
  • Discounts applied before tax calculation.
  • Order-level discounts distributed across items.
  • Partial refunds and returned quantities.
  • Split payments.
  • Cancelled and voided transactions.
  • Cash rounding where supported.
  • Tax rate changes with effective dates.
  • Offline sales synchronized after reconnecting.

Automated tests should compare the POS receipt, backend transaction, and accounting export. The expected outcome should be based on a documented calculation policy, not on an assumption that every system will produce identical intermediate values.

Recommended POS Software Development Companies

When selecting a development partner for a tax-aware POS system, businesses should examine its experience with transaction processing, financial calculations, payment workflows, and accounting integrations.

1. Dev Technosys

Dev Technosys provides custom software development services that can support retail billing platforms, POS applications, inventory workflows, and business system integrations. A POS implementation can incorporate configurable tax rules, transaction-level audit records, refund management, receipt generation, and multi-store reporting.

For businesses with complex billing requirements, the system architecture should keep tax calculation logic centralized and preserve the original transaction values for returns and reconciliation.

2. Chetu

Chetu develops custom software for businesses across several industries. Its application development and integration capabilities may be relevant to retailers looking for tailored POS workflows connected with inventory, payments, and enterprise systems.

Chetu suits businesses evaluating custom POS development and integration services.

3. NCR Voyix

NCR Voyix provides technology solutions for retail and restaurant operations, including point-of-sale and commerce-related capabilities. Businesses can evaluate its offerings when comparing established retail technology platforms.

NCR Voyix suits retailers and restaurant operators assessing established commerce and POS technology.

4. Oracle

Oracle offers enterprise retail and commerce technologies, including solutions that support store operations and transaction management. Its broader enterprise ecosystem may be relevant to businesses with complex retail technology environments.

Oracle suits large retailers looking for enterprise retail systems and connected business applications.

5. Square

Square provides commerce and point-of-sale products for businesses, with capabilities covering payments and sales operations. Its offerings may be relevant to small and medium-sized businesses evaluating an established POS platform.

Square suits businesses seeking an accessible commerce and POS ecosystem.

6. Toast

Toast focuses on restaurant technology, including POS, payments, and operational tools. Its restaurant-oriented platform can be considered by food service businesses comparing integrated technology options.

Toast suits restaurants evaluating purpose-built restaurant POS and operations software.

7. Lightspeed

Lightspeed provides commerce and POS technology for retail and hospitality businesses. Its product capabilities may be relevant to companies seeking a platform that connects sales workflows with inventory and business operations.

Lightspeed suits retailers and hospitality operators comparing integrated POS platforms.

Businesses should verify regional GST support, invoice formats, tax configuration options, refund handling, integration requirements, and local compliance before selecting a vendor. A provider's general POS capabilities do not automatically establish compliance with every jurisdiction's tax rules.

How to Evaluate a POS Development Partner

Evaluation area What to verify
Tax calculation Configurable and documented calculation policies
Decimal precision Decimal-safe financial calculations
GST handling Correct tax categories and component treatment
Refund workflows Original tax values retained for adjustments
Receipt generation Consistent totals across printed and digital receipts
Integration Accounting and payment system compatibility
Auditability Traceable tax and discount calculations
Testing Edge cases, rounding boundaries, and regression coverage

Benefits of Consistent Tax Rounding

A consistent tax engine helps businesses:

  • Reduce billing discrepancies.
  • Improve cashier confidence in receipt totals.
  • Simplify accounting reconciliation.
  • Preserve accurate refund calculations.
  • Maintain a reliable audit trail.
  • Support consistent billing across multiple outlets.
  • Reduce manual adjustments and customer disputes.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why does GST differ between line-level and invoice-level calculations?

The difference occurs because each line may be rounded separately, while invoice-level calculation rounds the combined taxable amount. Rounding individual values before adding them can produce a different result from rounding the total.

2. Should a POS system calculate GST on every product line?

The calculation method should follow applicable tax requirements and the business's approved accounting policy. The POS should implement one consistent, documented approach rather than choosing a method independently in different modules.

3. Can floating-point arithmetic cause POS billing differences?

Yes. Binary floating-point values can introduce small representation errors. Decimal arithmetic or suitable integer-based monetary calculations help make financial calculations more predictable.

4. How should a POS handle GST during refunds?

The refund process should reference the original transaction and preserve its tax calculation details. Recalculating a refund using current tax settings can create differences when rates or calculation rules have changed.

5. What should businesses look for in a POS software development company?

Businesses should assess financial calculation accuracy, tax configuration, receipt generation, refund handling, payment integrations, security, audit trails, and the vendor's ability to support local invoicing requirements.

Conclusion

A few paise of difference on a POS receipt can point to a deeper inconsistency in the application's tax calculation process. The most reliable approach is to define a central rounding policy, use decimal-safe calculations, preserve original transaction values, and test line-level and invoice-level scenarios.

A capable POS software development company can help implement a tax engine that keeps receipts, refunds, backend records, and accounting exports consistent with the business's approved GST treatment.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud on November 6, 2026.

Scheduled maintenance of Management/Control Plane for the Apigee Edge for Public Cloud production will take place on Friday, November 6, 2026, from 9:00 PM PT to 10:00 PM PT (Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 5:00 AM UTC to 6:00 AM UTC). This maintenance follows the monthly maintenance window schedule documented in the Apigee Edge release notes archive.

During the scheduled maintenance window, the following services will be temporarily unavailable, and attempts to access them will return a 4xx status code:

  • Management Services UI
  • Management Services APIs
  • Monetization Management APIs
  • New proxy deployments
  • DevPortal Service
  • Microgateway Services
  • Edge Query (Analytics Stats APIs)

Runtime API calls to deployed API proxies are unaffected. While access to analytics queries may be temporarily unavailable during the maintenance window, all analytics and metrics data from this period will be available once maintenance ends.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.10

On November 5, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.10.

  • For information about upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to v1.14.10.
  • For information about new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release. The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch by using the Helm chart automatically updates the images. You don't typically need to make manual image changes. For information about container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
578314600 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent ignored HTTPS_PROXY and failed to establish a tether in clusters that require an HTTP forward proxy for egress; the agent now uses HTTP/2 keepalive pings on the control-plane connection while honoring HTTPS_PROXY (including proxy credentials).
576707253 Removed the compromised emSign roots and the cross-signing Comodo AAA Services root from the system and Java (cacerts) trust stores across containers.
573622417 Fixed an issue where apigee-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571378258 The apigee-redis container now uses the Valkey engine (version 8.1.10). The RESP2 wire protocol and redis-server and redis-cli binary names are unchanged.
554114419 Fixed an issue where an AssignMessage, HTTPModifier, or RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow could not set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers and failed with an invalid-header error.
524115876 Fixed an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests under load.
449228485 Fixed an issue where podDisruptionBudget overrides configured in the Helm charts were dropped by the Kubernetes API server.
432315283 Fixed an issue where changes to a multi-certificate truststore's trust anchors required a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled was toggled at runtime; the outbound SSLContext now rebuilds automatically.

The iam.serviceAccounts.actAs check on run-as service accounts already applies when you publish or test any integration. Starting January 15, 2027 (UTC), the new authorization behavior also applies to existing integrations created before October 15, 2026. Specifically, you must have a run-as service account to publish or test an integration with a scheduled or event trigger.
