title: SQL Server Statistics Explained: Why Your Query Plans Go Wrong
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

When a query suddenly picks a terrible plan, the root cause is very often statistics. SQL Server's optimizer does not look at your data when it builds a plan; it looks at statistics about your data. If those are missing or out of date, it guesses wrong, and a wrong guess can mean a scan instead of a seek, the wrong join type or a memory spill.

What statistics are

A statistics object describes how values are distributed in one or more columns. SQL Server creates one automatically for every index, and, with AUTO_CREATE_STATISTICS on, for columns you filter or join on. The optimizer uses them to estimate how many rows each step will return, and those estimates drive almost every plan choice.

How to read a statistics object 

DBCC SHOW_STATISTICS ('dbo.PayrollLine', 'IX_PayrollLine_Run_PayCode');

The output has three parts:

  • Header: when the statistics were last updated, how many rows the table had, and how many rows were sampled.
  • Density vector: how unique the column combinations are, used when the actual value is unknown.
  • Histogram: up to 200 steps showing, for ranges of values in the first column, how many rows match. This is what lets SQL Server know that Status = 'Closed' matches 2 million rows but Status = 'Error' matches 12.

When statistics update automatically

With AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS on (the default), statistics are refreshed when enough rows have changed and a query needs them. On modern versions (compatibility level 130 and above) the threshold is dynamic, so large tables are refreshed after a smaller percentage of changes than in old versions. Even so, on a table with hundreds of millions of rows, a lot can change before an automatic update kicks in.

Automatic updates also use a sample of rows by default, which can miss skewed values in very large tables.

Check how stale your statistics are 

SELECT
    OBJECT_NAME(s.object_id)  AS table_name,
    s.name                    AS stats_name,
    sp.last_updated,
    sp.rows,
    sp.rows_sampled,
    sp.modification_counter
FROM sys.stats s
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_db_stats_properties(s.object_id, s.stats_id) sp
WHERE OBJECTPROPERTY(s.object_id, 'IsUserTable') = 1
ORDER BY sp.modification_counter DESC;

A high modification_counter means many rows have changed since the last update. A low rows_sampled compared with rows means the statistics are based on a small sample.

Update statistics manually when it matters 

-- One table, default sample
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.PayrollLine;

-- One statistics object, reading every row (most accurate, most expensive)
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.PayrollLine IX_PayrollLine_Run_PayCode WITH FULLSCAN;

-- All statistics in the database that have had modifications
EXEC sp_updatestats;

Use FULLSCAN for important, skewed columns on large tables; it costs more I/O but gives the most accurate histogram. After a big data load, updating statistics on the affected tables before users run queries prevents a wave of bad plans.

The ascending key problem

Columns that always grow, such as identity values or CreatedAt dates, cause a classic issue: new rows are added beyond the highest value in the histogram, and until statistics are updated, SQL Server may estimate that very few rows exist there. Queries on "today's" or "the latest" data then get plans built for tiny row counts. Newer cardinality estimator versions handle this better, but frequent statistics updates on these tables are still the most reliable fix.

Index rebuilds vs statistics updates

  • Rebuilding an index also updates that index's statistics with a full scan.
  • It does not update auto-created column statistics.
  • Reorganizing an index does not update statistics at all.

So a maintenance job that only reorganizes or rebuilds indexes can leave important column statistics stale. Include a statistics step in your maintenance.

Practical routine

  • Keep AUTO_CREATE_STATISTICS and AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS on.
  • Schedule a regular statistics update, such as nightly or weekly, for busy tables.
  • Update statistics after large loads, purges or migrations.
  • When a plan goes bad, compare estimated and actual rows; if they differ a lot, check the statistics on those columns first.

Related reading:

  • SQL Server Parameter Sniffing: What It Is and How to Fix It
  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan
  • SQL Server Index Tuning for Beginners

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
description:
arXiv:2611.15481v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

title: Feat Looks Like Spring Boot. So Why Does It Work Differently?
description:
A question came up recently in the Feat repository:

"What is the difference between this project and Spring?"

It's a fair question. If you look at Feat Cloud code, you'll find familiar concepts: controllers, beans, dependency injection, and annotations.

But the similarity is mostly in the developer experience.

Compile-time generation instead of runtime scanning

In a typical Spring Boot application, the framework performs a lot of work during startup: discovering components, processing annotations, wiring dependencies, and building runtime infrastructure.

Feat Cloud takes a different approach.

Its annotation processor handles controller mappings and dependency wiring during Maven compilation. The generated Java code can be inspected under:

target/generated-sources/annotations/

This means Feat Cloud does not need runtime annotation scanning for those generated mappings and wiring.

There is a trade-off: changes to relevant annotations or compile-time configuration require rebuilding the application.

No Servlet container

Feat does not build its web server on the Servlet model.

Feat Core provides HTTP server and routing capabilities on top of smart-socket. You can use its Router and Handler APIs directly, without annotations or a container.

Feat Cloud adds a higher-level programming model for developers who prefer annotation-based controllers.

What Feat does not try to do

Spring Boot has a much broader ecosystem. Security, data access, messaging, monitoring, and countless integrations are major strengths.

Feat does not aim to reproduce every Spring project or starter. Integrations such as MyBatis, Nacos, and XXL-Job are available, but some Spring ecosystem capabilities still require custom integration or a different solution.

If your application is deeply coupled to Spring Security or many Spring-specific starters, migration may not be worthwhile.

Why build another Java framework?

The question behind Feat is simple:

Can we keep a familiar Java development experience while moving more work from runtime to compile time?

Feat is one attempt to explore that direction.

It may be a better fit for resource-sensitive services, lightweight HTTP applications, and projects that value a simpler runtime model. It is not intended to be a universal Spring Boot replacement.

Project: https://github.com/smartboot/feat

Documentation: https://smartboot.tech/feat/

Spring migration guide: https://smartboot.tech/feat/practices/from-spring/

title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
description:
arXiv:2611.14804v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training.
  Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

title: 5 Ways to Implement File Export: Temporary Download Links with Presigned URLs
description:
5 Document Pipelines: Matching Large-File Throughput to Expiry Rules

A signed-document export has two clocks: the file must move quickly enough for a large download, and the link must die on schedule. For an edtech platform retaining signed enrollment documents until an explicit deletion deadline, I would choose a private object store plus a short-lived presigned download URL. I would test the path with real document sizes before choosing a provider.

The useful answer is a decision rule, not a vendor popularity contest: pick the service that passes your largest-file throughput test, keeps the object private, and lets your deletion job meet its deadline. A presigned URL grants temporary access to one object without handing the browser storage credentials.

The field guide: which path fits?

Option Pick this when Watch closely
Amazon S3 presigned URLs Your team already operates AWS and wants the broadest surrounding storage ecosystem. IAM policy design, region choices, and the operational surface around the export service.
Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs The workload is already close to Cloudflare and S3-compatible tooling is useful. Check the exact compatibility and egress assumptions for your clients.
Azure Blob SAS Your identity, audit, and document workflows already live in Microsoft Azure. SAS scope and expiration policy need the same review as any bearer link.
Infrai storage presigning You want storage beside other backend capabilities behind one REST API, with one key and one bill. It is not a public-asset host, a WORM store, or a cross-cloud migration service.

The comparison is deliberately practical. S3 is the ecosystem default for many teams. R2 is compelling when the surrounding Cloudflare setup is already the center of gravity. Azure Blob is the natural fit for an Azure-governed identity boundary. Infrai belongs in the trial when consolidating backend access matters and the storage workflow fits its private-object model.

What should the experiment measure?

Start with three inputs: the largest export size you expect, the slowest client network you support, and the maximum link lifetime your policy permits. For an edtech system, include a signed PDF, a scanned bundle, and the biggest multi-file export that a registrar can request. Use the same bucket region, object key shape, and client behavior for every option.

Test the boundary.

Record time to upload, time to first byte, completed download time, retry count, and deletion completion time. Do not call a run a success because the link opened once. Run each size several times, keep the results, and inspect the failure cases. A 2 GB export that is fast on a wired laptop but fails on a constrained campus connection is not a passing user workflow.

Use these pass/fail rules:

  1. The object is private before and after the test.
  2. The link works during its permitted window and fails after it expires.
  3. The largest export completes within your product timeout, including a resumed or retried client path where your provider supports it.
  4. The deletion worker removes the object by the stated deadline.
  5. A retry cannot create a second document or silently extend retention.

The decision rule is simple: reject any option that fails a hard policy check, then choose the passing option with the best large-file result and the smallest operational boundary your team can actually own. Throughput is the primary axis here. Price is not a substitute for a failed deletion guarantee.

How can Node.js implement file export with temporary download links?

Keep generation and hosting as two explicit steps. The model or document generator produces bytes; the storage write keeps the object private; the presign call returns a temporary link; the browser downloads directly from that link. Diagram in words: generator -> private object -> expiring URL -> browser.

Here is the small handoff shape. generateExport() represents the application's existing generation step. Its returned bytes are sent through the same base URL and the same Authorization value used for storage. The route names are the storage routes available for this workflow.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function callWithBackoff(
  url: string,
  init: RequestInit,
  attempts = 4,
): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < attempts; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, init);
    if (response.status !== 429 || attempt === attempts - 1) return response;

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const waitSeconds = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter
      : 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitSeconds * 1000));
  }
  throw new Error("Retry loop ended unexpectedly");
}

async function storeAndPresign(
  bucket: string,
  key: string,
  bytes: Uint8Array,
  expiresInSeconds: number,
): Promise<string> {
  const headers = {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/pdf",
    "Idempotency-Key": `export-${key}`,
  };

  const putResponse = await callWithBackoff(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
    { method: "PUT", headers, body: bytes },
  );
  if (!putResponse.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Object write failed: ${putResponse.status} ${await putResponse.text()}`);
  }

  const presignUrl = new URL(
    `${baseUrl}/storage/object/presign/${encodeURIComponent(bucket)}/${encodeURIComponent(key)}`,
  );
  presignUrl.searchParams.set("expires_in", String(expiresInSeconds));
  const linkResponse = await callWithBackoff(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/signed-documents/student-42%2F2026-10%2Fexport.pdf?expires_in=900",
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );
  if (!linkResponse.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Presign failed: ${linkResponse.status} ${await linkResponse.text()}`);
  }

  const payload = (await linkResponse.json()) as { url?: string };
  if (!payload.url) throw new Error("Presign response did not contain a URL");
  return payload.url;
}

const generatedBytes = await generateExport();
const downloadUrl = await storeAndPresign(
  "signed-documents",
  "student-42/2026-10/export.pdf",
  generatedBytes,
  900,
);
console.log(downloadUrl);

The browser receives only downloadUrl. It must not receive the Infrai bearer key, and the bearer header must not be sent to the returned presigned URL. Treat the URL as a bearer credential during its short lifetime. A 900-second window is an application choice for the experiment, not a claim about every export.

For an AI-generated document, the same application boundary can feed generated output into the private object write. The single-key advantage is concrete: an OpenAI-plus-S3 stack would mean an OpenAI account and an AWS account, two credential sets, and glue for moving generated bytes between them. A consolidated API removes that account and credential handoff, while still leaving you with one vendor boundary, one bill, and one outage surface. That trade-off belongs in the decision record.

Where the candidates stop fitting

Do not use this design for permanent public links, static website hosting, or an image CDN. The storage capability does not provide a public-read ACL or a permanent public URL. It also lacks object versioning and object lock, so an overwritten document cannot be recovered through WORM semantics; regulated immutability needs an external design.

Browser-direct uploads need special care because CORS rules are not self-service here. Strict write concurrency also needs coordination in a queue or database rather than an If-Match condition. Lifecycle expiration is measured in days, with a one-day minimum, so it cannot express an hourly cleanup promise. There is no cross-region automatic replication or bulk cross-cloud migration tool, either.

Those are useful boundaries, not footnotes. If your hard requirement is legal hold, public distribution, automatic replication, or hour-level lifecycle cleanup, the specialist with that feature should win. If your hard requirement is a repeatable large-file export test plus a common backend account, try Infrai for the storage leg and record the result rather than assuming it wins. If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage presigned-download guide.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • Azure Blob SAS overview
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
  • Infrai documentation

title: A settlement record, thirteen tests, eight mutants, one file
description:
@mickyarun asked for the template, then told me not to sell it. His sentence: a document a stranger can publish is not a product. He was right, so here is the file with no price on it. Copy it, no attribution needed.

It answers the question a payment reconciliation job asks and usually cannot answer. Given a commitment written before the money moved, and a settlement record written after, is the comparison between them valid?

Two rules do most of the work.

The verdict is derived at read time. render() takes the commit, the settlement, the caller's clock and the set of parties who can invalidate the basis. It returns a string. Nothing on the record stores PASS. A stored verdict is a decision that survives the evidence it was made from.

Expiry carries an owner, and the owner is whoever can invalidate the basis, not the counterparty. A merchant comparing against an issuer's authorisation window is bounded by that window because the issuer can revoke it. Rule it as a counterparty condition and one clock produces two verdicts.

The settlement record has exactly four fields: call_id, reference_rev, settled_at, value. No delta. No verdict. No provenance label written by the writer.

The thirteen cases

case record read result
3a no settlement 06:20 vs commit 06:00 NO_SETTLEMENT basis=8812 age=20m
3a twice same commit, two reads 06:20 and 06:35 age=20m, then age=35m; the clock is the caller's
reference moved settlement at rev 8900, commit at 8812 06:10 NOT_COMPARABLE reason=reference_mismatch 8812:8900
3b settled 07:41, expiry 06:15, issuer in the invalidators 08:00 NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expired owner=issuer
3b, other list same bytes, issuer not in the invalidators 08:00 NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expiry_owner_cannot_invalidate
equal 100.00 against 100.00 in window PASS basis=8812 delta=0.00
short 97.00 against 100.00 in window FAIL basis=8812 delta=-3.00

The two 3b rows are the point of case 3b: the verdict changes because of the list the caller passes, not because of anything in the record. A record that decides its own comparability cannot be checked by the party reading it.

Four schema tests sit behind the seven above. Settlement has exactly four fields, and verdict, status and delta are not among them. Commit carries no provenance label. render() takes no default clock and no default invalidator set, because a function that supplies its own basis cannot fail on a test that always supplies one. And render(commit, None, None, ...) must refuse rather than invent a time.

Provenance degrades in one direction only: self_attested when there is no acknowledgement and no issuance attempt, issued when an attempt exists or when the acknowledgement comes from the writer's own holder, witnessed only when the digests match and the holder is someone else. An acknowledgement about your own record is a self-report wearing a second word.

The file 

"""
Settlement record + render, and a mutation harness that actually runs the tests.

Four-field settlement (call_id, reference_rev, settled_at, value), verdict derived
at read time by render() over the (commit, settlement) pair.  Expiry carries an
owner; the owner bounds the comparison only if that owner can invalidate the basis.

The harness below is the point of this file: every mutant is a variant
implementation executed against the same test list.  A mutant is caught when at
least one test fails, not when the mutant's own function says so.  A no-op
mutation must survive; if it is reported caught, the harness is broken.

Run: python3 settlement.py   (exit 0 iff every invariant holds)
"""

import inspect
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

SETTLEMENT_FIELDS = {"call_id", "reference_rev", "settled_at", "value"}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the implementation under test
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

SOURCE = r'''
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

SETTLEMENT_FIELDS = {"call_id", "reference_rev", "settled_at", "value"}


def dt(s):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace("Z", "+00:00"))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Expiry:
    at: datetime
    owner: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Commit:
    call_id: str
    reference_rev: int
    observed_at: datetime
    value: Decimal
    expiry: Expiry = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settlement:
    call_id: str
    reference_rev: int
    settled_at: datetime
    value: Decimal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Ack:
    digest: str
    holder: str


def render(commit, settlement, now, invalidators):
    """now and invalidators are required: the function under test does not
    supply the clock, and does not default the parties that can invalidate
    the basis."""
    if settlement is None or settlement.call_id != commit.call_id:
        age = int((now - commit.observed_at).total_seconds() // 60)
        return "NO_SETTLEMENT basis=%d age=%dm" % (commit.reference_rev, age)

    if settlement.reference_rev != commit.reference_rev:
        return ("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=reference_mismatch %d:%d"
                % (commit.reference_rev, settlement.reference_rev))

    if commit.expiry is not None and settlement.settled_at > commit.expiry.at:
        if commit.expiry.owner in invalidators:
            return ("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expired owner=%s at=%s"
                    % (commit.expiry.owner, commit.expiry.at.isoformat()))
        return ("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expiry_owner_cannot_invalidate owner=%s"
                % commit.expiry.owner)

    delta = settlement.value - commit.value
    if delta == 0:
        return "PASS basis=%d delta=0.00 settled_in_window" % commit.reference_rev
    return "FAIL basis=%d delta=%s" % (commit.reference_rev, delta)


def provenance(digest, ack, attempts):
    if ack is not None and ack.digest == digest and ack.holder != "operator":
        return "witnessed"
    if attempts:
        return "issued"
    return "self_attested"
'''


def load(source):
    ns = {}
    exec(compile(source, "<variant>", "exec"), ns)
    return ns


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# fixtures and tests, written against a namespace so they can run on any variant
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def fixtures(ns):
    C = ns["Commit"]("c1", 8812, ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T06:00:00Z"), ns["Decimal"]("100.00"),
                     ns<a href="ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T06:15:00Z"">"Expiry"</a>, "issuer"))
    S = ns["Settlement"]
    return dict(
        C=C,
        S_OK=S("c1", 8812, ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T06:04:12Z"), ns["Decimal"]("100.00")),
        S_LOW=S("c1", 8812, ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T06:04:12Z"), ns["Decimal"]("97.00")),
        S_STALE=S("c1", 8900, ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T06:04:12Z"), ns["Decimal"]("100.00")),
        S_LATE=S("c1", 8812, ns["dt"]("2026-11-12T07:41:03Z"), ns["Decimal"]("100.00")),
        t=ns["dt"],
        D=ns["Decimal"],
    )


def test_equal(ns):
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], f["S_OK"], f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:10:00Z"),
                        {"issuer"}) == "PASS basis=8812 delta=0.00 settled_in_window"


def test_unequal(ns):
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], f["S_LOW"], f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:10:00Z"),
                        {"issuer"}) == "FAIL basis=8812 delta=-3.00"


def test_no_settlement_3a(ns):
    # case 3a: read at 06:20 against a commit observed at 06:00 is 20 minutes
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], None, f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:20:00Z"),
                        {"issuer"}) == "NO_SETTLEMENT basis=8812 age=20m"


def test_no_settlement_clock_is_the_callers(ns):
    f = fixtures(ns)
    a = ns["render"](f["C"], None, f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:20:00Z"), {"issuer"})
    b = ns["render"](f["C"], None, f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:35:00Z"), {"issuer"})
    assert a.endswith("age=20m") and b.endswith("age=35m")


def test_reference_mismatch(ns):
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], f["S_STALE"], f["t"]("2026-11-12T06:10:00Z"),
                        {"issuer"}).startswith("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=reference_mismatch 8812:8900")


def test_expired_issuer_bounds_merchant_basis(ns):
    # the issuer's authorisation clock governs a merchant comparison because the
    # issuer can invalidate the basis, even though the issuer is not the counterparty
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], f["S_LATE"], f["t"]("2026-11-12T08:00:00Z"),
                        {"issuer", "rail"}).startswith("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expired owner=issuer")


def test_expiry_owner_who_cannot_invalidate(ns):
    f = fixtures(ns)
    assert ns["render"](f["C"], f["S_LATE"], f["t"]("2026-11-12T08:00:00Z"),
                        {"rail"}).startswith("NOT_COMPARABLE reason=expiry_owner_cannot_invalidate")


def test_settlement_is_four_fields(ns):
    assert {x.name for x in ns["fields"](ns["Settlement"])} == ns["SETTLEMENT_FIELDS"]


def test_commit_has_no_label(ns):
    assert "provenance" not in {x.name for x in ns["fields"](ns["Commit"])}


def test_settlement_has_no_verdict(ns):
    names = {x.name for x in ns["fields"](ns["Settlement"])}
    assert not names & {"verdict", "status", "delta"}


def test_render_takes_no_defaults(ns):
    # a default clock or a default invalidator set is a record that supplies its
    # own basis; no call that always passes them can fail on it
    sig = inspect.signature(ns["render"])
    for name in ("now", "invalidators"):
        assert sig.parameters[name].default is inspect.Parameter.empty


def test_render_refuses_a_missing_clock(ns):
    # a fallback clock is invisible to every test that always supplies one, so the
    # suite needs the test where the argument is absent and refusal is the answer
    f = fixtures(ns)
    try:
        ns["render"](f["C"], None, None, {"issuer"})
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return
    raise AssertionError("render invented a clock instead of refusing")


def test_provenance_degrades(ns):
    P, Ack = ns["provenance"], ns["Ack"]
    assert P("d1", None, 0) == "self_attested"
    assert P("d1", None, 3) == "issued"
    assert P("d1", Ack("d1", "operator"), 1) == "issued"   # holder is the writer
    assert P("d1", Ack("d1", "client-a"), 1) == "witnessed"
    assert P("d1", Ack("d2", "client-a"), 1) == "issued"   # digest mismatch


TESTS = [
    test_equal, test_unequal, test_no_settlement_3a, test_no_settlement_clock_is_the_callers,
    test_reference_mismatch, test_expired_issuer_bounds_merchant_basis,
    test_expiry_owner_who_cannot_invalidate, test_settlement_is_four_fields,
    test_commit_has_no_label, test_settlement_has_no_verdict,
    test_render_takes_no_defaults, test_render_refuses_a_missing_clock, test_provenance_degrades,
]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# mutations: source substitutions, each applied to the module text
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

MUTATIONS = [
    ("rev rewritten to match at settlement",
     'if settlement.reference_rev != commit.reference_rev:',
     'if False:'),
    ("one window for every party",
     'if commit.expiry is not None and settlement.settled_at > commit.expiry.at:',
     'if commit.expiry is not None and settlement.settled_at > commit.expiry.at + timedelta(minutes=120):'),
    ("stored delta",
     '    value: Decimal\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Ack:',
     '    value: Decimal\n    delta: Decimal = Decimal("0.00")\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Ack:'),
    ("provenance label written by the writer",
     '    expiry: Expiry = None',
     '    expiry: Expiry = None\n    provenance: str = "witnessed"'),
    ("render supplies its own clock",
     '    if settlement is None or settlement.call_id != commit.call_id:\n        age',
     '    now = now or commit.observed_at + timedelta(minutes=30)\n    if settlement is None or settlement.call_id != commit.call_id:\n        age'),
    ("expiry owner ignored, counterparty rule back",
     'if commit.expiry.owner in invalidators:',
     'if True:'),
    ("holder check dropped",
     'and ack.holder != "operator"',
     ''),
    ("verdict field stored on the settlement",
     '    settled_at: datetime\n    value: Decimal\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Ack:',
     '    settled_at: datetime\n    value: Decimal\n    verdict: str = "PASS"\n\n\n@dataclass(frozen=True)\nclass Ack:'),
]


def run_suite(ns):
    failures = []
    for t in TESTS:
        try:
            t(ns)
        except AssertionError as e:
            failures.append((t.__name__, str(e)))
        except Exception as e:
            failures.append((t.__name__, "error: %r" % (e,)))
    return failures


def main():
    base = load(SOURCE)
    base_fail = run_suite(base)
    print("baseline: %d/%d pass" % (len(TESTS) - len(base_fail), len(TESTS)))
    for n, m in base_fail:
        print("  baseline failure %s: %s" % (n, m))

    escaped, caught = [], []
    for name, old, new in MUTATIONS:
        if old not in SOURCE:
            raise SystemExit("mutation did not apply, so it proves nothing: %s" % name)
        src = SOURCE.replace(old, new, 1)
        fails = run_suite(load(src))
        if fails:
            caught.append((name, [f[0] for f in fails]))
        else:
            escaped.append(name)

    # the no-op mutation must escape. a harness that reports this caught is
    # measuring itself, not the tests.
    noop_src = "# a mutation that changes no behaviour\n" + SOURCE
    noop_caught = bool(run_suite(load(noop_src)))

    print("mutants caught: %d/%d" % (len(caught), len(MUTATIONS)))
    for name, ts in caught:
        print("  caught %-45s by %s" % (name, ", ".join(ts[:3])))
    print("escaped: %s" % (escaped or "none"))
    print("no-op mutation escaped (harness is not self-agreeing): %s" % (not noop_caught))

    ok = not base_fail and not escaped and not noop_caught
    print("RESULT:", "OK" if ok else "BROKEN")
    return 0 if ok else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())```
{% endraw %}


Run it with nothing but the standard library:
{% raw %}

python3 settlement.py


plaintext

What mine prints, verbatim:

baseline: 13/13 pass
mutants caught: 8/8
caught rev rewritten to match at settlement by test_reference_mismatch
caught one window for every party by test_expired_issuer_bounds_merchant_basis, test_expiry_owner_who_cannot_invalidate
caught stored delta by test_settlement_is_four_fields, test_settlement_has_no_verdict
caught provenance label written by the writer by test_commit_has_no_label
caught render supplies its own clock by test_render_refuses_a_missing_clock
caught expiry owner ignored, counterparty rule back by test_expiry_owner_who_cannot_invalidate
caught holder check dropped by test_provenance_degrades
caught verdict field stored on the settlement by test_settlement_is_four_fields, test_settlement_has_no_verdict
escaped: none
no-op mutation escaped (harness is not self-agreeing): True
RESULT: OK




Two of those eight mutants are invisible to `render()`. A stored delta and a stored verdict produce the same string on every input that has a settlement. Only the schema assertion catches them, which is why the file asserts on fields and not only on behaviour.

And the no-op mutant has to survive. A harness that reports its own no-op as caught is measuring its own bookkeeping. If someone hands you a mutation tester with no surviving mutant, that is the first thing to check.

## What this does not do

The agent writes the record. A compromised writer writes a matching one. Every rule above passes, and the money is still gone. This catches the case where the record is written honestly and the comparison is made wrongly, which is the common case and the boring one. It does not catch the writer whose intent was the problem.

`witnessed` is a word, not a witness. It means an acknowledgement row exists with a matching digest from a holder that is not the writer's. If that row lives in a store the write path can reach, the word is worth nothing. Something outside the writer has to hold the copy, or the label is decoration.

There is no reader in this file. A record nobody diffs is a second log agreeing with the first.

## If you want it run on your numbers

That is a different job from owning the file. Send the pair: one commitment with its revision and its clock, one settlement with its revision and its time, and say who can invalidate the basis. You get the case table above filled in with your rows and the two places your rule would print two different verdicts. USD 20, and I write you a link after you say yes, not before.

Otherwise take the file. The cases are the part worth stealing.

title: October 21, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

Changed in this release

  • Upgraded the Apigee Emulator runtime JVM to Eclipse Temurin JRE 21 (21.0.12.1.0+1-0, from JRE 11 11.0.31+11), adding JVM 21 compatibility flags (-Djava.security.manager=allow and --add-opens module flags) for JavaCallout, JavaScript (Rhino), and Python (Jython) policies while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra 4.0.19 datastore pinned to Eclipse Temurin JRE 8.
  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
  • Upgraded shaded Apache Log4j (log4j-api and log4j-core) in ConfigUtil.jar to 2.25.5 (from 2.17.1 and 2.25.4).
  • Upgraded BouncyCastle (bcprov-jdk18on, bcpkix-jdk18on, and bcutil-jdk18on) to 1.85 (from 1.84).
  • Upgraded Apache CXF (cxf-*) to 3.6.12 (from 3.5.11).
  • Upgraded gRPC to 1.82.3 (from 1.62.2), Protobuf (protobuf-java and protobuf-java-util) to 4.33.6 (from 3.25.5), and Guava to 33.5.0-jre (from 33.4.8-jre).
  • Removed unused org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-* (9.4.58.v20250814) and commons-collections:commons-collections (3.2.2) JARs from the emulator distribution.
  • Refreshed the Cassandra base image to pick up Go standard library 1.27.0 (from 1.25.11) in the embedded /opt/apigee/ready health-check binary.

Announcement

v1.15.9

On October 21, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.15.9.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.15.9.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

title: I Built a Free Tool to Track AI Tokens and API Costs
description:
I’ve been spending a lot of time exploring AI tools and working with prompts recently.

One thing I noticed is that it’s not always easy to understand how much a prompt actually costs when using AI APIs.

You write a prompt, send it to a model, get a response, and move on.

But what if you’re testing multiple prompts or comparing different AI models? Keeping track of token usage and API costs can become confusing.

Why I Built It

I wanted a simple place where I could:

  • Count the tokens in a prompt.
  • Estimate API costs before sending requests.
  • Compare the costs of different AI models.
  • Make prompts shorter and more efficient.

Instead of constantly switching between different tools, I decided to build a small project that brings these features together.

Introducing PromptBurn

PromptBurn is a free tool designed for people who work with AI prompts and APIs.

It currently includes:

  1. Token Counter

Check how many tokens your prompt contains.

  1. API Cost Calculator

Estimate potential API costs based on token usage and model pricing.

  1. Model Comparison

Compare costs across supported AI models.

  1. Prompt Compression

Experiment with making prompts shorter while keeping their meaning.

Privacy Was Important to Me

I also wanted to keep the experience simple and privacy-conscious.

PromptBurn is designed to process prompt text directly in the browser, rather than sending it to a server.

What’s Next?

This is still a work in progress.

I’d like to improve the accuracy, add useful features, and make the experience better for developers working with AI APIs.

You can check it out here:

https://prompt-burn.com

I’d genuinely appreciate feedback from other developers.

A few questions:

  • What would you improve first?
  • What feature is missing?
  • How do you currently track token usage and API costs?

Thanks for reading!

title: One Engine, Seven Open-Source Projects: PageSift 1.4 and the yolow Family
description:
PageSift started as the ingestion layer of an AI research platform I was building: something had to fetch web pages and documents and turn them into clean Markdown that an LLM pipeline could actually use. It grew into a self-hosted web scraper, crawler and document parser — Firecrawl- and Jina-compatible API, MCP server, Python/Node SDKs, one Rust binary.

Over the 1.x series I kept doing one thing: every time a piece of the engine turned out to be generally useful, I cut it out and gave it its own repository, its own versioning, and an MIT license. PageSift 1.4 finishes that split — and adds the subsystem the extraction was making room for.

PageSift 1.4

The split, completed. Wave one (1.2.7) turned the base64, PDF, HTML and content crates into thin shims over standalone libraries. Wave two (1.4.0) does the same for the remaining three: pagesift-office → yolowdoc, pagesift-syntax → yolowsyntax, pagesift-compress → yolowzstd. The engine is now a composition of seven independently versioned open-source projects — and since 1.3, PageSift itself is Apache-2.0 (it was AGPL before).

DataGraph. The new crate, pagesift-graph (~4,000 lines), is what the cleanup was for. A normal scraper returns text and forgets everything else. DataGraph keeps the receipts:

  • Every fetch becomes a node; links between documents become citations.
  • Provenance is recorded as edges: redirect chains, canonical alias clusters, attachments and their parent documents.
  • Refetch the same resource and you get version lineage instead of an overwrite.
  • Extracted fields carry evidence spans — byte offsets into the source document, so any claim can be pointed back at the exact text it came from.
  • Claims about the same entity (keyed by subject keys like sku) are clustered into facts across sources, and when sources disagree you get a conflict record: both variants, both excerpts, and a preferred variant with its reason. Two pages pricing the same product at $10 and $12 stop being a silent data-quality bug and become a queryable fact.

It's exposed everywhere PageSift is: CLI (scrape --graph, crawl --graph, graph inspect), the HTTP API (a graph slice on scrape responses, plus /v2/graph/history and /v2/graph/conflicts), the MCP tool pagesift_graph_query, and the Python and Node SDKs.

An LLM pipeline doesn't just need text. It needs to know where a claim came from, what it contradicts, and which version is current. That's the layer DataGraph adds.

The six libraries

yolow64 0.3.0 — base64, ~20 GB/s

A fast Base64 codec with runtime-dispatched SIMD (AVX2/NEON), zero runtime dependencies, streaming and data-URL APIs. The 0.3 release added dedicated short-input kernels and fused hash-table tail processing: around 20.4 GB/s from 8 KiB to 1 MiB, and short payloads (8–64 bytes) got 1.5–2.8× faster than in 0.2. Short inputs are the common case in real pipelines — tokens, hashes, embedded blobs — so that's where the work went.

cargo add yolow64 · GitHub · crates.io

yolowpdf 0.1.2 — PDF to Markdown, no C libraries

A PDF-to-Markdown library and OCR engine that parses the format itself — no Poppler, no MuPDF, nothing to link against. The workspace includes GPU-accelerated OCR (PP-OCRv6). The README benchmark clocks 1,900 pages/s on born-digital documents (i7-10700). This is the component that taught the family its hardest rule: every allocation a hostile file can influence is budgeted before it happens.

cargo add yolowpdf · GitHub · crates.io

yolowhtml 0.1.0 — arena HTML5 parsing and extraction

Two crates: yolowhtml-dom, a zero-copy HTML5 parser over a contiguous arena (Vec<Node>, u32 ids, CSS selectors), and yolowhtml, a single-pass main-content extractor that produces Markdown, metadata and publication dates from the same parse. On the README's test corpus it scores 1.000 structural F1 for Markdown across 15 page categories, and 0.945 F1 for publication-date extraction across 20 languages. Both crates are #![forbid(unsafe_code)].

cargo add yolowhtml · GitHub · crates.io

yolowzstd 0.1.2 — pure-Rust Zstandard

A Zstandard (RFC 8878) encoder/decoder written from the spec: zero dependencies, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], multi-core encode/decode that emits standard concatenated frames — interoperability is tested against the official zstd CLI. It's built for the small-record end of the world: on 64-byte payloads it decodes at 3,257 MB/s (1.6× C libzstd) and encodes at 264 MB/s (4.1×) on an i7-10700, which is exactly the shape of PageSift's cache records. One stated gap: no dictionary support yet.

cargo add yolowzstd · GitHub · crates.io

yolowsyntax 0.1.2 — tree-sitter, without the C

A pure-Rust runtime for tree-sitter grammars: the C runtime reimplemented in Rust, with 41 languages' parse tables converted and embedded — 6.22 MiB total, Zstd-compressed (with yolowzstd, its only runtime dependency) and decompressed lazily per language. It extracts code outlines for 32 symbol-bearing languages. No C FFI, #![forbid(unsafe_code)]. Stated limits: no Query DSL and no incremental re-parsing.

cargo add yolowsyntax · GitHub · crates.io

yolowdoc 0.1.1 — every document format, one call

Documents to Markdown behind a single convert(bytes, format, opts): Office (DOCX/XLSX/PPTX, plus legacy DOC/XLS/PPT and XLSB), OpenDocument, RTF, WordPerfect, HWP/HWPX, e-books (EPUB/MOBI/FB2), email (EML/MBOX/MSG), archives (ZIP/TAR/7Z/GZ/BZ2/XZ — the decompressors are pure Rust too), SQLite, dBASE, CSV and Jupyter notebooks. The per-format parsers go deep — pivot tables, charts, equations — and a Limits budget is checked before any work starts.

cargo add yolowdoc · GitHub · crates.io

How they fit together

The family is a small lattice, not a pile: PageSift depends on all six libraries; yolowsyntax depends on yolowzstd; yolowdoc builds on both; yolowpdf uses yolow64. The rules are shared across all of them — pure Rust, no C dependencies, unsafe code forbidden in the libraries, and resource budgets enforced before allocation, because every one of these parsers eats untrusted input for a living.

PageSift is the engine. These six are its organs, now living their own lives — each usable without the others, each on crates.io under MIT, with PageSift itself under Apache-2.0.

Links: PageSift · yolow64 · yolowpdf · yolowhtml · yolowzstd · yolowsyntax · yolowdoc

Try them, break them, and tell me where they break — issues and benchmarks from other machines are the most useful feedback I can get.

title: Secure, Lightweight Secret Management for Node.js Without Heavy External Vaults
description:
The Secret Management Dilemma: Heavy Vaults vs. Fragile .env Files

Modern Node.js deployment architectures suffer from a structural split that forces teams into a bitter trade-off: surrender to the operational gravity of enterprise-grade external vaults, or drift into the silent, catastrophic vulnerabilities of decentralized text files. This friction is not merely theoretical; it directly fractures developer velocity and introduces severe failure vectors into the software supply chain.

The Enterprise Vault Failure Mode

When engineering teams adopt heavy external secret management solutions for modest or mid-tier applications, they introduce unnecessary architectural mass. An external vault requires a continuous network handshake, sidecar proxy maintenance, explicit IAM role bindings, and token renewal daemons.

The mechanical failure chain: During a cold container boot, if the external secret provider experiences network latency or token expiry, the Node.js application process hangs mid-initialization or throws an unhandled promise rejection. The system fails not due to application logic, but because an external, stateful dependency choked the runtime bootstrap sequence. Operational overhead expands exponentially with every new microservice or staging environment, draining cognitive bandwidth into infrastructure plumbing rather than core business logic.

The Fragile .env File Failure Mode

To dodge this enterprise complexity, teams routinely retreat to the path of least resistance: local, plain-text .env files scattered across developer laptops and deployment pipelines. This introduces a silent, highly volatile security decay.

  • Git History Pollution: When a developer runs a casual git add ., unencrypted secret strings cross the boundary from working directory to staging index. The plaintext credentials are permanently written into the local .git/objects database. Once pushed to a remote host, pulling the repository exposes those keys to every contributor and automation log.
  • State Drift and Overwrites: Decentralized environment files mutate independently across staging, production, and local environments without atomic versioning. A misplaced character or mismatched key name silently corrupts runtime configuration, manifesting as erratic, hard-to-diagnose authentication faults hours after deployment.

Decision Dominance: Choosing the Pragmatic Equilibrium

Evaluating these options reveals a distinct inflection point. Heavy vaults break deployment agility for simple apps; plain text files break security hygiene entirely. The optimal solution must eliminate network dependencies while preserving cryptographic rigor.

The Decision Rule: If an application footprint does not demand complex dynamic secret lease rotation across thousands of distributed enterprise domains, discard external vaults. Instead, centralize credentials into a single, encrypted file artifact (such as a local app.safebox) locked down with authenticated encryption like AES-256-GCM and derived via scrypt. This binds the secrets directly to the deployment package, stripping out runtime network fragility while ensuring that if the file is intercepted without its master key, it remains entirely inert mathematical noise.

Anatomy of a Lightweight Solution: Inside pavex/safebox

Traditional secret architectures rely on continuous network handshakes, sidecar proxy maintenance, explicit identity-and-access-management role bindings, and token renewal daemons. During a cold container boot, network latency or token expiration against an external provider typically fails, triggering unhandled promise rejections or application hangs mid-initialization via external stateful dependencies. Conversely, decentralized plain-text environment files induce silent state drift and permanent git history pollution whenever an unvetted git add . commits plain-text secrets directly into the local object database.

To eliminate this operational friction, pavex/safebox consolidates all credentials into a single encrypted artifact named app.safebox that lives directly beside the application code in both the repository and the deploy package. Without the master password supplied at runtime, the file remains structurally inert ciphertext.

Cryptographic Rigor and Zero-Dependency Execution

The internal mechanics of pavex/safebox rely entirely on Node.js built-in modules, maintaining zero runtime dependencies to minimize supply-chain exposure risks. The cryptographic pipeline operates through two deterministic phases:

  • Key Derivation via scrypt: The master password feeds into the memory-hard scrypt algorithm, forcing high CPU cycles and RAM allocation during derivation. This mechanical resistance thwarts high-speed parallel brute-force cracking attempts by inflating the thermal and computational cost per guess.
  • Authenticated Encryption via AES-256-GCM: The derived key feeds a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard cipher operating in Galois/Counter Mode. This provides both confidentiality and an integrity tag; if an attacker alters a single bit of the ciphertext within app.safebox, the decryption math fails catastrophically during authentication, throwing a runtime exception before any malformed payload reaches memory.

Decision Mechanics: When to Adopt Safebox Versus Enterprise Vaults

Choosing a secret management paradigm depends entirely on operational scale and rotation requirements:

  • Decision Rule: If dynamic secret lease rotation across thousands of distributed microservices is unneeded, enterprise vaults are architecturally over-engineered. Use app.safebox when deployment footprints require self-contained immutability without external network dependencies.
  • Failure Threshold: The safebox approach stops working effectively when multiple distributed engineering teams require independent, concurrent write access to overlapping secret namespaces without a centralized coordination server, as manual file merging introduces state collisions.
  • Typical Choice Errors: Teams often choose complex external vaults out of perceived enterprise compliance norms, only to introduce cascading failure modes where transient DNS outages take down entire application fleets during startup.

Risk Analysis, Operational Trade-offs, and Production Scenarios

Choosing a secret management architecture forces an immediate trade-off between operational complexity and exposure surface. Teams frequently default to enterprise-grade vaults or fragmented plaintext files without analyzing the failure mechanics embedded in each approach.

Enterprise Vault Failure Modes

Heavy external vault architectures introduce fragile network dependencies during application startup. When a container performs a cold boot, its initialization script depends on synchronous network handshakes with sidecar proxies, IAM token generators, or external renewal daemons. If transient network latency spikes, DNS resolution lags, or the remote token expires mid-handshake, the application thread stalls or crashes entirely via unhandled promise rejections. The system fails not due to bad code logic, but because an external, stateful service blocked the local process from acquiring its configuration variables.

Plaintext .env Failure Modes

At the opposite extreme, decentralized .env files create permanent risk vectors through developer workflow friction. When a developer runs git add ., raw plaintext API keys and private database credentials are ingested into the local .git/objects directory as compressed database blobs. Pushing that commit broadcasts those bytes to remote repositories, permanently exposing credentials in git history even if the file is later deleted from the working tree. Furthermore, decentralized manual mutations across local development environments induce silent state drift, causing erratic runtime authentication faults when mismatched configurations hit production.

Cryptographic Mechanics of File-Based Encrypted Artifacts

Lightweight, zero-dependency tools like pavex/safebox resolve these friction points by consolidating all named secrets into a single encrypted file (app.safebox) deployed directly beside the application code. At rest, the file is entirely inert ciphertext; without the correct master password, interception yields zero usable data.

The security posture relies on a rigorous cryptographic pipeline executed entirely through Node.js built-in modules:

  • Key Derivation (scrypt): The master password feeds into scrypt, a memory-hard function that forces high CPU cycles and massive RAM block allocations per guess. This computational friction penalizes parallel brute-force attacks by spiking thermal loads and memory bandwidth consumption on attacking hardware.
  • Authenticated Encryption (AES-256-GCM): The derived key powers 256-bit AES in Galois/Counter Mode, providing both confidentiality and an integrated authentication tag. If a single bit in the ciphertext is altered—whether by storage corruption or malicious tampering—the mathematical tag verification fails instantly, throwing a runtime exception that halts execution before malformed payloads can leak into memory variables.

Decision Rules and Production Boundaries

File-based secret encryption changes the deployment footprint by eliminating external network calls entirely during container initialization. However, it comes with strict operational boundaries.

Adoption Threshold: If your architecture does not require dynamic, automated secret lease rotation across thousands of distributed microservices, heavy external vaults are architectural over-engineering. For standard Node.js applications deployed as unified artifacts, bundling an encrypted app.safebox eliminates cold-boot network failure modes while maintaining cryptographic rigor.

Failure Threshold: Safebox stops working effectively when multiple distributed engineering teams require independent, concurrent write access to overlapping secret namespaces without a centralized coordination server. Because app.safebox is a single file, concurrent manual updates across different branches create state collisions and merge conflicts that destroy data consistency.

The Core Decision Rule: If deployment relies on immutable, self-contained packages where secrets are updated atomically through a controlled CLI pipeline, use file-based encryption. If you require real-time, dynamic lease revocation across a multi-tenant cluster, accept the operational overhead of an enterprise vault.

title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
description:
arXiv:2611.14960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.
