title: Sandbox blocking npm install in Claude Code, Cursor and Codex
description:
Originally published on KitQuarry. Written by Eliran Kotzero for KitQuarry.

In short: when an agent's npm install, pip install or curl fails but the same command works in your own terminal, the sandbox is usually the reason. Each tool's sandbox lets commands reach only the hosts you allow and write only inside the project. Allow the registries you use by name, allow the package cache folder, and leave everything else closed. Turning the sandbox off isn't the fix.

Is it the sandbox? Read the error

Agents often misreport these failures as a bad token, a broken registry or a flaky network. The error text usually tells you which limit you hit:

What you see What it usually means
Could not resolve host, Temporary failure in name resolution, Network is unreachable The command has no network route at all: Codex with network off, or a tool that ignores the proxy variables in Claude Code's sandbox
403 Forbidden, Tunnel connection failed: 403, or a prompt asking about a host The sandbox proxy is working and this host isn't on the allowlist
EROFS, Read-only file system, Operation not permitted The command wrote outside the folders the sandbox allows, often a cache in your home folder
Works for curl, fails for ssh, psql or a database driver The tool doesn't use the HTTP proxy, so an allowed host still can't be reached

To check rather than guess, ask the agent to run the probe script below. It prints what the sandbox lets that command reach and write.

The three sandboxes side by side

Claude Code Cursor Codex
On by default? No. Turn it on with /sandbox or sandbox.enabled Yes in Auto-review (the default mode); optional in Allowlist; none in Run Everything Yes. The default workspace-write sandbox has no network
Config file .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude/settings.json, key sandbox .cursor/sandbox.json or ~/.cursor/sandbox.json ~/.codex/config.toml, or .codex/config.toml in a trusted project
Hosts allowed out of the box None. You get asked (in Manual mode) the first time Cursor's default list: npm, PyPI, crates.io, GitHub, Docker Hub and many more None until you set network_access, and then every host unless the network proxy is on
Allow a host network.allowedDomains networkPolicy.allow [features.network_proxy] domains
Allow a folder outside the project filesystem.allowWrite additionalReadwritePaths writable_roots
What it covers Bash, PowerShell and Monitor commands only Terminal commands Commands Codex runs; not web search or MCP

Claude Code

1. Know what's blocked

The sandbox is off until you run /sandbox or set sandbox.enabled. Once it's on, a sandboxed command can write only to the working directory, a per-user temp directory and folders you've added. It has no direct network route. Traffic goes through a proxy on your machine that checks each host against your allowed domains, and that list starts empty.

What happens with a host that isn't on the list depends on your permission mode: Manual and acceptEdits prompt you, auto mode refuses unless the command named the host and the classifier approved it (v2.1.271 or later; if auto mode is missing or its classifier keeps failing, see Claude Code auto mode unavailable or classifier blocked), dontAsk refuses, and bypassPermissions lets it through. Answering Yes allows the host for the session. Yes, and don't ask again saves a WebFetch(domain:...) allow rule to your local settings, and the sandbox picks those rules up as allowed domains.

2. Allow the hosts and the cache folder

In .claude/settings.json (commit it) or ~/.claude/settings.json (just you):

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "network": {
      "allowedDomains": ["registry.npmjs.org", "pypi.org", "files.pythonhosted.org"]
    },
    "filesystem": {
      "allowWrite": ["~/.npm"]
    }
  }
}
  • Use exact hosts where you can. The docs' examples use a leading *. wildcard such as *.npmjs.org, and they warn that a broad entry like github.com can be used to send data out.
  • allowWrite is for tools that write outside the project. The docs name npm among them: its cache lives in ~/.npm. Path rules use ~/ and absolute paths here, not the // prefix that permission rules use.
  • Filesystem path lists from different settings files are merged, not replaced.
  • To refuse every other host instead of prompting, set network.strictAllowlist to true in your user settings (v2.1.219 or later). A repo's settings file can't turn it on.

3. The commands that still fail

  • Tools that ignore the proxy (plain ssh, most database drivers, anything over UDP) can't connect, even to an allowed host. Take that exact command out of the sandbox with sandbox.excludedCommands, and add an ask rule for it so you approve each run.
  • Docker doesn't work inside the sandbox. The docs suggest a narrow exclusion such as docker compose *. An excluded command runs with your full access.
  • A server on localhost: on Linux and WSL2, each sandboxed command has its own private localhost, so it can't reach your dev server or a database in a container. Use excludedCommands for the command that needs it. On macOS, set network.allowLocalBinding to true.
  • git over SSH fails on macOS even with the host allowed. Switch the remote to HTTPS, or exclude git fetch *, git pull * and git push *.
  • jest hangs because watchman doesn't work in the sandbox. Run jest --no-watchman.

When a command fails in the sandbox, Claude may offer to retry it unsandboxed. Your mode decides whether that retry prompts. If you'd rather it never happens, set allowUnsandboxedCommands to false. Also note that if the sandbox can't start (missing bubblewrap or socat on Linux), Claude Code runs commands unsandboxed unless you set failIfUnavailable.

Cursor

1. Know when the sandbox is in play

In Auto-review, the default Run Mode, allowlisted calls run as they are and other shell commands run in the sandbox when they can. If a sandboxed command fails on a sandbox limit, the agent can rerun it outside the sandbox, and the Auto-review classifier checks that rerun. In Allowlist mode the sandbox is optional. Run Everything has no sandbox at all. Cloud Agents don't use Run Modes; they run on their own machine.

Cursor's sandbox starts more open than the other two. In the default network mode, sandbox.json + Defaults, a long built-in list is already allowed, including registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, github.com, crates.io and Docker Hub. So when npm install fails in Cursor, look for a host that isn't on that list: a private registry, a Git dependency on another host, or an API your tests call.

2. Add the hosts it's missing

In .cursor/sandbox.json (one repo) or ~/.cursor/sandbox.json (all projects):

{
  "networkPolicy": {
    "default": "deny",
    "allow": ["npm.pkg.github.com", "api.stripe.com"]
  },
  "enableSharedBuildCache": true
}
  • Entries can be exact hosts, wildcards or CIDR ranges. In Cursor, *.example.com also matches example.com itself. URL paths are ignored, and deny always beats allow.
  • The two files are merged: allow lists are combined, and a "deny" default wins over "allow". A team admin allowlist replaces the combined list.
  • The network mode setting has two other options. sandbox.json Only drops Cursor's defaults, so you have to list your registries yourself. Allow All opens every host inside the sandbox.
  • enableSharedBuildCache sends npm, pip, cargo and similar caches to a shared temp folder, so sandboxed and unsandboxed runs use the same caches. additionalReadwritePaths grants other folders outside the project.

3. The commands that still fail

  • Local and private addresses (127.x, 10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x and the cloud metadata address) are blocked by default. The reference lists CIDR ranges as allow patterns, but it doesn't say whether one re-opens a blocked private range, and we haven't tested it. Expect a command that talks to your local dev server or database to need a run outside the sandbox.
  • Docker on Linux: inside the sandbox, id -u returns 0. Scripts that pass your user ID to docker run --user should read CURSOR_ORIG_UID and CURSOR_ORIG_GID instead.
  • Linux needs kernel 6.2 or later with Landlock v3 and unprivileged user namespaces. Without them, Cursor asks before running commands instead of sandboxing them.
  • Some paths stay read-only whatever you write in sandbox.json, including .cursor/*.json, .claude/*.json, .vscode/, .git/hooks/ and .git/config.

Codex

1. Know what the default blocks

Codex's default workspace-write sandbox lets commands write in the workspace and temp folders, with no network. In our test, every host failed with Temporary failure in name resolution, which is easy to read as a DNS problem. Your home folder is read-only, and so are .git, .agents, .codex and .aws inside the workspace. A git commit inside the sandbox failed on .git/index.lock, so with the default on-request approvals Codex has to ask to run it outside the sandbox, or you commit yourself.

2. Open the network to your registries only 

# ~/.codex/config.toml, or .codex/config.toml in a trusted project
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
approval_policy = "on-request"

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = true          # off by default
writable_roots = ["~/.npm"]    # npm's cache lives outside the workspace

[features.network_proxy]
enabled = true                 # without the proxy, network_access means every host
domains = { "registry.npmjs.org" = "allow", "pypi.org" = "allow", "files.pythonhosted.org" = "allow" }

Two settings, and both matter:

  • network_access = true alone opens every host. In our test, example.com was reachable with only that line. The docs say the same thing: network on with the proxy off means "unrestricted direct outbound access".
  • [features.network_proxy] routes commands through a local proxy that enforces domains. Domain rules do nothing until the proxy is on, and the proxy does nothing while the network is off. With both on, registry.npmjs.org worked and example.com got 403 Forbidden with the header x-proxy-error: blocked-by-allowlist.
  • Codex wildcards differ from Cursor's: *.example.com matches subdomains only, and **.example.com matches the domain and its subdomains. "*" allows every public host.
  • The proxy also refuses hostnames that resolve to non-public addresses, even when they're on your list. In our test, our machine's DNS answered a reserved address for pypi.org, and the proxy blocked it. If an internal registry resolves to a private IP, that's why.

For one session, pass the same settings as flags:

codex -c 'sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true' \
  -c 'features.network_proxy.enabled=true' \
  -c 'features.network_proxy.domains={ "registry.npmjs.org" = "allow" }'

The proxy only covers commands Codex runs. Web search, MCP servers and connectors have their own settings.

3. Let installs write their cache

With the network open, npm install still failed in our test:

npm error code EROFS
npm error path /home/box/.npm/_cacache/tmp/***

npm keeps its cache in ~/.npm, outside the workspace. Adding it to writable_roots, as in the file above, fixed it. The docs' example uses an absolute path; "~/.npm" also worked in codex-cli 0.166.0. Do the same for pip (~/.cache/pip) or cargo if you use them.

4. Reach localhost on purpose

With the proxy on, local and private addresses are blocked. Our test server on 127.0.0.1:8765 returned 403 until we added both literals:

domains = { "registry.npmjs.org" = "allow", "localhost" = "allow", "127.0.0.1" = "allow" }

Wildcards don't count as local exceptions. allow_local_binding = true opens local and private addresses more broadly, so use it only if a hostname you need resolves to one.

Codex also has newer permission profiles (marked beta) that describe the same filesystem and network rules as one named profile. Don't mix them with sandbox_mode: if sandbox_mode appears in any loaded config, Codex uses the older settings and ignores the profile.

Wildcards don't mean the same thing

Pattern Claude Code Cursor Codex
example.com That host That host That host
*.example.com Leading *. is supported; the docs don't say whether it includes example.com Subdomains and example.com Subdomains only
**.example.com Not documented Not documented Subdomains and example.com
Port "127.0.0.1:8080"; no port means every port Not documented Ports are stripped

If you keep one list of hosts for all three tools, write exact hosts. They mean the same thing everywhere.

A probe to run inside the sandbox

Ask the agent to run this with the hosts your project needs, for example python3 sandbox_probe.py registry.npmjs.org npm.pkg.github.com. It has to be the agent that runs it. A command you type in your own terminal isn't sandboxed.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Ask the agent to run this inside its sandbox to see what the sandbox blocks.
Usage: python3 sandbox_probe.py [host ...]   (defaults: registry.npmjs.org pypi.org github.com)
Exit code 1 if a host or an existing cache folder is blocked. Standard library only."""
import os, sys, pathlib, tempfile, urllib.request, urllib.error

HOSTS = sys.argv[1:] or ["registry.npmjs.org", "pypi.org", "github.com"]
FOLDERS = [".", ".git", "~", "~/.npm", "~/.cache/pip", "~/.cargo/registry", "~/go/pkg/mod", "~/.gradle"]

def can_write(folder):
    path = pathlib.Path(folder).expanduser()
    if not path.is_dir():
        return None
    try:
        with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(dir=path, prefix=".sandbox-probe-"):
            return True
    except OSError:
        return False

def reach(host):
    req = urllib.request.Request(f"https://{host}/", method="HEAD")
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8)
        return True, "reachable"
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:  # the server answered, so the network path works
        return True, f"reachable (HTTP {e.code})"
    except urllib.error.URLError as e:
        reason = str(e.reason)
        if "Tunnel connection failed" in reason:
            return False, f"BLOCKED by the sandbox proxy ({reason})"
        return False, f"NO ROUTE ({reason})"
    except OSError as e:  # timeouts and resets
        return False, f"NO ROUTE ({e})"

proxies = sorted(k for k in os.environ if k.lower() in ("http_proxy", "https_proxy", "all_proxy"))
print("Sandbox markers:")
print("  CURSOR_SANDBOX =", os.environ.get("CURSOR_SANDBOX", "(not set)"))
print("  proxy variables:", ", ".join(proxies) if proxies else "none (direct network, or no network)")

failed = False
print("Write access:")
for folder in FOLDERS:
    ok = can_write(folder)
    if ok is None:
        continue
    print(f"  {'ok     ' if ok else 'BLOCKED'} {folder}")
    failed |= (not ok) and folder.startswith("~/.")  # a read-only package cache breaks installs

print("Network (HTTPS):")
for host in HOSTS:
    ok, why = reach(host)
    print(f"  {host}: {why}")
    failed |= not ok
sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)

"BLOCKED by the sandbox proxy" means add the host to the allowlist. "NO ROUTE" means there's no network at all, or the host doesn't resolve. A blocked ~/.npm or ~/.cache/pip means installs will fail even with the network open. A blocked .git is expected in Codex. In Claude Code's Manual mode, a host that isn't allowed may bring up a prompt while the probe waits.

We ran it in Codex's sandbox (codex-cli 0.166.0 on Linux) with the network off, with only network_access, and with the config above, and outside any sandbox. The results matched what's described in the Codex section. We didn't run it inside Claude Code or Cursor, which weren't installed on the test machine; it only reads standard proxy variables and CURSOR_SANDBOX, which Cursor sets in sandboxed commands.

When to stop allowlisting

If the list of exceptions keeps growing (Docker, databases, SSH, local servers), run the agent inside a dev container and make the container the boundary. Claude Code's docs describe a reference container with an outbound firewall, running as a non-root user, and the CLI refuses --dangerously-skip-permissions when it runs as root. Codex's docs suggest --sandbox danger-full-access inside a container when the container is the boundary, so Codex doesn't try to build a second sandbox. A container still lets a command send out anything inside it, so keep host secrets such as ~/.ssh out of it.

For fewer prompts without widening the sandbox, see how to stop Claude Code, Cursor and Codex asking permission for every command. To keep secrets out of reach, see how to stop agents reading your .env file.

A ten-minute setup

  1. List the hosts your installs and tests need: the package registries, any private registry, Git hosts for Git dependencies, and APIs your tests call.
  2. Claude Code: /sandbox, then add those hosts to allowedDomains and the cache folder to allowWrite.
  3. Cursor: leave the network mode on sandbox.json + Defaults and add only the hosts that aren't on Cursor's default list.
  4. Codex: turn on network_access and [features.network_proxy] with a domains table, and add the cache folder to writable_roots.
  5. Have the agent run the probe. Fix what it reports, commit the project files, and keep personal hosts in your home-folder config.

FAQ

Why does npm install fail when my AI agent runs it?

Usually the agent's sandbox, not npm. Codex's default workspace-write sandbox has no network, Claude Code's sandbox only reaches hosts on its allowlist (empty at first), and Cursor's sandbox, in its default network mode, only reaches its built-in list plus your sandbox.json. Even with the network open, npm writes its cache to ~/.npm, which is outside the workspace, so the install can still fail with EROFS until you allow that folder.

How do I allow a domain in the Claude Code sandbox?

Add it to sandbox.network.allowedDomains in .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude/settings.json, or answer "Yes, and don't ask again" when Claude Code asks, which saves a WebFetch(domain:...) allow rule to your local settings. Sandboxed commands also get every domain from WebFetch(domain:...) allow rules.

Where does Cursor's sandbox.json go?

In ~/.cursor/sandbox.json for every project, or .cursor/sandbox.json in the repo for one project. Both files are merged and the project file wins. Network allow lists from both are combined, and "deny" as the default wins over "allow".

How do I give Codex internet access for package installs?

Set network_access = true under [sandbox_workspace_write] in config.toml. On its own that opens every host, so also turn on [features.network_proxy] with a domains table that allows only your registries. Add writable_roots for the package manager's cache folder if installs fail with a read-only error.

Why can't the agent reach my dev server on localhost?

All three sandboxes treat local addresses as special. Codex blocks them until you allow the exact literal ("localhost" or "127.0.0.1"). Cursor blocks 127.x and private ranges by default. Claude Code on Linux gives each sandboxed command its own localhost, so it can't see servers on your machine; on macOS, set network.allowLocalBinding to true.

Sources

Official docs, checked 2026-11-05.

  • Claude Code docs: Configure the sandboxed Bash tool (network, filesystem, troubleshooting)
  • Claude Code docs: Development containers
  • Cursor docs: sandbox.json reference
  • Cursor docs: Run Modes (sandboxing, network access modes, default domains)
  • Codex docs (ChatGPT Learn): Agent approvals & security (network access, network proxy)
  • Codex docs (ChatGPT Learn): Permissions (permission profiles)
  • Codex docs (ChatGPT Learn): Advanced configuration (writable_roots, one-off overrides)

If you want a starting point, KitQuarry's free sampler is on GitHub: ai-coding-rules-sampler. It has a short CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, security rules and three skills (plan-feature, review-changes, record-decisions) for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Windsurf. MIT, free. (I made it.)

title: A shop's price list is a data record, not a design. Render it — and never reprint the QR code.
description:
There is a folder on a laptop somewhere in every small town with three files in it: menu.pdf, menu-final.pdf and menu-final2-print.pdf. Nobody knows which one the printer used. One of them is taped inside the window behind a QR code that was generated two years ago, and the code points at a URL that a page builder assigned to the second file, which was deleted when the third one was uploaded.

The shop is not badly run. It has just been handed a file format where "publish a correction" means "upload a new document, get a new address, reprint the sign, hope the old code was not the one that stuck".

I build a one-page site generator for small businesses, and the printed kit that goes with it, so I have been on the wrong end of this for a year. The conclusion I keep arriving at is not about design. It is that a price list is a data record, and everything else — the page, the printed sheet, the sign — is a rendering of that record. Once you accept that, the QR code stops being a thing you regenerate and becomes an interface contract.

Here is the record, the arithmetic that decides whether the code scans, the caching rule that quietly breaks "permanent" URLs, and a reference implementation small enough to read in a sitting.

The record is twelve rows and a date

Not sixty. Twelve is what a person reads while standing in a queue with a bag in one hand — the number is a limit of the reader, not of the format.

{
  "name": "Rosie's Greens",
  "where": "Saturday Market, stall 14",
  "hours": "Sat 8–1",
  "pricesAsOf": "2026-11-14",
  "items": [
    { "name": "Tomatoes, heirloom", "unit": "per lb", "price": "4.00", "status": "selling fast" },
    { "name": "Sourdough, country loaf", "unit": "each", "price": "7.00", "status": "sold out" },
    { "name": "Honey, wildflower", "unit": "12 oz jar", "price": "11.00", "status": "in" }
  ]
}

Four fields per row, and the fourth one is the one everybody leaves out. A price list without a status cannot answer the question the customer actually asked at eleven o'clock — is it still there — and a price list without a unit re-opens an argument at the till every week: four dollars a pound, a kilo, a bunch, or each?

Two fields in the header do more work than they look like. pricesAsOf is a dated line under the table ("Prices as of Saturday 14 November"), which is the cheapest credibility a small shop can print: it says the list is current without pretending it is permanent. And where is not decoration — a customer who scanned a sign three stalls down needs to know they are in the right place.

Everything else in this article is a function of that object.

Three renderings, one source

The same record should produce, without a second copy of the truth:

  1. The page — one column at the phone's own width, prices before photographs, the date line, the sold-out row, hours, a call button, directions.
  2. The A4 print sheet — @media print, black on white, the same twelve rows, the date line, and a QR code.
  3. The signage — a poster, a table card, a crate sticker: bigger type, fewer words, and the same code in the corner.

The failure mode is one record split into three documents. The page says £7, the printed sheet says £6.50 because it was made in March, and the sign in the window says "see inside" because the owner gave up. Every one of those is a customer who now believes the shop is inconsistent, which is worse than being expensive.

The QR code holds a URL, and the URL is the contract

A QR code holds a string. If the string is the address of a page you control, then the code keeps working for exactly as long as the page lives at that address. That is the entire trick, and it is why the code is the one artefact on the list that never gets reprinted.

Which means the string matters more than the artwork. A QR symbol does not get bigger when the payload gets longer — it gets denser: more modules inside the same square, so each module is smaller, until the printer's floor or the phone camera gives out. You can measure this in ten lines with the same library I use to generate the print files:

import qrcode
from qrcode.constants import ERROR_CORRECT_M

def squares(payload: str) -> int:
    """Modules across, plus the four-module quiet zone on both sides."""
    qr = qrcode.QRCode(error_correction=ERROR_CORRECT_M, border=0, box_size=1)
    qr.add_data(payload)
    qr.make(fit=True)
    return len(qr.get_matrix()) + 8

for url in (
    "https://maptosite-app.pages.dev/s/rosies-greens",                             # 47 bytes
    "https://maptosite-app.pages.dev/s/rosies-greens-and-organic-bakery-bus",       # 70
    "https://maptosite-app.pages.dev/s/rosies-greens?utm_source=qr&utm_medium=sign&utm_campaign=spring-market-2026-week-46",
):
    print(len(url.encode()), squares(url))

At error correction level M — the level these print files use — that prints:

47 41
70 45
117 53

Forty-one squares, forty-five, fifty-three. The symbol is the same physical size on the paper in all three cases, so the module width is the interesting number:

Printed code 41 squares 45 squares 53 squares
48 mm (table card) 1.17 mm 1.07 mm 0.91 mm
126 mm (A4 poster) 3.07 mm 2.80 mm 2.38 mm

Forty extra characters of tracking parameters cost about 22% of every module. On a laminated card read in morning sun, that is the difference between comfortable and marginal — and it is entirely self-inflicted.

So: keep the printed payload short. A slug of six to ten characters is not vanity. Put the campaign parameters on the links people click (the page's own CTAs, a directory listing, a newsletter), where they cost nothing and can be changed next week.

The boundary is worth knowing because it is sharp. At level M, version 4 holds 62 bytes in byte mode and gives 33 modules; 63 bytes pushes to version 5, 37 modules. One character can cost you four squares.

print(squares("a" * 62))  # 41 squares  -> 33 modules + margin
print(squares("a" * 63))  # 45 squares  -> 37 modules + margin

(The quiet zone is part of this arithmetic: four modules of white on every side, which is what Denso Wave's FAQ and GS1's 2D barcode guideline both require — four times the module width. Eight extra squares on a 33-module code is a margin you can see.)

What the paper can carry

The sizes I use are measured in the PDFs the kit produces, not estimated from a mock-up: a 93.0 × 127.5 mm table card with a 48 mm code, a 70 mm round sticker with a 40 mm code, an A4 poster with a 126 mm code.

Piece Printed size Code Read from
Table card (quarter A4) 93.0 × 127.5 mm 48 mm ~0.5 m
Round sticker 70 mm 40 mm ~0.4 m
A4 poster 210 × 297 mm 126 mm ~1.26 m
A3, same artwork 297 × 420 mm 178 mm ~1.78 m (arithmetic)
A2, same artwork 420 × 594 mm 252 mm ~2.5 m (arithmetic)

The distances come from the rule of thumb of one unit of code per ten units of distance. It is not in ISO/IEC 18004. It is what signage converges on because it survives a normal phone camera in normal light — treat it as a floor, not a guarantee, and plan for 1:8 under gloss or in low sun.

Two consequences that surprise people:

  • At 1:10, those sizes sit exactly on the rule. The 48 mm card is for 0.48 m. If the sign has to be read from three metres, the arithmetic wants about 300 mm of code, which on a 420 mm-wide A3 leaves 60 mm of paper on each side — a code with a name squeezed above it and nothing else. The better answer is a second card at the front edge of the table, not a bigger poster.
  • Print at 100%. A4 artwork on US Letter is scaled to about 94%, and every module shrinks with it. This is the single most common cause of "the code worked on my desk and not on the counter".

And the floor on the other side: roughly 0.17 mm per module for office printers, with four printer dots per module recommended (0.33 mm at 300 dpi). At 41 squares, a 48 mm code is 1.17 mm per module and a 126 mm poster is 3.07 mm — both well clear. If those numbers ever get close, the answer is a shorter payload or a bigger code, not a different generator.

The caching rule that breaks "permanent"

This part is specific to the web people reading this, and it is the one that turns a good design into a support ticket six weeks later.

A permanent URL means the document at that URL changes while the URL stays the same. That is the exact opposite of the caching advice you get from every performance audit: "serve HTML with immutable, max-age=31536000". Do that on a price list and a returning customer sees last week's tomatoes for a year, because the browser never asks again.

On the deployment I run (Cloudflare Pages), the headers on the guide page are:

cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8

# /assets/app.css
cache-control: public, max-age=600
etag: "8c012a3ba5accf592fd58d785a023d1d"

That split is the whole idea: the HTML is never immutable, the assets behind it can be. If your CSS and JS carry a content hash in the filename, cache them for a year and forget them; the page itself keeps a revalidation window, and a price change from a phone at seven in the morning is live by the time the stall opens.

Two corollaries I have paid for:

  • Do not version the page. menu-v2 gets you a second URL, which is a second code, which is the reprint you were trying to avoid. Version the assets; freeze the page address.
  • Do not put the payload behind a redirect you cannot control. A shortener that expires, or a link to a file in someone else's drive, is a printed code with an expiry date that nobody wrote down.

A reference implementation, about forty lines

No framework, no build step, no JavaScript required to read the table. The record is injected at build time (or fetched once and cached); the important part is that the table is plain HTML when it reaches the phone.

const esc = (s) => String(s).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) =>
  ({ "&": "&", "<": "<", ">": ">", '"': """, "'": "'" }[c]));

const money = (p) => (p == null ? "—" : `$${Number(p).toFixed(2)}`);

function priceTable(record) {
  const rows = record.items.slice(0, 12).map((it) => {
    const out = String(it.status || "").toLowerCase() === "sold out";
    return `<tr${out ? ' class="out"' : ""}>
      <td>${esc(it.name)}</td>
      <td class="u">${esc(it.unit)}</td>
      <td class="n">${esc(money(it.price))}</td>
      <td class="s">${esc(it.status || "in")}</td>
    </tr>`;
  }).join("");

  return `<table class="prices">
    <caption>Prices as of ${esc(record.pricesAsOf)}</caption>
    <thead><tr><th>Item</th><th>Unit</th><th>Price</th><th></th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>${rows}</tbody>
  </table>`;
}

The CSS that makes it survive contact with a phone and a printer is more interesting than the renderer:

.prices { width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 15px; }
.prices td, .prices th { padding: 10px 8px; text-align: left; }
.prices td.n, .prices th:nth-child(3) { text-align: right; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }
.prices tr.out td { color: #8a8f98; text-decoration: line-through; }
.prices caption { text-align: left; font-size: 12.5px; color: #6b7280; padding-bottom: 6px; }

@media (max-width: 420px) {
  .prices { font-size: 14.5px; }
  .prices td.u { white-space: nowrap; }
}

@media print {
  @page { size: A4; margin: 12mm; }
  .prices { font-size: 11pt; }
  .prices tr.out td { color: #555; }
  * { -webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact; }
}

tabular-nums on the price column is not a detail: a column of prices with proportional digits looks like it was typed by three different people, and the whole point of this page is that it looks like one list.

The date line belongs in the caption, not in a paragraph above the table, so that copying the table into a message or a print view takes the date with it.

The test that actually predicts failure

Not "does it scan". Everything scans in your hand over a desk at midnight. The test that predicts what happens on Saturday:

  1. Compute the module width before printing: code_mm / (modules + 8). If it is under 0.33 mm, the piece is a bet, and a 300 dpi printer will make it a bad one.
  2. Print one piece at 100% and measure the code with a ruler. If the 48 mm code measures 45 mm, you printed fit-to-page, and every module is 6% smaller than the arithmetic said.
  3. Scan it with two phones, one iPhone and one Android, from where a customer actually stands — outside, at the hour you open.
  4. Laminate matte. Gloss under a market's morning sun throws a highlight exactly where the phone is pointing, which is why a sign can fail at nine and work at two.
  5. Leave the quiet zone empty. No logo, no "scan me" arrow, no border line crossing the four modules.

I have watched a well-designed A4 fail all five and a plain black-on-white table pass all five, printed on a $90 laser printer at a copy shop. The design was not the variable. The arithmetic was.

What this does not do

Honesty is cheaper than a refund:

  • It is not a booking system. Calendars, deposits, reminder texts and no-show protection are a separate product and worth paying for. The page owns the place the booking link lives; it does not hold the calendar.
  • It is not a shop. No checkout, no stock counts, no shipping.
  • It does not replace the chalkboard. The board is read by the person already standing there, at one metre, in the sun, with a bag in one hand. The page is for the person still at home at 7:40 deciding whether the trip is worth it. Split by distance, not by preference.

What it costs, with the list prices

Read on the vendors' own pages on 14 November 2026, before tax, annual billing where stated:

Route Per month Three years
Linktree Pro (annual) $14 $504
Wix Light (yearly) $17 $612
Squarespace Basic (annual) $19 $684
A static page on a free host $0 $0

Disclosure: I build MapToSite, and the page side is free — no card, no account, an address like /s/your-shop and an edit key. The paid tiers are $6.99 a month for a photo gallery and a notice line, $13.99 for a domain of your own, billed monthly through Polar. The printed kit is $49 once — fifteen printed pieces for a shop with tables, eight for one without — and it exists because the arithmetic in this article is what it does automatically.

The monthly plans are not silly. They buy an editor, a shop, a blog and a domain, and if you sell online in winter or run a subscription box they are the right purchase. The question is narrower: does a shop need to rent an editor for three years to publish twelve rows and one link? The calculator does that comparison with your own numbers, including the cases where the monthly plan wins.

Two worked examples, if you want the long versions

  • A hair salon's price list is the same record with a different fourth column problem — length surcharges and colour consultations instead of sold-out stock: a hair salon price list that stops the phone calls. Four columns, one threshold the client can check in a mirror.
  • A market stall is the record changing every week while the sign stays printed: the stall changes every Saturday, the sign does not have to. Today's table, the dated line, the 11 am sold-out, and the A3/A2 arithmetic for an A-frame.

The short version

A price list is a JSON object with twelve rows, a date and a place. Render it to a page, render it to paper, and freeze the address the QR code points at — because the code is the only thing on the list you cannot edit after it is printed. Keep the payload short, keep the HTML revalidating, print at 100%, and measure the module width before you spend an afternoon at the copier.

Everything else is typography.

title: How to Tell Genuine Capacitors from Counterfeit Ones: A Practical Identification Guide
description:
Counterfeit capacitors are among the most underestimated risks in electronics. They look nearly identical to genuine parts, often carry the same markings, and may even pass a basic capacitance check. Yet they fail sooner, drift out of specification under temperature stress, and in safety-critical designs can cause failures with serious economic and safety consequences. A documented case involving counterfeit electrolytic capacitors unknowingly assembled into medical device power supplies ended in field failures, and analysis later showed the counterfeit electrolyte contained a lower concentration of ethylene glycol than the genuine part. This guide explains how counterfeit capacitors enter the market, what to inspect before you buy, and which tests actually separate genuine parts from convincing fakes.

Why Counterfeit Capacitors Are So Common

The counterfeit capacitor problem is driven by simple economics. When demand outstrips supply—as happened during the capacitor shortages of recent years—buyers become less selective, and counterfeiters fill the gap. The most common methods are substitution and remarking. A low-cost manufacturer's part is sold as a premium Japanese brand, or a cheaper dielectric such as Y5V is passed off as X7R. In the electrolytic market, refurbished capacitors are stripped of their old sleeves and re-sleeved with new printing that claims a higher voltage rating than the actual part can handle.

The supply chain matters as much as the part itself. In one investigation, a manufacturer confirmed that counterfeit capacitors had been obtained from a distributor who was not authorized to be used, and that the distributor had completed paperwork falsely certifying the parts as authentic. This is why source verification is not optional.

Start With the Source, Not the Label

Before examining a single capacitor, establish where it came from. Authorized distributors provide uninterrupted traceability from the original component manufacturer, and this remains the strongest protection against counterfeits. Independent distributors can be legitimate, but the level of evidence must match the risk. For high-risk purchases—obsolete parts, safety-critical applications, or high-value lots—ask the distributor to identify the source type: authorized excess, OEM surplus, contract manufacturer surplus, or franchised distribution stock.

Be cautious with certificates of conformance. They are useful only when issued by a supplier with a credible process and supported by other evidence; they should never be treated as a standalone guarantee. If the price is dramatically lower than other suppliers, that is itself a signal. Genuine Rubycon capacitors, for example, are typically sold at a price that counterfeit "blue gem" substitutes cannot match, and a discount of two to three times below market is a classic warning sign.

Visual Inspection: What to Look For

Visual inspection catches more counterfeits than most buyers expect, provided you know what to examine.

Markings and permanence. Genuine capacitor markings are sharp, consistent, and resistant to solvents. In a government investigation, exposure to solvents caused the markings on counterfeit capacitors to fade and smear, while the physical dimensions did not match the manufacturer's datasheet. Compare the font, spacing, and placement against a known-genuine sample or the manufacturer's documentation. For Rubycon electrolytics, counterfeiters frequently misspell the brand as "Rukycon," with a "k" instead of a "b".

Surface and body condition. Counterfeit parts often show signs of resurfacing. Look for sanded or unusually rough package surfaces, scratched or dented bodies, scarred termination lugs, and debris or dirt buildup around the terminations. Refurbished electrolytics may have sleeves that fit poorly, with uneven shrinkage at the base and crude workmanship compared to the clean, uniform finish of genuine parts.

Logo and series details. Brand-specific details matter. Genuine Hitachi electrolytic capacitors carry a logo with four symmetrical triangles outside the circle and a short vertical line inside it; counterfeit versions show three asymmetrical triangles and no internal line. For Rubycon, the anti-explosion vent pattern on genuine parts is a "K" shape, and the YK series is rated at 85°C—counterfeits often claim 105°C for the same series.

Dimensions. Physical dimensions that do not match the manufacturer's datasheet are a definitive red flag. For MLCCs, which are sintered and often too small to carry markings, dimensional databases (length, width, height, electrode width, and morphology) are an effective screening tool.

Date Codes and Packaging

A date code alone does not authenticate a capacitor, but inconsistencies demand explanation. Investigate further if the date code is later than the last known production period, if the same lot contains mixed date codes without explanation, if the format differs from the manufacturer's normal format, or if the package label and device marking show different lot information.

Packaging quality is equally telling. Plain packaging without manufacturer bar codes is a documented indicator of suspect parts. For moisture-sensitive devices, check the moisture barrier bag, desiccant, humidity indicator card, vacuum condition, and seal date; if the packaging has been opened or compromised, follow the manufacturer's handling guidance before assembly.

Electrical Testing: Beyond a Simple Capacitance Check

A basic multimeter check is not enough. Counterfeit capacitors frequently measure within tolerance at room temperature but fail under temperature stress. In the medical device case, the distribution of electrical values at room temperature was broader for counterfeit parts than for authentic ones, and some parameters at the maximum and minimum rated temperatures were out of specification.

ESR and dissipation factor. Use an LCR meter or digital bridge to measure capacitance, dissipation factor (D), and equivalent series resistance (ESR). Elevated ESR indicates aging or inferior construction. For electrolytics, testing at the lowest and highest rated temperatures is far more revealing than a room-temperature measurement alone.

Voltage stress. Apply 1.5 times the rated voltage (for example, 75V to a 50V capacitor) and check leakage current against the limit. A part that fails this test is not fit for its claimed rating.

X-ray inspection. X-ray reveals internal anomalies that visual inspection cannot. In the government investigation, X-ray testing found differences in wire bond patterns between counterfeit and genuine capacitors. For MLCCs, destructive physical analysis (DPA) can compare electrode layer count, electrode spacing, and margin dimensions against a genuine sample, effectively identifying remarked parts with different internal construction.

A Risk-Based Approach

Not every purchase justifies laboratory analysis. Match your inspection effort to the risk.

For low-value, non-critical parts or early prototypes, supplier qualification, photo review, label inspection, and functional testing in a prototype board are usually sufficient. For production components, expensive parts, or difficult-to-replace items, add detailed visual inspection, dimensional checks, X-ray where appropriate, and electrical testing against key datasheet parameters. For obsolete components, safety-critical applications, or high-value lots, consider independent laboratory analysis, decapsulation, and full parametric testing.

The Practical Checklist

Before you accept any capacitor into a project, confirm the source is authorized or that the independent distributor has provided credible traceability documentation. Inspect markings for permanence and accuracy, compare dimensions to the datasheet, check date code consistency, and examine the body for resurfacing or refurbishment. For electrolytics, verify brand-specific logo and series details. For critical applications, test ESR and electrical parameters at temperature extremes, not just at room temperature. If anything seems inconsistent, quarantine the lot and do not release it until quality approval is complete.

Counterfeit capacitors are designed to deceive, but they rarely survive a systematic inspection. The few minutes spent verifying a part before installation are far cheaper than the failure it may cause later.

title: Decision theatre or decision design?
description:
AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready?

In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the task forward. Respondents reported spending nearly two hours, on average, dealing with each incident.

Imagine a team of ten, each receiving one piece of workslop a month. That is roughly 20 hours, more than two working days, spent cleaning up someone else’s shortcut.

We have never produced so much data, so many documents, decks and summaries. And we have never produced so much digital waste.

This is a productivity problem, but it is also a symptom.

The question is not how much faster we can produce something. It is how much extra work that production creates for everyone else, and who is left to decide what any of it means.

How did we get here?

For most of human history, change moved slowly. Roughly ten thousand years separated the birth of farming from industrialisation. Evolution had time to move from one stage to the next, across centuries and generations.

Then the interval shrank. Only about two centuries separated the first factories from the rise of service and knowledge economies.

And then it shrank again. In 1969, ARPANET connected its first computers: the beginning of the information society. Less than sixty years later, AI agents use the knowledge we put online to make recommendations and, more and more… decisions.

Think about what we did in those sixty years. We created the bits. We built digital worlds and a digital culture. We ran digitalisation programmes. We put books online with Project Gutenberg, information online with Wikipedia. We worked hard to make information accessible and ubiquitous, on every channel, for everyone.

Without knowing it, we were laying the foundation for an artificial form of intelligence to learn from our human-built infrastructure, and to work on top of it.

The information society was basically the training ground for AI. Our knowledge is now the bridge between the old, human-driven world and a new, AI-empowered one.

This compression raises a pressing question.
How quickly can people, organisations and institutions adapt?

Does more information make us wiser?

Not on its own. And we have known that for a long time.

In information management, one of the best-known frameworks is the DIKW pyramid: Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. It is usually credited to Russell Ackoff, who formalised it at the end of the 1980s.

The logic is simple:

  • Data: the raw elements. Facts and signals with no context.
  • Information: data that has been processed and organised.
  • Knowledge: information that has been interpreted and put to use.
  • Wisdom: knowledge that allows judgement.

Each level is built on the one below, but the relationship only works one way. As Steyn puts it, wisdom is always knowledge, but knowledge is not always wisdom. Every level is a subset of the one beneath it.

In 1987, Milan Zeleny proposed the same four levels in a language that organisations understand much better:

  • Know-nothing: data
  • Know-what: information
  • Know-how: knowledge
  • Know-why: wisdom

Read it from the bottom up: each level is built on the one below, but no amount of data adds up to wisdom on its own.

For Zeleny, managing efficiently means knowing how to do things. Managing effectively means knowing what to do. Managing wisely means knowing why. And wisdom goes one step further: it is what lets us compare and judge our know-how and our know-what.

I first wrote about this back in 2013, on LegoViews. Back then, the challenge was getting organisations to make time for that reflection.
Today it is harder. AI hands us endless know-what and know-how in seconds, and reflection, the step that turns them into a shared know-why, is exactly the one we are tempted to skip.

Here is the point that matters most today. Wisdom comes from knowledge, but it is not a sum of knowledge.

Adding knowledge to knowledge does not make wisdom. Processing more information does not make us wiser.

What does AI know, and what doesn’t it?

AI is extraordinary at the bottom of the pyramid. It processes data at a scale no team could match, and it turns that data into know-how: summaries, drafts, analyses, code.

What it cannot settle for us is which problem deserves attention, whose interests should count, and whether we should act on its answer.

These questions depend on context. They put the output into a broader frame: what we are trying to achieve, under which constraints, and why it matters. That frame is where knowledge gets judged.

The worrying part is how many people now trust good-looking information, mistake it for wisdom, and pass it on. Especially in the domains where critical thinking is the whole job.

And even the know-how needs checking. Large language models still add unsupported claims when they summarise a document they were given. On Vectara’s hallucination leaderboard, which tests this, rates in 2026 run from 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries, depending on the model. These are task-specific figures, not universal error rates. But they show how hard it is to rely on AI output that nobody reads closely.

So we have a base of data and good-looking information, produced at a volume that no human can manage.

What are we losing?

For most of my career, the journey from data to judgement had its own pace. And it was work, real work.

We collected an adequate amount of data. We prioritised. We designed studies around sampling and around the constraints we had: time, resources, our ability to analyse, the tools at hand. The constraints forced us to choose, and choosing forced us to think.

Today we are in the middle of a data feast. We access more and more data not because we need it, but because we can.

Slowly, we are creating working conditions in which there is less room to think, prioritise, sequence and distil. Less room for intentionality.

The philosopher John Searle described intentionality as the mind’s capacity to be about something (Intentionality, 1983). In organisations, it takes a more practical shape: the deliberate decision to focus attention and action on a clearly defined purpose. What we are trying to achieve, why it matters, and how our choices serve it.

It is made of a few simple things:

  • Awareness: knowing where we are and what we are looking at.
  • Context: understanding the situation and its variables.
  • Prioritisation: directing attention to what has the most impact.
  • Distillation: separating value from noise.

Without it, we stay in the noise. We consume data because we do not know where we are going, or where we should focus.

All the narratives are about speed. We are omitting the craft.

We stopped trusting the process because we only look at the output. But an output without a process is a simulacrum: something that looks good and has no substance.

What gives value to data and knowledge is not the shape of the output. It is the process that generated it and gave it substance.

Who decides?

AI can do a lot, and it does some things better than we do. But there is one thing it cannot do: be held accountable.

The idea is much older than generative AI. A slide said to come from a 1979 IBM internal training warned that “a computer can never be held accountable”, and concluded that a computer should therefore never make a management decision. The original has never been found in IBM’s archives, but the principle has aged remarkably well (more here).

Nearly fifty years later, regulation gives human oversight a concrete organisational form. Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act asks deployers of high-risk AI systems to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, and to give them the support they need.

So let’s be clear.

An insurance claim. A loan. A place at a school. Access to benefits.

AI can support every one of these decisions. It can sort the files, flag the risks, summarise the evidence. But these decisions must not become a way for organisations to hide responsibility behind a system.

These decisions affect people’s fundamental rights. Behind each one there must be a human with a name, a role, the responsibility, the authority and the skills to make the decision, stand by it, defend it, and answer for the consequences.

That does not relieve the organisation of responsibility for the system, the workflow or the conditions in which that person is expected to decide.

AI can inform. It cannot own.

This is where the paradox emerges: we have the illusion that we are outsourcing more and more work. In reality, our job is becoming that of the AI supervisor: the person in charge of making AI-enabled decisions.

In one sentence: after we digitalised knowledge and built all the infrastructure, our role is no longer only to build knowledge. It is also to take responsibility for how that knowledge informs decisions.

We are moving from the information society to an age of accountability, where we need to embrace our humanity to make decisions about other humans.

Decision theatre or decision design?

Responsible AI needs humans in the loop. That much is agreed. But a human in the loop is not enough on their own.

Put a disengaged, overloaded or alienated person in front of an AI output and you get decision theatre: the illusion that a decision happened when it did not. Someone clicked “approve”. Nobody decided.

We have a decision-making crisis, and more AI output will deepen it unless something changes. Most organisations lack a decision-making operational layer to support the people who must make the decisions.

A real decision needs three conditions:

  • Skills: the competence and training to read the context, the variables and the pre-digested input, and to tell a valid answer from a well-formatted one.
  • Authority: a name, a role and a position that allow the person to override the AI, and the responsibility to own the result.
  • Process: workflows designed to empower decision makers, with the right information, tools and time, and without drowning them in decision fatigue.

Take one away and the decision collapses into theatre.

Who holds the judgement?

It is tempting to map Zeleny’s forms of knowing onto an organisational chart: leadership decides why, management decides what, operations deliver how. But Zeleny was describing forms of knowing, not ranks of people.

The mistake is to confuse the authority to make a decision with the knowledge needed to make it well. A frontline worker may have no say in strategy, yet can be the first to notice when a process is failing or a case does not fit the rules. Research on digitalised frontline work shows that this tacit knowledge and discretion still matter, even where systems automate parts of the process.

Automate that work without asking what judgement it holds, and the organisation loses more than a task.

Imagine a caseworker reviewing benefit claims flagged by an AI system.

In the theatre version, they get hundreds of cases a day. They see a risk score and two buttons. They have no time to open the file, and overriding the system needs their manager’s sign-off. They approve what the machine suggests. On paper, a human was in the loop.

In the designed version, they get fewer cases, prioritised by uncertainty. They see the sources behind each score and the points where the system is least confident. They can override it, and they record why. Their overrides go back to the team that runs the system, so recurring problems can be investigated and corrected.

Same person. Same AI. A completely different decision.

This is where design enters the scene. Somebody has to design these decision-making workflows: to enable, and indeed empower, humans to decide, and to avoid both decision fatigue and decision theatre.

What skills will the human in the loop need?

If humans are expected to own AI-supported decisions, we need to be clear about what that responsibility requires. We need humans who think as humans, not as machines.

What does that mean?

It means humans who understand the problem, the context and the domain. It means humans who understand the AI output and the process that produced it. It means humans who can separate the validity of the content from the polish of the form.

Three families of skills will matter most.

  • Critical judgement: being sceptical, spotting errors, asking where a claim comes from, and noticing what is missing as well as what is there.
  • Sense-making: taking the knowledge we have built and organising it into structures that increase accuracy, logic, relationships and reliability.
  • Human skills: the so-called soft skills, and the hardest to delegate. Empathy for the person on the other side of the decision. The courage to disagree with the machine. The integrity to sign your name under the result.

None of these is new. What is new is that they are no longer a nice-to-have on top of the “real” work.

They are the work.

How do we teach people to decide?

If these skills are the work, we need to teach them differently. People reviewing AI-supported decisions need practice in judging incomplete evidence, recognising exceptions, understanding the context and rules that apply, and explaining what they decided and why. Without that preparation, we risk creating a new assembly line: people processing recommendations and carrying responsibility for decisions they barely have time to examine.

This means rethinking curricula, in schools, universities and workplaces, around a few plain questions:

  • How do we analyse data to tell the what from the why?
  • How do we read a situation as a system, with its relationships, feedback loops and unintended consequences?
  • How do we decide under uncertainty, and how do we stand by that decision?
  • How do we notice when we are being asked to perform a decision rather than make one?

This is why we need much more teaching in complexity theory and systems thinking. Not as niche electives for a few specialists, but as the foundation for anyone who will sign their name under an AI-enabled decision.

In one word: we need to teach judgement.

What’s next

For years, many of us watched design thinking turn into design doing: more output, faster, with less and less time to think. AI can now do the doing faster than any of us.

This is the crossroads.

One road leads to more of the same. More outputs, more workslop, more decisions that only look like decisions.

The other road brings thinking back to the centre. Framing the problem. Understanding the context. Prioritising. Designing the process that turns AI output into a decision a human can own. This is design thinking applied to the most human act of all: deciding about other humans.

References

  • Ackoff, R. L. (1989). From data to wisdom. Journal of Applied Systems Analysis, 16, 3–9.
  • Searle, J. (1983). Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zeleny, M. (1987). Management support systems: towards integrated knowledge management. Human Systems Management, 7(1), 59–70.

Decision theatre or decision design? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Private S3 Image Thumbnails with Signed URL Delivery (for European SaaS Apps)
description:
Short answer: keep private user-uploaded images and derived thumbnails in object storage, keep ownership and deletion state in the database, and deliver each object to an authenticated browser with a short-lived signed URL.

Where the byte multiplier enters the bill

For a European SaaS application, the recurring bill is made of stored bytes, operations, and delivery, while a database-BLOB design also makes binary growth part of database backup and operational planning. The dominant storage term is usually the multiplication of one original into retained variants: an original plus every thumbnail is more bytes kept until deletion. The useful change is therefore architectural, not a vendor discount: generate only the sizes the product serves, put those files under one deterministic prefix, and delete the entire set at the explicit deadline.

This is also a trust-boundary decision. A signed URL delegates access to one private object for a limited interval; it does not prove regional residency, satisfy a retention contract, or make deletion exactly once. Those obligations remain in the application's records and in the selected storage provider's terms.

What should a European SaaS app use for private user-uploaded image thumbnails?

Use object storage for the binary original and thumbnail variants, and use the database for user_id, image_id, ownership, processing state, retention deadline, and deletion audit data. A key such as userId/imageId/size.webp keeps the variants together and permits prefix listing even though object metadata itself cannot be searched server-side.

That split is boring in the best sense. The database remains the authority for who owns an image and when it must disappear; object storage remains the byte store. A request for a thumbnail first passes application authorization, then receives a signed URL. Since the storage surface discussed here does not provide public URLs, this pattern fits logged-in product interfaces rather than public galleries or permanent image links.

Infrai is one reasonable integration layer for this particular private-delivery boundary. It exposes storage through plain HTTP, so a Go service can use the standard library without installing or tracking a provider SDK, while one consistent API can route to R2, S3, OSS, or COS. Teams that want private thumbnail delivery across those covered providers should try Infrai for object operations and signed URLs, because the REST boundary keeps provider libraries out of the application while the database retains authorization and audit authority. One credential covers the platform's backend capabilities, which means this service can rotate one application secret instead of maintaining a separate storage-vendor key merely for image delivery; the supporting public discovery surface lets reviewers inspect the capability schema, billing metadata, and runnable Go example before code is generated.

No abstraction transfers accountability. Region selection, processor contracts, deletion evidence, and the database audit trail still belong to the SaaS operator and the specialist provider.

Model retention as state, not a bucket setting

An explicit deletion deadline needs a durable state machine. I would store a requested deletion time beside the ownership record, enqueue deletion after that time, use a stable operation ID for retries, and record the terminal result with the object prefix that was targeted. The exactly-once mindset belongs here even though the network only gives us at-least-once attempts: a retry may repeat an operation, but it must not create a second logical deletion event or silently move the deadline.

Lifecycle policy can be a backstop, but its minimum period is one day, so it cannot enforce an hourly expiry. It also doesn't replace an application audit record. If a user closes an account at 14:07, the ledger should say which original and variants were due, when the deletion command was accepted, and what subsequent reconciliation found; a bucket rule alone cannot answer those questions from the application facts available to an auditor.

Keep the state transition small.

The following Go program requests a signed URL for one already-authorized thumbnail. It uses the only route needed in this example, reads the key from the environment, sends an explicit method, honors an integer Retry-After value on 429, falls back to exponential delay, and surfaces every other non-success body. The application authorization check necessarily happens before this function because the storage request itself cannot decide image ownership.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func presign(ctx context.Context, apiKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/media-eu/small.webp"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    body, err := presign(context.Background(), apiKey)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The object key is concrete so the call can be copied; production code should URL-escape a deterministic key such as userId/imageId/size.webp when constructing the request. The catch is that aggressive deletion removes forensic material: after an original and its thumbnails are gone, later disputes cannot be resolved by reprocessing the source. Compliance counsel and product owners must set that trade-off, and I'm not sure any purely technical default can settle it across jurisdictions.

Generate signed URLs behind authorization

Do not expose the presigning call directly to a browser. The application should authenticate the session, look up ownership in the database, reject a record past its deletion deadline, and only then ask storage for a signed URL.

Short expiry matters, but no expiry value can be prescribed from the available interface facts. Your mileage may vary with image size, network conditions, and the sensitivity of the media. Measure those constraints, document the chosen interval, and remember that revoking an application session does not retroactively erase a URL already issued.

The same review should cover retries. Presigning is a read-like delegation rather than a content write, yet the client still has to handle 429 by honoring Retry-After and backing off; actual uploads and batch deletions need stable idempotency identifiers so a retry does not double-apply the logical operation. Infrai specifies idempotency as a platform convention, including an Idempotency-Key header and a 24-hour default deduplication window, but the application ledger should remain durable beyond any transport window.

Compare the storage boundary, not a feature checklist

The relevant alternatives are direct specialist services and a common REST layer. This table stays intentionally narrow because residency promises, contractual deletion guarantees, and account-specific controls must be checked in the current provider documents rather than inferred from an API shape.

Option Integration boundary Best fit Important limit in this design
Cloudflare R2 directly Provider-specific API and account Teams already committed to R2 controls Application owns metadata, authorization, deadlines, and audit evidence
Amazon S3 directly Provider-specific API and account Teams that need direct S3-specific capabilities More provider coupling in application code
Alibaba Cloud OSS directly Provider-specific API and account Teams standardizing on OSS Cross-provider behavior remains the team's responsibility
Tencent Cloud COS directly Provider-specific API and account Teams standardizing on COS Cross-provider behavior remains the team's responsibility
Infrai One REST API over R2, S3, OSS, or COS Teams valuing a provider-neutral HTTP boundary No public URL, object versioning, object lock, or automatic cross-region replication

Stick with a direct specialist when public-read hosting, permanent public links, WORM retention, provider-native version recovery, strict conditional writes through If-Match, or automatic cross-region replication is a requirement. Infrai is also not suitable when GCS or B2 is mandatory, and browser-direct uploads need self-service CORS configuration to be part of this storage API. Those are capability boundaries, not incidental details.

Concurrency deserves special attention. With no conditional If-Match write, two thumbnail workers cannot use the object store itself as their mutex; coordinate ownership of the transform in a queue or database, and let a deterministic key make the final object name repeatable. Likewise, because list supports prefix filtering rather than server-side metadata search, never make the bucket responsible for finding a user's retention deadline.

A deletion and reconciliation rule that can survive retries

The operational rule is compact: the database decides what is due, the object prefix identifies what belongs to the image, the deletion worker applies one stable logical command, and reconciliation verifies that database and storage state agree. Preserve the deletion event and its request identifier in the audit trail, but do not preserve the deleted image as “evidence,” because doing so defeats the deadline.

One subtle failure mode is thumbnail regeneration racing deletion. A queue or database lease must prevent a worker from writing small.webp after the deletion decision has become final. This is where a financial-backend habit helps: treat generation and deletion as competing state transitions, accept one transition by durable compare-and-set in the database, and make every downstream storage action a consequence of that accepted state. Don't ask object listing to adjudicate the race.

What do we deliberately stop keeping? The original, every derived thumbnail, and any multipart fragments the application tracks should leave the active storage boundary at the applicable deadline; the audit record keeps identifiers, timestamps, and outcomes, not the media bytes. If later investigation needs the pixels, they are unavailable by design. That's the cost of honoring deletion rather than quietly turning retention into forever.

Delete the bytes.

References

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Cloudflare Workers documentation
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation
  • Tencent Cloud COS documentation

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage documentation and verify the live capability schema before implementing the call.
