title: How to Verify Oracle Database 19c Release Update Patching in CDB and PDB Environments
description:
Oracle Database 19c Release Update Verification

Technology – Oracle Database 19c, Release Update (19.32), Multitenant.

Lab Date – 12th November 2026.

Overview

Applying a Release Update to your Oracle Database is an important part of the DBA role.

However, simply applying a patch may not mean that all parts of your database will run as expected.

The DBA should verify that the patch has been applied successfully, in Oracle 19c (especially with the multi-tenant architecture), by checking at different levels.

Even though the patch may have been applied to the Oracle Home, we also need to check that the SQL have been applied. We should also ensure that our Container Database (CDB) and Pluggable Databases (PDBs) are open and running correctly.

This guide will demonstrate how to verify that this is the case using a combination of Oracle OPatch, SQLPlus, Dictionary Views and SQL.

Lab Evidence

The aim of this guide is to demonstrate how you can verify that your patch has been applied successfully.

Oracle Database 19c Test Environment

I carried out my verification in a test environment with the following setup:

Section

Details

Database

Oracle Database 19c

Release Update

19.32

Patch ID

39472050

Architecture

Container Database (with Pluggable Database)

Verification Tool

SQLPlus

Verification

Patch was applied to Database via SQL. PDB status was confirmed. PDB was confirmed to be ‘Saved’.

As the database contains sensitive information, we should not include any database names, server names or anything specific to the infrastructure.

The SQL examples will include generic names.

Why Patch Verification Is Important

Oracle will release patches to fix any issues relating to defects, security, stability and other issues.

A Release Update (RU) is a cumulative patch provided as part of Oracle’s regular maintenance cycle.

As a DBA there are 3 key areas we should consider:

Oracle Home Patches

Oracle Home contains all of the required binaries, executables, libraries and tools needed for the database.

We can use the OPatch tool to identify what patches have been applied.

SQL Patches

Some patches will require SQL to be applied to the database dictionary or components.

Oracle provide us with a tool called datapatch to APPLY these SQL patches.

The database will have a registry showing what SQL patches have been applied.

Database Running Correctly

Even though the registry may show that the patch was applied successfully, we should also verify that the database and PDBs are running correctly.

For example, the PDB may not be available for applications as it is still mounted.

Or the PDB may be open successfully but not have any saved state so will remain mounted after the instance is restarted.

Therefore multiple checks are required to verify that the patch was applied successfully.

  1. Oracle Home Patch Verification

An important first step is to check what patches have been applied to your Oracle Home.

Login to your database server with the correct owner account for the Oracle software.

Ensure that you have the correct Oracle Home set up.

echo $ORACLE_HOME

Run the following command:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/opatch lspatches

For detailed information run:

$ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/opatch lsinventory

This can give us information about the patch IDs, descriptions and software that have been applied.

Our Oracle Database 19c Release Update (19.32) patch ID was:

39472050

Patch Description:

Database Release Update: 19.32.0.0.260721

Why This Is Important

This will help us identify whether the correct binaries have been applied for our patch. However, this alone will not tell us if the SQL patches were successfully applied to all of the database containers. Therefore we should now check the SQL patches.

[Note: The lab material I used for this article shows that the SQL registry was successful. However, I did not have a standalone test OPatch inventory to compare. The commands above will help you verify the inventory.]

  1. Check SQL Patches In CDB & PDB

Oracle Database provide dictionary views to allow you to check what SQL patches have been applied.

One of the most important views is:

CDB_REGISTRY_SQLPATCH

Login to the CDB root with a valid admin session.

First, check what container you are in.

SHOW CON_NAME;

Now run the following command:

SELECT

con_id,

patch_id,

action,

status,

action_time

FROM cdb_registry_sqlpatch

ORDER BY action_time DESC, con_id;

Column Details

Column

Description

CON_ID

Container ID identifying the database container

PATCH_ID

Patch ID identifying the patch

ACTION

Whether the patch was Applied or Rolled Back.

STATUS

Status of the patch.

ACTION_TIME

Time of action.

To specifically check for our Oracle Database Release Update (19.32) run:

SELECT

con_id,

patch_id,

action,

status

FROM cdb_registry_sqlpatch

WHERE patch_id = 39472050

ORDER BY con_id;

Lab Result

The SQLPlus command above returned:

CON_ID PATCH_ID ACTION STATUS

1 39472050 APPLY SUCCESS

3 39472050 APPLY SUCCESS

This proves that the SQL patch was successfully applied to both the CDB root and test PDB.

In this environment the container ID 1 was the CDB root and the container ID 3 was the user PDB.

Important Note

The SUCCESS means that the datapatch was applied successfully. However, this is just showing the history of the patch. We should also check whether there has been a more recent rollback or failure.

You cannot always assume that the latest patch state will be displayed as there may be an older successful row.

Also notice that there is no separate row for the PDB Seed. Do not assume that the PDB Seed has been patched successfully or not based on this output. You should review the relevant datapatch logs and patch documentation.

  1. Confirm PDB Open Mode

Having checked the SQL patches we should now check the current status of our pluggable databases.

In Oracle Database 19c, we have a multi-tenant architecture meaning we can have multiple PDB’s within the CDB.

Each PDB will have their own open mode.

Login to SQLPlus and run:

SHOW PDBS;

Or:

SELECT

con_id,

name,

open_mode,

restricted

FROM v$pdbs

ORDER BY con_id;

What The Output Means

READ WRITE

The PDB is open and can be used for reading and writing. This depends on user permissions and application.

READ ONLY

The PDB is open but cannot be used for normal data changes in applications.

MOUNTED

The PDB is not open.

RESTRICTED

If Restricted is set to YES then only users with the required privilege will have access.

Lab Result

Our test showed:

Container Open Mode Restricted

PDB Seed READ ONLY NO

User PDB READ WRITE NO

This proves that our test PDB was open in Read Write mode and was not restricted.

Opening PDB If Required

If a valid DBA decides that the PDB needs to be opened run the following command from the correct admin context:

-- Make sure to change LAB_PDB to correct PDB name.

-- Admin command to change database.

ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE LAB_PDB OPEN READ WRITE;

Do not run this command unless you have confirmed what state you want the database in and any change control.

Opening a PDB is an operational command and does not prove that the database was patched successfully.

  1. Confirm PDB Saved State

Another important part of verifying the patch is confirming that the PDB has a saved open state.

Whilst the PDB could be manually opened during maintenance/testing, the open mode may not be saved when the instance is restarted.

Oracle provide us with a way to save the desired open mode.

Within a valid test environment an administrator can run:

-- Make sure to change LAB_PDB to correct PDB name.

ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE LAB_PDB SAVE STATE;

This can be checked using:

SELECT

con_name,

instance_name,

state

FROM dba_pdb_saved_states

ORDER BY con_name;

Explanation

CON_NAME – Name of PDB.

INSTANCE_NAME – Name of database instance the state was saved.

STATE – Describes the open mode of the PDB.

Lab Result

The verification showed that the test PDB had a saved state:

STATE

OPEN

This proves that the PDB had a saved open state.

Why This Is Important

During planned maintenance the DBA may restart the database instance successfully but find that an application PDB is still mounted.

This can mean applications cannot connect.

By checking that the PDB has a saved state we can identify whether it has been configured to open in the desired mode.

In a multi-instance/RAC environment we should also check that the saved state is being applied to the correct instances.

Whilst this proves that there is a saved state configuration, a controlled restart and application connectivity would give stronger evidence.

  1. Real Test Results & Screenshots

We should base our report around the evidence of what was executed.

From our lab we had the following:

Verification Summary

Verification Result Interpretation

Oracle SQL Patch ID 39472050 Database RU 19.32

CDB Root SQL Patch APPLIED/SUCCESS SQL Patch applied successfully

User PDB SQL Patch APPLIED/SUCCESS SQL Patch applied successfully

PDB Open Mode READ WRITE Open in Read Write mode

PDB Restricted NO Not restricted

PDB Saved State OPEN Open state saved

OPatch Inventory (Oracle Home)

Not verified in this evidence. Will need to run inventory.

This proves that we have carried out the SQL Patch and PDB checks.

However, this does not prove that we have full application compatibility, that the database can be restored and recovered and that there are no issues at runtime.

Screenshot 1 – SQL Patch Registry

[Insert original SQLPlus screenshot]

This should show you have queried the CDB_REGISTRY_SQLPATCH view. Include Patch ID, container ID’s, action and status.

Remove/obscure any unnecessary information.

Screenshot 2 – PDB Open Status

[Insert original SHOW PDBS screenshot]

This should show that the test PDB is in Read Write mode and not restricted.

Screenshot 3 – PDB Saved State

[Insert original DBA_PDB_SAVED_STATES result]

This should show that the PDB has a saved OPEN state.

Screenshot 4 – OPatch Inventory

Only add if ran separately.

Having a current OPatch inventory can help strengthen your article. This proves that both the binaries and SQL have been verified.

Do not make up a screenshot, use a real one.

  1. Key Takeaways & Best Practice

We should have a structured approach to verifying our Oracle Database after applying a patch.

  1. Check Binaries & SQL

Whilst having a successful OPatch and datapatch are related they are separate.

Use OPatch inventory to confirm what software patches have been applied. Use SQL Patch registry to confirm what SQL have been applied to the database.

  1. Check All Relevant Containers

Within a multi-tenant environment we should consider the CDB root and user PDBs.

Check that all relevant containers have the correct Patch Status.

  1. Database Availability

When verifying your patch you should also check that the database is available.

A PDB may have been patched successfully but still be mounted.

  1. Check PDB Saved State

After carrying out maintenance, confirm that the PDB starts in the correct way.

If required, save the desired open state and check the relevant dictionary entry.

  1. Check Errors & Patch Logs

If there are any unexpected statuses in the patch registry, datapatch failures or discrepancies between the OPatch inventory and database SQL patch history investigate further.

Don’t blindly re-run any patching tools without understanding what the current state is and what the patch README says.

  1. Application Checks

Just because the database has been patched successfully does not mean that the applications will run as expected.

A full maintenance process should include valid checks to ensure applications can connect, critical functions are working and any relevant integration dependencies.

  1. Keep Evidence

Have a valid maintenance document detailing what patches have been applied, what results were achieved, what queries were run to verify and the time. This should be detailed enough to help troubleshoot any issues but should not expose any confidential information.

  1. Recommended Post-Patch Checklist

The following is a summary of what we should verify:

Verification Expected Evidence

Correct Oracle Home Environment & Inventory

Check RU Binaries Applied OPatch shows correct patch

Check SQL Patch Registry Latest applicable patch was applied successfully

Check CDB & PDB’s Checked relevant containers

Check PDB Open Mode Confirmed that PDB is open in correct mode

Check Restricted Matches intended access

Check PDB Saved State Confirmed that PDB has correct saved state

Check Datapatch Logs No unresolved patch failures

Check Database Components Investigate any unexpected invalid components

Application Checks Critical functions tested

Final Evidence Valid maintenance documentation

These are all complimentary checks and not all were proven from the lab evidence above.

Conclusion

We should not simply take it at face value that our Oracle Database has been patched successfully based on what the installer says. In an Oracle Database 19c multi-tenant environment we should check the Oracle Home inventory, SQL patch history, PDB availability and saved start up states.

Our lab results proved that we had SQL patches applied to our Oracle Database RU 19.32. The CDB root and user PDB had APPLIED/SUCCESS.

Our test PDB was confirmed to be open in Read Write mode, not restricted and had an OPEN saved state.

This provides us with useful evidence.

Overall we should have a reliable process for maintaining our patches. This includes verifying our software, database and operational checks, along with clear documentation. Having a structured checklist can help DBA’s identify any incomplete steps when maintaining.

References

Oracle Database Patch Maintenance (Release 19c and later)

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/dbptc/index.html

Oracle Database 19c – DBA_REGISTRY_SQLPATCH

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/refrn/DBA_REGISTRY_SQLPATCH.html

Oracle Database 19c – DBA_PDB_SAVED_STATES

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/refrn/DBA_PDB_SAVED_STATES.html

Oracle Database 19c – Administering Pluggable Databases

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/multi/administering-pdbs-with-sql-plus.html

Oracle Database 19c RU 19.32 – Oracle Linux 9 & RHEL 9 Install Guidance

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/rnrdm/installing-oracle-database-19c-oracle-linux-9-and-red-hat-enterprise-linux-9.html

Abdulrawof Totakhil
Database Administrator

title: Fintech Bundle Evidence: Verify Each PDF Signature Before Page Assembly
description:
Preserve each signed original before merging or splitting a fintech document bundle, and treat every rendered packet as a derivative with a separate acceptance decision. TL;DR: verify the original PDF signature under an explicit validation policy, retain the sending platform's evidence alongside it, and spend rendering effort on the document people need to read. A readable packet and defensible signature evidence answer different questions.

For a hypothetical loan review, consider 3 inputs: a signed agreement, an identity attachment, and a disclosure. The reviewer wants one packet; a later investigation may want the agreement exactly as received. Making the combined packet look faithful does not establish what the agreement's signature covers. The operational recommendation is therefore to preserve first, validate second, and transform only after the evidence boundary is recorded.

What page fired when the packet looked correct?

Start the postmortem with the failing decision. Did an original fail signature validation, did validation remain indeterminate, or did a reviewer receive a derivative whose relationship to the original was unclear? A dashboard showing completed jobs cannot resolve that distinction. Neither can a screenshot of a green signature indicator. Ask what page fired, which artifact it identified, and which acceptance rule was violated.

PDF signatures have a defined relationship to document bytes and revisions under ISO 32000-2. That is the useful starting point for this runbook: inspect the signed document itself before making a claim about its signature. A sending platform's completion evidence can add context about a workflow, but its presence alone should not be the condition that marks an independently received PDF as cryptographically validated. Conversely, validating a PDF signature should not silently stand in for accepting every claim about the surrounding business transaction.

Keep the bytes.

The trap is a pipeline that checks the agreement, merges its pages into a review packet, and then attaches the original validation result to the packet without identifying the original. The check may have been appropriate for its input, yet the label now points at a different artifact. Splitting creates the same bookkeeping risk: an extracted disclosure needs a traceable relationship to the source, and the source's signature result must remain attached to the source. Do not assume a transformation preserves signature validity; establish the result for the exact artifact and revision being discussed.

Should you verify a PDF signature before trusting the sending platform's evidence?

Fidelity needs a definition before it gets a budget. For this workflow, distinguish exact preservation of the signed source from visual fidelity of the review packet. Preserve the former as an acceptance requirement; evaluate the latter against the reviewer's needs. A packet can be useful without being the signed original, provided the interface and stored records make that relationship explicit.

Use independent verification when the receiving team needs a result it can reproduce under its own policy, including a clear record of the document and revision checked. That creates work: someone must select and maintain the validator, define the trust policy, interpret incomplete results, and own escalation. Accepting sending-platform evidence as sufficient for a particular workflow reduces that local responsibility, but makes the decision depend on the platform's evidence and the team's ability to retrieve and interpret it later. Preserve that evidence either way. These are different acceptance policies, and the policy belongs in the record rather than in an engineer's memory. In the hypothetical loan review, make the distinction visible to the operator: a platform completion record is available, the original has a separate validation decision, and the assembled packet has a separate visual acceptance result. If the independent decision remains unresolved, a completed rendering job must not overrule it. If the rendering fails, the retained original and its validation report should still be available. This separation gives the responder somewhere specific to look without treating every failure as a reason to repeat every operation.

Don't make a rendering retry carry the authority to accept a signature.

For the loan packet, render a review copy only after retaining the signed agreement and associating its validation record with it. If a reviewer only needs the disclosure, produce that derivative and retain its source mapping. Avoid rendering the same original merely to rediscover a signature decision already recorded for those exact bytes under the same policy; if the policy or validation context changes, decide explicitly whether another check is required.

Rendering cost is an operational budget here: work performed, queue occupancy, and the time a reviewer waits. Do not invent a universal conversion between those quantities and fidelity. Measure the candidate implementation with representative inputs, including difficult layouts, and choose the least work that meets the defined review requirement. Exact source retention stays outside that visual compromise.

Gate transformation on a recorded validation decision

The safe implementation separates evidence storage, signature evaluation, derivative generation, and publication. Stage the outputs until the acceptance decision is complete. For this proposed policy, only an accepted original proceeds automatically; a rejected or indeterminate result goes to review, with its evidence retained. An indeterminate result is not a clean bill of health.

The following Go example implements that gate. It deliberately delegates PDF parsing and cryptography to an injected validator: the code controls the workflow and does not pretend to implement signature verification. Its evidence store must retain the original and the supplied sending record together before validation starts. The policy ID identifies a versioned acceptance policy, and the validator's report is retained even when the document is not accepted.

package evidence

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

type Status string

const (
    Accepted      Status = "accepted"
    Rejected      Status = "rejected"
    Indeterminate Status = "indeterminate"
)

type Decision struct {
    Status Status
    Report []byte
}

type Validator interface {
    Check(context.Context, []byte, string) (Decision, error)
}

type Store interface {
    RetainSource(context.Context, []byte, []byte) (string, error)
    RetainDecision(context.Context, string, string, Decision) error
}

func Admit(ctx context.Context, store Store, validator Validator,
    original, sendingRecord []byte, policyID string,
) (string, error) {
    if policyID == "" {
        return "", errors.New("validation policy is required")
    }
    sourceID, err := store.RetainSource(ctx, original, sendingRecord)
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    decision, err := validator.Check(ctx, original, policyID)
    if err != nil {
        return sourceID, err
    }
    if err := store.RetainDecision(ctx, sourceID, policyID, decision); err != nil {
        return sourceID, err
    }
    if decision.Status != Accepted {
        return sourceID, errors.New("original requires review")
    }
    return sourceID, nil
}

The caller must check the returned error before scheduling a merge or split. A source ID returned with an error is a handle for investigation, not authorization to publish. The store and validator implementations also need explicit contracts for concurrency, input ownership, and durable writes; this small gate does not supply those guarantees.

Record a failed validation attempt against the retained source when the validator returns an operational error. Keep that attempt distinct from a completed decision that rejects a signature. Otherwise a timeout can quietly become a statement about document authenticity. Retry policy belongs to the job controller, with a stable job identity so a retry does not create an unrelated evidence chain.

The derivative record should identify its source inputs, selected page ranges, transformation configuration, and acceptance record. Record page ranges against a specific source and make the numbering convention explicit.

An unqualified instruction to extract page 2 is a poor incident artifact when the job has 3 inputs.

Verify the release against evidence, then against appearance

Before enabling automatic publication, exercise the entire path with a deliberately small fixture set whose expected outcomes are established independently of this gate. Include an accepted signed original, an altered input expected to fail, an indeterminate case under the chosen policy, and a validator error. These are proposed release cases, not claims about measured performance. Check that only the accepted case reaches transformation and that the others retain an investigable source.

Then test the loan packet itself. Confirm that the retained original can be retrieved unchanged, that its report identifies the policy used, and that the merged packet and extracted disclosure both resolve to their intended sources. Inspect appearance separately: page order, clipped content, and whether the review copy clearly identifies itself as a derivative. Passing that inspection does not replace the signature decision.

Instrument the decisions that can change an operator's action: validation failures, indeterminate results, failed evidence writes, and publication attempts without a complete source relationship. Keep rendering duration and queue depth as capacity signals. Define paging around the acceptance boundary; a busy queue and a published packet lacking required evidence need different responses.

A green dashboard is insufficient.

Roll back publication while retaining the evidence

Deploy a changed validator policy or transformation configuration to a limited cohort first, retaining its version in each decision or derivative record. If the release produces unacceptable review copies or breaks source relationships, pause publication from that version and route affected jobs to review. Keep their originals, reports, and sending records available for investigation.

Rollback should restore a known configuration without rewriting historical validation decisions. Reprocessing creates a new decision or derivative linked to the same retained input, so investigators can distinguish the earlier outcome from the replacement. For fintech bundle assembly, the governing trade-off is straightforward: budget visual rendering around the review task, and preserve the evidence needed to explain exactly what was accepted.

References

  • ISO 32000-2 — Portable Document Format: https://www.iso.org/standard/75839.html

title: How many Shopify stores sell coffee? Size a niche per country with one free API
description:
Before you build a Shopify app for coffee roasters, pitch a packaging service to them, or write "the market is huge" in a deck, it helps to know how many such stores there are and who the biggest ones are. This post answers that for coffee in five countries with a 40-line Python script and 21 API requests. The numbers are from a run made on 14 November 2026.

The data

Shopify Stores Database is a REST API over 57,202 Shopify stores that appear in two open popularity lists (Chrome UX Report top 1M and Majestic Million). Each record has the store name, description, country, currency, city and catalog size. Three endpoints:

  • GET /v1/stores: filtered list, most popular first, up to 25 stores per request
  • GET /v1/stores/{domain}: is this domain in the database?
  • GET /v1/stats: store counts per country and currency

The free plan gives 50 requests a month, which is enough for everything below.

One request 

curl "https://shopify-stores-database.p.rapidapi.com/v1/stores?country=DE&q=coffee&limit=2" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: $RAPIDAPI_KEY" \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Host: shopify-stores-database.p.rapidapi.com"

{
  "data": [
    {
      "domain": "berserker-coffee.com",
      "url": "https://berserker-coffee.com",
      "tld": "com",
      "trafficRank": 500000,
      "majesticRank": null,
      "name": "Berserker Coffee Company",
      "description": "Berserker Coffee ist der stärkste und leckerste Kaffee ...",
      "country": "DE",
      "currency": "EUR",
      "city": "Fürth",
      "productCount": 64,
      "myshopifyDomain": "berserkercoffee.myshopify.com",
      "position": 6829
    },
    {
      "domain": "thebarn.de",
      "name": "THE BARN Coffee Roasters",
      "country": "DE",
      "city": "Berlin",
      "productCount": 206,
      "position": 20548
    }
  ],
  "count": 2,
  "nextCursor": 20548,
  "dataUpdatedAt": "2026-11-13"
}

(The second record is shortened here.) position is the store's place in the popularity ordering, and nextCursor is what you pass as after to get the next page. When nextCursor is null, there is nothing left.

The API does not return a total count. To count a niche you page through it, which is what the script does.

The script

Standard library only, so there is nothing to install.

import csv, json, os, statistics, sys, urllib.parse, urllib.request

HOST = "shopify-stores-database.p.rapidapi.com"
HEADERS = {"X-RapidAPI-Key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"], "X-RapidAPI-Host": HOST}
FIELDS = ["country", "position", "domain", "name", "city", "currency",
          "productCount", "trafficRank", "description"]

def get(path, **params):
    url = f"https://{HOST}{path}?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params)
    with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, headers=HEADERS), timeout=30) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def stores(keyword, country):
    """Every store matching the keyword in one country, most popular first."""
    after = 0
    while after is not None:
        page = get("/v1/stores", q=keyword, country=country, limit=25, after=after)
        yield from page["data"]
        after = page["nextCursor"]

keyword, countries = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2].upper().split(",")
totals = {c["country"]: c["count"] for c in get("/v1/stats")["countries"]}
rows = []
print(f"{'country':8}{'stores':>8}{'in niche':>10}{'share':>8}{'median products':>17}")
for country in countries:
    found = list(stores(keyword, country))
    rows += found
    sizes = [s["productCount"] for s in found if s["productCount"] is not None]
    median = int(statistics.median(sizes)) if sizes else "-"
    print(f"{country:8}{totals[country]:>8}{len(found):>10}"
          f"{100 * len(found) / totals[country]:>7.1f}%{median:>17}")

with open(f"{keyword}_stores.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=FIELDS, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)
print(f"\n{len(rows)} stores written to {keyword}_stores.csv")

export RAPIDAPI_KEY=your-key
python niche_size.py coffee US,GB,DE,CA,AU

The result 

country   stores  in niche   share  median products
US         16697       291    1.7%               83
GB          4296        62    1.4%              127
DE          2202         9    0.4%              126
CA          1637        26    1.6%               86
AU          1912        33    1.7%              119

421 stores written to coffee_stores.csv

That took 21 requests (one for the country totals, twenty pages of stores) and a few seconds.

The first rows of the CSV for the US are Peet's Coffee, AeroPress, The Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf, Fellow, Death Wish Coffee and Trade Coffee: the list is ordered by popularity, so the names you would expect come first.

Reading the numbers honestly

Coffee is about 1.5% of popular Shopify stores in English-speaking countries. The share is nearly the same in the US, Canada and Australia (1.6 to 1.7%) and a little lower in the UK (1.4%).

Germany's 0.4% is a keyword artifact, not a market fact. The q filter looks for the word in the store name, description and domain. German stores write "Kaffee". Searching kaffee in Germany finds 15 stores, and 22 match either spelling, which brings Germany to 1.0%. For non-English markets, run the script once per local term and merge by domain.

Catalogs are small. The median US coffee store lists 83 products, and 172 of the 291 have 100 or fewer. If your product is priced per SKU or assumes a large catalog, this niche will disappoint you.

This is a count of popular stores, not of all stores. The database covers stores that are visible in public top-1M rankings. A roaster that opened last month with forty visitors a day is not in it. Treat 291 as "US coffee stores with measurable traffic or links", which is usually the set you can sell to anyway.

A keyword match is not a category. In this run, 9 of the 421 matches are furniture and homeware stores whose descriptions mention coffee tables. Skim the CSV before you quote the number to anyone; the description column makes that quick.

Variations

Stores with a large catalog and real traffic, any niche:

GET /v1/stores?country=US&minProducts=1000&maxTrafficRank=100000&limit=25

Everything priced in euros that mentions "bio":

GET /v1/stores?currency=EUR&q=bio&limit=25

Is a domain from your CRM a known Shopify store?

GET /v1/stores/gymshark.com

A 404 here means "not in this database". It does not prove the site runs on something else.

What to do with the list

The CSV gives you domains, names and sizes. If you need to know which apps those stores run (Klaviyo, Recharge, a reviews app) or their public contact details, the companion guide shows that step: Build a targeted list of Shopify stores by country, niche and installed apps.

Costs and limits

  • Free plan: 50 requests a month, up to 1,250 stores. The run above used 21.
  • Paid plans start at $9.99 a month for 1,500 requests (37,500 stores).
  • Data is rebuilt monthly; every response carries dataUpdatedAt.
  • No emails or personal data in this API.

The API is here: Shopify Stores Database on RapidAPI. If a filter you need is missing, say so in the comments or in the API's Discussions tab.

title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
description:
arXiv:2611.14924v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

title: gat
description:
<!DOCTYPE html>


🏙️ Street Life - Mini City Game
<br> * { margin:0; padding:0; box-sizing:border-box; font-family:Arial, sans-serif; }<br> body { background:#1a472a; text-align:center; color:white; padding:10px; }<br> canvas { background:#333; border:4px solid #222; }<br> .ui { position:fixed; top:10px; left:10px; text-align:left; background:rgba(0,0,0,0.6); padding:10px; border-radius:8px; z-index:10; }<br> .controls { position:fixed; bottom:10px; left:50%; transform:translateX(-50%); background:rgba(0,0,0,0.6); padding:8px 15px; border-radius:8px; font-size:14px; }<br> 

💰 Money: <span id="money">0</span>
🚗 Vehicle: <span id="vehicle">Walking</span>
📍 Mission: <span id="mission">None</span>
⏱️ Time: <span id="time">60</span>s

⬆⬇⬅➡ Move | E=Enter/Exit Car | SPACE=Complete Mission

const canvas = document.getElementById('game');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');

// Player
let player = { x:400, y:300, w:24, h:32, speed:3, inCar:false, car:null };
let money = 0;
let timeLeft = 60;
let gameTime = 0;
let mission = null;
let missionText = 'None';

// World
let buildings = [];
let roads = [];
let cars = [];
let pickups = [];

// Input
const keys = {};
document.addEventListener('keydown', e=>keys[e.key]=true);
document.addEventListener('keyup', e=>keys[e.key]=false);

// Generate city
function initWorld() {
// Roads
roads = [
{x:0,y:250,w:800,h:100},
{x:0,y:450,w:800,h:100},
{x:250,y:0,w:100,h:800},
{x:500,y:0,w:100,h:800}
];
// Buildings
let bData = [
{x:20,y:20,w:200,h:200,c:'#4a6fa5',n:'Apartments'},
{x:300,y:20,w:150,h:200,c:'#8b4513',n:'Warehouse'},
{x:580,y:20,w:200,h:200,c:'#d68029',n:'Mall'},
{x:20,y:320,w:200,h:100,c:'#555',n:'Bank'},
{x:580,y:320,w:200,h:100,c:'#2e8b57',n:'Hospital'},
{x:20,y:520,w:200,h:60,c:'#777',n:'Garage'},
{x:580,y:520,w:200,h:60,c:'#b8860b',n:'Casino'}
];
bData.forEach(b=>buildings.push({...b}));

// Parked cars
cars = [
    {x:120,y:210,w:40,h:24,c:'#e63946',dx:0,dy:0},
    {x:360,y:210,w:40,h:24,c:'#457b9d',dx:0,dy:0},
    {x:620,y:210,w:40,h:24,c:'#2a9d8f',dx:0,dy:0},
    {x:120,y:490,w:40,h:24,c:'#f4a261',dx:0,dy:0},
    {x:620,y:490,w:40,h:24,c:'#9b5de5',dx:0,dy:0}
];

// Money pickups
spawnPickup();
newMission();

}

function spawnPickup() {
pickups.push({
x: 80 + Math.random()*640,
y: 80 + Math.random()*440,
w:20,h:20,
value: Math.random()>0.8 ? 100 : 25
});
}

function newMission() {
let missions = [
{text:'Drive to Hospital', target:'Hospital', reward:150},
{text:'Go to Bank', target:'Bank', reward:200},
{text:'Visit Garage', target:'Garage', reward:100},
{text:'Go to Mall', target:'Mall', reward:120},
{text:'Deliver to Apartments', target:'Apartments', reward:180}
];
mission = missions[Math.floor(Math.random()*missions.length)];
missionText = mission.text;
timeLeft = 45;
}

function updateUI() {
document.getElementById('money').textContent = '$' + money;
document.getElementById('vehicle').textContent = player.inCar ? '🚗 Driving' : '🚶 Walking';
document.getElementById('mission').textContent = missionText;
document.getElementById('time').textContent = timeLeft;
}

function checkBuildingCollision(rect) {
for(let b of buildings) {
if(rect.x < b.x+b.w && rect.x+rect.w > b.x &&
rect.y < b.y+b.h && rect.y+rect.h > b.y) return b;
}
return null;
}

function update() {
gameTime++;
if(gameTime % 60 === 0 && timeLeft>0) timeLeft--;
if(timeLeft<=0 && mission) { missionText='Failed!'; mission=null; }

let moveX=0, moveY=0;
let speed = player.inCar ? 5 : player.speed;
if(keys['ArrowUp']) moveY=-speed;
if(keys['ArrowDown']) moveY=speed;
if(keys['ArrowLeft']) moveX=-speed;
if(keys['ArrowRight']) moveX=speed;

// Enter/Exit car
if(keys['e'] || keys['E']) {
    keys['e']=keys['E']=false;
    if(!player.inCar) {
        for(let c of cars) {
            let dist = Math.hypot(player.x-c.x, player.y-c.y);
            if(dist < 40) {
                player.inCar = true;
                player.car = c;
                c.dx=0; c.dy=0;
                break;
            }
        }
    } else {
        player.inCar = false;
        player.x = player.car.x + 30;
        player.y = player.car.y;
        player.car = null;
    }
}

// Movement
if(player.inCar) {
    player.car.x += moveX;
    player.car.y += moveY;
    // Boundaries
    player.car.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width-player.car.w, player.car.x));
    player.car.y = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.height-player.car.h, player.car.y));
    player.x = player.car.x; player.y = player.car.y;
} else {
    let nx = player.x + moveX;
    let ny = player.y + moveY;
    if(!checkBuildingCollision({x:nx,y:player.y,w:player.w,h:player.h})) player.x=nx;
    if(!checkBuildingCollision({x:player.x,y:ny,w:player.w,h:player.h})) player.y=ny;
    player.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width-player.w, player.x));
    player.y = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.height-player.h, player.y));
}

// Pick up money
pickups = pickups.filter(p=>{
    if(player.x < p.x+p.w && player.x+player.w > p.x &&
       player.y < p.y+p.h && player.y+player.h > p.y) {
        money += p.value;
        return false;
    }
    return true;
});
if(gameTime % 180 === 0) spawnPickup();

// Complete mission
if(keys[' '] && mission) {
    let b = checkBuildingCollision({x:player.x,y:player.y,w:player.w,h:player.h});
    if(b && b.n === mission.target) {
        money += mission.reward;
        missionText = 'Complete! +$'+mission.reward;
        mission=null;
        setTimeout(newMission, 1500);
    }
    keys[' ']=false;
}

updateUI();

}

function draw() {
// Ground
ctx.fillStyle='#3d6b34';
ctx.fillRect(0,0,canvas.width,canvas.height);

// Roads
roads.forEach(r=>{
    ctx.fillStyle='#444';
    ctx.fillRect(r.x,r.y,r.w,r.h);
    ctx.strokeStyle='#fff';
    ctx.setLineDash([30,20]);
    ctx.lineWidth=2;
    ctx.beginPath();
    if(r.h>r.w) { ctx.moveTo(r.x+r.w/2,r.y); ctx.lineTo(r.x+r.w/2,r.y+r.h); }
    else { ctx.moveTo(r.x,r.y+r.h/2); ctx.lineTo(r.x+r.w,r.y+r.h/2); }
    ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
});

// Buildings
buildings.forEach(b=>{
    ctx.fillStyle=b.c;
    ctx.fillRect(b.x,b.y,b.w,b.h);
    ctx.strokeStyle='#222'; ctx.lineWidth=3; ctx.strokeRect(b.x,b.y,b.w,b.h);
    ctx.fillStyle='#fff'; ctx.font='12px Arial'; ctx.fillText(b.n, b.x+8, b.y+18);
    // Windows
    ctx.fillStyle='#ffff99';
    for(let i=0;i<Math.floor(b.w/40);i++) {
        for(let j=0;j<Math.floor(b.h/35);j++) {
            if(Math.random()>0.3) ctx.fillRect(b.x+10+i*40, b.y+25+j*35,12,15);
        }
    }
});

// Money pickups
pickups.forEach(p=>{
    ctx.font='20px Arial'; ctx.fillText('💰',p.x-2,p.y+16);
});

// Cars
cars.forEach(c=>{
    ctx.fillStyle=c.c;
    ctx.fillRect(c.x,c.y,c.w,c.h);
    ctx.fillStyle='#222';
    ctx.fillRect(c.x+4,c.y+4,c.w-8,c.h-8);
    ctx.fillStyle='#fff';
    ctx.font='11px Arial'; ctx.fillText('🚗',c.x+8,c.y+18);
});

// Player
if(!player.inCar) {
    ctx.font='26px Arial'; ctx.fillText('🧍',player.x-4,player.y+26);
}

// Mission arrow
if(mission) {
    let tgt = buildings.find(b=>b.n===mission.target);
    if(tgt) {
        ctx.strokeStyle='#ffff00'; ctx.lineWidth=3;
        ctx.beginPath();
        ctx.moveTo(player.x+12, player.y+16);
        ctx.lineTo(tgt.x+tgt.w/2, tgt.y+tgt.h/2);
        ctx.stroke();
    }
}

}

function loop() { update(); draw(); requestAnimationFrame(loop); }
initWorld();
loop();

title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
description:
arXiv:2611.14942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.

title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.15091v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT. Our framework transforms the GPU-optimized variable logits to high-confidence assignments and transfers them to CPU solvers via two complementary modes: partial guidance, which injects the most confident perturbed partial variable assignments as soft clauses into $N$ parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which guides the CDCL solver's internal branching polarity with the full GPU assignment as a warm start to preserve the problem's originality. We evaluate on all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 (most recent due to cancellation in 2025) anytime weighted benchmark with the top 2 winners as baselines; our hybrid framework improves the average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second time limit, with the potential to obtain better solutions surpassing the best known solution recorded in the competition evaluation.

title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark
description:
arXiv:2611.15225v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2611.14794v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

title: Querying 7,636 Small Music Venues Under 500 Capacity: Schema, Pay Data and Corridor Routing
description:
Independent bands and solo musicians booking their own shows rarely play 2,000-seat theaters. The core of a working regional tour is the under-500-capacity circuit: 75-to-350 capacity rock clubs, neighborhood bars, brewery taprooms, winery patios, and seated acoustic listening rooms. Finding those stages and verifying who books them requires structured data rather than generic map searches.

As of November 2026, the No Stairs Please catalog tracks 38,223 open live music venues across 10,286 towns in all 50 US states, the District of Columbia, and British Columbia. Within that catalog, 7,636 open rooms have a verified capacity of 500 or fewer, 7,325 publish a dedicated talent-booking contact, and 121,954 dated shows appear in the 90-day calendar window. You can explore the full small music venues under 500 capacity hub on the web or query the catalog programmatically through the remote Model Context Protocol endpoint.

National Breakdown by Room Type

Every open stage in the catalog is classified by its primary room type, capacity, 90-day show count, weekday activity mask, and booking contact route. The table below summarizes the seven primary room categories across North America.

Room category Open venues Rooms at or under 500 capacity Verified booking contacts Active in 90-day window Median capacity
Dedicated music venues 3,489 1,731 1,806 2,713 320
Bars and pubs with live music 6,419 1,508 1,554 3,365 150
Breweries and taprooms 2,084 463 661 1,039 121
Restaurants with live music 1,929 450 440 1,021 140
Wineries and tasting rooms 1,440 289 269 619 125
Listening rooms 158 133 93 128 100

Dedicated music venues have a median capacity of 320 and hold the highest density of verified talent-buyer routes (1,806 rooms). Bars and pubs make up the largest total count at 6,419 open stages with a median capacity of 150. Breweries (median capacity 121), wineries (median capacity 125), and listening rooms (median capacity 100) give solo acts, duos, and acoustic trios daytime and early-evening performance windows that pair well with weekend club dates.

Comparing Six Regional Touring Markets

When routing a tour across the Midwest, South, and Mountain West, comparing open stage counts and median room sizes helps you balance weekend club anchors against weeknight taproom stops.

In the Upper Midwest, the Minneapolis music venues directory tracks 145 open stages (51 at or under 500 capacity, 54 with verified booking contacts, and 112 with dated shows in the 90-day window), alongside 83 open venues across the Mississippi River in Saint Paul. A band routing along Interstate 94 can link Minneapolis and Saint Paul with Eau Claire, Madison, Milwaukee, and Chicago across 2,556 open rooms in the Great Lakes corridor.

Querying the Catalog via MCP

To query these records from Claude Code, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, or Gemini CLI, register the stateless Streamable HTTP endpoint at https://nostairsplease.com/mcp:

claude mcp add --transport http nostairsplease https://nostairsplease.com/mcp

You can then filter rooms by capacity, room category, and highway corridor in a single tool call:

{
  "tool": "search_venues",
  "arguments": {
    "stops": ["Minneapolis, MN", "Madison, WI", "Milwaukee, WI", "Chicago, IL"],
    "max_capacity": 350,
    "radius_miles": 15,
    "has_booking_contact": true
  }
}

Performer Pay Benchmarks Across 393 Reviewed Venues

Across 393 reviewed performer pay records in the catalog, deal structures follow clear patterns by room category:

  • Dedicated clubs under 500 capacity typically offer 70% to 85% of net door receipts after a $100 to $300 house sound and door deduction, or a $250 to $750 guarantee versus a door split.
  • Breweries and taprooms typically pay a flat guarantee of $150 to $250 for a solo or duo act and $300 to $500 for a full band, plus a drink tab and tip jar.
  • Neighborhood bars and pubs typically pay $150 to $400 flat, 10% to 15% of bar ring during the set, or 100% of a $5 to $10 door cover.
  • Seated listening rooms typically pay 70% to 100% of the ticket or suggested-donation door pool, with early 7:00 PM to 9:30 PM show times and strong merchandise sales.

Lead-Time Windows and Hold Etiquette

When you inspect the 766 venues in the catalog that publish explicit booking rules, lead time is the primary filter that separates confirmed tours from ignored emails. Dedicated clubs under 500 capacity typically book 8 to 16 weeks in advance for local and regional bills, and 3 to 6 months ahead for Friday and Saturday touring anchors. Brewery taprooms, wineries, and neighborhood bars usually finalize their monthly entertainment calendars 4 to 8 weeks out.

To route a multi-city loop without leaving expensive empty nights on the calendar, request pencil holds on your Friday and Saturday club dates first. Give each talent buyer two specific date options in your subject line so they can match your request against open slots on their hold sheet. Once a weekend anchor confirms your hold, fill Wednesday, Thursday, and Sunday along the highway with taprooms, college-town pubs, or co-bills where your band shares the night with two local acts that already draw 40 to 80 people in that market.

Keep your cold outreach email under 150 words of plain text. Put your dates, band name, genre, and proposed local bill partner in the subject line, include one direct link to an unedited live performance video, name two comparable bands from the venue's 90-day calendar, and paste your plain-text one-sheet below your signature with no file attachments. If you do not hear back within 7 to 10 business days, send one polite follow-up in the same email thread so the buyer can see your original dates and live video link without searching their inbox.

title: agentscrub: a local-first Rust CLI that redacts secrets and PII from AI agent transcripts
description:
Agent transcripts often keep API keys, cloud credentials and email addresses in plain text on disk. I wanted a tool that stays on the machine, prints only masked values, and refuses writes it cannot yet do safely.

That tool is agentscrub. I am Jarvis Osorio, and I released it as open source under Apache-2.0.

  • Project page: jarvisosorio.com/agent-session-scrubber
  • Source: github.com/JarvisOsorio/agent-session-scrubber

What it does

agentscrub is a local-first Rust CLI that discovers, scans and redacts secrets and PII in AI agent session transcripts. It runs offline, with no accounts and no telemetry.

Commands in v0.1.0:

  • discover — list recognized session files
  • scan — detect secrets and PII (exit 8 if the scan is incomplete)
  • report — re-render a saved JSON report, or re-scan
  • scrub — dry-run redaction by default; pass --confirm to write
  • verify — post-remediation check
  • retention — status / plan / apply / verify (apply refuses while the flag is off)
  • config — show effective config (the current binary expects config show)

Scan output is masked values and fingerprints only. It never logs raw secrets.

Adapters in v0.1

Adapter Read Redact Notes
claude_code yes yes JSONL sessions
codex yes yes JSONL sessions
cursor yes no JSONL + SQLite state.vscdb — rewrite is intentionally disabled
generic_jsonl yes yes Configurable text fields
generic_json yes yes Single JSON documents

Unsupported or malformed files are skipped and reported, not silently modified. Writes that are allowed use an exclusive lock, a pre-write hash recheck, and an atomic same-filesystem replace. Symlink targets are refused.

Cursor rewrite is held back until SQLite and transcript mutation are proven safe. Retention planning is in the tree, but retention.enabled is false by default and retention apply will not delete. This is not a credential revocation service — rotate anything the scan finds at the provider.

Install

agentscrub is not on crates.io or Homebrew yet. It requires Rust 1.89+:

git clone https://github.com/JarvisOsorio/agent-session-scrubber.git
cd agent-session-scrubber
cargo install --path .
# or: cargo build --release && ./target/release/agentscrub --help

A short fixture walk-through (copy fixtures first — do not scrub the originals in-tree):

mkdir -p /tmp/agentscrub-demo/.claude
cp tests/fixtures/claude/session_secrets.jsonl /tmp/agentscrub-demo/.claude/

agentscrub discover --path /tmp/agentscrub-demo
agentscrub scan --path /tmp/agentscrub-demo --format terminal
agentscrub scrub --path /tmp/agentscrub-demo/.claude/session_secrets.jsonl
agentscrub scrub --path /tmp/agentscrub-demo/.claude/session_secrets.jsonl --confirm
agentscrub verify /tmp/agentscrub-demo/.claude/session_secrets.jsonl --format json
# expect: clean=true, remaining_findings=0, exit 0

A name collision to be aware of

The binary is called agentscrub. An unrelated Python project, ppravdin/agentscrub, already exists on GitHub and PyPI. pip install agentscrub is not this tool. Use the GitHub repository above.

Status

The public version is 0.1.0. The GitHub release tag exists; prebuilt binary assets were not attached at publish time, so install from source as shown. Docs in the repository cover the security policy, privacy, threat model and redaction behavior.

If you try it, I would like feedback on the Cursor-rewrite hold and on detector precision. Issues and discussions belong on the GitHub repository.

— Jarvis Osorio

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Designing Inclusive Mobile Apps: Accessibility Done Right
description:
Designing Inclusive Mobile Apps: Accessibility Beyond Just Contrast Ratios

When developers hear "accessibility," they often think of automated Lighthouse scores or ensuring text has a 4.5:1 contrast ratio. While these technical specifications are important, they barely scratch the surface of true inclusive design.

Building an accessible mobile app means recognizing that your users are navigating the digital world with varying levels of vision, hearing, motor skills, and cognitive processing.

1. Dynamic Type and Layout Fluidity

Many developers hardcode font sizes, assuming users will view the app exactly as it appears in Figma. This completely breaks when a visually impaired user increases their system font size by 200%.

Best Practice:
Never use fixed heights for text containers. Allow your UI to wrap and flow dynamically. If a user sets their system text to maximum, your elegant single-line button might need to become a multi-line, stacked layout. Embrace the fluidity.

2. The Nuance of Screen Readers

Testing with VoiceOver (iOS) or TalkBack (Android) should be a mandatory part of your QA process.

  • Avoid using vague labels like "Click Here".
  • Use "aria-hidden" or "excludeFromSemantics" on purely decorative images so the screen reader doesn't waste the user's time reading out useless file names.
  • Group related elements together. If you have a custom card with a user's name, avatar, and bio, the screen reader should read it as a single cohesive unit, not three disconnected pieces of data.

3. Designing for Motor Impairments

Not everyone can perform precise gestures or reach the top corners of massive modern smartphones.

  • Touch Targets: Ensure every tappable element is at least 44x44 points.
  • Gesture Alternatives: If your app relies heavily on complex swipe gestures, always provide a simple button alternative for users with limited dexterity.

Inclusivity isn't a post-launch "nice-to-have." It is a fundamental architectural decision that expands your user base and improves the UX for absolutely everyone.

Originally published at uzairxdev.online

title: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies
description:
arXiv:2611.14928v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hybrid bonding terminal (HBT) legalization assigns every terminal of a face-to-face 3D IC to its own pitch-grid site with minimum total Manhattan displacement. Open3DBench reports that a reinforcement-learning (RL) legalizer reduces displacement by 19-22% relative to a sliding-window (SW) heuristic, but none of its legalizers is publicly released. We ask how much displacement any legalizer can still recover. We build an open benchmark of 21 design/pitch instances from Open3DBench placement data, with reconstructed greedy, SW (ViaLegal-style) and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, an exact solver that runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate proves its assignment optimal on all 21 instances (relative primal-dual gap at most $8.2 \times 10^{-16}$). Against these optima, our SW reconstruction with ViaLegal's default configuration is on average 0.011% above optimal (worst 0.119%), while on the 16 contended instances BTAssign-style, a density-guided heuristic (DGHL) and greedy are 3.0%, 6.9% and 64.5% above. Headroom does appear outside this regime: with 2x2 windows SW reaches 34.1%, and above about 58% utilization, on three of six swept designs, it reaches 21.1% on bp, 27.5% on swerv and 8.9% on jpeg (217 further certified instances, and ten bp points checked against an independent exact solver). If the published 19-22% gain were measured on instances like ours, SW would have to be at least 24-28% above optimal on average, far more than any SW variant we tested at nominal pitch; the RL paper's own comparison with the Hungarian optimum puts its SW 3.05% above optimal on average. GEO-Exact is also about an order of magnitude faster than DGHL and SW in our harness (geometric means 8.1x and 40x; a compiled core against Python baselines on a shared server). Code, optimal values and certificates are released.

title: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution
description:
arXiv:2611.15178v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.
