title: Typed Verification Timelines for React Forms
description:
Email verification looks like a small form feature: collect an address, send a code, and show a success message. In a real product, it is a timeline with several actors: the browser, the API, the mail provider, a user who may open two tabs, and a timer that eventually expires.

When those actors disagree, a React component often falls back to a handful of booleans:

const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false)
const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)

This works for the happy path. It gets confusing when a resend request finishes after an old verification request, or when a user returns to a tab after the code has expired. A typed timeline makes the UI easier to reason about and gives tests something more useful than a screenshot to assert.

Why a boolean is not enough

loading, verified, and error can all be true at the same time. That means the component can accidentally render “Verified” while a newer request is still pending. The UI should not guess what the API mean; it should render a state that already explains the server decision.

A useful model starts with mutually exclusive states:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending"; requestId: string }
  | { kind: "awaiting_code"; expiresAt: number; attempt: number }
  | { kind: "checking_code"; attempt: number }
  | { kind: "verified"; verifiedAt: number }
  | { kind: "expired"; expiredAt: number }
  | { kind: "failed"; message: string; retryable: boolean }

The names are intentionally plain. They describe what the user can do next, not which component happened to run last. The state names are boring, but they makes the product behavior much easier to discuss with support and QA.

Model the verification timeline

The transition rules belong in one place. A reducer is a good fit because every event can be logged and replayed:

type VerificationEvent =
  | { type: "SEND_STARTED"; requestId: string }
  | { type: "CODE_SENT"; expiresAt: number }
  | { type: "CODE_CHECK_STARTED" }
  | { type: "CODE_ACCEPTED"; verifiedAt: number }
  | { type: "CODE_REJECTED"; message: string }
  | { type: "CLOCK_EXPIRED"; expiredAt: number }
  | { type: "RESET" }

function reduceVerification(
  state: VerificationState,
  event: VerificationEvent,
): VerificationState {
  switch (event.type) {
    case "SEND_STARTED":
      return { kind: "sending", requestId: event.requestId }
    case "CODE_SENT":
      return { kind: "awaiting_code", expiresAt: event.expiresAt, attempt: 0 }
    case "CODE_CHECK_STARTED":
      return state.kind === "awaiting_code"
        ? { kind: "checking_code", attempt: state.attempt + 1 }
        : state
    case "CODE_ACCEPTED":
      return { kind: "verified", verifiedAt: event.verifiedAt }
    case "CODE_REJECTED":
      return { kind: "failed", message: event.message, retryable: true }
    case "CLOCK_EXPIRED":
      return state.kind === "verified"
        ? state
        : { kind: "expired", expiredAt: event.expiredAt }
    case "RESET":
      return { kind: "idle" }
  }
}

The reducer does not need to know whether the message arrived through a normal inbox, a run-scoped email fixture, or a service such as tempmailso. That boundary is useful: the provider produces events, while the product owns the meaning of those events. For a broader fixture strategy, see run-scoped email fixtures.

The server should still be authoritative. A client-side timer can show that a code is probably expired, but only the API can confirm whether a code is valid. When the timer expire, dispatch an event that changes the hint in the UI; do not pretend it has changed the server record.

Keep the React UI honest

Render from state.kind, then make each action explicit:

function VerificationPanel({ state }: { state: VerificationState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "idle":
      return <button type="submit">Send code</button>
    case "sending":
      return <p role="status">Sending a new code…</p>
    case "awaiting_code":
      return <CodeEntry expiresAt={state.expiresAt} />
    case "checking_code":
      return <p role="status">Checking the code…</p>
    case "verified":
      return <p role="status">Email verified.</p>
    case "expired":
      return <ResendButton />
    case "failed":
      return <RetryMessage message={state.message} retryable={state.retryable} />
  }
}

This prevents stale success messages from competing with a resend action. It also makes accessibility behavior more deliberate: transient updates can use role="status", while the code input remains available when a retry is valid.

Keep the timer separate from the state reducer. A hook can schedule one timeout for the current expiresAt, clean it up when the value changes, and dispatch CLOCK_EXPIRED. In practise, that separation makes fake-clock tests much less fragile. Its a small detail, but it avoids a timer callback reading an old closure.

If an OAuth or login flow also carries a state value, treat that value as another replay boundary rather than mixing it into the form booleans. This related explanation of a replay boundary for authentication state is a useful companion when the verification page is part of a larger sign-in flow.

Test transitions instead of screenshots

The highest-value tests assert event sequences. For example:

it("does not expire an already verified address", () => {
  const verified = reduceVerification(
    { kind: "verified", verifiedAt: 100 },
    { type: "CLOCK_EXPIRED", expiredAt: 200 },
  )

  expect(verified).toEqual({ kind: "verified", verifiedAt: 100 })
})

Add cases for a late rejection after a resend, an expired code followed by a successful new send, and two tabs receiving different results. These tests expose the contract between API responses and UI states. They also fail with a compact diff when behavior changes, instead of requiring someone to inspect a pixel-level snapshot.

Some teams label their disposable fixture a “temp mailid” in test data. The label is less important than its lifecycle: assign it to one run, record the message identifier, and clean it up when the test ends.

A small rollout checklist

  1. Replace related booleans with a discriminated union.
  2. List every API response as an event before changing the component.
  3. Keep server truth separate from client timeout hints.
  4. Test late, duplicated, and out-of-order responses.
  5. Make retry and resend actions visible from the current state.
  6. Log a request or correlation ID for failures, but never log verification codes.

This approach scales beyond email. The same timeline works for phone challenges, payment confirmation, and background imports. Once the UI has one honest state at a time, React stops being the place where async ambiguity gets hidden.

Common questions

Should the client mark a code as expired?

It can show an expired hint when its local clock passes the deadline, but the API must decide whether a submitted code is accepted. Client time is feedback, not authority.

Do I need a state machine library?

No. A TypeScript union and a small reducer are enough for many forms. Consider a library when the workflow has nested states, parallel actors, or a team that benefits from visualized transitions.

What if the email provider is slow?

Keep sending and awaiting_code distinct, show a clear status message, and offer a safe retry policy. This avoid making a slow inbox look like a broken form while still giving the user a next action.

title: Evals Deep: Beyond RAGAS, Build Your Own Eval Harness
description:
Evals Deep: Beyond RAGAS, Build Your Own Eval Harness

Deep Part 6 settled chunking and Deep Part 7 measured retrieval, but every number in both parts came from a test set we scored by hand. That works for one article. It does not work for a system that changes every week. This part turns the hand scoring into a repeatable gate: a question set with known answers, a script that runs every retriever change against it, and a rule that blocks a deploy when a score drops. We built the harness as a single Python file using only the standard library, with no API calls, no model, and no bill. Then we ran it on 20 questions and three small systems, and the numbers taught us something RAGAS alone would never show: a completely wrong answer can score token F1 of 0.857 and perfect faithfulness at the same time.

Our position is simple. RAGAS is a good starting point and a bad finish line. It grades your system with the same kind of model that built it, it charges you per question, and it hands you one number that hides the exact failure you care about. A hand built harness costs nothing, runs in milliseconds, and shows you the failing question by name. Run the cheap harness on every change. Run the LLM judge on a sample, once a week, calibrated against human labels. Never ship on a single aggregate number.

What RAGAS actually measures

RAGAS, from Es and colleagues in 2023, proposed three reference free metrics for RAG pipelines, each scored by prompting a language model. Faithfulness splits the answer into statements and checks each one against the retrieved context, then scores supported statements over total statements. Answer relevance asks the model to generate questions the answer would fit, then measures embedding similarity between those questions and the original. Context relevance asks the model to extract the sentences from the context that are needed to answer, then scores extracted sentences over total sentences in the context. The paper tested this on WikiEval, a dataset the authors built from 50 Wikipedia pages with human judgments, using gpt-3.5-turbo-16k as the judge. If you want the hands on version of the same tool, our earlier guide walks through it step by step: Evaluate Your RAG System with RAGAS.

The agreement numbers from the paper are worth reading closely, because they are better than most people remember and worse than most people assume. On pairwise comparisons against human annotators, RAGAS agreed with humans 0.95 of the time on faithfulness, 0.78 on answer relevance, and 0.70 on context relevance. A baseline that simply asked ChatGPT to assign a score from 0 to 10 managed 0.72, 0.52, and 0.63. A baseline that asked it to rank two answers managed 0.54, 0.40, and 0.52. So the structured metrics beat naive prompting by a wide margin, and faithfulness at 0.95 is genuinely strong. But 0.70 on context relevance means the judge disagrees with humans on nearly one comparison in three, and the authors say themselves that context relevance was the hardest dimension, because the judge struggles to pick the crucial sentences out of longer contexts.

Two more facts matter before you adopt it. First, the paper is from 2023 and the library moved on. The current release, ragas 0.4.3, ships six text metrics, and the names changed: answer relevance is now response relevancy, and context precision now has a reference free path and a reference based path. Three of the six metrics need a reference answer in every documented mode, which quietly breaks the original promise of reference free evaluation. Second, every RAGAS metric needs at least one LLM call per question. Faithfulness needs two, one to extract statements and one to verify them. Answer relevancy needs one generation plus an embedding call. Context relevancy needs one extraction. That is 4 LLM calls and 1 embedding call per question, or 80 LLM calls and 20 embedding calls for a 20 question test set. That is the price of every run, and it is also the reason most teams run evals rarely, which is exactly when regressions slip through.

The problem with judge only evaluation

The first problem is cost and speed. Eighty judge calls for 20 questions means a 200 question test set needs 800 calls. At that price teams shrink the test set until it stops catching anything, or they run evals once a month instead of on every change. The second problem is correlation. Zheng and colleagues showed that GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences more than 80 percent of the time, about the same rate at which human judges agreed with each other. That sounds good until you flip it: the judge disagrees with people about one time in five, and when the judge and the generator are the same family of model, their blind spots overlap. A judge that shares your generator's training will forgive the same phrasing habits and the same confident mistakes. The third problem is aggregation. A single faithfulness score of 0.92 tells you nothing about which question failed, and the one question that failed is usually the one your users will ask first.

ARES, from Saad-Falcon and colleagues at Stanford in 2023, is the honest answer to the trust question. It fine tunes lightweight judge models on synthetic data for context relevance, faithfulness, and answer relevance, then corrects those judges with prediction powered inference, a statistical technique that uses a small set of human labelled examples to put confidence intervals on the scores. Across eight knowledge intensive tasks in KILT, SuperGLUE, and AIS, it scored RAG systems accurately with only a few hundred human annotations, and the authors ask for about 150 labelled examples as the validation set. That is the standard we hold our own harness to: a number without a confidence interval and without a named failing example is a press release, not an evaluation.

The setup: one corpus, three systems, twenty questions

We built a small fictional corpus about Kiln Coffee Roasters, a made up company with 12 short passages: founding year and city, a second roastery, bag prices, cafe hours, decaf process, shipping rules, subscription price, roast levels, sourcing countries, wholesale terms, and composting. Fictional matters. A real corpus lets the model answer from memory and inflates every score. A fictional corpus forces the system to use only the retrieved text, which is the entire point of RAG evaluation. We wrote 20 questions against it, each with a short gold answer and the passage that contains it.

Then we built three answerers from the same keyword overlap retriever, so the only difference between them is the policy under test. System A retrieves the top 1 passage and answers with the best matching sentence in it. System B retrieves the top 3 passages and answers with the best matching sentence across all three. System C is System A with one invented detail appended to every answer, the words with free worldwide shipping, which appear nowhere in the corpus. System C is the trap detector: any metric that cannot tell C from A is not measuring groundedness at all. All three systems answer by copying a sentence from the corpus, which is deliberate. Extractive answers isolate the retrieval and selection logic from generation quality, so a failure points at the retriever, not at the wording.

The metrics, implemented from scratch

We implemented six metrics in plain Python, no libraries beyond the standard library. Recall at k is the share of questions where a gold passage appears in the top k retrieved. Context precision at k is the share of the retrieved passages that are gold. Exact match is 1 only when the predicted tokens equal the gold tokens exactly. Token F1 is the harmonic mean of token precision and token recall between prediction and gold. Substring accuracy is 1 when the gold answer appears inside the predicted answer. Faithfulness, our proxy for the RAGAS idea, is the share of the answer content words that appear anywhere in the retrieved context. Two of these functions carry the whole idea, and they fit in a few lines.

def token_f1(pred, gold):
p, g = set(tokens(pred)), set(tokens(gold))
common = len(p & g)
if common == 0:
return 0.0
prec, rec = common / len(p), common / len(g)
return 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)

def faithfulness(answer, passage_ids):
ctx_words = set(tokens(" ".join(PASSAGES[i] for i in passage_ids)))
words = content_tokens(answer)
if not words:
return 0.0
return sum(1 for w in words if w in ctx_words) / len(words)

Note what faithfulness can and cannot see. It checks whether the answer words exist in the context, not whether the sentence is true, not whether it answers the question, and not whether the right sentence was picked. That limitation is the point of the experiment. We wanted to find out how far word level checks get you, and where they stop.

The measured table

We ran all three systems over the same 20 questions. The full run took 0.010 seconds of wall time for 60 system question pairs, at zero cost and zero API calls. For comparison, scoring the same 20 questions the RAGAS way needs 80 LLM calls and 20 embedding calls. Here is what the harness reported.

SystemRecallContext precisionExact matchToken F1Substring accuracyFaithfulness
A: top 1 passage0.850.850.000.3120.801.00
B: top 3 passages1.000.330.000.3320.851.00
C: top 1 plus invented detail0.850.850.000.2250.800.70

Read the recall column with the retrieval size in mind. System A retrieves one passage, so its 0.85 is recall at 1. System B retrieves three, so its 1.00 is recall at 3. The extra context fixed every retrieval miss, and the price is visible in the next column: only one of the three passages B retrieves is gold, so context precision falls to 0.33. That is the trade Deep Part 7 already measured from the other side: more context helps recall and adds noise for the model to wade through. If you want the retrieval numbers behind this, read RAG Deep: Hybrid Search and Reranking, Measured and RAG Deep: Chunking Strategies Tested at Scale.

What the numbers actually say

Exact match is 0.00 for all three systems, and that is a finding, not a bug. The gold answers are short, like 16 dollars, and the systems answer with full sentences, like the single origin bag costs 16 dollars. Exact match punishes complete sentences, so a system that answers correctly in a full sentence scores zero. If exact match is your gate, you will reject every system that speaks in sentences. Token F1 has the same disease in milder form: 0.312 for A and 0.332 for B look like failing grades, but substring accuracy says 0.80 and 0.85 of the answers contain the gold answer verbatim. The low F1 mostly measures verbosity, not wrongness. This is why our series part on evals warned against single metric thinking in the first place: Evals: The Skill 56 Percent of Jobs Want.

Faithfulness is 1.00 for both A and B, even though both systems answer three questions wrong. Extractive answers are faithful by construction: every word comes from the context, so a word level faithfulness check passes by design. It catches invented content and nothing else. System C proves it: the same answers with one invented phrase appended drop faithfulness to 0.70, while token F1 only falls to 0.225 and substring accuracy stays at 0.80. Faithfulness is the only metric in our set that separates C from A, and that separation is exactly its job. But a faithful answer can still be the wrong sentence, and our harness shows that happening three times in 20 questions.

The three misses are worth naming, because they are three different failure modes. On how much is shipping outside the United States, the system retrieved the right passage and picked the wrong sentence from it: orders over 40 dollars ship free in the United States, when the answer was in the next sentence, international shipping costs 12 dollars per order. On how often does the single origin change, it picked the single origin bag costs 16 dollars, because keyword overlap cannot tell costs from changes. On what is the minimum wholesale order, it retrieved a passage about wholesale orders that never mentions the minimum, because the words wholesale orders matched and the number did not matter to the scorer. Retrieval found the topic. Selection picked the wrong fact. No aggregate score names these. Only the per question table does.

The adversarial probe: a wrong answer that scores 0.857

The most important number in this whole part did not come from the three systems. It came from a probe we ran after the main experiment, to test what token F1 actually rewards. We fed the harness a hand written wrong answer, Kiln Coffee was founded in 2019 in Seattle, against the gold Kiln Coffee was founded in Portland in 2019, with both the Portland and Seattle passages in the retrieved context. The result: exact match 0.00, token F1 0.857, faithfulness 1.00. Every word of the wrong answer appears in the context, and seven of the eight gold tokens appear in the answer, so F1 calls it nearly perfect. The answer is wrong on the one fact the question asked about, the city, and two of the three metrics cannot see it. The only checks that catch it are the substring check for Portland, which fails, and a human reading the sentence.

This is the core argument of this part. Token overlap metrics measure word sharing, not truth. A wrong city, a wrong year, or a wrong price can hide inside a high F1 score whenever the rest of the sentence matches. RAGAS faithfulness has the same blind spot by design: it asks whether claims can be inferred from the context, and Seattle is in the context, just attached to the wrong event. The fix is not a better aggregate metric. The fix is a test set where the wrong entity is present as a distractor, plus a human reading the five worst examples on every run. Our corpus has the distractor built in: the Seattle roastery passage exists precisely so a careless retriever can pick the wrong city, and it did, in the probe and in spirit in the wholesale miss.

The cost ledger

Here is the full ledger for scoring 20 questions three ways. Our harness ran 60 system question pairs in 0.010 seconds, with zero API calls and zero cost, on a laptop, using only the Python standard library. Scoring the same 20 questions the RAGAS way needs 80 LLM judge calls and 20 embedding calls, because faithfulness needs two calls per question, answer relevancy needs one generation plus embeddings, and context relevancy needs one extraction. That is before retries, before rate limits, and before the judge model changes version and quietly moves every score. The judge route also has a failure mode the local route does not: when the judge API is down, your deploy gate is down. A local harness runs in CI on every commit, offline, deterministically, with the same numbers every time. That determinism is what makes it a gate instead of a report.

The gate: thresholds that block a deploy

A harness earns its keep when it can say no. We set three thresholds before looking at the results, and we did not move them after: recall at 3 of at least 0.90, faithfulness of at least 0.90, and substring accuracy of at least 0.80. System B passes all three and ships. System A fails recall at 0.85 and does not ship. System C fails faithfulness at 0.70 and recall at 0.85 and does not ship. The gate is a few lines at the end of the script, and it exits nonzero on failure so CI blocks the deploy.

GATE = {"recall@3": 0.90, "faith": 0.90, "substring": 0.80}

def gate(aggregate):
failed = [m for m, t in GATE.items() if aggregate[m] < t]
return (not failed), failed

passed, failed = gate(aggregate)
print("GATE PASS" if passed else f"GATE FAIL: {failed}")
raise SystemExit(0 if passed else 1)

Three rules keep the gate honest. First, thresholds are set before the run, never after, or the gate becomes a rubber stamp. Second, the gate runs on the same frozen test set every time, and the test set only grows: new failures get added as regression questions, never edited away. Third, the gate prints the failing questions by name. A red build that says recall dropped to 0.85 is useful. A red build that says the shipping question now returns the free shipping sentence instead of the 12 dollar sentence is actionable.

Our opinionated take

Most teams we see do evaluation backwards: they buy the fanciest judge, run it once, quote the number, and never look at a single answer. That is theatre. The order that works is the reverse. First, build the cheap deterministic harness and run it on every change, because it is free and it catches retrieval and selection failures the same day you introduce them. Second, read the five worst examples on every run, because the aggregate will lie to you and the examples will not. Third, run the LLM judge weekly on a sample, not on every commit, and calibrate it the ARES way: about 150 human labelled examples, confidence intervals on the scores, and a check that the judge still agrees with people on your domain. Fourth, keep the two layers separate in your head. The harness answers did we break retrieval. The judge answers does the answer read well and stay grounded. One number cannot answer both questions, and any tool that promises it is selling you the average of two different failures.

We also think the test set matters more than the metric. Twenty hand written questions caught three real failure modes and one adversarial trap, because the corpus had distractors built in: two cities, two bag prices, two shipping sentences in one passage. A test set without distractors will give you perfect scores and teach you nothing. If your test set has never failed, it is not a test set. It is a demo.

What to do this week

Start with 20 questions on your own corpus, each with a short gold answer and the passage that contains it. Add one distractor per question type: a second city, a second price, a second date that a careless retriever could pick. Implement recall at 3, token F1, substring accuracy, and the faithfulness proxy from this part, in one file, standard library only. Run it against your current retriever and read every miss by name. Then set three thresholds before your next change, wire the script into CI with a nonzero exit on failure, and add every new failure to the test set as a regression question. After that, and only after that, run RAGAS or DeepEval on a weekly sample, and compare the judge scores against your harness scores on the same questions. Where they disagree, trust the harness until a human reads both answers.

What is Next in This Series

Deep Part 9 takes the retrieval stack into LangGraph, where state and memory decide what the agent remembers between turns. We will build a small agent that keeps working notes across turns, measure how much memory helps and how much it costs, and show where memory becomes a liability: stale facts that outlive the documents they came from. The eval harness from this part comes along, because a memory change is a retriever change, and it goes through the same gate.

title: What Is a Rage Click? 7 Causes, Dead Clicks and Fixes
description:
We build Opti-Behavior, the WordPress plugin discussed here. Originally published on optiuser.com.

A rage click is when a visitor clicks the same spot several times in a very short time, usually 3 or more clicks within about one second. Rage clicking almost always means the visitor expected something to happen, and it did not. Think of an elevator button you press again and again: that is exactly what rage clicks are, but on a website.

A dead click is the quiet version: a single click on something that looks clickable and does nothing.

Rage clicks are one of the clearest signs of a frustrated visitor. And frustrated visitors do not buy, sign up or come back. The good news: rage clicks are easy to find and often easy to fix.

Simple definition: A rage click is 3 or more quick clicks on the same small area, usually within about one second. A dead click is a single click that does nothing at all. In Opti-Behavior, rage, dead and error click detection is a Pro feature; the free plugin gives you click heatmaps, where dead clicks show up as hot spots on things that are not links.

Rage clicks vs dead clicks vs error clicks

These three often come together. Here is the difference.

Type What happens What the visitor feels
Rage click Many fast clicks on the same spot "Why is this not working?!"
Dead click One click, nothing changes on the page "Hmm, I thought that was a button."
Error click A click that triggers a JavaScript error Often nothing visible, the feature is broken

A dead click can turn into a rage click. The visitor clicks once, nothing happens, so they click again, harder.

What causes rage clicks?

Here are the most common causes we see on WordPress sites.

  1. Things that look clickable but are not. A product image, an icon, bold blue text, a card. People expect a link.
  2. Slow buttons. The button works, but it takes two seconds to react. The visitor clicks again because they think it failed.
  3. Broken JavaScript. A plugin conflict or an error stops a menu, a slider or an "Add to cart" button from working. On a shop, a broken checkout script is a common reason behind an abandoned cart.
  4. Tiny tap targets on mobile. The link is too small, so the finger misses it again and again.
  5. Form buttons that do not give feedback. The visitor presses "Send", nothing shows, so they press again.
  6. Pop-ups that will not close. The close button is too small or covered.
  7. Disabled buttons with no explanation. The button is grey because a field is missing, but nothing tells the visitor.

How to find rage clicks on your WordPress site

Option 1: Watch recordings (slow)

You can open session recordings one by one and look for fast clicks. It works, but it takes hours on a busy site.

Option 2: Let a tool flag them (fast)

Opti-Behavior Pro detects friction events on its own. It flags rage clicks, dead clicks and error clicks, groups them by page and element, and links each one to the recording where it happened. Each line is one element where visitors got stuck, with the number of events. Open an event to see the page, the element and the recording.

This turns hours of watching into a short to-do list, for example: "The 'Size guide' link on product pages gets the most rage clicks." Now you know exactly what to fix.

Option 3: Check your click heatmap

A click heatmap shows hot spots on things that are not links. That is where dead clicks live. It is included in the free version of Opti-Behavior. Hot spots on images or plain text often mean dead clicks.

Dead clicks: the quiet cousin of rage clicks

A rage click is loud. Someone hits the same spot five times in a second. A dead click is quiet. Someone clicks once on something that looks clickable, nothing happens, and they just leave. No drama, no noise. That is why dead clicks are easy to miss, and why they often cost more.

Here is a typical example. Imagine a shop with a "Size guide" line under the price, in blue and underlined. It looks exactly like a link, but it is plain text. Visitors click it and nothing opens. Some of them never add to cart, because they are not sure which size to pick.

Why a click can be "dead"

When Opti-Behavior Pro records a dead click, it also saves the details: the element that was clicked, whether it was really interactive, whether something was covering it, what happened after the click, and the screen size, browser and device. The button "View element on page" highlights the element on your live page, so you see exactly what visitors saw.

Most dead clicks come from one of these three causes:

  • Covered by an overlay. A pop-up, a cookie banner or a sticky bar sits on top of the button. The visitor sees the button but clicks the invisible layer above it. This is very common on mobile.
  • Not interactive. The element looks like a link or a button (blue, underlined, an arrow, a card with a shadow) but it is just text or an image.
  • A script problem. The button should work, but its JavaScript failed to load or crashed.

The verdict tells you who should fix it

In Opti-Behavior Pro, each group of friction events gets a verdict, so you know if it is a design job or a developer job:

Verdict What it means Who fixes it
Probable code bug Clicks on this element triggered a captured error Developer
Needs review Could be a bug or the network (ad blockers, offline) Check a few recordings first
Visitor behavior Normal behavior, like impatient clicking Usually nobody, or a small design tweak

With Pro, Smart Insights measures rage clicks per 100 visits, so a busy page does not flood you with cards. You see the elements that frustrate a real share of visitors, not every single double-click.

How to fix dead clicks

  • Covered by overlay: move or shrink the pop-up, cookie banner or sticky bar, or delay it until the visitor scrolls.
  • Not interactive: make it a real link, or change its look so it does not pretend to be one. No blue underline on plain text.
  • Probable code bug: open the linked JavaScript error and fix or replace the script that breaks.

After the fix, check the same element two weeks later. Dead clicks on it should drop close to zero.

How to fix rage clicks

Fix the cause, not the symptom. Here is a simple guide.

Cause Fix
Image or icon looks clickable Make it a link, or change the style so it does not look clickable
Button is slow Show a loading state right away ("Adding…") so people know it worked
JavaScript error Check the error log, update or replace the plugin that breaks
Tiny mobile link Make tap targets at least 44 by 44 pixels
Form button gives no feedback Show a message or spinner right after the click
Pop-up close button hard to hit Make it bigger and let people close it by tapping outside
Disabled button Tell people what is missing, next to the button

Measure before and after

Before you fix anything, look at the verdict. Opti-Behavior Pro tells you if the clicks look like a design problem (people click something that is not a button) or a code bug (the clicks trigger an error).

After a fix, compare the number of rage clicks on that element for the next two weeks. If it drops, you fixed it. If you want to be sure the change also helped sales or sign-ups, run an A/B test. Opti-Behavior's A/B testing is free.

Are rage clicks always bad?

Almost always, but not every time. Some people double-click out of habit. A game or a quiz may need fast clicks. That is why good tools look for a pattern: many visitors, same element, again and again. One person with a fast finger is not a problem. Fifty people on the same button is.

Slow buttons and rage clicks often go together. If your page reacts slowly to taps, Core Web Vitals (especially INP) are worth a look.

Rage clicks FAQ

What are rage clicks?
Rage clicks are several fast clicks on the same spot, usually within about one second. They show that a visitor expected something to happen and it did not.

What is the difference between rage clicks and dead clicks?
A dead click is one click that does nothing. A rage click is many fast clicks in the same place. A dead click often becomes a rage click when the visitor tries again.

How do I track rage clicks in WordPress?
Use a behavior analytics plugin that detects friction events. Opti-Behavior Pro flags rage clicks, dead clicks and error clicks and links each one to a session recording.

Do rage clicks hurt conversions?
They can. A rage click means a visitor tried to do something and could not, so it often marks a step where people give up. Fix the elements with the most rage clicks first, then check the effect with an A/B test.

Full guide with screenshots of the friction events report: What Is a Rage Click? 7 Causes, Dead Clicks and Fixes

Drafted with AI assistance, reviewed by the Opti-Behavior Team.

title: Scrape Property Finder Data with Python: What Furniture Adds to a Dubai Rent
description:
A furnished 1-bedroom apartment in Al Barsha listed on Property Finder this week asks a median AED 85,000 a year. An unfurnished one asks AED 65,000. That is 30.8% more for a sofa, a bed and a fridge, and it is the largest gap I found for 1-bedroom flats in ten Dubai areas.

Tenants moving to Dubai ask the same question every year: is it cheaper to rent unfurnished and buy the furniture? Landlords ask the mirror question: does furnishing a flat pay? Both start with one number, the premium a furnished flat commands over an unfurnished one in the same area. Property Finder has a furnishing filter, so I pulled both sides with Python and compared them. The median premium across the ten areas is 11.3% for 1-bedroom flats and 12.5% for 2-bedroom flats. The bigger lesson is in Dubai Hills Estate, where furnished flats look cheaper and are not.

The data

Every listing here was pulled through the Property Finder API. Its /search-rent endpoint takes a furnishing parameter (furnished, unfurnished or partly), so the split costs nothing extra: one call per area, bedroom count and furnishing state.

On 4 November 2026 I made 40 calls: ten areas, 1- and 2-bedroom apartments, furnished and unfurnished, the first page of yearly rentals sorted by newest. That returned 1,465 rows. After dropping project cards and a few broken rows (more on both below), 1,307 listings were left, about 33 per area, bedroom count and furnishing state. Each response also carries total_count, the number of matching listings on the site, which shows how much of each market is furnished: 15,800 furnished against 16,920 unfurnished listings in these twenty segments.

The ten areas fall into three groups: the waterfront (Dubai Marina, Emaar Beachfront, Palm Jumeirah), the central towers (Downtown Dubai, Business Bay, Jumeirah Lake Towers or JLT) and the suburbs (Jumeirah Village Circle or JVC, Dubai Hills Estate, Al Barsha, Dubai Silicon Oasis). /autocomplete-location turns each name into a location ID.

The code

This is the whole comparison for one area and bedroom count. Install requests, set the RAPIDAPI_KEY environment variable to your RapidAPI key, and run it.

import json
import os
import statistics

import requests

HOST = "uae-real-estate-property.p.rapidapi.com"  # Property Finder API on RapidAPI
BASE = os.environ.get("API_BASE", "https://" + HOST)


def headers():
    if "API_BASE" in os.environ:
        return json.loads(os.environ.get("API_HEADERS", "{}"))
    return {"x-rapidapi-host": HOST, "x-rapidapi-key": os.environ["RAPIDAPI_KEY"]}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(BASE + path, params=params, headers=headers(), timeout=120)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def location_id(name):
    found = get("/autocomplete-location", query=name)["data"]
    exact = [x for x in found if x["name"].lower() == name.lower()]
    return (exact or found)[0]["id"]


def rents(loc, bedrooms, furnishing):
    """Newest yearly rents for one furnishing state: (rent, size in sq ft) pairs, and the total count."""
    body = get("/search-rent", location_id=loc, property_type="apartment", bedrooms=bedrooms,
               rent_frequency="yearly", furnishing=furnishing, sort="newest", page=1)
    rows = []
    for x in body["data"]:
        price, size = x.get("price") or {}, (x.get("size") or {}).get("value")
        # Skip new-project cards (sale prices), non-yearly prices and rows with no size
        if (x.get("listing_type") != "property" or not price.get("value")
                or price.get("period") != "yearly" or not size):
            continue
        if price["value"] / size > 1000:  # a sale price, or a size typed in square metres
            continue
        rows.append((price["value"], size))
    return rows, body["total_count"]


area, beds = "Jumeirah Lake Towers", 1
loc = location_id(area)
furn, furn_total = rents(loc, beds, "furnished")
unfurn, unfurn_total = rents(loc, beds, "unfurnished")

for name, rows in (("furnished", furn), ("unfurnished", unfurn)):
    print("%-12s %2d listings, median AED %s a year, AED %.0f per sq ft" % (
        name, len(rows), format(statistics.median(r for r, s in rows), ",.0f"),
        statistics.median(r / s for r, s in rows)))

premium = statistics.median(r for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r for r, s in unfurn) - 1
premium_psf = statistics.median(r / s for r, s in furn) / statistics.median(r / s for r, s in unfurn) - 1
print("furniture premium: %+.1f%% on the median rent, %+.1f%% per sq ft" % (premium * 100, premium_psf * 100))
print("furnished share of listings: %.0f%%" % (100 * furn_total / (furn_total + unfurn_total)))

For a 1-bedroom in JLT it printed:

furnished    33 listings, median AED 95,000 a year, AED 110 per sq ft
unfurnished  33 listings, median AED 79,999 a year, AED 101 per sq ft
furniture premium: +18.8% on the median rent, +8.9% per sq ft
furnished share of listings: 58%

The API_BASE switch is there so the same script can point at a test server; with only RAPIDAPI_KEY set it calls RapidAPI. The full version loops over the ten areas, caches every response and also compares listings building by building. Two numbers come out of every pair, and you need both: the premium on the median rent and the premium per square foot.

Furnished flats ask about 11% more

For 1-bedroom apartments, furnished listings ask more than unfurnished ones in 7 of the 10 areas. The median premium is 11.3%.

Al Barsha leads at 30.8%, then Downtown Dubai at 25.0% (AED 150,000 furnished against AED 119,999) and JLT at 18.8%. Business Bay shows no premium at all: both sides have a median of AED 90,000. Palm Jumeirah furnished 1-beds ask 3.1% less, and Dubai Hills Estate 12.7% less.

For 2-bedroom flats the median premium is 12.5%, and furnished asks more in 9 of 10 areas. Downtown Dubai stands out again at 33.3%: AED 220,000 against AED 165,000. Dubai Silicon Oasis shows 64.7%, but only 24 furnished 2-bedroom flats were listed there in total, and they are much bigger than the unfurnished ones (a median of 1,501 sq ft against 1,082). That is a sample to note, not a finding.

Area 1-bed unfurnished (AED) 1-bed furnished (AED) 1-bed premium 1-bed per sq ft 2-bed premium 2-bed per sq ft
Dubai Marina 85,000 95,000 +11.8% +17.5% +3.9% +6.8%
Downtown Dubai 119,999 150,000 +25.0% +47.8% +33.3% +51.6%
Palm Jumeirah 160,000 155,000 -3.1% +4.1% +13.6% +27.2%
Business Bay 90,000 90,000 0.0% +3.3% +6.3% +8.5%
JVC 72,000 80,000 +11.1% +5.5% +9.5% +5.9%
Dubai Hills Estate 106,500 93,000 -12.7% +16.2% -21.9% +14.7%
Emaar Beachfront 130,000 145,000 +11.5% +8.3% +11.4% +17.8%
Dubai Silicon Oasis 62,000 64,999 +4.8% +28.7% +64.7% +36.9%
Al Barsha 65,000 85,000 +30.8% +35.6% +26.3% +28.0%
JLT 79,999 95,000 +18.8% +8.9% +14.3% +16.0%

Medians of the newest yearly listings, about 33 per cell, collected on 4 November 2026. "Per sq ft" compares the median yearly rent per square foot.

In money, the premium is easy to read. A furnished 1-bed in JVC asks AED 8,000 a year more than an unfurnished one; in JLT the gap is AED 15,001, and in Downtown Dubai about AED 30,000. That Downtown figure compares different buildings, though: in the 6 Downtown buildings with both kinds of 1-bed listing, the median furnished flat asked 13.5% less than the unfurnished one. Whether that beats buying your own furniture depends on how long you stay, but it is a yearly cost, paid again at every renewal.

Divide by the size and every gap turns positive

Dubai Hills Estate was the result that made me look twice. On the median rent, furnished flats there are 12.7% cheaper for 1-bedrooms and 21.9% cheaper for 2-bedrooms. That would make it the one area where landlords pay you to take their furniture.

They don't. The furnished flats in Dubai Hills are smaller. The median furnished 1-bed is 645 sq ft against 743 sq ft unfurnished, and the median furnished 2-bed is 748 sq ft against 1,118. My reading is that the compact 2-bedroom units are the ones landlords furnish, while the large family layouts are let empty. Per square foot, furnished flats in Dubai Hills ask 16.2% more for 1-bedrooms and 14.7% more for 2-bedrooms.

The same thing happens on Palm Jumeirah, where furnished 1-beds look 3.1% cheaper and are 4.1% dearer per square foot. Measured per square foot, furnished flats ask more in all 20 area and bedroom pairs. The median premium per square foot is 12.6% for 1-bedrooms and 16.9% for 2-bedrooms.

Per square foot is still not a perfect control, because a furnished flat can sit in a newer or better building. So I also matched listings building by building. In 132 cases the same building had both furnished and unfurnished listings in my sample. Comparing the medians inside each building, furnished asked more in 91 of them (69%), and the median premium was 9.6%: 6.5% for 1-bedrooms and 13.6% for 2-bedrooms. That is the cleanest estimate here, and it is a little lower than the area figures, which suggests part of the area premium is the building, not the furniture.

How common furnished flats are does not set the premium

The total_count field gives the share of each market that is furnished, and it varies more than the premium does.

Downtown Dubai (67.9%), Palm Jumeirah (65.7%) and Emaar Beachfront (64.4%) list most 1-beds furnished. My guess is that they draw more short stays and new arrivals, though this data cannot show it. At the other end, only 19.9% of 1-bed rentals in Al Barsha and 12.6% in Dubai Silicon Oasis are furnished.

It would be neat if scarcity set the price, but the data does not say so. Al Barsha has one of the smallest furnished shares and the largest 1-bed premium, 30.8%. Dubai Hills Estate is mostly unfurnished too (23.7% furnished), and its furnished 1-beds ask 12.7% less, because they are smaller. Dubai Silicon Oasis, where furnished is rarest, asks only 4.8% more. And in Downtown, where furnished is the norm, the area median still shows 25.0% more for a 1-bed, perhaps because furnished Downtown flats are often serviced units in branded towers, even though the same-building comparison above points the other way. Across all twenty segments, 48.3% of the listings are furnished.

Pitfalls I hit in the listings

Project cards ignore the filter. 154 of the 1,465 rows were new-project cards (listing_type is project), with a "from" sale price instead of a yearly rent. 77 of them were identical in the furnished and unfurnished results for the same search, so the furnishing filter does not apply to them. Keep only listing_type == "property" with a price.value and price.period == "yearly".

Some rents are not rents. One unfurnished 1-bed in Dubai Hills Estate was listed at AED 4,000,000 a year for 757 sq ft, which is a sale price in the wrong box. Two others had sizes of 11 and 135 sq ft, most likely square metres typed as square feet. A ceiling of AED 1,000 per sq ft a year removes all three and nothing else. The median barely notices them; an average does.

The median rent hides the size mix. This is the Dubai Hills lesson. Before you report a furnished premium for an area, check the median size on both sides. If they differ by more than a few percent, report the rent per square foot too.

There is a third option. Property Finder also has furnishing=partly. I left it out, so the furnished share above is furnished against unfurnished only, not against the whole market.

"Newest" can reach back months. Where a segment is small, the first page of the newest listings is most of the segment. The oldest listing in my sample was posted on 20 May 2026. In Dubai Silicon Oasis the 24 furnished 2-beds are the whole furnished market for that size, not a sample of it.

Asking is not signed. All of these are asking rents. The registered lease records in /get-transactions do not say whether a flat was furnished, so this data cannot check the premium against signed rents. Treat the figures as what landlords ask for furniture, not what tenants end up paying for it.

Where I would take it next

I would repeat the building match with more pages per segment, so each building has five or more listings on each side, and add furnishing=partly as a middle group. I would also track the same buildings over a few months: if furnished listings stay on the market longer, the premium is partly wishful.

For the signed-rent side of these areas, the Al Barsha rent page and the Dubai Hills Estate rent page on UAEPropertyAPI show median lease rents by bedroom count, updated monthly. The parameters used here are documented in the Happy Endpoint reference for the Property Finder API, more Python and JavaScript examples sit in the GitHub repo, and a key is a sign-up away on RapidAPI. For every Property Finder listing with its price changes as one file, see the listings dataset, or contact us for something custom.

title: Half of Googlebot's requests to my Next.js site are for JavaScript. 176 pages were never crawled.
description:
I run two small Next.js sites on the same host. Google indexes neither of them well, and this week I read the crawl stats for both instead of guessing. They fail in opposite ways.

Site one: a calculator site, robots.txt allows everything

Search Console, crawl stats, last 90 days:

total crawl requests      988
average response time     173 ms
by response               200: 97 %    404: 2 %
by purpose                refresh: 100 %
by file type              JavaScript 50 %   HTML 37 %   CSS 7 %   image 4 %
by Googlebot type         page resource load 57 %   smartphone 34 %

And the Pages report:

indexed                                  32
discovered - currently not indexed      176
crawled - currently not indexed          40

Read together: Google made 988 requests in three months, and more than half of them were not pages. They were the scripts and stylesheets it needs to render pages it already knows. About 37 % were HTML, which is roughly 365 page fetches in 90 days, four a day, for a sitemap of 263 URLs. Every request was a refresh of something known. None went to discovering anything new, and 176 URLs sit in "discovered" with no crawl date at all.

Nothing is broken. The server answers in 173 ms, nothing is blocked, the sitemap is read. Google gives this site a very small allowance and spends more than half of it on JavaScript.

Site two: a resume builder, robots.txt blocked /_next/

Same host, same framework, and one line that had been in robots.txt since May: Disallow: /_next/. It was there to keep "infrastructure" out of search. /_next/static is where every stylesheet and script lives.

total crawl requests      about 1,680
by file type              HTML 80 %   JavaScript 2 %   image 4 %
by Googlebot type         smartphone 57 %   page resource load 4 %
crawled - currently not indexed         411

Here Google fetched far more HTML, because it was not allowed to fetch anything else. It read 411 pages and declined to index them. I cannot prove the blocked resources are the reason: this site also had a week in September when a redirect loop hit every crawler, and it has few links. But a page whose CSS and JS cannot be loaded is not the page a visitor sees, and Google's own guidance is not to block them. I removed the line today.

What I take from the two together

  • The same complaint, "Google does not index my site", had two different shapes: never crawled on one site, crawled and declined on the other. The Pages report tells you which one you have, and the fix is different.
  • Blocking /_next/ does not save crawl budget in any useful way. It trades rendering for raw HTML fetches.
  • Allowing it has a cost on a site with little authority: the rendering requests come out of the same small allowance. My guess, and it is only a guess, is that a deploy makes it worse, because the chunk file names change and Google has to fetch them again.
  • Crawl stats sit under Settings, not in the main reports, and I had never opened them. Ten minutes there replaced weeks of theories.

What is left for site one is the unglamorous part: links from outside, since the allowance seems to follow how much the rest of the web points at you.

The calculator site is AllSmartCalculators; a typical page is the PPF calculator. Written by an AI assistant from my own Search Console data.

title: Small SaaS Shipment Scheduling: Go Queue Push, HTTPS Webhooks, and Polling Workers
description:
Short answer: Choose polling when one small team needs private, controlled execution; choose HTTPS push when delivery latency matters enough to justify a public receiver; choose a queue subscription when sustained fan-out and explicit backpressure matter more than the fewest moving parts. For a fintech SaaS sending shipment updates to subscribers in Europe and the US, the default I would operate is a durable queue with regional consumers and an idempotent delivery boundary. It gives up some setup simplicity to keep latency, concurrency, and retry pressure visible.

I've been paged by both missed scheduled jobs and duplicate deliveries. That history produces one invariant: scheduling decides when work becomes eligible, but a durable handoff plus an idempotent receiver decides whether the shipment update survives retries. Treat those as separate state transitions.

Duplicates still happen.

How should a small SaaS choose public HTTPS webhook push, queue subscribe, or polling?

Start with the failure mode the team is actually equipped to own. A public HTTPS push receiver can be the shortest path from an eligible task to a subscriber notification. It also becomes an internet-facing production service: authentication, replay defense, rate limits, deployment overlap, and traffic bursts all arrive on that endpoint. Low idle cost and low delivery delay are attractive, but the receiver must turn a burst into bounded work instead of letting request concurrency become the queue.

A queue subscription places a durable buffer between scheduling and delivery. Consumers can take work at a rate their dependencies tolerate, and queue depth makes backlog concrete. This is usually the cleanest operational shape for shipment fan-out because one shipment version may create many subscriber deliveries. The catch is that the team now owns consumer scaling, poison-message policy, retention decisions, and a clear acknowledgement rule. It isn't the easiest setup for a service that sends a handful of non-urgent updates each day.

A polling worker keeps the worker private and gives it direct control over batch size and cadence. For a small SaaS with relaxed latency targets, that can be the easiest deployment: one worker asks for eligible jobs, leases a bounded batch, processes it, then sleeps. The cost is paid in empty reads, database or queue load, and delay up to the polling interval. Tightening the interval cuts delay while increasing idle work. That's the latency-versus-cost dial in its least disguised form.

Delivery shape Best fit Operational catch Latency/cost tendency
Public HTTPS push Sparse events that need prompt delivery Public endpoint and burst control Low idle work; receiver capacity must absorb bursts
Queue subscription Sustained or bursty fan-out Consumer fleet and acknowledgement policy Fast while capacity is available; buffer adds infrastructure
Polling worker Low volume with relaxed deadlines Empty polls and interval delay Longer interval lowers idle work but raises delay

For Europe and the US, don't turn geography into one transatlantic critical path by accident. Keep an authoritative shipment version, create one delivery record per subscriber, and route each record to the region responsible for that subscriber. Whether data is allowed to cross regions is a legal and product requirement, not something an SRE should infer from a cloud diagram. I'm not sure which residency boundary applies to your customers; a written classification from counsel and security resolves that uncertainty.

The incident lesson is an idempotency boundary, not a retry count

A retry policy without a stable operation identity converts temporary uncertainty into duplicate side effects. The useful identity in this system is not merely a queue message ID. Use business fields that remain stable when the same work is republished: shipment ID, subscriber ID, and shipment version. The tuple means, "deliver this version of this shipment to this subscriber." A later shipment version is new work; a redelivery of the same version is not.

The long paragraph matters because the awkward failure window sits between systems. A worker can lease a delivery, send the HTTPS request, and lose its process before recording completion. On retry, its local state cannot prove whether the subscriber accepted the first request. Holding a database transaction open across the network doesn't repair that ambiguity and creates a different operational risk. The subscriber-facing contract therefore needs the same idempotency key, while the worker ledger uses a lease so an abandoned attempt becomes eligible again. A successful subscriber response is followed by completion in the ledger; a timeout or rate-limit response releases the lease for a later attempt. If the remote subscriber cannot deduplicate, the honest guarantee is at-least-once attempts with possible duplicate effects. Don't label that exactly once.

Keep the boundary boring.

The acknowledgement point follows from that model. A consumer acknowledges only after the durable delivery state is complete. It does not acknowledge when work starts, and it does not retry indefinitely inside one process. When a subscriber returns an overload signal such as HTTP 429, schedule the next eligible attempt with bounded backoff and jitter, then free the worker slot. Invalid or permanently unauthorized destinations need a terminal state and an operator-visible reason rather than a hot retry loop.

A preventative Go delivery path

The interfaces below avoid tying the core rule to a queue vendor. Claim must atomically create or renew a bounded lease for the operation key. Send forwards that same key to the subscriber. A crash after the remote side effect but before Complete is safe only when the subscriber also treats the key idempotently.

package delivery

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

var ErrLeaseHeld = errors.New("delivery lease held")

type Update struct {
    ShipmentID  string
    SubscriberID string
    Version     int64
    Payload     []byte
}

func (u Update) Key() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("shipment:%s:subscriber:%s:version:%d",
        u.ShipmentID, u.SubscriberID, u.Version)
}

type Ledger interface {
    Claim(ctx context.Context, key string, lease time.Duration) (bool, error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, key string) error
    Release(ctx context.Context, key string, nextAttempt time.Time, reason string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, update Update, idempotencyKey string) error
}

type Handler struct {
    Ledger Ledger
    Sender Sender
    Lease  time.Duration
    Delay  func(attempt int) time.Duration
}

func (h Handler) Deliver(ctx context.Context, update Update, attempt int) error {
    key := update.Key()
    claimed, err := h.Ledger.Claim(ctx, key, h.Lease)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("claim %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    if !claimed {
        return ErrLeaseHeld
    }

    if err := h.Sender.Send(ctx, update, key); err != nil {
        next := time.Now().Add(h.Delay(attempt))
        if releaseErr := h.Ledger.Release(ctx, key, next, err.Error()); releaseErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("send failed: %v; release failed: %w", err, releaseErr)
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("send %s: %w", key, err)
    }

    if err := h.Ledger.Complete(ctx, key); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("complete %s: %w", key, err)
    }
    return nil
}

The queue adapter around Deliver has one sharp rule: acknowledge on nil; otherwise leave or reschedule the message according to the ledger's next-attempt time. ErrLeaseHeld should not trigger concurrent work on the same operation. Exact adapter behavior depends on the queue's visibility and acknowledgement model, so verify it against the primary documentation rather than assuming all subscriptions expose the same controls.

Scheduling, deployment, and observability must share one state model

Delayed work starts as data. Store eligible_at, the stable operation key, attempt count, lease expiry, and terminal outcome. A scheduler promotes eligible records to the delivery queue; it does not perform subscriber I/O itself. That separation lets a delayed task remain inspectable during a deploy and stops a slow subscriber from consuming the scheduler's capacity.

Deploy consumers with overlap only after proving that the lease and idempotency paths work under concurrency. The minimum test suite races two claims for one key, kills a worker after Send but before Complete, advances a lease past expiry, and republishes the same operation. A separate load test should create one shipment update with a realistic subscriber fan-out and confirm that concurrency limits protect the slowest dependency. No benchmark number transfers cleanly between teams — payload size, subscriber response time, and regional network paths dominate it.

Observe the state transitions, not just process health. Queue age answers whether customers are waiting; queue depth without age can exaggerate a fast-moving burst. Track eligible-to-start delay by region, delivery completion latency, attempts per operation key, terminal failures by reason, active leases, and lease expirations. Alert on customer-impacting delay and a sustained failure ratio. A single retry is evidence for a trace, not necessarily a page.

Cost needs the same workload-shaped treatment. Estimate scheduled records, fan-out deliveries, empty poll reads, retained bytes, regional transfer, worker idle time, and peak concurrency. Then replay a representative day through each design. Public push often removes empty polls, polling makes the idle tax explicit, and subscriptions trade that tax for managed buffering plus active consumers. Your mileage may vary because subscriber distribution and burst shape move the answer more than an architecture label does.

When should you choose a different delivery shape?

Stick with a polling worker when delivery can wait for the polling interval, volume is low, and keeping workers private reduces more operational burden than empty reads create. Increase the interval until the observed eligible-to-start delay approaches the product objective, then leave headroom for backlog recovery. This is a good constraint, not a second-class architecture.

Use public HTTPS push when events are sparse, prompt delivery is important, and the team already operates authenticated public receivers with admission control. It is not suitable when a burst can exceed receiver capacity and there is no durable buffer before business processing. A push endpoint should validate and durably accept quickly; long subscriber work belongs behind its own queue.

Choose a queue subscription when fan-out is sustained or bursty, independent scaling matters, and operators need backlog visibility. Don't choose it merely because queues sound more serious. If the team cannot define acknowledgement, retention, terminal failure, and replay procedures, the extra component has created ambiguity rather than reliability.

The final decision rule is operational: select the least complex shape that meets the measured delivery deadline while preserving a durable handoff and an end-to-end idempotency key. Revisit it when fan-out, regional boundaries, or subscriber latency changes. The transport may change; the invariant should not.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview

title: Evaluate Vercel Flags from another project without sharing SDK keys.
description:
Project Connections let applications evaluate flags defined in another Vercel project within the same team, without managing SDK keys.

Previously, sharing flags between projects required copying a server SDK key into an environment variable and managing it manually. Connected projects authenticate using their deployment’s identity. For local development, vercel env pull retrieves your project’s OIDC token.

Manage access from the Connections page under your project's Flags section, or with vercel flags connections in the CLI. Connections grant read-only access across all environments. The consumer deployment determines the flag environment (production deployments evaluate production flags).

In the consumer application, create an adapter with the source project’s ID.

Access can be revoked without redeploying.

Project Connections are available on all plans and require @flags-sdk/vercel 1.6.0 or later, or @vercel/flags-core 1.11.0 or later when using the core library directly. Managing connections from the CLI requires Vercel CLI 63.0.0 or later.

Learn more in the Vercel Flags documentation
