title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

title: How to plan a Google Maps embed and directions section for a local business site
description:
A map is useful only when it helps someone arrive. For a local shop, clinic, studio, or service counter in India, pair any embedded map with plain-language directions and a clear address. Visitors may be on a slow connection, using a small screen, or trying to identify the right entrance from a busy road.

Begin by confirming the exact location with the people who work there. Check the map pin against the entrance customers should use, not merely the centre of a large building or market. Write the address in a copyable format, including the area, city, and PIN code where appropriate. If a building has multiple gates or floors, state the entry point, floor, and a recognizable nearby landmark only if the business can verify it.

Next, decide whether an embedded map is necessary. A map can provide useful visual context, but it adds third-party content and may load slowly. Keep the address and a link that opens directions available even if the embed is blocked, delayed, or disabled. Where privacy or performance matters, consider loading the map only after a visitor chooses to view it. Test what happens when scripts or cookies are restricted, and make sure the surrounding page still explains how to reach the business.

Write directions for more than one kind of journey. A short note might mention a nearby bus stop, railway station, main road, or parking arrangement, but avoid guessing travel times or claiming a route is accessible unless you have checked. Tell visitors whom to contact if the pin seems wrong or the entrance is difficult to find. For a lane, campus, or shared commercial building, a brief arrival instruction can prevent confusion.

On mobile, put the address and directions button near opening hours and contact details. Use descriptive button text such as “Get directions” rather than an unexplained icon. Check that the map is not wider than the screen, that text remains readable, and that tapping the address allows it to be copied. Ask a colleague who has not visited recently to follow the page’s directions and point out any gaps.

Before publishing changes, assign someone to verify the pin and arrival notes whenever the business moves or its entrance changes. A map should support good directions, not replace them. For ongoing website planning ideas, see the MGTech Labs blog.

title: Effective Teacher Support for Reasoning Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.14850v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

title: How to Scrape Google News Headlines and Real Article URLs
description:
How to Scrape Google News Headlines and Real Article URLs

Google News is still one of the fastest ways to see what is being written about a topic, a company or a person, across languages and countries. The painful part is the links: many scrapers leave you with Google redirect URLs instead of the publisher's article. This guide shows how to scrape Google News search results, topics and top stories, and keep the real article URL.

You will use the Google News Scraper on Apify. It covers keyword search, topic headlines and top stories in 47 country and language editions, and can resolve Google redirects to the publisher's own URL. You also get the title, publisher, date and related coverage.

By the end of this article you will have a CSV or JSON file on your machine, and a short Python snippet you can rerun or schedule. The same Actor is also callable from JavaScript and from AI agents through the Apify MCP server.

What you need

  • An Apify account. The Free plan is enough to try a small run.
  • A list of inputs for the Actor (URLs, IDs or search terms — details in the steps below).
  • Optional: Python 3 with the apify-client package if you want to automate the run.

No Google login and no proxy setup are required for normal use. Think of it as a small Google News API you do not have to maintain.

How to run it in the Apify Console

Step 1: Open the Actor

Open https://apify.com/veenkes/veenkes-google-news and click Try for free.

Step 2: Enter queries or topics

A search query such as artificial intelligence is enough. You can also add topic pages. Pick an edition such as US:en, GB:en, DE:de or JP:ja.

Step 3: Set a time range

Use a rolling window (for example the last 7 days) or explicit dates. Keep max items per query small on the first run, and leave URL resolution on if you want publisher links.

Step 4: Export

Start the run and download CSV or JSON. De-duplication can drop the same article if several queries return it.

Time range applies to search queries. URL resolution is the difference between a redirect and a link you can fetch or open directly.

How to run it from Python

Install the official client and call the Actor by its Store id veenkes/veenkes-google-news. Replace YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN with a token from Apify Console > Integrations. Do not commit the token to a public repository.

pip install apify-client

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("veenkes/veenkes-google-news").call(run_input={
    "queries": [
        "artificial intelligence"
    ],
    "region": "US:en",
    "timeRange": "7d",
    "maxItemsPerQuery": 50,
    "resolveUrls": True
})

# Write every dataset item, then export from the Console or keep going in code.
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(item)

The JavaScript client (apify-client on npm) uses the same Actor id and the same input object. You can also start the run with a plain HTTP POST to the Apify API if you prefer.

Sample output

Here is a shortened example of one dataset record (field values are illustrative of the schema, taken from a real sample run shape):

{
  "title": "1 killed, 4 injured in shooting in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle neighborhood; suspect is dead",
  "publisher": "CBS News",
  "publisherUrl": "https://www.cbsnews.com",
  "url": "https://www.cbsnews.com/news/washington-dc-shooting-gym-vida/",
  "googleNewsUrl": "https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMibkFVX3lxTE95dkVUTlk2aDQ5YWFfUFBxNWRuSDBoQkdsRlpwN2J6ZTZaSDF0STRpTktzVm0yQTBEd3Z1XzVJT2tXb2M3cVFyejJRZ2k1R3JuMlJpQ1pnRmw3YXJ1NEpaY0xKblVHcnd…",
  "articleId": "CBMibkFVX3lxTE95dkVUTlk2aDQ5YWFfUFBxNWRuSDBoQkdsRlpwN2J6ZTZaSDF0STRpTktzVm0yQTBEd3Z1XzVJT2tXb2M3cVFyejJRZ2k1R3JuMlJpQ1pnRmw3YXJ1NEpaY0xKblVHcnd1NmFoMkt3",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-12T19:28:18.000Z",
  "position": 1,
  "sourceType": "topic",
  "query": null,
  "topic": "TOP_STORIES",
  "language": "en",
  "country": "US",
  "relatedArticles": [
    {
      "googleNewsUrl": "https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMidEFVX3lxTFBxRDBQN3NNZV80TkVLTktzU0V2VzdEYVIwNWRqYkhsd1lZYnRCVkxSdzZzREg0cHVPVjNLSmxwclBxRERaR2Vwb1ducldyWDQybzdfZ2M3M1R1dFBBczd2ZFhESjFEd1B…",
      "title": "Live updates: 55-year-old alleged gunman identified after 1 killed and 4 injured in DC shooting",
      "publisher": "CNN"
    },
    {
      "googleNewsUrl": "https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMixgFBVV95cUxQV3BES0JvbS1IdmF6dG9uc3BvdUlUTmVrenVKUFl0cGFVTWM2ZEhtVWt2TUVMbFBmWGhQbDlFNXBCYTZSbllUeklFT1hUM3ZNODRjdHI0bm5HTzh0VGFmQ21PQW1yTkt…",
      "title": "Logan Circle mass shooting suspect was feuding with condo building management",
      "publisher": "NBC4 Washington"
    }
  ],
  "urlResolved": true,
  "scrapedAt": "2026-11-12T21:32:
  …
}

Once the run has finished, open the dataset in the Console and use Export > CSV if a spreadsheet is your destination. JSON is usually better for code and for language models.

What to use the data for

Media-monitoring teams watch brand and competitor names in several editions. Researchers build a headline corpus for a topic. AI briefing agents need a short list of recent stories with working URLs. A scheduled hourly or daily run is a simple news radar.

Pricing

Pay-per-result pricing starts at $2.00 per 1,000 articles on the Apify Free plan, with lower unit prices on paid Apify plans, plus a small per-run start fee. Always check the live pricing on the Actor page, because plans and unit prices can change. For a first test, keep the input tiny so you can inspect the schema before you scale up.

Scheduling and automations

In the Apify Console you can schedule the Actor (daily or hourly) and leave the same input in place. For incremental jobs, prefer a "since" or "posted after" style filter when the Actor offers one, so you are not paying to re-collect old rows. When a run finishes you can send a webhook, or connect the Actor in Zapier, Make or n8n. AI agents can discover and call veenkes/veenkes-google-news through Apify's MCP server using the same input.

Good practices and limits

This is not an official Google News API, and the Actor is not affiliated with Google. Headlines and snippets belong to their publishers; use them for monitoring and research rather than republishing a news site. Resolved URLs still point at the publisher, who may have their own access rules.

If a run returns fewer rows than you expected, check the input caps, language or country filters, and the Actor log. A zero-row run is usually a filter or an unavailable source, not a silent crash — read the log before you increase limits.

Next step

Open the Actor and run a small job: Google News Scraper: Search, Topics & Article URLs.

If you later want this on a schedule, save the input that worked, add a date filter where it applies, and export CSV automatically from the dataset or from the API snippet above.

title: Take the merge out of the agent's session, and let a skill do the checks before I merge (karasu weekly)
description:
karasu is a text modeling language for system architecture, inspired by the C4 model.
You describe your system in .krs files and karasu draws the views: system, deployment, and team structure.
I haven't written its code by hand; everything goes through Claude Code.

This is the sixth weekly update.
It covers changes merged from November 8 to 13.
Starting this week the update comes out on Saturday instead of Sunday, so this one covers six days instead of seven.

This week in numbers: 72 PRs merged (14 of them Dependabot) and 9 decisions recorded as ADRs.
All 9 ADRs came in ADR-only PRs.
No monthly release this week.
On November 11 the second weekly prerelease of the Visual Studio Code extension came out (0.5.2026111101).

What I learned building with agents this week

This week I changed how PRs get merged, in two places.
For Low PRs, whose diffs I don't read, the merge moved from the Claude session to a GitHub workflow.
For High PRs, which I do read, the checks before I merge became a skill.

Take the merge out of the agent's session

karasu sorts each PR into one of four risk tiers by the paths it changes.
The lowest tier, Low, covers PRs like ADR-only changes and the regenerated ADR index, and I merge them without reading the diff.
Until now, the Claude session that opened the PR ran gh pr merge --auto and left the merge to GitHub's auto-merge.

That had two problems.
The first is that the merge depended on the session.
In my local session records, 3 out of 128 --auto calls were denied by Claude Code's auto mode classifier.
When a call is denied or the session stops, the merge stops too.
One PR took about 7 hours to merge.
The second is that GitHub's auto-merge doesn't wait for the check that decides the tier (Review tier).
One PR merged 16 seconds after that check failed.

Now a workflow handles Low PRs in two jobs.
The judge job has read-only permissions and runs the tier script from main against the PR's head commit.
It doesn't put the PR's files on disk or run the PR's code.
Only the merge job holds a GitHub App key, and it merges with the commit it judged pinned.
The key lives in an environment that only workflows running from main can use.

This adds a key.
The previous design counted needing no new key as one of its reasons.
A leaked key could merge any PR that passes CI, not only Low ones.
I accepted that and created the GitHub App.
The workflow checks the conditions for merging, not whether the change is good.
The local review record is still self-reported by the agent.

The move is split into three stages.
In the first stage, the workflow only judges the open Low PRs and writes down the verdicts.
It merges and comments on nothing; the session's --auto still does the merging.
The PR for that stage ran the same judge script from my machine against real PRs.
It said "wait" while the required checks were running and "merge" once they finished.
In the second stage, the workflow merges according to its verdicts.
In the last stage, --auto comes out of the session's procedure and auto-merge gets turned off for the repository.

On November 13 the workflow merged a PR for the first time.
The first run failed because the private key I had registered in the environment couldn't be read.
After I registered the key again and re-ran it, it merged as low-pr-merger[bot].
Once five PRs in a row merge through the workflow alone, the last stage starts.

When a procedure keeps growing cases, make it a script

In the second stage, sessions were still running --auto.
Then GitHub's auto-merge merged a few seconds after the last required check passed, and the workflow never got its turn.
So I wrote a procedure into the session rules: leave Low PRs to the workflow and wait.
The first version was prose, and every review round found a gap in it.
There were too many cases.
The session has to decide whether to turn off auto-merge, fix a rejected PR, or re-run a stuck check.
If nothing moves for 30 minutes, it goes back to --auto.
In the end the waiting went into a tested script, and the rule kept only the command and a table of what to do for each outcome.

Last week's block on gh pr ready went the same way: listing the loopholes from the command string never ended.
This week the cases couldn't be written out in prose either, and things settled once they became a script that runs.
Next time I write a procedure for sessions, if it has many cases, I'll first ask whether it can be a script from the start.

Let a skill do the checks before I merge, and record videos

I still read and merge High PRs myself.
Before merging, I read the PR description, check CodeRabbit's findings and CI, and open the preview to try the acceptance items by hand.
The descriptions are long and in English.
Trying app changes by hand took the most time.

/pr-verify <PR number> is a skill that takes over the mechanical part:

  • If there is an unresolved CodeRabbit finding, a failed required check, or a conflict with the base, it stops there and writes a request in English to paste into the session that implemented the PR.
  • Otherwise it summarizes the PR, and the points that need my decision, in Japanese.
  • For a PR that changes acceptance tests or e2e tests, it drives the preview with Playwright, takes screenshots of the items to check by hand, records videos of the changed e2e tests, and publishes a report page.
  • It ends with an opinion on whether to merge. It merges only when I say OK in the session.

On the skill's own PR, three rounds of agent review plus CodeRabbit raised 41 findings.
The ones that stood out were gaps where a failed read from GitHub, or a check with no result yet, came out as "go ahead".
Now a failed read counts as "stop" or "wait".
It merges with --match-head-commit, so a push after the check makes the merge fail.
I evaluated the skill with skill-creator on three PRs.
With the skill, 97% of the assertions passed; without it, 87%.

Since it merged, I've been using it on High PRs.
The report puts the points that need my decision first, so I can spend my attention on what I actually need to check.
Recording the behavior checks as Playwright videos turned out well too.
In the videos, it's easier to spot what the agent probably didn't check.
A passing test doesn't tell you which parts of the screen it never looked at.
I think a video helps because it also shows the parts the test doesn't look at.

PRs by tier

Of the 72 PRs merged this week, 42 were High (14 of them Dependabot), 10 Design, 7 Medium and 13 Low.
73 PRs were closed; the one that wasn't merged was a spike for an experiment.
I merged the 13 Low PRs without reading their diffs, an auto-merge rate of 18% (24% last week).
They were 9 ADR PRs, 2 regenerations of the ADR and TPL indices, and 2 cleanups of TPL documents.

Getting ready for teams to try karasu: a payroll subject, a session script, and a feedback form

Last week's "coming next" mentioned a PR that walks the guide on a second subject. It has merged.
The "Design a service split" guide on karasu.kompiro.dev walks you through splitting an online shop into services in five steps.
On its first step you can now switch to doing the same five steps on a payroll system, and switch back.
Going back and forth reuses a copy you haven't edited, so it doesn't pile up projects.

Whether to add this subject at all was my call at the design stage.
Adding it means a sample, its text, a gallery page, and two new public constants in @karasu-tools/core.
Removing a public constant later is a breaking change.
The app has no usage tracking, so nothing will tell me whether anyone uses it.
The design doc recommended adding it because the first-run requirements document lists a second subject.
I went with adding it.

The first-run work is split into phases, and this PR finished the work of the second.
The third is about finding out, with real teams, whether looking at one shared model as a team is worth it.
This week two things went in to prepare for that.

A script for a 60-minute karasu trial session with a team.
It is in the guides on the docs site, in English and Japanese.
The session has three parts:

  1. Each participant walks the "Design a service split" guide in a private browser window.
  2. The team looks at a model of its own system. Before looking, they predict how the parts connect, then look and talk.
  3. A retrospective.

The agent drafted the Japanese version first and I revised it with it.
The revisions: fewer parts with room to spare, a short survey afterwards instead of an interview during the session, and a retrospective at the end.
The survey is four questions the same day and two more two weeks later.

A place for feedback, in GitHub Discussions.
It's a category called Feedback, and a new post there comes with a form.
The last step of every guide on karasu.kompiro.dev links to it ("Tell us what you thought ↗").
That is the only place in the app with this link.

The form starts with a warning and a required checkbox, so that nobody pastes a share link to a model of a non-public system.
A karasu share link carries the whole model after the # in the URL.
Browsers don't send that part to karasu's server, so the model isn't stored there.
But anyone who has the link can see the model.

I'm looking for teams to try it.
You don't need to follow the script.
If you walk one guide and tell me in Feedback where you got stuck, and whether your team could use karasu (or why not), that already helps a lot.
For now the script assumes Chrome or Edge.
In a private window of another browser, the app may fail because it can't use the browser storage it saves files to, and I haven't checked that yet.

Other changes this week

Fixed several cases where karasu misread the model you wrote.

  • With two edges whose node names contain ->, such as a -> "b->c" and "a->b" -> c, the color and direction of the edge written later applied to both. The key that told edges apart was the endpoints joined as plain text. The released 0.10.0 has this bug.
  • With both x -> y and x -> "y#sync", color rules and direction: up applied to both edges or to neither, depending on the order you wrote them. No diagnostic said so.
  • When the line after an edge started with an edge whose source name was quoted, that name was read as the label of the edge on the previous line. Inside a node block, this produced a wrong label and an edge you never wrote, with no error.
  • When two files @imported the same style sheet, karasu reported a circular import. A .krs file in a subdirectory had its @import resolved from the entry file's directory instead of its own.

All of these should reach the stable CLI and Visual Studio Code extension on the next monthly train (planned for November 29).

Diagnostics now have short IDs.
Every diagnostic has an ID from KRS001 to KRS114, and the CLI prints it like Warning[KRS041]: ....
karasu check --format json gives scripts and agents the same findings as JSON.
The skills in karasu-skills used to grep the diagnostic messages to decide whether a model was broken.
The messages are translated, so the grep could find nothing, and a broken model could pass the point where a skill should stop.
They now decide by the code in the JSON.
Showing the IDs in the app and the Visual Studio Code extension comes next.

Redaction in karasu-nest could get extremely slow on some inputs.
karasu-nest is a gallery where you can post and publish a .krs you generated from your own repository.
Every post is checked for secrets such as passwords and keys.
Three of those patterns took time proportional to the square of the input length.
On a 1 MiB input on Node.js 24 on my machine, the connection-string password check took 277 seconds; after the fix, the whole check takes 260 milliseconds.
On Cloudflare Workers each request is limited to 5 seconds of CPU time, and I haven't seen a request killed in production.

Decided on a design that puts my approval before anything reaches npm.
karasu ships three packages on npm.
Today the release workflow publishes straight to latest.
That will move to staged publishing, which npm made generally available in May.
CI only puts versions into an approval queue, and I approve them after comparing them against a build on my machine.
The security review of the implementation found that the queue doesn't show a version's manifest (what package.json becomes on npm).
So the design was revised before the implementation merged.
The job that installs dependencies and builds is split from the job that holds the npm token and stages the versions.
The implementation will be redone on the revised design.

Dependencies.
The 14 Dependabot PRs were triaged together and merged.
No new packages came in, and there were no known vulnerability advisories.

Coming next

  • Redo the staged publishing implementation on the revised design, and rehearse it again.
  • See whether five Low PRs in a row merge through the workflow alone. If they do, take --auto out of the session's procedure.
  • Show diagnostic IDs in the app and the Visual Studio Code extension too.
  • The next monthly train is planned for November 29. This week's fixes and the diagnostic IDs should reach the stable CLI and Visual Studio Code extension on it.
  • Site: karasu.kompiro.dev
  • Source: github.com/kompiro/karasu
  • Feedback: the Feedback category in GitHub Discussions

title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.15315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models.
  MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience.
  On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost.
  Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

title: Evaluating and Comparing Fragmented Go GUI Frameworks Through a Data-Intensive Inventory Specification
description:
Introduction: Navigating the Fractured Go Desktop Landscape

For years, evaluating Go GUI and desktop development options meant wading through a fragmented ecosystem characterized by abandoned repositories, sparse documentation, and a conspicuous absence of a single, batteries-included native framework. Developers historically risked wasting weeks building prototypes on unstable foundations, only to hit architectural walls when pushing data-heavy workloads through immature rendering pipelines. Rather than relying on theoretical documentation and README claims, a rigorous, hands-on empirical test was executed: building the exact same demanding desktop application five distinct ways across Fyne, Cogent Core, Wails, GoTTH (Go + templ + htmx), and Qt via MIQT.

This empirical approach was accelerated by modern AI coding agents. By leveraging AI to translate high-level specifications into divergent paradigm implementations, the iteration velocity barrier was bypassed, exposing the true runtime and ergonomic delta between web-hybrid frameworks and native canvas architectures.

The Benchmark Specification: Stress-Testing the Data Core

To eliminate framework-induced biases, all five implementations shared an identical backend data core, forcing variances to emerge purely from the GUI and rendering abstraction layers. The benchmark specification was deliberately punishing: a 1-million-row data grid supporting real-time sorting, high-speed searching, and background CSV export.

This scale exposes severe mechanical failure modes in desktop architectures:

  • UI Thread Starvation and Memory Bloat: Instantiating 1 million records as unvirtualized DOM nodes or native canvas draw calls floods the memory bus and locks the event loop, causing catastrophic frame drops during rapid scrolling.
  • Garbage Collection Pressure: Allocating millions of discrete Go structs for row data triggers excessive GC mark phases, introducing unpredictable stop-the-world pauses that freeze the user interface.
  • Cross-Language Boundary Penalties: Frameworks bridging Go and C++ via Cgo (such as Qt via MIQT) incur heavy stack-switching and data-serialization overhead during high-frequency filtering operations, heating up CPU caches and degrading responsiveness.

Paradigms Under Scrutiny: From Retained Canvas to Web-Hybrid

The evaluation spanned five distinct architectural models, each translating Go's concurrency and backend execution models into graphical output through radically different mechanical pathways:
Framework Rendering Architecture Observed Mechanical Trade-off
Fyne Retained-mode native canvas Surpassed expectations; efficient retained rendering minimizes layout thrashing, though complex custom widgets require strict adherence to its canvas pipeline.
Cogent Core Go-native scene graph Offers deep Go integration, but divergent styling paradigms place heavy demands on state synchronization.
Wails Web-hybrid (Go backend + native webview) Bridges Go concurrency with mature browser rendering engines, bypassing native widget limitations at the cost of webview binary footprint.
GoTTH DOM-over-HTTP (Go + templ + htmx) Proved surprisingly competitive by offloading layout computation and rendering entirely to optimized browser engines over local loopback.
Qt (MIQT) C++ binding layer via Cgo Delivers mature desktop widgets, but introduces Cgo boundary friction and complex build-time dependencies.

Empirical Surprises and Decision Rules

The results challenged several long-held dogmas in the Go community. Most notably, Go-native web stacks and web-hybrid approaches proved significantly more viable and performant than traditional assumptions suggest, effectively neutralizing the historical advantage of native desktop toolkits. Fyne outperformed expectations in retained-canvas stability, while GoTTH demonstrated that web-first architectures can serve as viable local desktop deployment patterns.

Decision Rule: If your application demands heavy tabular data throughput and complex UI layouts with minimal build complexity, prioritize web-hybrid solutions (like Wails) or web-native stacks (like GoTTH) to leverage browser rendering engines. Reserve native canvas toolkits (like Fyne) for lightweight utilities where single-binary distribution and zero-runtime dependencies outweigh complex data grid demands.

Introduction: Navigating the Fractured Go Desktop Landscape

For years, evaluating Go GUI and desktop development options meant wading through a fragmented ecosystem characterized by abandoned repositories, sparse documentation, and a conspicuous absence of a single, batteries-included native framework. Developers historically risked wasting weeks building prototypes on unstable foundations, only to hit architectural walls when pushing data-heavy workloads through immature rendering pipelines. Rather than relying on theoretical documentation and README claims, a rigorous, hands-on empirical test was executed: building the exact same demanding desktop application five distinct ways across Fyne, Cogent Core, Wails, GoTTH (Go + templ + htmx), and Qt via MIQT.

This empirical approach was accelerated by modern AI coding agents. By leveraging AI to translate high-level specifications into divergent paradigm implementations, the iteration velocity barrier was bypassed, exposing the true runtime and ergonomic delta between web-hybrid frameworks and native canvas architectures.

The Benchmark Specification: Stress-Testing the Data Core

To eliminate framework-induced biases, all five implementations shared an identical backend data core, forcing variances to emerge purely from the GUI and rendering abstraction layers. The benchmark specification was deliberately punishing: a 1-million-row data grid supporting real-time sorting, high-speed searching, and background CSV export.

This scale exposes severe mechanical failure modes in desktop architectures:

  • UI Thread Starvation and Memory Bloat: Instantiating 1 million records as unvirtualized DOM nodes or native canvas draw calls floods the memory bus and locks the event loop, causing catastrophic frame drops during rapid scrolling.
  • Garbage Collection Pressure: Allocating millions of discrete Go structs for row data triggers excessive GC mark phases, introducing unpredictable stop-the-world pauses that freeze the user interface.
  • Cross-Language Boundary Penalties: Frameworks bridging Go and C++ via Cgo (such as Qt via MIQT) incur heavy stack-switching and data-serialization overhead during high-frequency filtering operations, heating up CPU caches and degrading responsiveness.

Paradigms Under Scrutiny: From Retained Canvas to Web-Hybrid

The evaluation spanned five distinct architectural models, each translating Go's concurrency and backend execution models into graphical output through radically different mechanical pathways:
Framework Rendering Architecture Observed Mechanical Trade-off
Fyne Retained-mode native canvas Surpassed expectations; efficient retained rendering minimizes layout thrashing, though complex custom widgets require strict adherence to its canvas pipeline.
Cogent Core Go-native scene graph Offers deep Go integration, but divergent styling paradigms place heavy demands on state synchronization.
Wails Web-hybrid (Go backend + native webview) Bridges Go concurrency with mature browser rendering engines, bypassing native widget limitations at the cost of webview binary footprint.
GoTTH DOM-over-HTTP (Go + templ + htmx) Proved surprisingly competitive by offloading layout computation and rendering entirely to optimized browser engines over local loopback.
Qt (MIQT) C++ binding layer via Cgo Delivers mature desktop widgets, but introduces Cgo boundary friction and complex build-time dependencies.

Empirical Surprises and Decision Rules

The results challenged several long-held dogmas in the Go community. Most notably, Go-native web stacks and web-hybrid approaches proved significantly more viable and performant than traditional assumptions suggest, effectively neutralizing the historical advantage of native desktop toolkits. Fyne outperformed expectations in retained-canvas stability, while GoTTH demonstrated that web-first architectures can serve as viable local desktop deployment patterns.

Decision Rule: If your application demands heavy tabular data throughput and complex UI layouts with minimal build complexity, prioritize web-hybrid solutions (like Wails) or web-native stacks (like GoTTH) to leverage browser rendering engines. Reserve native canvas toolkits (like Fyne) for lightweight utilities where single-binary distribution and zero-runtime dependencies outweigh complex data grid demands.

Access the complete write-up, source code, and raw results at https://justinfx.com/2026/11/10/go-gui-five-ways, and track community addendums via the wiki at https://github.com/justinfx/go-gui-experiments/wiki.

Pure-Go Toolkits: Fyne and Cogent Core

When evaluating Fyne and Cogent Core through the crucible of a 1-million-row inventory specification, the illusion of an all-Go desktop paradise collides immediately with raw memory management and rendering physics. Fyne relies on a retained-mode native canvas, caching node hierarchies to minimize layout thrashing. Under normal utility conditions, this retained architecture shines: it bypasses the massive binary bloat of embedded webviews and packages into a lean, single-binary distribution with zero external runtime dependencies.

However, pushing Fyne’s retained canvas to render massive, unvirtualized tabular datasets exposes a catastrophic mechanical failure mode: garbage collection (GC) pressure and memory bus saturation. Because the framework instantiates distinct object graphs for widget elements, handling millions of discrete Go structs during high-speed searching and sorting floods the heap. This forces the Go runtime into aggressive mark-and-sweep cycles, triggering stop-the-world pauses that freeze the UI event loop and drop frames mid-scroll. The layout engine starves the main thread not from raw CPU execution limits, but from allocation-induced GC stutter.

Cogent Core takes a different path, leveraging a deep Go-native scene graph designed for complex applications. While this provides tight integration with Go's concurrency and typing models, it introduces structural friction via divergent styling paradigms. The separation between the underlying data core and Cogent Core's styling state machine increases state synchronization overhead. When data updates ripple through the scene graph, mismatched bindings force redundant node re-evaluations, inflating CPU cache churn and complicating reactive UI updates.

Comparing their effectiveness yields a stark operational divide:

  • Fyne is optimal for lightweight standalone utilities, system tray tools, and simple dashboards where single-binary distribution and zero-dependency footprints outweigh complex data-grid throughput.
  • Cogent Core suits developers deeply committed to pure-Go scene architectures, provided they can absorb the state-sync tax of its custom styling abstractions.

The Decision Rule: If your application is a lightweight utility or configuration panel where runtime dependencies must be zero, use Fyne. But if your specification demands heavy, high-frequency sorting and million-row data grids, stop-the-world GC pauses and canvas memory bloat will break pure-Go toolkits—forcing a pivot toward web-hybrid or DOM-over-HTTP architectures where browser engines absorb the heavy rendering load.

Hybrid Web-Bridge Architectures: Wails and GoTTH

When an inventory specification mandates a 1-million-row data grid featuring real-time sorting, high-speed searching, and background CSV export, native Go GUI toolkits encounter severe architectural limits. Pure-Go retained-mode canvases instantiate discrete Go structs for every individual widget node, flooding the heap and triggering aggressive garbage collection (GC) mark-and-sweep phases that freeze the UI event loop with stop-the-world pauses. To bypass this native thread starvation, developers turn to hybrid web-bridge architectures: Wails and GoTTH (Go + templ + htmx).

Wails: Native Webview Binaries and Inter-Process Boundaries

Wails pairs a high-performance Go backend with a native system webview (such as WebKit on macOS or WebView2 on Windows) through platform-specific bindings. Rather than relying on custom drawing loops or complex Cgo abstraction layers, Wails exposes Go methods directly to the frontend via an internal IPC bridge. This splits the execution model cleanly: heavy data crunching and database filtering execute in compiled Go code, while layout calculation, DOM reflows, and paint cycles are offloaded entirely to the browser engine's optimized C++/Rust core.

Failure Mode & Structural Friction: While Wails successfully eliminates native UI thread locking, it introduces cross-language serialization overhead. Passing massive JSON payloads across the bridge during high-frequency filtering operations forces memory allocation spikes and CPU cache churn on both sides of the bridge. Furthermore, bundling the operating system's webview runtime increases the final binary footprint significantly compared to single-binary native toolkits like Fyne.

GoTTH: DOM-over-HTTP via Local Loopback

GoTTH discards traditional desktop UI frameworks entirely, treating the desktop application as an embedded local web server. It integrates Go's backend execution with templ for type-safe component compilation and htmx for hypermedia-driven DOM fragment updates over a local loopback HTTP connection. The entire application executes inside a lightweight, borderless webview container pointing directly to localhost.

Mechanical Advantage: By utilizing DOM-over-HTTP, layout computations and rendering are delegated to mature browser layout engines that excel at incremental DOM diffing and hardware-accelerated painting. The Go backend retains state and streams pre-rendered HTML fragments or JSON updates, eliminating the complex client-side state synchronization overhead that typically plagues native Go scene graphs.

Framework Comparison and Decision Matrix

Evaluating Wails and GoTTH against data-intensive constraints reveals distinct operational boundaries:
Framework Rendering Architecture Primary Bottleneck Optimal Scaling Profile
Wails Go backend + Native Webview bindings IPC serialization overhead during massive data transfers Rich desktop apps requiring tight native OS integration and complex frontend logic
GoTTH DOM-over-HTTP (Go + templ + htmx) Local loopback latency and HTML string allocation Tabular, data-heavy interfaces relying on hypermedia state management

Decision Rules for Data-Heavy Desktop Development

Rule: If an application specification requires high-frequency sorting, complex search queries, and million-row data grids, bypass pure-Go retained canvases and deploy web-hybrid (Wails) or DOM-over-HTTP (GoTTH) architectures. Why? Native toolkits saturate the Go heap with millions of node allocations, causing GC pauses and memory bus saturation. Web-bridge architectures successfully isolate rendering pipelines into hardware-accelerated browser runtimes, preventing UI thread starvation and maintaining consistent frame rates under heavy operational loads.

Native C++ Wrappers: Qt via MIQT

Reaching for a mature, battle-tested GUI toolkit like Qt via Go bindings (such as MIQT) represents the classic instinct of a developer burnt by fragmented native ecosystems. Qt offers decades of widget maturity, comprehensive layout engines, and native desktop polish that pure-Go toolkits struggle to replicate. However, routing a demanding specification—such as a 1-million-row data grid requiring real-time sorting and filtering—through a cross-language bridge introduces severe structural and mechanical trade-offs.

Compilation Complexity and Build-Time Brittleness

The primary engineering penalty of Qt via MIQT manifests long before runtime, deep inside the build pipeline. Qt is a massive C++ framework governed by complex meta-object compilers and rigid header hierarchies. When wrapped via Cgo, the Go compiler must coordinate with external C++ toolchains, requiring local installations of Qt development libraries, specific header versions, and specialized binding generators.

This architectural coupling creates a brittle build state. When AI coding agents attempt to resolve compilation errors across the Go-C++ boundary, mismatched pointer types, missing library paths, and subtle ABI incompatibilities trigger cascading build failures. Unlike a pure-Go binary that compiles cleanly via a single command, a MIQT-backed application binds its deployment pipeline to the host system's dynamic link libraries, complicating cross-compilation and containerized builds.

The Cgo Boundary Penalty and Performance Degradation

At runtime, the friction shifts from compilation to the execution boundary. Passing data between Go's garbage-collected heap and Qt's C++ object model requires explicit translation layers. During high-frequency filtering and sorting operations across the 1-million-row inventory specification, this Cgo boundary penalty exacts a heavy toll on CPU instruction throughput:

  • Stack-Switching Overhead: Every cross-language call forces a transition from Go's cooperative scheduler runtime to native OS thread stacks, stalling instruction pipelines.
  • Data Serialization Churn: Translating massive arrays of inventory records across the boundary forces repeated memory allocations and copies, saturating the memory bus.
  • CPU Cache Pollution: Frequent context switching invalidates L1/L2 data caches, degrading the high-speed execution required for real-time grid responsiveness.

Ecosystem Depth Versus Architectural Mismatch

While Qt's widget inventory is unmatched—offering advanced native trees, custom item delegates, and robust accessibility hooks—forcing it to ingest a high-throughput, data-intensive Go backend exposes a fundamental architectural mismatch. The framework expects a C++ event loop and manual memory management, which clashes with Go's memory model and concurrency primitives, resulting in high synchronization overhead.

Decision Rule for Native C++ Wrappers

Rule: Avoid C++ bindings like MIQT for data-intensive, high-frequency tabular applications; restrict them strictly to desktop utilities where native widget fidelity outweighs cross-language maintenance overhead. Optimal Solution: For heavy data grids, bypass Cgo bridges entirely in favor of web-hybrid architectures (such as Wails) or DOM-over-HTTP models (such as GoTTH) that isolate rendering into hardware-accelerated browser engines without incurring cross-language stack-switching penalties.

Cross-Framework Quantitative Benchmarking

Pushing a standardized 1-million-row inventory data grid—complete with real-time sorting, high-speed searching, and background CSV export—across Fyne, Cogent Core, Wails, GoTTH, and Qt (MIQT) strips away documentation claims, exposing stark mechanical realities in memory management, rendering pipelines, and binary distribution footprints.

Memory Consumption and Heap Pressure under Heavy Data Loads

Pure-Go retained canvas frameworks like Fyne and Cogent Core instantiate distinct Go structs for every widget node in the hierarchy. Under a 1-million-row dataset, this object graph translation floods the heap with millions of discrete allocations. The causal mechanism is direct: this memory bus saturation forces aggressive Go garbage collection mark-and-sweep phases, triggering stop-the-world pauses that stall the UI event loop, drop frames, and freeze scrolling. Conversely, web-hybrid architectures like Wails offload DOM reflows and paint cycles to the browser engine's C++/Rust core, while GoTTH (Go + templ + htmx) relies on server-side pre-rendered HTML fragments and incremental DOM diffing over local loopback. GoTTH and Wails bypass native heap exhaustion for tabular data, though Wails incurs higher baseline memory footprints due to embedded webview runtimes.

Binary Sizes and Deployment Footprints

Binary footprint size exposes the trade-offs between static linking and external runtime dependencies. Fyne packages into a lean, single-binary distribution with zero external runtime dependencies because its retained canvas rendering engine compiles entirely into native machine code. Cogent Core similarly maintains a pure-Go distribution footprint, though its complex styling state-sync overhead increases code complexity and internal node re-evaluations. On the other end of the spectrum, Wails bundles the host operating system's native webview runtime (WebKit or WebView2), inflating the binary footprint significantly. Qt (via MIQT) requires dynamic link libraries and external C++ toolchains, creating severe build-time brittleness, ABI incompatibilities, and containerization friction due to Cgo dynamic linking dependencies.

Startup Latency and Cross-Language Boundary Penalties

Startup latency and runtime throughput reveal deep architectural penalties in cross-language binding layers. Qt (MIQT) suffers from severe Cgo boundary friction: cross-language calls force stack-switching from Go's cooperative scheduler runtime to native OS thread stacks, stalling instruction pipelines. Translating large arrays across this boundary causes repetitive memory allocations and copies, saturating the memory bus and polluting L1/L2 CPU caches. This context-switching overhead degrades high-speed grid filtering. In contrast, GoTTH maintains low operational latency by leveraging local loopback HTTP streams, avoiding cross-language serialization bottlenecks entirely.

Comparative Framework Evaluation

  • Fyne: Optimal for lightweight standalone utilities and system tray tools. Fails under million-row data grids due to GC pressure from retained canvas node allocation.
  • Cogent Core: Suited for pure-Go scene graph architectures where developers accept custom styling state-sync overhead and higher CPU cache churn.
  • Wails: Optimal for rich desktop applications requiring tight native OS integration and complex frontend logic, trading binary size for rendering offload.
  • GoTTH: Highly competitive for tabular, data-heavy interfaces, leveraging browser engine hardware acceleration via DOM-over-HTTP.
  • Qt (MIQT): Anti-pattern for data-intensive apps due to Cgo stack-switching penalties and build-time brittleness; restricted strictly to basic desktop utilities.

Decision Rule: For specifications requiring high-frequency sorting, complex search queries, and million-row data grids, bypass pure-Go retained canvases and C++ bindings; deploy web-hybrid solutions like Wails or DOM-over-HTTP architectures like GoTTH to isolate rendering into hardware-accelerated browser engines and prevent UI thread starvation.

Architectural Verdict and Selection Matrix

Navigating the fragmented Go desktop landscape requires looking past superficial documentation and README promises. By implementing an identical, demanding 1-million-row inventory specification across five distinct architectural paradigms—Fyne, Cogent Core, Wails, GoTTH, and Qt (via MIQT)—empirical testing reveals exact mechanical bottlenecks and failure thresholds that standard theoretical reviews miss entirely.

Framework Performance and Failure Mechanics

Every GUI framework imposes strict physical and computational costs governed by its rendering pipeline and memory model. Selecting the wrong abstraction layer does not merely degrade responsiveness; it triggers cascading system failures ranging from memory bus saturation to catastrophic UI thread starvation.

  • Pure-Go Retained Canvases (Fyne & Cogent Core): Instantiating discrete Go structs for every widget node floods the heap under high-density demands like a million-row grid. This memory footprint overloads the runtime, triggering aggressive Go mark-and-sweep cycles. The resulting stop-the-world pauses freeze the event loop and drop frames. Verdict: Fyne excels for lightweight utilities and system tray tools, but pure-Go retained architectures fail entirely under heavy data-intensive workloads due to garbage collection pressure and cache churn. Cogent Core introduces further structural friction via divergent styling state-sync models, increasing CPU cache pollution.
  • C++ Bridge Toolkits (Qt via MIQT): Routing high-throughput operations across the Cgo boundary forces expensive stack-switching transitions from Go's cooperative scheduler to native OS thread stacks, stalling instruction pipelines. Translating large arrays across this boundary saturates the memory bus and invalidates L1/L2 CPU caches. Verdict: Qt bindings are a severe anti-pattern for data-intensive grids. They must be strictly restricted to basic desktop utilities where native widget fidelity outweighs the brittleness of Cgo coordination, ABI incompatibilities, and containerization friction.
  • Web-Hybrid Architectures (Wails): By coupling a compiled Go backend with a native system webview (WebKit/WebView2) via an internal IPC bridge, Wails offloads layout calculations, DOM reflows, and paint cycles to the browser engine's C++/Rust core. While cross-language JSON serialization introduces minor CPU churn and binary sizes expand due to bundled runtimes, it completely bypasses native heap exhaustion. Verdict: Optimal for rich desktop applications requiring tight OS integration and hardware-accelerated rendering offload.
  • DOM-over-HTTP Models (GoTTH - Go + templ + htmx): Treating the desktop app as an embedded local web server communicating over local loopback HTTP eliminates client-side state synchronization overhead. Pre-rendered HTML fragments and incremental DOM diffing delegate rendering entirely to browser engines. Verdict: Highly competitive and mechanically robust for heavy tabular interfaces, bypassing native memory bottlenecks without sacrificing development velocity.

The Definitive Decision Matrix

To prevent project failure and eliminate wasted engineering cycles, framework selection must be driven by data throughput constraints and distribution requirements rather than aesthetic preference. Use the following operational rules:

  • Rule 1 (High-Density Data Grids): For specifications requiring high-frequency sorting, complex search queries, and million-row data grids, strictly bypass pure-Go retained canvases and C++ bindings. Deploy Wails or GoTTH to isolate rendering pipelines into hardware-accelerated browser runtimes and prevent UI thread starvation.
  • Rule 2 (Lightweight Standalone Utilities): For zero-dependency tools, system tray applets, or simple dashboards without massive datasets, use Fyne to maximize deployment simplicity and minimize binary overhead.
  • Rule 3 (Complex Pure-Go Scene Graphs): Choose Cogent Core only when building custom pure-Go scene architectures where your engineering team explicitly accepts the synchronization overhead of custom styling state-machines.

Comparative Architecture Summary

Evaluating trade-offs across distribution constraints and runtime performance clarifies why traditional assumptions about Go GUI development are obsolete:

  • Wails: Large binary size due to embedded webview runtime, excellent UI rendering performance, ideal for feature-rich hybrid apps.
  • GoTTH: Extremely lightweight backend payload, exceptional tabular throughput via htmx, ideal for data-heavy workflows without client-side state bloat.
  • Fyne: Smallest native footprint, zero external runtime dependencies, fails on large data grids due to GC pauses.
  • Qt (MIQT): Severe Cgo and build friction, high cache pollution, strictly for legacy or native-widget fidelity requirements.
  • Cogent Core: Pure Go flexibility, high styling complexity, suited for specialized scene graphs.

Ultimately, AI-assisted multi-stack prototyping has exposed the fragility of traditional documentation. Developers can now empirically validate these boundaries before committing to an architectural dead end.

title: Why Brilliant ML Research Dies in Big Tech
description:
In my time shipping ML models, I've watched more ideas die in internal review meetings than in production. But the latest news hits different.
John Langford, a 14-year Microsoft veteran and co-founder of their AI Frontiers lab, has resigned. His stated reason? Innovative research ideas couldn't find a path to reality. Not one dramatic boardroom battle—just a quiet, systemic inability to move from paper to product.
This isn't just a personal story. It's a structural pattern I've seen repeat across every major tech company, and understanding it matters if you're building ML systems today.

The Scaling Trap

Langford acknowledged something uncomfortable publicly: scaling models does improve predictions, and the ROI is clearer for leadership. But treating scale as the only lever creates a dangerous feedback loop. Teams optimize for benchmark metrics rather than decision quality under uncertainty. They pour compute into bigger models when better algorithms could achieve the same results with fewer resources.
Contextual bandits—a field Langford helped advance—are precisely the kind of approach that gets squeezed out. These techniques let systems make smarter decisions with incomplete feedback, which is actually closer to how most real products operate than any benchmark suite. Yet they rarely land on roadmap decks.

What Actually Happens When Research Gets Absorbed

Microsoft merged his roughly 50-person AI Frontiers team into Mustafa Suleyman's broader AI organization last September. On paper, this looks like strategic consolidation. In practice, it often signals the end of independent research trajectories. Integration means alignment with product OKRs—and those OKRs almost always prioritize near-term deliverables over exploratory work.
I've been on both sides of this merger dynamic. The people doing foundational methodological work don't get fired; they just stop having an audience. Their papers stop citing each other. The technical conversations shift from "what should we explore?" to "what can ship next quarter?"

The Practical Lesson

Here's what I'd tell any ML engineer or researcher feeling this friction:
First, build a bridge to deployment early. Even a small proof-of-concept integrated into a live system beats five perfect arXiv papers. Decision-makers respond to evidence, not potential.
Second, find pockets of autonomy. Some teams within large orgs genuinely protect research space. Learn who they are before you need them.
Third, document your failures publicly. When contextual bandit approaches or alternative architectures don't win internal buy-in, write about it. The community benefits, and sometimes the very person you're trying to reach reads it.
Langford's departure is a reminder that organizational design shapes technical outcomes more than raw intelligence does. We talk a lot about model architecture and training pipelines, but rarely enough about the incentives that determine which problems get solved at all.
The real question for anyone working in ML today: How do you stay technically ambitious when your organization optimizes for predictability over discovery?
