title: How to Modernize a VM-Based App to Kubernetes on Multi-Cloud: Five Paths, a VM-to-Kubernetes Map, and a Readiness Scorecard
description:
Modernize a VM-based application to Kubernetes on multi-cloud infrastructure by choosing a path per application (keep it as a VM inside Kubernetes, containerize it as is, refactor it, or replace parts with managed services), mapping each VM concern to its Kubernetes equivalent, and moving in phases from a low-risk pilot to a gradual cutover. Keep the data layer and the deployment definition portable so the same app can run on every cloud.

This guide provides three original reference tables you can score your own portfolio against: a modernization-path comparison, a readiness scorecard that tells you which path fits each application, and a VM-concept-to-Kubernetes map.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Five paths per application. Retain on VMs for now, keep as a VM inside Kubernetes with KubeVirt, containerize as is, refactor into services, or replace parts with managed services. Pick the path that matches each app’s readiness; most portfolios use several.
  • VM-to-Kubernetes mapping table. Fourteen VM concepts, from systemd services to host-based licensing, map to Kubernetes equivalents or to keeping the app as a VM.
  • Readiness scorecard. Eight signals (OS dependency, state, startup time, configuration style, licensing, vendor container support, network assumptions, and team familiarity) score each app toward “containerize or refactor” or “keep as a VM first.”
  • Phased plan. Inventory, score, pick a path, externalize config and state, build images, stand up clusters across clouds, migrate data, run in parallel, cut over with DNS or a global load balancer, then decommission VMs.
  • Portability. Use Helm or Kustomize with per-cloud overlays (or a platform with one definition), portable databases, workload identity per cloud, and mTLS between clouds. Avoid tying your data layer to a single provider without a migration plan.
  • Control Plane. Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) lets you define a workload once and run it across AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), your own Kubernetes clusters joined through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), or your own servers joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), including on premises. VM workloads run on MK8s locations with the KubeVirt add-on on KVM-capable nodes, so containers and VMs coexist under one platform.

How do I modernize a VM-based application to Kubernetes on multi-cloud infrastructure?

There is no single migration. You assess each application independently, assign it one of five modernization paths, translate its VM constructs into Kubernetes equivalents, and move it in phases. The phased plan keeps risk low and gives you a rollback at every step.

The phased plan

  1. Inventory and dependency mapping. Catalog every VM workload by business function, owner, SLA, compliance requirements, and upstream and downstream dependencies. Identify VMs that are unused or redundant and mark them for retirement. The seven Rs of cloud migration provide a useful framework for this classification.
  2. Score each application. Use the readiness scorecard to count signals. Applications that lean toward “containerize or refactor” go first. Applications that lean toward “keep as a VM” either stay on VMs or move into Kubernetes as VM workloads via KubeVirt.
  3. Pick a path. Assign one of the five paths (retain, VM-in-Kubernetes, containerize, refactor, replace with managed services) to each application.
  4. Externalize config, secrets, state, and logs. Move configuration into ConfigMaps, secrets into a Kubernetes Secret backed by an external secrets manager, persistent data into PersistentVolumeClaims or managed databases, and logging to stdout so a cluster-level agent collects it.
  5. Build images and manifests. For containerized apps, create a container image and a Deployment or StatefulSet manifest. For VM workloads, export the VMDK, qcow2, or VHD image and prepare it for import.
  6. Choose the cluster layer across clouds. Standardize cluster provisioning with Cluster API, Terraform, OpenTofu, or a platform that manages clusters for you. The goal is identical Kubernetes APIs on every cloud so your manifests are portable.
  7. Migrate data. Replicate databases to the target environment before cutover. Use logical replication for PostgreSQL, native replication for MySQL, or a vendor-supported tool for your database engine. Validate row counts and checksums.
  8. Run in parallel. Route a small percentage of traffic to the Kubernetes deployment while the VM deployment continues to serve the rest. Monitor error rates, latency, and data consistency.
  9. Cut over gradually with DNS or a global load balancer. Shift traffic weights from the VM environment to Kubernetes. Keep the VM environment running and ready for rollback until you are confident in the new deployment.
  10. Decommission VMs. After a soak period with no issues, shut down the old VMs and reclaim the infrastructure.

Which modernization path should each application take?

The five paths differ in effort, in what you gain, and in how portable the result is across clouds.

Modernization paths compared

Path What changes in the app Effort What you gain Multi-cloud portability Choose it when
Keep as a VM inside Kubernetes (KubeVirt; OpenShift Virtualization) Nothing in the application itself. The VM image runs inside a Kubernetes pod. Low. Package the existing disk image. Unified orchestration. VMs and containers share the same API, networking, and observability. Limited. KubeVirt needs KVM-capable nodes (bare metal or instances with nested virtualization), which not every cloud region offers as a managed option. The app cannot be containerized yet, but you want to retire standalone hypervisors and manage everything through Kubernetes.
Containerize as is (replatform) The same process runs inside a container image. Config moves to ConfigMaps and Secrets. Local state moves to volumes or an external store. Medium. Build a container image, write manifests, externalize config. Faster startup, smaller images, standard Kubernetes scaling and health checks. High. A container image runs on any Kubernetes cluster on any cloud with no special node capability. The app is a standard Linux process with documented dependencies and no kernel-level or OS-level requirements that prevent containerization.
Refactor (split into services, externalize state) The application is redesigned into independently deployable services with external state stores. High. Requires development time and new integration testing. Independent scaling, faster deployments, fault isolation between services. High. Each service is a container. The data layer’s portability depends on your database choice. The app is strategic, under active development, and the team has the skills and time to re-architect.
Replace parts with managed services (managed database, queue, object storage) Application code changes to call a managed API instead of a local component. Medium. Integration work per managed service. Reduced operational burden for databases, queues, and storage. Low to medium. Managed services tie you to one cloud unless a portable equivalent exists (for example, a self-managed PostgreSQL cluster instead of a cloud-native database). The component being replaced is a commodity (relational database, message queue, blob store) and the team wants to stop operating it.
Retain on VMs for now Nothing changes. None. No migration risk. N/A. The app stays where it is. The app is end-of-life, has an immovable licensing constraint, or the team lacks capacity to migrate it safely.

Readiness scorecard: which path fits each application

Score each application against these eight signals. Count how many fall in the left column versus the right column. A majority on the left points toward containerize or refactor. A majority on the right points toward keep as a VM first (either retain or run as a VM inside Kubernetes with KubeVirt).

Signal Points toward containerize or refactor Points toward keep as a VM or retain
OS dependency Linux userland only; no custom kernel modules Requires kernel modules, Windows desktop components, or an old unsupported OS
State Stateless, or all state lives in an external database Local writable state on disk that the process expects to survive restarts
Startup time Starts in seconds Takes minutes to initialize or requires a complex boot sequence
Configuration Reads environment variables or mounted files cleanly Hand-edited files in non-standard paths, or configuration baked into the OS image
Licensing Per-core, per-user, or open source Tied to a MAC address, host ID, or VM-specific hardware fingerprint
Vendor support for containers Vendor publishes container images or documents container deployment Vendor does not support or certify running in containers
Network assumptions Uses DNS for discovery; standard TCP/UDP Requires fixed IPs, multicast, raw sockets, or kernel-level networking
Team familiarity Team has built and operated containers before Team has never worked with containers or Kubernetes

Scoring rule. If five or more signals land in the left column, the application is a strong candidate for containerization or refactoring. If five or more land in the right column, keep it as a VM for now and plan a longer migration or use KubeVirt as an interim step. A four-four split means containerize only after the right-column blockers, usually state or licensing, are resolved.

How do VM concepts map to Kubernetes?

Each VM construct has a Kubernetes equivalent, a change to make, and a common trap.

On the VM Kubernetes equivalent What to change Common trap
systemd service or init script Deployment or StatefulSet Define the container command and arguments in the pod spec. Use lifecycle hooks for pre-stop cleanup. Assuming the container runtime will run your init system. Containers run a single process by default.
Cron job CronJob Move the schedule into a CronJob manifest. Make the job idempotent. Running cron inside a long-lived container instead of using the CronJob resource, which means no retry or concurrency control.
Config files in /etc ConfigMap mounted as a volume or injected as environment variables Extract config values and create a ConfigMap per environment. Baking config into the container image so every config change requires a new image build.
Secrets on disk or in environment files Secret (plus an external secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager) Store secrets in Kubernetes Secrets and reference them in the pod spec. Rotate regularly. Committing secrets to version control or leaving them as plain-text environment variables in the manifest.
Local disk for data PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) backed by a CSI driver Identify which directories hold data that must survive a pod restart and mount a PVC there. Using emptyDir for persistent data. It disappears when the pod is evicted.
Log files on disk stdout/stderr logging collected by a cluster-level agent (Fluentd, Fluent Bit, or a cloud-native agent) Reconfigure the application to log to stdout. If that is not possible, use a sidecar that tails the log file. Writing logs to a local file inside the container and losing them on restart.
OS patching Rebuild the container image with an updated base image and redeploy Automate image rebuilds in CI. Use a minimal base image to reduce the patch surface. Treating containers like VMs and trying to SSH in to apply patches.
Static IP or hostname Service DNS name (e.g., my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local) Update clients to use DNS names. Use a headless Service if each pod needs a stable hostname (StatefulSet). Hardcoding IP addresses in application config. Pods get new IPs when they are rescheduled or replaced.
Load balancer in front of VMs Service (type LoadBalancer) and Ingress or Gateway API Define a Service for internal traffic and an Ingress or Gateway for external traffic. Creating one LoadBalancer Service per microservice, which provisions a separate cloud load balancer for each and increases cost.
Sticky sessions in memory External session store such as Redis or a managed session service Move session data out of process memory into Redis, Memcached, or a database. Relying on sessionAffinity in the Service, which breaks when pods scale or restart.
VM snapshots and backups CSI volume snapshots and Velero for cluster-level backup Configure a VolumeSnapshotClass and schedule Velero backups. Backing up only the persistent volume but not the Kubernetes manifests and secrets needed to restore the workload.
Scaling by adding VMs HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics Set resource requests accurately so the HPA can make good scaling decisions. Setting requests too low, which causes the HPA to think the pod is overloaded and scale to too many replicas.
Host-based licensing (MAC address or host ID) License server or per-node licensing; check with the vendor Contact the software vendor to understand container licensing options before migrating. Migrating first and discovering the license check fails because the container has no stable MAC address or host ID.
Windows services Windows nodes (supported for Windows Server containers in AKS, EKS, and GKE) or keep as a VM Add a Windows node pool to your cluster and use a nodeSelector in the pod spec. Assuming Linux containers can run Windows binaries. Windows containers require Windows nodes, and not all Kubernetes features are available on Windows.

Guidance on the three hardest rows

Local state. This is the single biggest blocker. If an application writes to local disk and expects that data to survive restarts, you must either move the data to a PVC, migrate it to an external database, or use a StatefulSet with stable storage. For PostgreSQL in containers, dedicated operators like CloudNativePG or Crunchy Data PGO handle replication and failover.

Licensing. Host-based licenses that fingerprint a MAC address or host ID will fail inside a container. Contact the vendor before migration. Some vendors offer floating license servers or per-core models that work in Kubernetes. If the vendor does not support containers, this application is a strong candidate for the “retain” or “VM inside Kubernetes” path.

Windows. Windows Server containers run on Windows node pools in AKS, EKS, and GKE. They support .NET Framework and Windows Server workloads but not desktop applications or GUI-based services. If the application requires a Windows desktop, keep it as a VM.

When should you run VMs inside Kubernetes with KubeVirt?

KubeVirt is a Kubernetes add-on that lets you run virtual machines as Kubernetes resources alongside containers. It extends the Kubernetes API with custom resources like VirtualMachine and VirtualMachineInstance, so you manage VMs with kubectl, Helm, and the same CI/CD pipelines you use for containers.

KubeVirt requires KVM-capable nodes for production (it has a software-emulation fallback that is too slow for production). In practice this means bare-metal servers or cloud instances that support nested virtualization. Not every cloud instance type or region offers nested virtualization, so you need to verify node capability before planning a KubeVirt deployment.

Live migration requires that the VM’s PersistentVolumeClaims use a shared ReadWriteMany (RWX) access mode. If they don’t, the VM must be shut down and restarted on the new node, which means a brief outage for that workload.

OpenShift Virtualization is Red Hat’s supported distribution of KubeVirt, integrated into OpenShift. It provides the same core capability with additional enterprise support and integration with Red Hat’s ecosystem.

When KubeVirt is a good interim step

  • You want to retire a standalone hypervisor (VMware, Hyper-V, Proxmox) and consolidate onto Kubernetes so your team operates one platform.
  • The application cannot be containerized yet (kernel module dependency, Windows desktop, vendor restriction) but you want it in the same orchestration layer.
  • You plan to containerize the application later and want to start by unifying networking, observability, and deployment tooling.

Trade-offs

  • VMs add a virtualization layer, so benchmark I/O-intensive workloads before committing; overhead is higher on nested-virtualization cloud instances than on bare metal.
  • The node pool must be KVM-capable, which limits which cloud regions and instance types you can use.
  • Live migration requires RWX shared storage, adding infrastructure complexity.
  • Some Kubernetes tooling (HPA, service mesh sidecars) does not apply to VM workloads the way it applies to pods. Health checks run against the guest OS: HTTP and TCP probes work, but exec and guest-agent ping probes need qemu-guest-agent installed in the VM image.

How do you keep the modernized app portable across clouds?

Kubernetes alone does not make an app portable. Five areas need attention.

Deployment definition

Use Helm charts or Kustomize bases with per-cloud overlays for storage classes, ingress annotations, and node selectors. Each overlay captures the cloud-specific differences. The base stays identical. Alternatively, a platform that runs one workload definition in every location removes per-cloud overlays. The guide to avoiding cloud vendor lock-in covers this in depth.

Data layer

Managed databases (Cloud SQL, RDS, Azure Database) are convenient but tie your data to one cloud. If portability matters, run a self-managed database on Kubernetes (with an operator) or use a database service that replicates across clouds. Whichever you choose, make sure your backup and restore process works on the target cloud before you need it.

Identity

Each cloud has its own workload identity mechanism (IAM Roles for Service Accounts or EKS Pod Identity on AWS, Workload Identity Federation for GKE on Google Cloud, Microsoft Entra Workload ID on Azure). Your application code should not contain long-lived cloud keys.

Networking between clouds

Connecting clusters across clouds requires encrypted tunnels (WireGuard, IPsec) or a service mesh with multi-cluster support (Cilium ClusterMesh, Istio multi-cluster).

Egress cost

Moving data between clouds is not free. Architect so that most traffic stays within a single cloud region for a given request. Cross-cloud traffic should be limited to replication, failover, and control-plane synchronization.

How do you migrate data and cut over with minimal downtime?

Data migration is the riskiest part of any VM-to-Kubernetes move. A clean approach has four steps.

Database replication then switchover. Set up logical or physical replication from the source database (on the VM) to the target database (on Kubernetes or a managed service). Let replication run until the replica is caught up and validated. Then promote the replica and point the application at it.

Dual-run. Run both the old VM deployment and the new Kubernetes deployment simultaneously, serving real traffic. Point both deployments at the same primary database during dual-run, and compare outputs or error rates to confirm the Kubernetes deployment behaves identically.

DNS or global load balancer weighting for the cutover. Start with 100% of traffic on the VM deployment and 0% on Kubernetes. Gradually shift the weight (for example, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) while monitoring. Use a global load balancer or a weighted DNS record to set the weights.

Rollback plan. At every stage, the VM deployment is still running. After promotion, replicate from the new primary back to the VM database so a rollback does not lose writes. If something goes wrong, shift traffic back. Do not decommission VMs until you have completed a soak period with all traffic on Kubernetes and confirmed data integrity.

How Control Plane fits

A workload deployed to a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations, runs in every location of that GVC from one workload definition. Locations can be Control Plane-managed regions on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), Kubernetes clusters you already run joined through Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), or your own servers joined through MK8s, including on premises.

For VM-to-Kubernetes modernization, Control Plane supports both ends of the spectrum:

  • VM workloads. Import a VMDK, qcow2, or VHD image over HTTP(S) (Control Plane converts the format) or as a container disk image. VM workloads run only on MK8s locations with the KubeVirt add-on, on KVM-capable nodes. Limits: no live migration (a VM restarts when it moves to another node, so keep state on volumes), whole-core CPU allocation, a single network interface, manually set minimum and maximum replicas, and no Secure Boot support. Autoscaling does not apply to VM workloads.
  • Container workloads. A containerized app keeps the same workload definition on every cloud. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.
  • VM and container workloads together. Because both types are Control Plane workloads, they share networking, identity, and observability. Workload-to-workload traffic uses mTLS with a unique client certificate per workload, behind a deny-by-default internal firewall.

Every workload has its own canonical endpoint that DNS geo-routes clients to the nearest location where that workload passes its readiness checks. A gradually containerized application can serve traffic from every location of its containerized components while other components still run as VMs on MK8s locations.

With MK8s, Control Plane operates the Kubernetes control plane and your servers run the worker nodes. This lets you run VM workloads on your own bare-metal servers on premises while container workloads run in Control Plane-managed cloud regions, all under one platform.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations.

For teams that want to consolidate multiple clouds onto one platform or get Kubernetes benefits without building a platform team, Control Plane removes per-cloud overlay work and runs the multi-location infrastructure for you. The hybrid cloud platforms comparison covers the wider field.

FAQ

Short answers to common questions about modernizing VM-based applications to Kubernetes.

How do I modernize a VM based application to Kubernetes on multi cloud infrastructure?

Choose a modernization path for each application (retain on VMs, run as a VM inside Kubernetes with KubeVirt, containerize, refactor, or replace parts with managed services), map every VM concept to its Kubernetes equivalent, externalize config and state, and migrate in phases. Use a readiness scorecard to decide which path fits each app. Keep your deployment definitions and data layer portable so the same workload runs on any cloud.

Can I run virtual machines on Kubernetes?

Yes. KubeVirt extends Kubernetes with custom resources that let you run VM images as pods. The nodes must support KVM (bare metal or nested virtualization). On Control Plane, VM workloads run on MK8s locations with the KubeVirt add-on, and they run alongside container workloads under the same Control Plane org, policies, and tooling.

What is KubeVirt?

KubeVirt is an open-source Kubernetes add-on that lets you define, run, and manage virtual machines using the Kubernetes API. It adds VirtualMachine and VirtualMachineInstance custom resources so VMs are scheduled, networked, and monitored alongside containers. It requires KVM-capable nodes, and live migration requires RWX shared storage.

Should I containerize or refactor a legacy application?

Containerize first if the application is a standard Linux process with documented dependencies and no kernel-level requirements. Refactor only when the application is strategic, under active development, and the team has the capacity. The readiness scorecard in this guide helps you make the call by counting eight signals.

How do I migrate a stateful VM application to Kubernetes?

Move the persistent data to a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by a CSI driver, or migrate it to an external managed database. Set up replication from the source to the target, validate data integrity, then cut over. Use a StatefulSet if the application needs stable network identities or ordered startup.

Can Windows applications run on Kubernetes?

Windows Server containers run on Windows node pools supported by AKS, EKS, and GKE. They work for .NET Framework, IIS, and Windows Server workloads. Desktop applications or GUI-based services cannot run as containers and should be retained as VMs or run inside Kubernetes via KubeVirt.

How do I handle software licensing tied to a VM?

Contact the software vendor before migrating. Containers do not have a stable MAC address or host ID, so fingerprint-based licenses will fail. Ask about floating license servers, per-core licensing, or container-specific license models. If no container-friendly option exists, keep the application as a VM.

Do I need a service mesh to modernize to multi-cloud Kubernetes?

No. A service mesh (Istio, Cilium, Linkerd) helps with cross-cluster traffic management, mTLS, and observability. You can start with Kubernetes Services and Ingress and add a mesh when you need multi-cluster routing or fine-grained traffic control. On Control Plane, workload-to-workload mTLS and a deny-by-default internal firewall are built in, so you do not need to operate a separate service mesh.

How does Control Plane run VM and container workloads together?

Control Plane runs VM workloads by importing VMDK, qcow2, or VHD images onto MK8s locations with the KubeVirt add-on on KVM-capable nodes. Container workloads run on any location in the GVC, including Control Plane-managed cloud regions. Both workload types share the same networking (mTLS per workload), identity (Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity, which lets workloads reach AWS, GCP, and Azure services through one identity), and observability. Each workload gets a canonical endpoint that routes clients to the nearest healthy location.

To modernize VM-based applications across clouds without building a platform team, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free to start running workloads on multiple clouds from one definition.

title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
description:
arXiv:2611.15189v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

title: Google Cloud Pub/Sub and AWS SQS Dead Letter Recovery — 4 Edtech Failure Classes
description:
Google Cloud Pub/Sub and AWS SQS Dead Letter Recovery — 4 Edtech Failure Classes

Short answer: Google Cloud Pub/Sub dead-letter topics, AWS SQS DLQs, and Azure Service Bus dead-letter subqueues can all handle retries; choose the one whose recovery evidence and replay controls fit the cleanup job.

Choose a dead-letter design by how an operator will recover a failed cleanup, not by which queue has the shorter setup. For an education platform, the useful question is: can someone identify the bad enrollment record, replay only safe work, and prove that the web request was never part of the recovery path?

The request is already gone.

No magic.

A practical default is a scheduled worker that writes an idempotent job envelope, retries transient failures with bounded delay, and moves poison messages to a separately monitored dead-letter destination. The queue product matters after that. Its redrive rules, message metadata, retention behavior, and permissions decide how much detective work remains at 02:00.

The comparison below uses three common patterns: Google Cloud Pub/Sub dead-letter topics, Amazon SQS dead-letter queues, and Azure Service Bus dead-letter subqueues. They solve a similar failure problem, but they expose different operational handles.

Recovery question Pub/Sub dead-letter topic SQS DLQ Service Bus dead-letter subqueue
What is isolated? An undeliverable message is forwarded to a dead-letter topic after repeated delivery attempts A message is moved after its receive count exceeds the redrive threshold A message is placed in the entity's dead-letter subqueue
Main retry control Subscription retry policy and maximum delivery attempts Visibility timeout and maxReceiveCount Lock duration, delivery count, and dead-letter reason data
Operator's first task Check forwarding permissions and inspect the wrapped message Inspect receive count, retention, and redrive policy Read the dead-letter reason and description before deciding to resubmit
Best fit Topic-based fanout with subscription-level recovery Queue-shaped work with explicit redrive ownership Workflows where failure reason metadata is part of triage

The matrix is a starting point, not a ranking. The right choice is the one whose recovery evidence matches the failure you expect.

Should Google Cloud Pub/Sub or AWS SQS own dead-letter recovery?

Consider a nightly cleanup in an edtech system. It removes expired temporary exports and marks orphaned upload records. A web request starts the run, writes one message per account shard, and returns. The worker may run for hours after the request has disappeared.

That separation changes the failure contract. A timeout at the learning portal is not proof that cleanup failed. A worker crash is not permission to run the same database mutation twice. A poison message should become inspectable work, not an invisible retry loop.

I model each message with an operation identifier, a scope, and a reason for the cleanup. The identifier is stable across retries. The consumer records it with the mutation, so a replay can answer “already applied?” before changing data again. This is more important than the name of the dead-letter feature.

type CleanupJob = {
  operationId: string;
  accountId: string;
  shard: number;
  requestedAt: string;
  schemaVersion: 1;
};

type FailureClass =
  | "transient_dependency"
  | "invalid_scope"
  | "permission"
  | "unknown";

function shouldRetry(failure: FailureClass): boolean {
  return failure === "transient_dependency";
}

The queue should carry enough context to find the job. It should not carry a second, competing source of truth for the account's state. Keep the payload boring. Config bloat is a liability during recovery.

Which differences affect the operator, not the brochure?

Pub/Sub uses a dead-letter topic attached to a subscription. Google documents a maximum delivery-attempt setting in the range of 5 to 100, and the subscription can also use a retry policy with minimum and maximum backoff. Forwarding requires the relevant service agent permissions. That last detail is easy to miss: a valid retry policy can still produce a confusing recovery path if the service identity cannot publish to the dead-letter topic or acknowledge the original message.

The forwarded message also needs deliberate inspection. Pub/Sub documents that the forwarded message contains the original message and attributes that help identify the source subscription. Your replay worker should treat that envelope as an input format, not assume the dead-letter payload is byte-for-byte the original event.

SQS makes the boundary explicit with a redrive policy. maxReceiveCount controls how many receives are allowed before SQS moves the message to the dead-letter queue. Visibility timeout is a separate control: it determines when an un-deleted message becomes available again. Mixing those two numbers is a common operational mistake. A long visibility timeout can delay a retry; a low receive threshold can send a temporarily slow job to the DLQ before its dependency recovers.

AWS also documents retention behavior that affects recovery windows. For a standard queue, the message's original enqueue timestamp is retained when it moves to a DLQ, so the DLQ retention period must be chosen with that lifecycle in mind. FIFO queues have different timestamp behavior. This is not trivia if an education provider investigates a failed term-end cleanup days later.

Service Bus uses a dead-letter subqueue associated with the queue or subscription. It records dead-letter reason and description properties, and its delivery count and lock behavior are separate parts of the retry design. That makes it useful when a human needs to distinguish an expired lock from an application-level rejection, provided the consumer writes meaningful descriptions and does not flatten every exception into “failed.”

These are different operational shapes. A topic-based system makes fanout and subscription-specific recovery natural. A queue redrive policy is direct for one work stream. A dead-letter subqueue keeps failure context close to the original entity. None eliminates the need for an idempotent consumer.

Each option has a boundary. Pub/Sub is a poor fit if the team cannot operate subscription-level permissions and wrapped-message inspection. SQS is a poor fit if the workflow needs fanout but the team has no clear owner for each queue's redrive policy. Service Bus is a poor fit if its lock and dead-letter metadata will be discarded by a generic adapter. Those are trade-offs, not feature defects.

How should the cleanup worker classify a failure?

Dead-lettering every exception is lazy and expensive in engineering time. Retrying every exception is worse. The worker needs a small classification table that the on-call person can understand without opening the application source.

Failure Retry action Dead-letter action
Database connection reset Retry with bounded backoff Escalate only after the retry budget
Account identifier fails validation Do not retry Preserve payload and validation detail
Permission denied for one tenant Do not blindly retry Route to an access owner with the tenant scope
Worker loses its lease Let the message become visible again Avoid a second mutation by using the operation identifier

The exact number of attempts belongs to the dependency's recovery time and the cleanup's urgency. I would rather document “six attempts over 25 minutes, then operator review” than paste a large attempt count into infrastructure and call it resilience. The number is a policy. It needs an owner.

Start small. A four-message failure drill tells you more than another page of queue configuration: break the database connection, send an invalid account, revoke a tenant permission, and stop a worker while it holds a lease. Record which signal the operator sees first and which replay guard prevents a duplicate mutation.

The poison-message path should expose at least these fields in logs and metrics: operation identifier, account or tenant identifier, shard, first-seen time, delivery or receive count when available, failure class, and last error code. Do not put student data into a dead-letter payload merely because it makes a dashboard convenient.

What should a replay command guarantee?

A replay is a production mutation with a smaller blast radius. It deserves a dry-run mode, an allowlist of operation identifiers, and a limit on how many messages can be released in one invocation. The command should report why each message was selected and where the result was written.

type ReplayRequest = {
  operationIds: string[];
  dryRun: boolean;
  maxMessages: number;
};

type ReplayResult = {
  operationId: string;
  action: "released" | "skipped" | "already_applied";
  detail: string;
};

async function replay(
  request: ReplayRequest,
  load: (id: string) => Promise<CleanupJob | undefined>,
  apply: (job: CleanupJob) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<ReplayResult[]> {
  const selected = request.operationIds.slice(0, request.maxMessages);
  const results: ReplayResult[] = [];

  for (const operationId of selected) {
    const job = await load(operationId);
    if (!job) {
      results.push({ operationId, action: "skipped", detail: "not found" });
      continue;
    }
    if (request.dryRun) {
      results.push({ operationId, action: "released", detail: "dry run" });
      continue;
    }
    await apply(job);
    results.push({ operationId, action: "released", detail: "submitted" });
  }

  return results;
}

The example deliberately leaves queue-specific release calls behind an interface. That keeps the replay policy testable and prevents a provider SDK from becoming the business logic. In real code, I would also make apply consult the idempotency store before the mutation and write the result transactionally with the state change where the database supports it.

When is the runner-up the better fit?

A Pub/Sub design is a reasonable fit when one cleanup event must feed several independent subscriptions and each subscription needs its own retry and dead-letter behavior. SQS is a reasonable fit when the unit of work is a single queue and the team wants an explicit receive-count redrive policy with queue-specific retention decisions. Service Bus deserves consideration when dead-letter reason and description are central to triage or when the surrounding messaging model already uses its entities and locks.

Those are boundaries, not endorsements. The third option can be the best operational match even when it is not the first service a team reaches for. The decision should follow the recovery exercise: inject a transient database failure, an invalid account, a lost worker lease, and a permission failure. Then ask an engineer who did not write the worker to recover one message without replaying the whole night.

If that drill requires a dashboard search across opaque identifiers, the design is unfinished. Add the identifier, the failure class, and the replay guard before tuning another backoff value.

Then stop.

The dead-letter mechanism is successful when recovery is a small, auditable operation. For scheduled education cleanup, operational recovery is the decision axis: message retention, failure metadata, permissions, idempotency, and replay controls matter more than a feature checklist.

References

  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub dead-letter topics: https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/dead-letter-topics
  • Google Cloud Pub/Sub retry policy: https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscription-retry-policy
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • Azure Service Bus dead-letter queues: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-bus-messaging/service-bus-dead-letter-queues
  • Azure Service Bus message transfers, locks, and settlement: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/service-bus-messaging/message-transfers-locks-settlement

title: Fix OOM Kills and MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED on ClickHouse® Servers
description:
Introduction

ClickHouse® servers can experience two types of memory-related failures.

In the first, the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer terminates clickhouse-server. The service restarts, and all running queries fail.

In the second, multiple queries fail with MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (code 241). The error message contains (total), indicating that the entire server has reached its memory limit rather than an individual query exceeding its own limit.

Both failures have the same underlying cause: the server is attempting to use more memory than the host can provide.

In this guide, we'll explain how ClickHouse manages server memory, how to identify the source of memory failures, and how to configure appropriate limits to protect your server.

1. Why Memory Failures Happen

ClickHouse maintains a hard memory limit for the entire server. When a query attempts an allocation that would exceed this limit, the query is stopped.

Two steps determine the server's memory limit.

Step 1: Establishing the Memory Ceiling

At startup, ClickHouse calculates its memory ceiling using the available memory and the setting max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.

The default value is 0.9, meaning ClickHouse can use up to 90% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

The setting max_server_memory_usage defaults to 0, which means no fixed limit is configured. If you specify a fixed value, ClickHouse uses the lower of that value and the calculated ceiling.

For example, on a host with 13.55 GiB of RAM, setting a fixed limit of 15.63 GiB resulted in the following log message:

Lowered setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 12.20 GiB because the system has too little memory. The new value was calculated as 13.55 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

ClickHouse automatically lowered the configured limit because the host could not support the requested amount.

Step 2: Understanding the Runtime Memory Limit

ClickHouse also uses a background thread called the memory worker to recalculate the hard memory limit while the server is running.

The runtime limit is calculated using:

(resident memory + available system memory) * ratio

The result cannot exceed the previously established ceiling.

When other processes consume memory, the available system memory decreases, and the runtime limit can fall accordingly.

For example:

MemoryWorker: Adjusting total memory hard limit from 5.62 GiB to 5.69 GiB (resident: 364.99 MiB, available: 5.97 GiB, ceiling: 12.20 GiB, ratio: 0.9)

The calculation is approximately:

(0.36 GiB + 5.97 GiB) × 0.9 = 5.69 GiB

Although the ceiling remained at 12.20 GiB, the live limit stayed around 6 GiB because other processes were consuming some of the host's memory.

Why the Safety Margin Matters

The ratio provides a safety margin because ClickHouse's memory tracker does not account for every memory allocation.

In one test, MemoryResident was 940 MiB while TrackedMemory was only 365 MiB. The remaining memory was consumed by the kernel, other services, and allocator overhead.

A sudden memory spike can consume the available margin between memory-worker checks, potentially triggering the Linux OOM killer.

What Happens in Containers?

ClickHouse can read memory limits imposed through cgroups.

For example, after setting MemoryMax=8G with systemd and restarting the server, the log showed:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 7.20 GiB (8.00 GiB available memory * 0.90 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Without a container memory limit, ClickHouse may see the memory available on the entire host rather than the amount intended for the service.

The setting memory_worker_use_cgroup controls the use of cgroup memory information for runtime memory-limit calculations. However, a test on a host with similar free memory inside and outside the limit does not, by itself, prove the behavior.

Version note: In ClickHouse 26.3.9, memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit does not exist. The limit remains at the ceiling, making the memory ratio an important protection mechanism.

2. How to Confirm the Problem

Before changing settings, determine whether the operating system killed the process or ClickHouse stopped a query because of its own memory limit.

Step 1: Check for OOM Kills

Run:

sudo dmesg -T | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

You can also inspect kernel logs from the last 24 hours:

sudo journalctl -k --since "24 hours ago" | grep -i -E "out of memory|killed process"

Check when the ClickHouse service last started:

systemctl show clickhouse-server -p ActiveEnterTimestamp

If the service started recently and the kernel logs show that clickhouse-serv was killed, the operating system likely terminated the process due to memory pressure.

The kernel truncates process names to 15 characters, which explains why the process name may appear as clickhouse-serv.

Step 2: Find Server-Level Memory Errors

A ClickHouse server-level memory failure typically appears as MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED with error code 241 and (total) in the message.

For example, this error was observed on ClickHouse 26.8.36:

Code: 241. DB::Exception: (total) memory limit exceeded: would use 6.28 GiB (attempt to allocate chunk of 4.00 GiB), current RSS: 2.23 GiB, maximum: 6.08 GiB. OvercommitTracker decision: Query was selected to stop by OvercommitTracker. Untracked memory across all threads: -6.82 MiB: While executing AggregatingTransform. (MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED)

The maximum value represents the live server memory limit. It may be lower than the configured ceiling.

To find recent server-level memory errors, query system.query_log:

SELECT
    event_time,
    query_id,
    substring(exception, 1, 250) AS exception_start
FROM system.query_log
WHERE type = 'ExceptionWhileProcessing'
  AND exception_code = 241
  AND exception LIKE '%(total)%'
  AND event_time > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
ORDER BY event_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

The system.errors table contains error counts accumulated since the server started and is reset on restart. The query log provides historical records of individual failures.

Step 3: Compare Process Memory with Host Memory

Run the following query:

SELECT
    metric,
    formatReadableSize(value) AS size
FROM system.asynchronous_metrics
WHERE metric IN (
    'MemoryResident',
    'TrackedMemory',
    'OSMemoryTotal',
    'OSMemoryAvailable'
)
ORDER BY metric;

These metrics help you compare the memory used by ClickHouse with the total and available memory on the host.

Step 4: Read the Live Memory Limit

Use system.server_settings to inspect the current server memory limit:

SELECT
    formatReadableSize(toUInt64(value)) AS live_limit
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name = 'max_server_memory_usage';

This shows the effective limit, which may differ from the value in your configuration file.

For more information about runtime adjustments, inspect the server logs:

sudo grep -a "Adjusting total memory hard limit" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -5

These messages are available at Trace log level.

3. Understanding the Relevant Settings

The following defaults are based on ClickHouse 26.8.36. Verify them on your own server before making changes.

Run:

SELECT
    name,
    value,
    default,
    changed,
    changeable_without_restart
FROM system.server_settings
WHERE name LIKE 'max_server_memory%'
   OR name LIKE 'memory_worker%';

The important settings are:

Setting Default Purpose Restart required
max_server_memory_usage 0 Defines a fixed server memory limit in bytes. A higher value is lowered to the calculated ceiling. No
max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio 0.9 Controls the share of memory available to the server and determines the memory ceiling. A value of 0 disables the limits established by this ratio. No in the test described
memory_worker_dynamic_hard_limit true Allows the memory worker to recalculate the hard limit at runtime. Yes
memory_worker_use_cgroup true Uses cgroup memory information when calculating the runtime limit. Yes

The changeable_without_restart column may show No for the ratio setting. In the test described here, reloading the configuration still applied the change, and the logs showed a new Changed setting message.

If the expected log message does not appear after reloading the configuration, restart the server.

4. How to Fix Memory Failures

The recommended approach is to reserve memory for the operating system and configure explicit memory limits for containers.

Step 1: Set a Lower Memory Ratio

Create a configuration file at:

/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/memory.xml

Add the following configuration:

<clickhouse>
    <max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio>0.8</max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio>
</clickhouse>

A ratio of 0.8 allows ClickHouse to use up to 80% of the available memory for its server memory limit.

For example, on a host with 64 GiB of memory, the ceiling would be 51.2 GiB, leaving 12.8 GiB for the operating system and other processes.

Consider these starting points:

  • 0.8: A reasonable starting point for many hosts.
  • 0.7: Consider this when the host runs other services.
  • 0.85: Consider this only on a dedicated host with carefully monitored memory usage.

These values are starting points, not universal recommendations. The appropriate ratio depends on the host, workload, and memory consumed by other processes.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

Then verify the updated setting in the logs:

sudo grep -a "max_server_memory_usage" /var/log/clickhouse-server/clickhouse-server.log | tail -3

You should see a Changed setting message confirming the new value.

For example, a test using a ratio of 0.15 produced:

Changed setting 'max_server_memory_usage' to 2.03 GiB (13.55 GiB available memory * 0.15 max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio)

Configuration tip: Write the new file in a separate directory first, then copy it into config.d/. This reduces the chance of ClickHouse loading a partially written configuration file.

Step 2: Configure a Fixed Memory Limit

If you know how much memory ClickHouse should use on a shared host, you can set an explicit limit alongside the ratio.

Update memory.xml:

<clickhouse>
    <max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio>0.8</max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio>
    <max_server_memory_usage>53687091200</max_server_memory_usage>
</clickhouse>

The value 53687091200 represents 50 GiB in bytes.

A fixed limit makes the memory budget easier to understand and manage. ClickHouse uses the lowest applicable value among the fixed limit, the calculated ceiling, and the runtime limit.

Reload the configuration:

SYSTEM RELOAD CONFIG;

In the test described here, changing the configured value from 3 GiB to 2 GiB through a configuration reload caused the next memory error to report:

maximum: 2.00 GiB

Verify the effective limit in the logs and through system.server_settings.

Step 3: Set a Container Memory Limit

A container memory limit prevents ClickHouse from consuming the entire host's memory.

Docker example:

docker run -d --name clickhouse --memory=32g clickhouse/clickhouse-server

Kubernetes example:

resources:
  requests:
    memory: 32Gi
  limits:
    memory: 32Gi

Setting the Kubernetes memory request equal to the limit reserves the same memory amount for scheduling purposes and helps avoid unexpected memory-pressure evictions caused by overcommitting the requested amount.

With a 32 GiB container limit and a ratio of 0.8, the calculated ceiling is 25.6 GiB.

Systemd's MemoryMax provides a similar cgroup memory limit.

Remember that the container limit and ClickHouse's internal memory limit serve different purposes: the container constrains the process at the operating-system level, while ClickHouse's settings help it stop queries before reaching that boundary.

5. How to Verify the Fix

After changing the configuration, check the effective settings and confirm that the logs show the expected memory limit.

On a test server, you can trigger a memory-limit error using:

SELECT groupArray(number)
FROM numbers(100000000000)
SETTINGS max_memory_usage = 0
FORMAT Null;

Warning: Do not run this test on a production server. It is intended for controlled testing only.

The query should fail with code 241. The maximum value in the error should match the configured effective limit or be lower if the host has insufficient available memory.

For production, monitor the server for seven days after applying the changes.

The fix is working as intended when:

  1. Kernel logs show no new OOM kills.
  2. The query log contains no new unexpected (total) memory-limit errors.
  3. MemoryResident remains below OSMemoryTotal with a safe memory margin.

Continue monitoring workloads that generate large aggregations, memory-intensive queries, merges, and mutations.

6. Risks and Trade-Offs

Lower Limits Can Cause Queries to Fail Earlier

Reducing the memory limit means ClickHouse may reject queries that previously succeeded.

This is often the correct trade-off: a failed query is preferable to a server process being killed and disrupting all running queries.

Identify and tune the heaviest queries rather than simply increasing the server limit.

The Live Limit Can Change

On a shared host, the effective memory limit can decrease when other processes consume more memory.

As a result, queries may fail even when the configured settings have not changed. Investigate other processes and host-level memory usage before increasing ClickHouse's limits.

Merges and Mutations Have Their Own Memory Controls

Merges and mutations have a separate setting:

merges_mutations_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio

Its default is 0.5. Review it when diagnosing memory pressure related to background operations.

Caches Also Consume Memory

Caches contribute to memory consumption. Avoid increasing cache sizes when lowering the server's memory limit unless you have measured the impact and confirmed that sufficient memory remains available.

Be Careful When Using Swap

The setting description notes that low-RAM hosts with swap may require a ratio above 1 in certain situations.

This should only be done deliberately. Allowing ClickHouse to use swap before reaching its configured limit may delay an OOM event, but heavy swapping can make queries extremely slow and postpone rather than prevent a more severe failure.

For ClickHouse hosts, consider disabling swap or configuring a low vm.swappiness value according to your operational requirements.

7. Summary

When troubleshooting ClickHouse memory failures:

  • Check dmesg and the service start time to determine whether the operating system killed the process.
  • Look for MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED code 241 errors containing (total) to identify server-level memory failures.
  • Read the maximum value in the error message to understand the effective live limit.
  • Remember that the live limit is constrained by the fixed limit, the ratio-based ceiling, and the runtime limit calculated by the memory worker.
  • Configure a suitable max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio in config.d/ and reload the configuration.
  • Set an explicit container memory limit when running ClickHouse in Docker, Kubernetes, or another cgroup-managed environment.
  • Monitor kernel logs, query errors, and memory metrics after applying the fix.

The goal is not to let ClickHouse consume every available byte of memory. It is to establish a predictable memory budget that protects the server while allowing normal workloads to run reliably.

References

  • ClickHouse documentation: max_server_memory_usage and max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio.
