title: How to Run Kubernetes Across On-Premises and Public Cloud: Four Hybrid Architecture Models and the Seven Layers to Standardize
description:
You run Kubernetes across on-premises and public cloud by choosing one of four architecture models and then standardizing seven layers across every cluster. The four models are: one distribution everywhere, a hyperscaler extension, a multi-cluster manager over mixed clusters, or a platform that deploys one workload definition to clusters in both places. The seven layers are cluster lifecycle, networking, ingress and load balancing, storage and data, identity and policy, delivery, and observability. Each layer carries an on-premises gotcha, from the absence of a managed load balancer to IP range collisions to storage that cannot be stretched over a WAN.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Four architecture models. One distribution everywhere (OpenShift, RKE2). Hyperscaler extension (Azure Arc, Google Distributed Cloud, EKS Anywhere, EKS Hybrid Nodes). Multi-cluster manager (Rancher, Advanced Cluster Management). Platform that deploys one workload definition to clusters in both places (Control Plane).
  • Seven layers to standardize. Cluster lifecycle and versions. Networking. Ingress and load balancing. Storage and data. Identity and policy. Delivery. Observability.
  • Most common on-premises gotchas. No cloud load balancer, so you need MetalLB or kube-vip. Overlapping pod and service CIDRs with the corporate network. Storage classes that do not match the cloud side. Version skew after a missed upgrade window.
  • Never stretch synchronous block storage across a WAN. Replicate at the application or database layer instead.
  • Where Control Plane fits. Control Plane deploys one workload definition to Control Plane’s Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations, that spans Control Plane-managed cloud regions, your own Kubernetes clusters joined through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own servers joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), including on premises. Every workload gets a canonical endpoint with DNS geo-routing to the nearest healthy location passing its readiness checks.

How do I run Kubernetes across on premises and public cloud?

You need a plan that covers architecture selection, network design, cluster provisioning, connectivity, workload delivery, and failure testing, in this order.

  1. Choose an architecture model. Decide whether you want a single Kubernetes distribution on every site, a hyperscaler extension that brings a cloud provider’s managed Kubernetes to your data center, a multi-cluster manager that federates heterogeneous clusters, or a platform that deploys one workload definition to clusters in both places.
  2. Plan networks and IPs. Assign non-overlapping pod CIDRs and service CIDRs per cluster. Map out which private links (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect) or IPsec VPN tunnels connect each site.
  3. Build clusters from code. Use Cluster API, Terraform, OpenTofu, or your chosen platform’s provisioning tooling so every cluster is reproducible. Pin Kubernetes versions and enforce the upstream version skew policy.
  4. Connect sites. Establish private links or encrypted tunnels. Set up DNS so services in one site can resolve services in the other.
  5. Standardize ingress and storage. On premises, deploy MetalLB or kube-vip for LoadBalancer-type Services. Define storage classes per site using CSI drivers appropriate to each environment.
  6. Deploy through GitOps. Use Argo CD or Flux with a single repository and per-site overlays. Mirror your container image registry on premises so image pulls do not depend on internet availability during deployment.
  7. Unify identity, policy, and observability. Configure one OIDC identity provider for human access. Apply OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno policies identically across clusters. Ship logs, metrics, and traces to a location that survives a single-site outage.
  8. Test a site failure. Simulate link loss, load balancer failure, certificate expiry, and registry unavailability before you declare the environment production-ready.

Which hybrid Kubernetes architecture model should you choose?

The right model depends on how much Kubernetes operations you want to own, which clouds you use, and whether you need workloads to move between sites without rewriting deployment manifests.

Model Examples Where the Kubernetes control plane runs What you operate on premises How apps are deployed to both sides Best fit Main trade-off
One distribution everywhere Red Hat OpenShift; SUSE Rancher with RKE2 On premises and in the cloud, one control plane per cluster Full Kubernetes control plane, worker nodes, storage, networking Same Helm charts or operators applied to each cluster, often via GitOps Teams that want full control and a single support contract You run and upgrade every control plane yourself, in every site
Hyperscaler extension Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes with AKS on Azure Local; Google Distributed Cloud (formerly Anthos) with GKE fleets; Amazon EKS Anywhere; Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes; AWS Outposts EKS Anywhere: on-premises control plane. EKS Hybrid Nodes: control plane in AWS, worker nodes on premises. Google Distributed Cloud: control plane on premises in every mode, managed from Google Cloud except air-gapped. Azure Arc: existing cluster control plane stays where it is; AKS on Azure Local runs a local control plane managed from Azure. AWS Outposts: control plane in the AWS Region (extended clusters) or on the Outpost itself (local clusters). Varies by product. EKS Anywhere: full cluster. EKS Hybrid Nodes: worker nodes only. Google Distributed Cloud: full cluster on your own servers (software-only), on hardware Google maintains remotely (connected), or on hardware with no Google Cloud connection (air-gapped). Azure Local: Microsoft-validated hardware stack. Outposts: AWS-owned and maintained rack. Cloud-native tooling (kubectl, Flux, Arc GitOps, Config Sync) Teams already invested in one hyperscaler who want a consistent managed experience on premises Ties networking, identity, and billing to one cloud provider, to a degree that varies by product
Multi-cluster manager over mixed clusters Rancher managing EKS, AKS, GKE, and on-premises clusters; Open Cluster Management; Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management Each cluster keeps its own control plane; the manager runs separately On-premises clusters (control plane and workers), plus the manager if self-hosted Manager pushes manifests, policies, or Helm releases to registered clusters Teams with existing heterogeneous clusters that need unified visibility and policy The manager is another system to operate, and it does not abstract away per-cluster differences
Platform that deploys one workload definition to clusters in both places Control Plane Control Plane-managed regions: Control Plane operates them; you run no Kubernetes control plane. MK8s locations: Control Plane operates the Kubernetes control plane, your servers run the worker nodes. BYOK: your existing cluster’s control plane stays where it is. MK8s: physical servers and local networking. BYOK: the full cluster. In both cases, hardware, physical security, network links, and stored data are your responsibility. One workload definition deployed to a GVC; workloads run in every location of that GVC. Teams that want production workloads across clouds and on premises without having to operate Kubernetes themselves Control Plane is not a Kubernetes distribution you install and does not replace OpenShift or Rancher for teams that want to run Kubernetes themselves

This table reflects each vendor’s public documentation as of November 2026.

One distribution everywhere

Running OpenShift or RKE2 in every site gives you a single set of APIs, a single support vendor, and the freedom to place clusters anywhere you have hardware or cloud accounts. The trade-off is that you own every control plane upgrade, every etcd backup, and every certificate rotation in every site. On-premises clusters do not get automatic node replacement the way cloud-managed clusters do. If your platform team is small, the operational load of maintaining identical distributions across five or ten sites can consume most of their capacity.

Hyperscaler extension

Azure Arc, Google Distributed Cloud, EKS Anywhere, EKS Hybrid Nodes, and AWS Outposts each bring a hyperscaler’s managed Kubernetes experience closer to your data center, but they differ in where the control plane runs and what hardware you supply. EKS Hybrid Nodes keeps the control plane in AWS and attaches your on-premises servers as worker nodes, which means a WAN outage can prevent new pod scheduling. EKS Anywhere runs a full on-premises control plane but is a separate product with its own lifecycle. Google Distributed Cloud runs the whole cluster, control plane included, on premises in all of its forms: software-only on VMware or bare metal, connected hardware that Google maintains remotely, and air-gapped hardware fully isolated from Google Cloud. Azure Arc projects existing clusters into Azure’s management plane without moving the control plane. The trade-off is cloud lock-in: your networking, identity, billing, and operational tooling become tightly coupled to one provider.

Multi-cluster manager over mixed clusters

Rancher, Open Cluster Management, and Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management let you register clusters from any provider and apply policies, RBAC, and application bundles from a central interface. This model works well when you already have clusters in multiple clouds and on premises and need one place to manage them. The trade-off is that the manager does not erase the differences between clusters. You still need to handle per-cluster storage classes, CNI plugins, and ingress configurations. The manager itself is another component to operate, upgrade, and secure.

Platform that deploys one workload definition to clusters in both places

You define a workload once and assign it to a GVC, which is a named set of locations. Those locations can be Control Plane-managed regions on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), Kubernetes clusters joined through BYOK, or your own servers joined through MK8s. The workload runs in every location of that GVC. DNS geo-routing on each workload’s canonical endpoint sends clients to the closest location where the workload passes readiness checks. The trade-off is that Control Plane is not a Kubernetes distribution you install. It does not replace OpenShift or Rancher for teams that want to run Kubernetes themselves.

What do you need to standardize across on-premises and cloud clusters?

Standardize the application-facing contracts, policies, and workflows so they behave the same in every cluster, even where the infrastructure differs.

Layer What to standardize On-premises gotcha Cloud side Typical tools
Cluster lifecycle and versions Kubernetes version, upgrade cadence, version skew policy between control plane and kubelets No managed upgrade button; missed upgrades push clusters out of support and leave manifests on APIs that the next release removes Managed upgrades (EKS, AKS, GKE) with maintenance windows Cluster API, Terraform, OpenTofu
Networking Non-overlapping pod and service CIDRs; private links or VPN; DNS resolution between sites Pod CIDRs can collide with corporate RFC 1918 ranges already in use on premises Cloud VPCs with provider-assigned ranges; AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect Calico, Cilium, IPsec VPN, private interconnects
Ingress and load balancing Consistent LoadBalancer-type Service behavior; global DNS or GSLB in front of all sites No cloud load balancer on premises; you must run MetalLB, kube-vip, or use a hardware load balancer Cloud load balancers provisioned automatically by the cloud controller manager MetalLB, kube-vip, F5, global DNS
Storage and data CSI drivers per site; backup and restore procedures; replication strategy On-premises storage requires Rook-Ceph, vendor arrays, or local disks; never stretch synchronous block storage over a WAN EBS, Persistent Disk, Azure Disk, managed databases Rook-Ceph, vendor CSI drivers, Velero
Identity and policy One OIDC identity provider for people; workload identity per cloud; admission policies applied everywhere On-premises clusters lack native workload identity federation; you must configure OIDC manually Cloud IAM with workload identity (IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Microsoft Entra Workload ID) OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno, Dex, Keycloak
Delivery GitOps with one repo and per-site overlays; image registry reachable from both sides Registry pulls from on premises may fail if the internet link is down; mirror images locally Cloud-hosted registries with cross-region replication Argo CD, Flux, Harbor (on-premises mirror)
Observability Common metric, log, and trace formats; cluster and environment labels on every signal If logs are stored only on premises, a site outage takes its own logs with it; ship logs off-site Cloud-native monitoring (CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring, Azure Monitor) OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki

How do you handle networking and traffic between on-premises and cloud clusters?

Private links versus VPN

Dedicated private links such as AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, and Google Cloud Interconnect provide predictable bandwidth and latency between your data center and a cloud region. They cost more than IPsec VPN tunnels but eliminate the variability of internet-based connections. For workloads that tolerate occasional jitter, an encrypted VPN tunnel over the public internet is a reasonable starting point. Many teams start with VPN and upgrade to a private link once traffic volume or latency sensitivity justifies the cost. The guide to cross-cloud private networking for VPCs and VNets compares the options in more depth.

CIDR planning

The most common networking failure in hybrid Kubernetes is overlapping IP ranges. On-premises corporate networks often use 10.0.0.0/8 liberally, and Flannel’s default pod range (10.244.0.0/16) and kubeadm’s default service range (10.96.0.0/12) both fall inside it. Assign each cluster a unique pod CIDR and service CIDR before provisioning. Document every allocation in a central IPAM registry.

Global DNS routing for user traffic

For traffic from end users, place a global DNS or GSLB layer in front of all sites. DNS health checks detect when a site’s ingress is unhealthy and stop routing traffic to it. This layer works with any ingress controller and does not require a service mesh. The guide to routing users to the nearest healthy region compares DNS-based and anycast options.

How do you handle storage and data in hybrid Kubernetes?

Per-site storage

Each site should have its own storage classes backed by the infrastructure available there. On premises, that means Rook-Ceph, a vendor storage array with a CSI driver, or local NVMe disks for latency-sensitive workloads. In the cloud, use the provider’s managed block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk, Azure Disk). Define storage classes with the same name and performance tier on both sides so that workload manifests do not need per-site changes.

Replication at the application or database layer

Synchronous block-level replication over a WAN introduces latency into every write and creates a single failure domain that spans both sites. Do not stretch synchronous storage across a WAN. Instead, replicate at the application or database layer. PostgreSQL streaming replication, CockroachDB multi-region, and MongoDB replica sets all handle cross-site replication at the database layer, each with its own consistency and failover rules. Object stores like MinIO can replicate buckets between sites asynchronously.

Backups

Velero backs up Kubernetes resources and persistent volume snapshots. Run Velero in each cluster and store backup artifacts in a location that survives the loss of that cluster. For on-premises clusters, that means shipping backups to a cloud object store or a separate data center.

Which workloads should run on premises, in the cloud, or both?

Workload trait Run on premises when Run in public cloud when Run in both when
Data residency or sovereignty Regulations require data to stay in a specific facility or jurisdiction you control The cloud region is in the required jurisdiction and the provider meets your compliance framework Different data subjects reside in different jurisdictions served by different sites
Latency to on-premises systems (factory, trading, mainframe data) The workload must respond in single-digit milliseconds to on-premises data sources The data source has already been migrated to the cloud or latency is not a constraint A local copy processes real-time data on premises while a cloud copy handles analytics or reporting
Spiky or seasonal demand (cloud bursting) Demand is steady and fits within existing on-premises capacity Demand is unpredictable or seasonal and would require over-provisioning on premises A base load runs on premises and overflow runs in the cloud
GPU or specialized hardware The required hardware is already installed on premises or is unavailable in the target cloud region Cloud GPU instances are available on demand without long-term commitment Training runs in the cloud on large GPU pools while inference runs on premises near the data
Steady base load with paid-off hardware Hardware is already purchased and has remaining useful life The workload is new and does not justify a hardware purchase The base runs on existing hardware while new capacity is added in the cloud
Customer-facing services that need regional failover All customers are near the on-premises site and failover is handled by a secondary on-premises site Customers are globally distributed and need low-latency access from multiple regions Active-active deployment across on-premises and cloud sites provides failover and geographic reach

What breaks first in hybrid Kubernetes, and how do you test it?

Hybrid environments have more failure modes than single-cloud deployments. Test each of these before production.

  • Link loss between sites. Disconnect the VPN or private link in a maintenance window. Verify that each site continues serving traffic independently, that each cluster keeps running its last synced state and GitOps catches up when the link returns, and that database replication resumes without data loss.
  • On-premises load balancer failure. Shut down MetalLB or kube-vip speakers on a subset of nodes. Confirm that the VIP moves to a healthy node in L2 mode, or that upstream routers withdraw the route in BGP mode, and that global DNS stops routing to the site if all speakers fail.
  • Certificate expiry. Issue a short-lived test certificate and confirm that cert-manager or your CA integration renews it and that alerts fire if renewal fails. Check kubeadm control plane certificates too, which expire after one year unless renewed or rotated by an upgrade.
  • Version skew after a missed upgrade. Intentionally skip an upgrade cycle on one cluster. Confirm that CI flags the version drift between clusters, that a scanner such as Pluto or kubent finds manifests using APIs removed in the next release, and that kubelets stay within the supported skew of the API server.
  • Registry unreachable from on premises. Block outbound access to your container registry from the on-premises cluster. Confirm that the on-premises image mirror serves cached images and that new deployments that cannot pull an image fail with a clear error.
  • DNS split-brain. Cut the link and confirm that global DNS health checks remove the unreachable site, and that internal split-horizon zones keep giving the same answer on both sides.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. Control Plane-managed compute runs in AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud regions.

A workload deployed to a GVC runs in every location of that GVC from one workload definition. You do not maintain a separate deployment per site. Add a location to the GVC and the workload runs there too.

Control Plane’s Cloud Wormhole connects workloads to TCP or UDP endpoints in VPCs and other private networks, including on-premises data centers, by running a Control Plane agent inside the private network. Workload-to-workload traffic uses mTLS with a unique client certificate per workload, behind a deny-by-default internal firewall.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity lets workloads reach AWS, GCP, and Azure services through one identity, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. The CLI, console, Terraform and Pulumi providers, and the Control Plane MCP server all work through the same Control Plane API.

The 9 best hybrid cloud platforms in 2026 compares the wider platform field, and the guide on how to deploy hybrid cloud covers the plan beyond Kubernetes. For teams that want the benefits of Kubernetes without building a platform team, Control Plane runs the platform while you choose where workloads run and where data resides. The guide on how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in covers portability across clouds.

FAQ

Short answers to common questions about hybrid Kubernetes.

How do I run Kubernetes across on premises and public cloud for hybrid cloud application deployment?

Choose one of four architecture models: one distribution everywhere, a hyperscaler extension, a multi-cluster manager over mixed clusters, or a platform like Control Plane that deploys one workload definition to locations in both places. Then standardize seven layers across every cluster: cluster lifecycle and versions, networking, ingress and load balancing, storage and data, identity and policy, delivery, and observability. Connect sites with private links or VPN, deploy workloads through GitOps, and test site failure before going to production.

What is hybrid cloud Kubernetes?

Hybrid cloud Kubernetes is the practice of running Kubernetes clusters in both on-premises data centers and public cloud environments, connected and managed as a unified system. The goal is to place workloads where they make the most sense for latency, compliance, cost, or resilience while giving developers a consistent deployment experience.

Can one Kubernetes cluster span on premises and the cloud?

Stretched clusters are technically possible, and products like EKS Hybrid Nodes attach on-premises worker nodes to a cloud-hosted control plane. However, etcd and the Kubernetes control plane are latency-sensitive. A WAN link with variable latency can cause leader election failures, slow API server responses, and scheduling delays. Most teams run a separate cluster per site and connect them at the application, DNS, or service mesh layer.

Do I need a service mesh for hybrid Kubernetes?

Not always. A service mesh like Istio, Linkerd, or Cilium Cluster Mesh is valuable when workloads in one cluster need to discover and call workloads in another cluster by service name with mutual authentication. If your cross-site traffic is limited to database replication, API gateway calls, or queue-based messaging, a service mesh adds operational complexity without proportional benefit.

How do I get a load balancer for Kubernetes on premises?

On premises, there is no cloud controller manager to provision a load balancer automatically. MetalLB assigns IP addresses from a pool you define and announces them via ARP (Layer 2) or BGP. kube-vip provides a virtual IP for the Kubernetes API server and can also handle LoadBalancer-type Services. Hardware load balancers from F5 or similar vendors work as well, integrated through their respective Kubernetes ingress controllers or CRDs.

What is the difference between Azure Arc, Google Distributed Cloud, and EKS Anywhere?

Azure Arc projects existing Kubernetes clusters into Azure’s management plane, enabling Azure Policy, GitOps, and monitoring on clusters running anywhere. Google Distributed Cloud (formerly Anthos) runs GKE-compatible clusters, control plane included, on premises, managed from Google Cloud or fully air-gapped. EKS Anywhere runs a full Kubernetes control plane on your hardware using EKS-compatible tooling, separate from the EKS Hybrid Nodes product, which keeps the control plane in AWS and runs only worker nodes on premises. Each locks you into its respective cloud’s identity, networking, and billing model to varying degrees.

Should I use Rancher or OpenShift for hybrid Kubernetes?

Choose OpenShift for a curated, integrated platform; choose Rancher to manage mixed distributions from one interface. OpenShift provides a tightly integrated platform with built-in CI/CD, a container registry, and enterprise support from Red Hat. Rancher is more flexible, managing clusters across multiple distributions and providers from a single interface. OpenShift requires more resources per cluster and has a more opinionated upgrade path. Rancher gives you more freedom to mix distributions but leaves more integration work to your team.

How do I keep on-premises and cloud clusters in sync?

Use GitOps. Store all cluster configuration, policies, and application manifests in a Git repository. Argo CD or Flux continuously reconciles the desired state in Git with the actual state in each cluster. Per-site differences are handled through Kustomize overlays or Helm value files. Flux corrects drift on its next reconciliation by default; Argo CD corrects it when self-heal is enabled.

How does Control Plane run workloads on premises and in the cloud?

You define a workload and assign it to a GVC containing the locations where it should run. Locations can be Control Plane-managed cloud regions on AWS, GCP, Azure, or OCI, Kubernetes clusters you already run joined through BYOK, or your own servers joined through MK8s. With MK8s, Control Plane operates the Kubernetes control plane and your servers run the worker nodes. The workload runs in every location of that GVC from one workload definition, with DNS geo-routing directing traffic to the nearest location passing its readiness checks. On BYOK and MK8s locations, your hardware, physical security, network links, and the data you store remain your responsibility.

To run production workloads across on-premises and cloud without having to operate Kubernetes yourself, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

Originally published on the Control Plane blog.

title: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
description:
arXiv:2611.14544v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Digitizing handwritten chess scoresheets has been studied as a handwriting-recognition problem: read the move in each box and check that it is legal. This framing misses the errors that matter most. A misread that yields an illegal move is loud. One that yields a legal-but-wrong move is silent, because a legality-only pipeline accepts it and reads every later move against a wrong position. We therefore treat the task as game reconstruction and present Zugwise, which repurposes computer-chess machinery (quiescence search, static exchange evaluation, pin detection) to ask not "what should be played?" but "could a human plausibly have written this?" An absurdity detector makes silent errors loud at or near where they occur, and a backward search traces late symptoms to their cause. Candidate ranking excludes chess-quality signals. A Needleman-Wunsch merge adds the second player's sheet as evidence, and review stops send every disagreement between the sheets' legal readings to a human. In oracle replay of two tournament sections, a release adding them cuts silent errors from 16 to 1 and from 50 to 13. Two learned signals, CTC re-scoring against the recognizer's raw output and a Maia-style human-move prior, raise the correct fix's top-rank rate from 58.8% to 78.0% of the replacement decisions where it is a candidate, and hold without refitting on a later section. On the first section, the human-verified output matches an independent expert transcription move for move on 34 of 45 games, and adjudication against the sheets found errors in both records, on different plies. We do not establish that either workflow is faster or more accurate. The system runs entirely in the browser and is free, private, and offline-capable; alongside it we offer a three-way adjudication protocol for a domain where no single record is ground truth.

title: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.15600v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

title: Weight-space programming at 50 forward passes: Qwen hit 48.1%, Gemma 7.0%
description:
GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights with no training. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%. On the same budget of 50 forward passes, Gemma 3 270M went from 6.8% to 7.0%.

It fixed a bug. It did not teach math.

The work is by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL, published Nov 2, 2026. The logs are public, so you can check the numbers without running a model.

Pull the numbers

Run this and you get the score and the share of answers cut at the token limit, for each Qwen run:

base=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/main/exp8_math
for run in unedited p10c p25c p50c; do
  curl -s "$base/eval/$run/merged.json" \
    | jq -c --arg run "$run" '[$run, .math500.acc, .math500.cut_share]'
done

["unedited",0.079,0.93]
["p10c",0.1235,0.8725]
["p25c",0.141,0.8635]
["p50c",0.481,0.3305]

The matched-budget table

Forward passes Qwen MATH-500 Qwen cut at token limit Gemma MATH-500
Unedited 7.9% 93.0% 6.8%
10 12.3% 87.2% 7.6%
25 14.1% 86.4% 7.7%
50 48.1% 33.1% 7.0%

One pass is up to 512 generated answers or 1,024 texts read for Qwen. Gemma's generation pass is larger, at 2,048.

Limits:

  • Each budget is one run, and each run chose a different edit. The 10-pass run changed 30 matrices. The 25-pass run zeroed one attention head. The 50-pass run edited 64 MLP columns in each of layers 15 and 19.
  • Gemma's setup differs: no thinking mode, 8,192 tokens, temperature 1.0 and format-agnostic grading. Read the columns separately.
  • The Gemma gain isn't established. Four other runs, told a stricter grading rule, scored 6.1% to 6.7% on the same scale.
  • No model was rerun for this post. akhaliq's re-run of the 50-pass checkpoint got 51.0% with 31.6% cut off. Its base-model check was a 25-problem smoke test.

The edit

The rules banned backward passes, autograd, optimizers and iterative fitting. Astra had a CPU Python kernel over the weights and could only run the model through the forward-pass tool.

The arithmetic: 2 layers × 64 columns × 1,024 = 131,072 weights. Against a nominal 0.8 billion, that's 0.016384%. The report rounds it to 0.016%.

Astra traced the loops to one direction written by those MLPs, then subtracted it. A steering vector works on the same idea at inference time, by adding a contrast direction to activations. Here the direction went into the weights. On Hacker News, yurimo, who says part of their research is in weight-space learning, reads the fix as close to that established technique.

Split the gain

From the same table:

  • 93.0 − 33.1 = 59.9 points fewer answers cut off.
  • 48.1 − 7.9 = 40.2 points more answers correct.

Those compare shares, so they don't show which answers changed. Astra's confirmation run gets closer, on 1,152 held-out practice problems: 579 answers went from wrong to right, and 576 of them had been cut off. Accuracy on finished answers didn't change. Those are Astra's own numbers, on practice data.

Gemma has no such bug. Only 8.5% of its answers reach its limit, and Astra found ordinary arithmetic and algebra errors.

You can split any score jump this way. Count the answers cut off at the limit first, then compare only the ones that finished.

Check the brief

Astra was told what to look for, as one example:

curl -s "$base/runs/p50c/turns/t001/prompt.txt" | grep -o "if the model often fails[^.]*\."

if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts.

That brief runs to 10,315 bytes. It names no layer or direction. Astra still needed 158 turns, 80 Python runs and 20.3 hours, including a 4.7-hour wait when the model could not be reached. Qwen's model card also warns this model is prone to thinking loops.

The limit

The authors write that editing could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but could not add one the model lacked. In experiments 5 and 6, Astra wrote small game networks from scratch, so that limit is about language models that already exist. A third of Qwen's answers still hit the limit.

My reading, not theirs: one AI can now debug another. Teaching it something new still takes training.

The maintained version, with the chart and the comment thread, is on argbe.tech.

title: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
description:
arXiv:2611.14654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.

title: 7 JavaScript interview questions where the follow-up decides the offer
description:
You write debounce in four minutes. The interviewer nods, then asks:

"Nice. Now I need to cancel it when the component unmounts. And sometimes I need it to fire right now, before the user navigates away."

That second question is where the round is actually decided. The first answer shows you have seen the problem before. The follow-up shows whether you understand it.

Below are seven questions that come up again and again in frontend interviews, each with the first answer most people give, the follow-up that comes next, and code that holds up. Every snippet is plain JavaScript you can paste into a console.

1. Debounce, then "cancel it" and "fire it now"

The ask: delay calling a function until the user stops typing for wait ms.

The common first answer works, but loses this, has no way to cancel, and drops the last call if the page closes.

The follow-ups: keep this and the latest arguments, add cancel() for unmounts, add flush() to run the pending call immediately.

function debounce(fn, wait) {
  let timer = null;
  let lastArgs;
  let lastThis;

  function invoke() {
    timer = null;
    const args = lastArgs;
    const context = lastThis;
    lastArgs = lastThis = undefined;
    fn.apply(context, args);
  }

  function debounced(...args) {
    lastArgs = args;
    lastThis = this;
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(invoke, wait);
  }

  debounced.cancel = () => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = null;
    lastArgs = lastThis = undefined;
  };

  // Run the pending call now (for example before the user leaves the page).
  debounced.flush = () => {
    if (timer === null) return;
    clearTimeout(timer);
    invoke();
  };

  return debounced;
}

What they are really checking: that you think about the lifecycle of the thing you built, not just the happy path. cancel is how you avoid calling setState on an unmounted component; flush is how you avoid losing the user's last keystroke.

2. Predict the output: the event loop

The ask: what does this print?

console.log("1");
setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4"));
(async () => {
  console.log("5");
  await null;
  console.log("6");
})();
console.log("7");

Answer: 1 5 7 3 4 6 2

Why:

  • 1, 5 and 7 are synchronous. The body of an async function runs synchronously until its first await, which is why 5 comes before 7.
  • 3, 4 and 6 are microtasks, queued in that order: the .then callback, then queueMicrotask, then the code after await.
  • 2 is a macrotask. Microtasks always drain completely before the next macrotask runs, so setTimeout(..., 0) comes last.

The follow-up: "What happens if a microtask keeps queueing more microtasks?" The macrotask never runs and the page freezes, because the microtask queue must be empty before the browser can render or run timers. That is the one-line answer that separates "memorised the order" from "understands the loop".

3. Promise.all from scratch, then the edge cases

The ask: implement Promise.all.

The follow-ups are all edge cases, and they are where most implementations fail:

  1. Results must keep the input order, not the order promises settle in.
  2. An empty array must resolve immediately with [].
  3. Plain values (not promises) are allowed in the input.
  4. The first rejection rejects the whole thing. 
function promiseAll(iterable) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const items = Array.from(iterable);
    const results = new Array(items.length);
    let remaining = items.length;

    if (remaining === 0) {
      resolve(results);
      return;
    }

    items.forEach((item, index) => {
      // Promise.resolve wraps plain values, so 42 works like a promise.
      Promise.resolve(item).then((value) => {
        results[index] = value; // by index, so order matches the input
        remaining -= 1;
        if (remaining === 0) resolve(results);
      }, reject);
    });
  });
}

A common bug is results.push(value): it passes a quick test and returns results in the wrong order as soon as one promise is slower than another.

4. Run async tasks with a concurrency limit

This one shows up a lot in mid-level and senior rounds, because it is a real production problem: upload 200 files, but never more than 3 at a time.

The ask: mapLimit(items, limit, fn) runs fn on every item, at most limit at once, and returns results in input order.

async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;

  // Each worker takes the next index until none are left.
  async function worker() {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const index = next++;
      results[index] = await fn(items[index], index);
    }
  }

  const workers = Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker);
  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;
}

// Usage
const pages = await mapLimit(urls, 3, (url) => fetch(url).then((r) => r.text()));

Why it works: JavaScript is single-threaded, so next++ can never be read by two workers at once. No locks needed.

The follow-up: "If one request fails, the others keep running. How do you stop them?" Pass an AbortController's signal into fn, call abort() in a catch, and check signal.aborted before a worker picks up the next item. Interviewers love this because it shows you know cancellation is not automatic in JavaScript.

5. Memoize, then "what's your cache key?" and "won't this leak?"

The common first answer stores results in an object keyed by the first argument. The follow-ups break it immediately:

  • What about multiple arguments? Or objects as arguments?
  • The cache grows forever. On a long-lived page that's a memory leak. 
function memoize(fn, { key = (...args) => JSON.stringify(args), max = 500 } = {}) {
  const cache = new Map();

  return function memoized(...args) {
    const k = key(...args);

    if (cache.has(k)) {
      // Move to the end, so the least recently used entry is always first.
      const value = cache.get(k);
      cache.delete(k);
      cache.set(k, value);
      return value;
    }

    const value = fn.apply(this, args);
    cache.set(k, value);

    // Map keeps insertion order, so the first key is the oldest: evict it.
    if (cache.size > max) cache.delete(cache.keys().next().value);
    return value;
  };
}

Things worth saying out loud in the interview:

  • JSON.stringify is a reasonable default key, but it treats {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} as different and drops functions and undefined. That's why the key function is configurable.
  • If fn is async and the promise rejects, you probably don't want to cache the failure forever. Delete the entry in a .catch.

6. Function.prototype.bind, then "what if I call it with new?"

The ask: write your own bind with partial application.

Most answers handle this and preset arguments. The follow-up is: "What should new boundFn() do?" With the native bind, new ignores the bound this and constructs a new instance of the original function.

Function.prototype.myBind = function (thisArg, ...preset) {
  const fn = this;

  return function bound(...args) {
    // Called with `new`: construct the original function, ignore thisArg.
    if (new.target) return new fn(...preset, ...args);
    return fn.apply(thisArg, [...preset, ...args]);
  };
};

function Point(x, y) {
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}

const PointAtX5 = Point.myBind(null, 5);
const p = new PointAtX5(10);
console.log(p.x, p.y, p instanceof Point); // 5 10 true

new.target is the detail that impresses here: it tells you whether the function was called with new, without any instanceof tricks.

7. React: a setInterval that doesn't go stale

The ask: a counter that ticks every second with setInterval inside useEffect.

The common first answer:

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []); // count is captured once: the counter gets stuck at 1

The callback closes over the first render's count, so it sets 0 + 1 forever. Adding count to the dependency array "fixes" it by tearing down and recreating the interval every second, which drifts.

The follow-up answer is a hook that keeps the interval stable and the callback fresh:

function useInterval(callback, delay) {
  const saved = useRef(callback);

  // Always point at the latest callback, without restarting the timer.
  useEffect(() => {
    saved.current = callback;
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (delay === null) return; // null pauses the interval
    const id = setInterval(() => saved.current(), delay);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [delay]);
}

// Usage
useInterval(() => setCount((c) => c + 1), running ? 1000 : null);

Explaining why the first version gets stuck (closures capture a render's values) is worth more than the fix itself.

The pattern

Look at what the follow-ups have in common:

  • Lifecycle: cancel, flush, cleanup, abort.
  • Edge cases: empty input, plain values, order, new.
  • Cost: memory that grows forever, intervals that restart every tick.

When you practise, don't stop at "it works". Ask yourself the next question an interviewer would ask, and make your code answer it.

Practise these with real tests

I built UIRound around this idea: the first answer gets you started, the follow-up gets you the offer. Every question there runs in a browser editor against real tests, and each answer walks through the follow-ups interviewers ask next.

All seven questions above are free to solve there, with tests:

  1. Debounce with cancel and flush
  2. Predict the event loop order
  3. Promise.all from scratch
  4. mapLimit with a maximum of N at once
  5. Memoize with custom cache keys
  6. Function.prototype.bind with partial application
  7. useInterval without stale closures

Which follow-up has caught you out in an interview? Tell me in the comments and I'll write up the best answer.

title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
description:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.

title: Why A 14-Year Microsoft AI Vet Just Walked Away
description:
I read a post last week that hit differently than most industry news. It wasn't about a new model release or another funding round. A senior researcher who helped build one of Microsoft's core AI labs was leaving — and saying why out loud.
John Langford spent over 14 years at Microsoft. He co-founded the AI Frontiers lab. His work on contextual bandits fundamentally changed how we think about learning from incomplete feedback. Offline policy estimation, exploration strategies, problem reduction theory — these are the things people still cite today.
And now he's gone. Not for a competing job at Google or OpenAI. Not for a startup. He simply said the work had nowhere to go.
His 50-person team was absorbed into Mustafa Suleyman's consolidated AI division this September. The merger made organizational sense on paper. But according to reports, the research direction and the paths to actually ship ideas diverged sharply from leadership priorities.
Langford didn't pretend otherwise. He acknowledged that scaling models works. Bigger architectures, more data, better performance curves — the empirical trajectory is clear. Companies love it because the ROI path is predictable. You feed it GPU hours and you get results.
But treating scale as the default answer quietly kills other lines of inquiry. It doesn't announce itself with fanfare. It just starves everything else slowly, methodically.
Here's the uncomfortable part I've thought about since reading his departure note: most of us benefit from this system right now. We ride the compute wave. Our benchmarks look good. We publish papers about marginal improvements on established architectures. We get promoted.
The people who might have asked different questions — the ones worth asking — are the ones getting filtered out. Not dramatically. Nobody fires them. Their projects just never get greenlit. They watch their teams reassigned. Then one day they resign.
Langford's background makes this more pointed than usual. Contextual bandits were never about brute force. They were about smart decision-making under uncertainty with minimal information. That philosophy — efficiency through intelligence rather than scale through volume — is exactly what gets crowded out when the metric becomes parameter count.
I'm not romanticizing this. Corporate priorities exist. Shareholders don't fund pure research forever. Some of my best shipping has also come from riding trends others dismissed as noise.
But I also know what happens when you spend five years optimizing toward the same objective function. You stop noticing which questions became untellable. The field narrows. The safe bets multiply. And the people who noticed first just leave.
What's your team doing with the research ideas that don't fit the current roadmap? The ones that would require different measurements, different timelines, maybe even different kinds of failure?
