title: Catch a stale opening caption with a small SRT test in Python
description:
The opening of a caption tutorial shows “glaze,” and so does the final playback. At least that’s what you want. If the ending still says “glass” after you fixed the opening, a quick search for “glaze” won’t catch it. And “glass” belongs in the middle of the file, where you demonstrate the original error.

Give the check two ranges, one for the opening and one for the ending. Ask for the corrected cue exactly once in each. Leave the demonstration outside both ranges so you can change that part of the tutorial without breaking the check.

Disclosure: AI assisted the drafting of this tutorial. The included script and fixture were run locally.

Set up the fixture

Use a plain UTF-8 SRT export. The following example is a small local fixture, independent of a video project. Save it as sample.srt.

1
00:00:00,300 --> 00:00:01,900
Glaze.

2
00:00:03,200 --> 00:00:05,100
Start with the raw clip.

3
00:00:19,200 --> 00:00:20,600
Glass.

4
00:00:42,400 --> 00:00:44,100
Glaze.

In this fixture the opening copy is entirely inside the first two seconds. The final segment starts at 42 seconds. Those are test values. On an actual job, use the times of the cut you are handing off. A source timecode from the raw recording will miss the shifted edit.

Compare the text inside the correct windows

This script is dependency-free and runs on Python 3.9 or newer. It uses ordinary SRT numbering, blank lines, and comma-separated timestamps. It reads a UTF-8 BOM and supports multiple text lines within a cue. The expected phrase is compared to the whole cue after normalizing case and punctuation, so a caption containing additional words will fail the test. That choice is useful for a one-line fixture and may be too strict for a longer subtitle.

import argparse
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path
import re
import sys

TIMESTAMP = r"[0-9]{2,}:[0-5][0-9]:[0-5][0-9],[0-9]{3}"
CUE_TIMES = re.compile(rf"({TIMESTAMP})\s+-->\s+({TIMESTAMP})")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Cue:
    start: int
    end: int
    text: str


def milliseconds(timestamp):
    hrs, mins, secs, ms = map(int, re.split(r"[:,]", timestamp))
    return ((hrs * 60 + mins) * 60 + secs) * 1000 + ms


def read_cues(path):
    text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig").strip()
    if not text:
        raise ValueError("empty subtitle file")

    cues = []
    for block in re.split(r"\n[ \t]*\n+", text):
        lines = block.splitlines()
        if len(lines) < 3 or not lines[0].strip().isdecimal():
            raise ValueError("expected cue number, time range and text")
        match = CUE_TIMES.fullmatch(lines[1].strip())
        if match is None:
            raise ValueError(f"invalid time range for cue {lines[0]}")
        start, end = map(milliseconds, match.groups())
        if end <= start:
            raise ValueError(f"nonpositive duration for cue {lines[0]}")
        cues.append(Cue(start, end, " ".join(lines[2:])))
    return cues


def normalized(line):
    return " ".join(re.findall(r"[\w']+", line.casefold()))


def review(cues, expected, opening_end, closing_start):
    expected = normalized(expected)
    if not expected:
        raise ValueError("expected text must contain words")
    if not 0 < opening_end < closing_start:
        raise ValueError("use nonoverlapping opening and closing ranges")

    opening = [cue for cue in cues if 0 <= cue.start < cue.end <= opening_end]
    closing = [cue for cue in cues if closing_start <= cue.start]
    for label, candidates in (("opening", opening), ("closing", closing)):
        exact = [cue for cue in candidates if normalized(cue.text) == expected]
        if len(exact) != 1:
            print(f"CHECK {label}: {len(exact)} exact matches for '{expected}'")
            return False
    print(f"PASS opening and closing each contain one cue for '{expected}'")
    return True


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("srt", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("expected")
    parser.add_argument("--opening-end", type=int, required=True, help="milliseconds")
    parser.add_argument("--closing-start", type=int, required=True, help="milliseconds")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        ok = review(read_cues(args.srt), args.expected, args.opening_end, args.closing_start)
    except (OSError, ValueError) as exc:
        print(f"ERROR {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    return 0 if ok else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Run a passing and a failing example 

python check_cues.py sample.srt "Glaze" --opening-end 2000 --closing-start 42000

The fixture prints:

PASS opening and closing each contain one cue for 'glaze'

Now duplicate the file as stale.srt and change only the last cue text to “Glass.” Repeat the command with stale.srt. It reports CHECK closing: 0 exact matches for 'glaze' and exits with code 1. The earlier wrong caption in the tutorial remains outside the checked ranges, so it never affects either test. A malformed cue exits with code 2. In a build script those codes can distinguish an expected review failure from a fixture that needs repair.

Check the export as well

After the script passes, open the actual export. It can still have the wrong SRT attached, the line can come in early, or the playback controls can cover the word. Play the opening and the end from the rendered media and listen across both boundaries. At phone size, inspect the lower area for any collision between sample captions, a tutorial label and the video player.

Some projects intentionally split the phrase across two cues. In that case set the expected text for each opening and closing cue or define a richer rule for adjacent cues. Avoid running a global substring search to compensate. It would hide the stale-copy failure this check exists to catch.

title: Tenant-Isolated Image Uploads: Choosing an Audit-Safe Storage Boundary for Logistics
description:
For a logistics system that must keep the original receipt image, the hard choice is not how to upload bytes. It is who can ever address those bytes. Put each tenant behind a bucket or an equally strict key namespace, keep the original immutable by policy, and choose the storage API that lets the rest of your backend use the same operational contract. A plain REST upload is enough for the write; the isolation model is what deserves the design time.

The short decision matrix

Option Best fit Tenant-isolation shape Important boundary
Amazon S3 Teams already standardized on AWS IAM and S3 tooling IAM, bucket policy, account and prefix controls Many controls are powerful, so the policy surface needs discipline
Cloudflare R2 Teams serving objects near Cloudflare workloads Bucket and application-level authorization Public delivery and edge behavior still need a separate access design
Google Cloud Storage Teams operating primarily in Google Cloud IAM, project, bucket, and object-prefix controls A multi-cloud storage abstraction can hide provider-specific behavior
Infrai storage A backend that wants one key and one REST API across several capabilities Application-selected bucket and key boundaries No public ACL, versioning, object lock, or conditional If-Match write

For a new receipt pipeline, use a private bucket boundary per tenant when the tenant count is manageable. At larger scale, use a carefully generated tenant prefix, but make the authorization service the only component allowed to turn a receipt ID into a key. The upload client should never choose an arbitrary bucket or path.

The boring part is the point.

The practical reason to consider the unified REST option here is breadth behind a small surface: storage can sit behind the same REST contract as other backend capabilities, so adding another capability does not require another SDK, credential family, and integration shape. One key can cover the broader platform, and the calls remain ordinary HTTP, so a Node.js service does not need another SDK just to persist a file. The platform currently exposes 295 routes across 20 modules. That helps a small engineering team. It does not remove the need to design isolation.

What should the upload boundary guarantee?

Receipts are audit material, not disposable thumbnails. The system should preserve the original bytes, derive the object key from trusted tenant and receipt identifiers, and record enough application metadata to find the receipt in the database. The object store is the byte vault. It is not the source of truth for authorization.

I use a key such as tenants/{tenantId}/receipts/{receiptId}/original.png. The tenant ID comes from the authenticated request context. The receipt ID comes from a database record. Neither comes from a browser-provided path. That small distinction prevents a surprisingly large class of cross-tenant mistakes.

Keep the original extension only when the detected content type agrees with it. Store the content type alongside the database record, and hash the received bytes before or during persistence if audit verification needs it. Do not treat a successful HTTP response as proof that the right tenant owns the object; that check belongs in your service.

There is a sharp caveat for any audit claim here. Storage without object versioning or object lock cannot provide WORM-style immutability by itself. An overwrite can be unrecoverable. If a regulator requires tamper-resistant retention, add an external retention design or choose a provider and configuration that explicitly meets that requirement.

How do you upload the original image in Node.js?

The write is deliberately boring. The route takes a bucket and key, and the request body is the binary image data. This example assumes an image has already been generated or downloaded into a Buffer; it shows the storage boundary rather than inventing an image-generation endpoint.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const storageBaseUrl = process.env.STORAGE_API_BASE_URL;
if (!apiKey || !storageBaseUrl) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and STORAGE_API_BASE_URL are required");
}

type UploadInput = {
  bucket: string;
  tenantId: string;
  receiptId: string;
  image: Buffer;
  contentType: string;
};

async function putReceiptImage(input: UploadInput): Promise<string> {
  const key = `tenants/${encodeURIComponent(input.tenantId)}/receipts/${encodeURIComponent(input.receiptId)}/original`;
  const path = ["/v1", "storage", "object", "put", encodeURIComponent(input.bucket), key].join("/");
  const url = `${storageBaseUrl}${path}`;
  const idempotencyKey = `receipt-original-${input.tenantId}-${input.receiptId}`;

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "PUT",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": input.contentType,
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: input.image,
    });

    if (response.ok) return await response.text();

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
      continue;
    }

    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Object upload failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  throw new Error("Object upload failed after retries");
}

const original = await readFile("./generated-receipt.png");
await putReceiptImage({
  bucket: "logistics-receipts",
  tenantId: "tenant-42",
  receiptId: "receipt-2026-00107",
  image: original,
  contentType: "image/png",
});

Node.js supplies Buffer as binary request data, so there is no base64 expansion in this path. The explicit method matters. The stable idempotency key matters more: if a transient 429 causes a retry, the operation has a client-selected identity instead of becoming two logically separate writes. The key must be derived from a receipt operation, not from a random value generated on every attempt. A retry after a timeout is the awkward case: the client may not know whether the first write reached the service, while a fresh random key would make the second attempt look like a new receipt. Deriving the key from tenant and receipt identity keeps the retry tied to the same business operation, and the database record can reject a different tenant before this function is ever called. That is the kind of glue worth keeping because it protects the audit record; generic upload wrappers that hide the key decision are not.

Keep authorization outside the upload helper.

The sample uses a private server-side call. Do not move this credential into browser code. Browser uploads also require a CORS configuration, and this storage capability does not expose an independent route for setting CORS rules. A direct browser-to-store workflow therefore needs an approved external CORS and authorization design; the server upload is the safer default for receipts.

Where do the alternatives fit better?

S3 is the stronger choice when the company already has AWS identity policies, bucket tooling, replication expectations, and compliance processes. Its ecosystem is the feature. The cost is surface area: a team must understand how identity policy, bucket policy, object ownership, and application keys combine. For a receipt system, that complexity can be justified when the surrounding AWS controls are already mature.

R2 is attractive when the object workload belongs close to Cloudflare’s network and the team wants an S3-compatible storage model. It is a sensible runner-up for an edge-heavy application. I would still make tenant authorization an application concern and verify the exact delivery and retention behavior needed for private audit files before choosing it.

Google Cloud Storage fits a Google Cloud estate with IAM, project boundaries, and existing operational ownership. It is a poor fit for a team that wants one vendor-neutral abstraction while also depending on provider-specific retention or replication semantics. Those details do not disappear because the client library is pleasant.

The one-contract option fits when time-to-first-call and integration count dominate. Its storage coverage includes S3, R2, OSS, and COS vendors, but not GCS or B2. There is no public or public-read ACL, no permanent public URL, no object versioning, no object lock, and no conditional If-Match write. That rules it out for a static website host, a public image CDN, WORM financial retention, or strict optimistic-concurrency updates without a queue or database coordinator.

Other limits are concrete. Lifecycle expiration bottoms out at one day, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and object metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix listing. Cross-region automatic replication and cross-cloud bulk migration are absent. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes. These are selection criteria, not footnotes.

The decision I would ship

Choose the unified REST storage boundary when the receipt workflow is private, server-mediated, and already shares a backend with other capabilities. Use a tenant-derived key, a database record for authorization, an idempotency key for retries, and an external retention strategy if the audit requirement is truly immutable.

Choose S3, R2, or Google Cloud Storage instead when its surrounding identity, replication, retention, or delivery controls are the actual product requirement. A small upload function cannot compensate for a missing storage primitive.

The upload is one PUT. The architecture is the part that decides whether that byte belongs to the right tenant five years later.

Sources

  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: Building a headless ERP: one codebase, a database per client
description:
The easiest way to see what I am talking about is to click around a live store.

https://demo-ecommerce.rivil.app/en

It is an Astro storefront on our shop API. The brand, Casa Lumen, is a demo. You can browse the catalog, add items to the cart, use the wishlist, and go through checkout without creating an account. On the account page there is a prepared demo login if you do not want to register.

I am Paul. I build RIVIL (https://rivil.app) with a small team in Romania. I do the engineering. This is a write-up of how the product took its shape, and of the architectural choice I still think about the most: one codebase, and a database per client.

It did not start as an ERP.

A colleague made very good reports in Google Sheets and had no clean way to send them to clients. That is a small problem when you write it down, and a large one when it is the weekly rhythm of the business. I moved our existing clients onto a CRM so those reports could be produced and shared from one place.

The CRM grew in the direction the work was already going. We added a WordPress tracking plugin, with attribution paths, so we could see how a lead had actually arrived. Then we integrated with the old systems those clients were already running. I will not name the products. What matters is what the integrations exposed: the same gaps, again and again, in systems that had been forked, patched, and then left behind.

That is why I built the ERP, on the same design as the CRM, and why I made it API-first. If the data and the workflows already live in one backend, a website, a mobile app, or a store should be able to use them. They should not be a second product with a second database and a second idea of what a customer or an order is.

The architecture, said simply, is this. The real infrastructure is more complex, but the rule is not:

There is one codebase.
Features are split into modules and enabled per client.
Each client has their own database.
We add features to the shared codebase instead of maintaining a rewritten fork for every install. With a traditional ERP, 100 clients often means 100 codebases. Those copies barely get updated, because every upgrade is a custom project. I did not want to run the company that way. If we improve checkout, or stock handling, or the way a storefront reads the catalog, that work should be able to reach the clients who are already on the system, not only the next deal.

A separate database per client is the trade I chose in the other direction. It is more operational work than a single shared tenant table with a client_id column. Migrations have to be applied many times, not once. I still prefer it. Client data stays isolated by default. A heavy client does not sit on a neighbour's row lock. When something goes wrong, you are looking at one tenant's database, not a shared pile. Modules stay in the same codebase; turning one on for a client is a configuration choice, not a new branch that slowly diverges.

The shop API is one surface of that backend. The public shape is a versioned HTTP API under a per-store Bearer key. In outline:

Base: https://erp.rivil.app/api/shop/v1/
Catalog: GET /products
Cart: POST /carts, then lines and discounts on /carts/{token}
Checkout: POST /carts/{token}/checkout, which creates the order in the ERP and decrements stock
The Astro app does not call that API from the browser as a raw third-party client. It uses same-origin routes, /api/cart, /api/search, and /api/wishlist, in front of it. Checkout is described as idempotent, so a retried request should not create a second order. We also describe signed webhooks for changes. Documentation is available on request, or to partners. It is not on a public docs host today, on purpose.

I care about the storefront being fast enough that the API work is not wasted. I ran PageSpeed Insights on the homepage and got 92 on mobile and 99 on desktop. I also timed the cart API with TLS already up, from a machine that is not in Romania, without placing an order. Median GET /api/cart was 131ms. Median POST to add a line was 201ms. Median GET /api/search was 168ms. Those numbers include the network, not just application time.

I am not claiming this is the only way to build an ERP, or that multi-tenant-with-one-database is wrong. I am saying this is the model I could stand behind after watching forked installs go stale. The demo is there so you can judge the storefront and the API shape yourself, not so I can tell you it is fast.

If you have a minute with it, the feedback I would like is specific. If you were wiring your own frontend to this API, what is missing or badly named? If you have operated a single codebase with a database per customer, what broke first for you: migrations, module boundaries, reporting, or something I have not hit yet? And if you go through the cart or the account flow, what feels awkward?

The demo is here:

https://demo-ecommerce.rivil.app/en

More context on the headless side is here:

https://rivil.app/en/headless/ecommerce

Thanks for reading.

title: I Built a Free English Dictionary API Using Wiktionary Data extract
description:
I wanted to build something useful for developers: a free English dictionary API that anyone could integrate into their applications without worrying about API keys, registration, or complicated onboarding.

That idea eventually turned into my Free Dictionary API.

🔗 Try it: https://api.suvankar.cc/docs/dictionary

In this article, I'll share what I built, where the dictionary data comes from, the technology behind it, and some of the engineering challenges I encountered along the way.

Why build another dictionary API?

There are already several dictionary APIs available. However, I wanted to build something that was:

  • Free to use.
  • Accessible without an API key.
  • Easy to integrate into applications.
  • Based on a comprehensive, openly available dictionary dataset.
  • Simple enough for developers to experiment with.

I also wanted to learn more about processing large dictionary datasets and building a public-facing API that could serve real-world applications.

Rather than starting with manually curated dictionary entries, I decided to explore Wiktionary.

The data: Wiktionary

The foundation of this project is data derived from Wiktionary, the collaborative, multilingual dictionary project.

I used structured Wiktionary data available through Kaikki.org, which makes Wiktionary content available in machine-readable formats.

This was particularly interesting because dictionary entries contain much more than just a word and its definition.

An entry can include information such as:

  • Definitions and senses.
  • Parts of speech.
  • Pronunciations.
  • Etymology.
  • Examples of usage.
  • Translations.
  • Grammatical information.

Processing this information into a structure that could be efficiently queried through a REST API was one of the interesting parts of the project.

Designing the database

One of the first challenges was deciding how to represent dictionary data in a relational database.

A dictionary entry isn't necessarily a simple one-to-one relationship between a word and a definition.

A single word can have multiple meanings, different parts of speech, examples, translations, and additional metadata.

I use PostgreSQL as the primary database and a relational structure to represent these relationships.

The objective was to keep the data structured while making common dictionary lookups efficient.

The data ingestion and processing pipeline is maintained separately from the API repository. The repository linked below contains the API application itself.

Building the API

I used Java 21 and Spring Boot 3 to build the REST API.

The API exposes dictionary information through straightforward HTTP endpoints that return structured JSON responses.

Some of its current capabilities include:

  • Looking up English word definitions.
  • Searching for words by prefix.
  • Retrieving translations.
  • Accessing Word of the Day.

For example, retrieving a definition is as simple as:

curl "https://api.suvankar.cc/dictionaryapi/v1/definitions/en/happy?compact=true"

You can also search for words:

curl "https://api.suvankar.cc/dictionaryapi/v1/words/en/?filter=happ&page=0&size=5"

And retrieve translations:

curl "https://api.suvankar.cc/dictionaryapi/v1/translations/en/?word=secure&pos=verb"

The API returns JSON that can be consumed by web applications, mobile applications, scripts, or other backend services.

You can explore the available endpoints and response structures in the interactive documentation:

https://api.suvankar.cc/docs/dictionary

Some engineering decisions

Building the endpoints was only one part of the project. Making them efficient and suitable for public consumption required additional infrastructure.

Here's a look at some of the technologies involved.

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL stores the structured dictionary data.

Given the relationships between words, senses, definitions, examples, and translations, a relational database was a natural choice.

Redis

I introduced Redis caching to avoid repeatedly querying PostgreSQL for frequently requested dictionary entries.

Dictionary lookups are particularly suitable for caching because the underlying data doesn't change with every request.

Rate limiting

Since the API is publicly accessible without API keys, I also needed a way to protect the service from excessive request volumes.

I implemented rate limiting using Bucket4j.

The idea is to keep the service accessible while protecting the underlying infrastructure from excessive traffic.

Docker

The application is containerised using Docker, making deployment and environment management easier.

Making it accessible without API keys

One decision I deliberately made was not to require API keys.

I wanted developers to be able to open the documentation, make their first request, and get a response immediately.

No registration forms, no API key generation, and no complicated setup.

Of course, public access doesn't mean unlimited resources. The API has rate limits to help maintain service availability.

What can you build with it?

There are plenty of possible applications for a dictionary API.

For example:

  • English dictionary applications.
  • Vocabulary learning tools.
  • Word-of-the-day applications.
  • Language learning platforms.
  • Browser extensions for instant word lookup.
  • Writing assistants.
  • Educational applications.

I'm also building an Android dictionary application called Lexicall, which is one of the projects that makes this API particularly interesting to me.

Building an actual client application has helped me think beyond simply returning JSON responses. API usability, response structures, search performance, and caching all become much more important when there's a real application consuming the service.

What's next?

This is an ongoing project, and there's still plenty I'd like to improve.

Some areas I'm interested in exploring further include:

  • Improving dictionary data coverage.
  • Optimising search and database queries.
  • Expanding language and translation support.
  • Improving caching and API performance.
  • Making the documentation and developer experience better.

I'd also love to hear how other developers use the API and what features they would find useful.

Try the API

If you're building something that needs English dictionary data, feel free to give it a try.

API Documentation: https://api.suvankar.cc/docs/dictionary

Source Code: https://github.com/suvankar-mitra/free-dictionary-rest-api

No API key required. Just make a request and start building.

The API code is open source under the Apache License 2.0. The dictionary data is sourced from Wiktionary and licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. Please refer to the repository for licensing and attribution details.

If you have feedback, suggestions, or ideas for improvement, I'd genuinely love to hear them.

Thanks for reading!

title: Migrating a Backbone.js app to React without a rewrite: Web Components as the bridge
description:
How I moved a Backbone.js and Marionette product toward React micro-frontends one screen at a time, using Web Components as the boundary both worlds understand.

At Thynk Web I worked on App Studio, a product built on Backbone.js, Marionette and jQuery. I led its migration toward React micro-frontends. The constraint that shaped everything: the product had to keep working, and keep shipping features, the whole time. A big-bang rewrite was never on the table. This post is about the approach — and why Web Components turned out to be the right bridge.

Why not rewrite

Rewrites look clean on a whiteboard and go badly in practice. The old app keeps changing while you rebuild it, behaviour that nobody documented gets lost, and for months you ship nothing users can see. The alternative is an incremental, strangler-style migration: new code grows around the old system, one piece at a time, until the old piece can be removed.

The hard question with incremental migration is the boundary. How does a Marionette view host a React component, pass it data and hear back from it, without either side knowing the other's internals?

Web Components: a boundary both sides speak

A Custom Element is just an HTML tag. Backbone and Marionette already know how to render HTML and listen to DOM events. React knows how to render into any DOM node. So a custom element that mounts a React tree inside itself gives you a contract both worlds understand natively:

  • Inputs go in as attributes or properties.
  • Outputs come out as DOM CustomEvents.
  • Lifecycle is handled by the browser through connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback. 
// define-react-element.tsx
import { createRoot, type Root } from 'react-dom/client';
import type { ComponentType } from 'react';

export function defineReactElement<P extends object>(tag: string, Component: ComponentType<P>) {
  class ReactElement extends HTMLElement {
    private root?: Root;
    private props = {} as P;

    set data(value: P) {      // rich inputs as a property
      this.props = value;
      this.render();
    }
    connectedCallback() {
      this.root = createRoot(this);
      this.render();
    }
    disconnectedCallback() {
      this.root?.unmount();   // no leaked React trees when Marionette tears down
    }
    private render() {
      this.root?.render(<Component {...this.props} emit={this.emit} />);
    }
    private emit = (type: string, detail?: unknown) =>
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(type, { detail, bubbles: true }));
  }
  if (!customElements.get(tag)) customElements.define(tag, ReactElement);
}

On the Backbone side, the new screen is just markup and an event listener:

// stage-view.js
const StageView = Marionette.View.extend({
  template: () => '<app-stage-editor></app-stage-editor>',
  events: { 'stage:save app-stage-editor': 'onSave' },
  onRender() {
    this.$('app-stage-editor')[0].data = { stage: this.model.toJSON() };
  },
  onSave(e) {
    this.model.save(e.originalEvent.detail);
  },
});

The Marionette view doesn't know React exists. The React component doesn't know Backbone exists. That's the point.

Tip: Pass objects through a property, not an attribute. Attributes are strings; serialising models into them is slow and loses types.

Migrating screen by screen

With the bridge in place, the order of work becomes a product decision instead of a technical one. Pick a screen, rebuild it in React behind a custom element, swap the tag in, and remove the old view once it's stable. Old and new code live side by side in the same build (we used Webpack) while the migration progresses.

A few rules kept this safe:

  1. Keep the model as the source of truth during the transition. The React component receives data and emits intentions; the existing model layer still saves.
  2. Make the contract small. One data property and a handful of named events per element. If a component needs ten inputs, the boundary is in the wrong place.
  3. Clean up on disconnect. Marionette re-renders and destroys views often. Unmounting the React root in disconnectedCallback prevents memory leaks and ghost listeners.

Warning: Watch styling leaks in both directions. Global legacy CSS will reach into your React markup unless you scope it, and new component styles can break old screens. Decide early whether to use Shadow DOM or a scoping convention.

Not just migration: fixing what was there

Migration work forces you to read the old code closely, and that surfaces bugs. On App Studio I resolved 90% of the API Builder bugs and did performance work on metadata and stage logic. I also shipped 5+ enhancements while the migration was ongoing — stage duplication, copy-paste, actions, rules and automation — which is the real argument for incremental migration: users kept getting improvements instead of waiting for a rewrite.

Components were built from Figma designs, and I documented the approach in Confluence so the rest of the team could build new screens the same way.

What I'd keep doing

  • Choose the boundary before the framework. The custom-element contract mattered more than any React pattern inside it.
  • Ship value during the migration. Features and bug fixes alongside the rewrite keep the business on board.
  • Write it down. A migration is a team effort over months; a short, clear guide is what makes the tenth migrated screen look like the first.

Web Components are often pitched as a way to build design systems. Their quieter superpower is being the one interface every framework — including a long-lived Backbone app — already agrees on.

Originally published at sumankumarkhan.com.

title: Building a Sticky Mobile Call Bar for a Law Firm Website
description:
Most visitors to a criminal defense website arrive on a phone, and many of them want to call rather than read. A sticky call bar, a strip pinned to the bottom of the screen with a tap-to-call button, is one of the most common patterns on law firm sites for that reason. It is also one of the most commonly broken. Bars cover footer links, collide with chat widgets, sit under the iPhone home indicator or hide the last line of every page.

This post walks through building one that behaves well: correct on notched phones, accessible, easy to measure and out of the way of the content. The examples use plain HTML and CSS with a few lines of JavaScript, so they port to any CMS or framework.

Start with the markup

Keep the bar simple. One primary action, the phone call, and at most one secondary action, such as a link to the contact form. Two buttons fit comfortably on small screens. Three usually do not.

Use a real tel: link with the number in international format, and put the human-readable number in the visible text. Screen reader users and people who distrust buttons both benefit from seeing the actual number. Wrap the bar in a landmark element with a label so assistive technology can identify it.

Handle the safe area on notched phones

On phones with a home indicator, content at the very bottom of the viewport can sit underneath it. CSS environment variables solve this, but only if the viewport meta tag opts in with viewport-fit=cover. Without that, env(safe-area-inset-bottom) returns zero and the bar may be partly covered.

.call-bar {
  position: fixed;
  inset: auto 0 0 0;
  display: flex;
  gap: 8px;
  padding: 10px 12px calc(10px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  background: #0c1a33;
  z-index: 50;
}
.call-bar a { flex: 1; min-height: 48px; display: grid; place-items: center; }
body.has-call-bar { padding-bottom: calc(72px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); }
@media (min-width: 900px) { .call-bar { display: none; } body.has-call-bar { padding-bottom: 0; } }

The body padding matters. Without it, the bar covers the last part of every page, which on a law firm site is often the footer with the disclaimer and office addresses. Match the padding to the bar's real height, and test with large text settings, since the bar grows when the user increases the font size.

Make the tap targets generous

WCAG 2.2 added a target size criterion at level AA that sets a minimum of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for most targets, with some exceptions. That is a floor. For the main call button on a defense site, aim much larger, around 44 to 48 pixels tall, since the person tapping it may be stressed, in a car or using one hand.

Check contrast too. A white phone number on a pale brand color may look fine in a design file and fail outdoors on a phone. Run the colors through a contrast checker and aim for at least the AA ratio for normal text.

Avoid collisions with other fixed elements

Law firm sites often load a chat widget, a cookie banner and sometimes an accessibility overlay, each of which wants the bottom corner of the screen. If your bar and a chat bubble overlap, users may tap the wrong one or neither.

Decide on a stacking order and stick to it. Common choices are to move the chat launcher above the bar with a bottom offset, or to fold chat into the bar as the secondary action. Hide the bar while the on-screen keyboard is open on form pages, since it can cover the field the user is typing in. Listening for focus on inputs and toggling a class works on most devices.

Show it only where it helps

A call bar on every page is the default, but it is worth reconsidering. On a long charge page, the bar keeps the number in reach. On the contact page, which already shows the number and a form, it adds clutter. On a printable page, such as courthouse directions, hide it in a print stylesheet.

Some sites reveal the bar only after the visitor scrolls past the first screen, so the hero section stays clean. That can work, but test it. A visitor who wants to call immediately should not have to scroll to find the number.

Content matters as much as code. The words on the button affect whether people tap it, and plain labels such as "Call now" next to the actual number tend to be clearer than vague promises. This article on writing the words around the call button on a defense site covers the copy side.

Measure taps without breaking calls

Track taps on the call link as an event in your analytics tool. Attach the listener to the link and do not prevent the default action, so the dialer still opens if the analytics script is slow or blocked. Record which page the tap came from, since that is the data the marketing side will ask for.

Remember that a tap is not a call. Some users tap and hang up before connecting. If the firm uses a call tracking service, compare tap events with connected calls by page every month to see how far the numbers drift apart.

Test on real devices

Emulators catch layout problems, but they miss the details that matter here: the home indicator, the dynamic toolbar in mobile browsers that changes the viewport height while scrolling, and how the bar behaves when the keyboard opens. Test on at least one recent iPhone and one Android phone, held upright and turned sideways, with the system font size turned up.

For more on design for defense firm websites, the law firm website design guides cover layout, typography and mobile patterns.

Questions about sticky call bars

Does a sticky call bar hurt SEO?

A small bar that does not cover the main content is generally fine. Avoid anything that hides most of the screen on page load, since intrusive overlays can create a poor experience on mobile.

Should the bar show on desktop?

Usually not. Desktop visitors rarely place calls from the browser, and a header with the phone number serves them better.

Can the bar include a text message option?

Yes, with an sms: link, if the firm actually monitors that number. Make sure someone replies quickly and that texting fits the firm's intake rules.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one per city. It designs and builds websites for defense practices, handles SEO for the charges they defend, runs SEO audits and works on visibility in AI search tools.

title: How AIClaw 3.11.1 Routes Audio Without Assuming Every Model Can Hear
description:
Audio attachments look simple at the interface: attach a clip and ask a question. The routing decision behind that interaction is less simple. A model endpoint may accept text while rejecting audio, and even an audio-capable endpoint may expose a different wire format.

AIClaw 3.11.1 makes that decision from the selected model’s declared capability and service protocol. When native audio is unavailable or unknown, it uses the configured speech-to-text route instead of silently sending audio bytes to a text-only request.

The routing decision

The audio preparation code enables native input only when AudioInput is explicitly marked supported and the selected protocol is Chat Completions or Gemini. WAV and MP3 attachments can follow this path; other formats go through the transcription fallback.

That is a deliberately narrow claim. A provider being compatible with a protocol does not establish that every model or endpoint accepts audio. The capability setting needs to match the actual service. Responses and other protocols are not treated as native audio routes by this version of the code.

For native input, the protocol adapters format the same audio differently:

  • Chat Completions sends an input_audio content part with a format and base64 data.
  • Gemini sends inline data with the appropriate audio MIME type.

When a route is not explicitly capable, AIClaw prepares a transcription instead. That depends on a working configured transcription service; it is not a guarantee that any arbitrary attachment will be understood.

Keep the request bounded

Native audio is subject to an 8 MiB limit per file and a 180-second request budget. For WAV files, the implementation estimates duration from the data size and byte rate. When it cannot determine duration, it conservatively charges the entire budget. This also matters for MP3 in this implementation: compressed file size is not used as a duration estimate.

When conversation history is assembled for another model call, the code walks from the newest messages backward and includes clips within the duration budget. Missing files and clips outside the budget are represented by an omission note rather than silently treated as audio the model received. A stored SHA-256 is also checked before reuse when present, so a changed local file is not silently substituted for the original attachment.

A rejection is evidence, not a reason to replay

If a service returns one of the recognized audio-specific HTTP 400 codes, the agent records a rejection against the model route only when the request contained exactly one clip. With multiple clips, the response cannot identify which clip caused the failure, so the code does not attribute it to one of them. The corresponding agent tests cover duration and fallback behavior, durable rejection, and the no-retry path. The adapter tests cover native wire formats and unsupported protocols.

Those are repository tests, not evidence that every provider has been exercised with live audio. In particular, the rejection tracking described here applies to later requests; it should not be read as an automatic replay of the failed request.

The result is a clearer boundary between capability configuration, protocol serialization, and the evidence the agent actually has. It is a small architectural distinction, but it prevents an attachment UI from promising more than the selected model route can deliver.

title: Accept crypto payments in Next.js
description:
A Moonvex integration for Next.js (App Router): a server Route Handler creates a checkout and redirects to it, the customer picks the coin and network there, and a second Route Handler receives the webhook, verifies the signature and marks the order paid.

Step by step

1. Get an API key and a webhook secret

In the Moonvex dashboard go to “Integration” → “Create key” → type “Secret” (sk_live_…). The key is shown only once: store it on your server as MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY. On the same page add a webhook pointing to an https URL on your server and store its signing secret as MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET. In Next.js never prefix these names with NEXT_PUBLIC_, or the key ends up in the browser.

npm install @moonvex/node pg

# .env — server only, never commit it
MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...
MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/shop

2. Create a checkout in a Route Handler

The POST handler in app/orders/[id]/pay/route.ts loads the order from the database and calls moonvex.checkouts.create without a network: the customer picks the coin and network on the Moonvex page. description is shown as “You are paying for”, returnUrl (https only) is where the Back buttons lead. The API key stays on the server; the client component just submits a form with method="post".

// lib/moonvex.ts
import { Moonvex } from '@moonvex/node';

export const moonvex = new Moonvex({ apiKey: process.env.MOONVEX_SECRET_KEY! });

// app/orders/[id]/pay/route.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { moonvex } from '@/lib/moonvex';

export async function POST(_req: Request, { params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params;
  const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT id, total::text AS total FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [id]);
  const order = rows[0];
  if (!order) return new Response('not found', { status: 404 });

  const checkout = await moonvex.checkouts.create(
    {
      orderId: String(order.id),
      amount: order.total,
      currency: 'USD', // the customer picks the coin and network on the checkout page
      description: 'Order #' + order.id, // shown as “You are paying for”
      returnUrl: 'https://shop.example.com/orders/' + order.id, // the Back buttons
    },
    { idempotencyKey: 'order-' + order.id + '-1' },
  );
  // a method="post" form → 303 to the checkout page
  return NextResponse.redirect(checkout.paymentUrl, 303);
}

3. Send the customer to paymentUrl

paymentUrl is the Moonvex checkout page: the customer picks the coin and network, then sees the exact amount including the fee, the address, a QR code, the official token contract and a timer, with a status that updates by itself. Your description is shown as “You are paying for”, and the Back and “Back to the shop” buttons lead to returnUrl. If you know the customer's language, add ?lang=ru, ?lang=uk or ?lang=en to paymentUrl; otherwise the page picks the language itself. Open the page with a redirect or in a new tab; it cannot be embedded in an iframe. A customer returning to your site is not proof of payment: mark the order paid only from a webhook. NextResponse.redirect(url, 303) after the form opens the payment page.

4. Receive the webhook and verify the signature

Moonvex sends a POST with a Moonvex-Signature header: t=,v1=. The signature is a hex HMAC-SHA256 of the string “t.raw_body” keyed with the webhook secret. Compute it over the body bytes before parsing JSON, compare in constant time and reject events older than 5 minutes. For 24 hours after a secret rotation the header carries two v1 values; either one is valid. In a Route Handler read the body with await req.arrayBuffer(): those are the original bytes. Do not call req.json() before verifying. Set runtime = 'nodejs', since verifyWebhook relies on node:crypto.

// app/api/moonvex/webhook/route.ts
import { verifyWebhook, type Payment, type WebhookEvent } from '@moonvex/node';
import { markOrderPaidOnce } from '@/lib/orders';

export const runtime = 'nodejs'; // needs node:crypto, not Edge
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  // read the bytes as is, not req.json()
  const raw = Buffer.from(await req.arrayBuffer());
  let event: WebhookEvent<Payment>;
  try {
    event = verifyWebhook<Payment>(raw, req.headers.get('moonvex-signature'), process.env.MOONVEX_WEBHOOK_SECRET!);
  } catch {
    return new Response('bad signature', { status: 400 });
  }

  if (event.type === 'payment.confirmed' || event.type === 'payment.overpaid') {
    await markOrderPaidOnce(event.id, event.data.orderId!);
  }
  // payment.cancelled also arrives when the customer switches coins: do not cancel the order on it
  return new Response('ok');
}

5. Mark the order paid exactly once

A redelivered event keeps the same id, so store it in a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the order update: a duplicate then changes nothing. Fulfil on payment.confirmed and payment.overpaid, never on payment.detected. Events arrive for the payment the customer starts: data.id is its pay_… id and data.orderId is your order number. If the customer switches coins, the previous payment gets payment.cancelled: do not cancel the order on it while the checkout is open.

// lib/db.ts
import { Pool } from 'pg';

export const db = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

// lib/orders.ts
// CREATE TABLE processed_events (event_id text PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now());
import { db } from '@/lib/db';

export async function markOrderPaidOnce(eventId: string, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  const client = await db.connect();
  try {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    const fresh = await client.query(
      'INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING',
      [eventId],
    );
    if (fresh.rowCount === 1) {
      // first delivery of the event: fulfil the order
      await client.query(
        "UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid', paid_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND status <> 'paid'",
        [orderId],
      );
    }
    await client.query('COMMIT');
  } catch (err) {
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
    throw err;
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
}

6. Test the integration

Moonvex has no test network: everything runs on mainnets. The “Send test” button under “Integration” sends a webhook.test event, which is how you check the signature. Then pay a small invoice, for example 1 USDT on TRON: it is a regular payment and the money lands on your balance. The delivery log with response codes and a “Retry” button is on the same page.

Pitfalls

  • Create and use the key only in server code (Route Handlers, Server Actions). Any variable prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is shipped in the client bundle.
  • If middleware checks authentication, exclude /api/moonvex/webhook in its matcher, or Moonvex gets redirected to your login page.
  • The Edge runtime does not work for the webhook in this example: it needs node:crypto and pg. Keep runtime = 'nodejs'.
  • Do not cache the handler: dynamic = 'force-dynamic' and the POST method make sure every webhook reaches your code.
  • With next-intl or another i18n setup you know the locale: redirect to withLanguage(checkout.paymentUrl, locale) from @moonvex/node (ru, uk or en) so the checkout opens in the same language.
  • Need one fixed coin instead of the customer's choice? moonvex.payments.create with network (and asset when currency is USD), for example network: 'TRON', asset: 'USDT', still works. The checkout above is the recommended flow.

FAQ

Can I create the checkout in a Server Action?

Yes: call moonvex.checkouts.create inside a 'use server' function and redirect(checkout.paymentUrl) from next/navigation. The webhook still needs its own Route Handler.

Why is amount in the webhook higher than the order price?

The checkout returns your price as is in amount and currency. The payment the customer starts (data in webhooks) is in the chosen coin, and its amount is the total due including the Moonvex fee on top. Your price stays in pricing.amount, and what you receive on a full payment is in merchantAmount. Reconcile orders by orderId and pricing.amount.

Is there a test mode or a sandbox?

No, there is no test network: Moonvex runs on mainnets only. Check the signature with the “Send test” button (a webhook.test event) and the whole payment flow with a real payment of a small amount, for example 1 USDT on TRON.

Originally published at: moonvex.org/en/guides/nextjs

title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
description:
arXiv:2611.14781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
description:
arXiv:2611.15006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

title: Controlling Databricks Costs with Cluster Policies and Tagging
description:
Giving data scientists and engineers direct access to create clusters is the fastest way to turn a cloud budget into a smoking crater. Most platforms attempt to solve this with "process"—asking users to check a box or follow a naming convention—but manual governance in distributed systems is a fantasy that fails the moment a deadline approaches.

If you aren't using Databricks Cluster Policies to constrain the compute environment, you aren't managing costs; you are merely witnessing them.

The contenders

The choice here is between unrestricted cluster creation (the default state) and policy-based enforcement.

Unrestricted creation allows maximum flexibility, letting users pick any instance type, runtime version, or library configuration. In environments where "move fast" is the only directive, this leads to massive instances being spun up for trivial tasks and forgotten when the notebook session closes.

Cluster Policies, conversely, act as a schema for cluster creation. When a user creates a cluster via the UI or API, the policy acts as a gatekeeper. It can force specific configurations, hide dangerous options, or mandate tags. You are moving from a "please play nice" culture to a "the system prevents you from doing otherwise" architecture.


Photo by Nika Benedictova on Unsplash

Cost and resource constraints

At the level of the Spark driver and executor, cluster policy is your primary tool for enforcing resource limits. You can use the spark_conf attribute in a policy to force specific configurations or set absolute maximums for instance types.

Consider an illustrative scenario where you want to prevent users from accidentally selecting memory-optimized instances for a simple ETL job. You can define a policy that restricts the node_type_id to a specific list of general-purpose instances.

{
  "node_type_id": {
    "type": "fixed",
    "value": "Standard_DS3_v2"
  },
  "autotermination_minutes": {
    "type": "fixed",
    "value": 30
  }
}

By forcing the autotermination_minutes to 30, you ensure that even if a user forgets to shut down their cluster after a job runs, the platform terminates the compute automatically. This is a mechanism that operates at the cloud provider level (e.g., terminating the VM instances) rather than just pausing the Spark application.

Enforcing organizational accountability with tags

In regulated industries, knowing exactly which cost center or project owns a specific cluster isn't just about accounting; it's a security and audit requirement. Databricks policies allow you to force the inclusion of custom tags.

If you don't enforce tags via policy, they will be missing. It is that simple. By using the custom_tags attribute in a cluster policy, you can mandate that users provide a ProjectID or CostCenter before they are even allowed to click "Create Cluster."

{
  "custom_tags.ProjectID": {
    "type": "unlimited"
  },
  "custom_tags.Environment": {
    "type": "fixed",
    "value": "production"
  }
}

When a user attempts to create a cluster using this policy, the API will reject the request if the ProjectID tag is missing. This pushes the data quality of your billing logs to the point of origin, ensuring that cloud provider invoices are sliced by tag without needing a separate, error-prone manual reconciliation process.

Operational burden and failure modes

The primary failure mode of implementing cluster policies is "policy drift" or being overly restrictive. If you lock down the spark_version to a specific runtime that hits end-of-life, every cluster creation request will fail simultaneously.

Policies require maintenance. You must treat them as code. If you define your policies through the Databricks UI, you lose the ability to version control your governance strategy. I recommend managing these policies via Terraform using the databricks_cluster_policy resource. This allows you to peer-review changes to your infrastructure governance just like you would review a change to a PySpark transformation.

Another failure mode is the "permission trap." If you remove the canUse permission from a user or service principal, their existing automated jobs—if they rely on that policy—will fail to start during their next run. Always test policy updates in a staging workspace before applying them to a production environment.

Comparison Summary

Feature Unrestricted Policy-Enforced
Cost Control None Hard limits via instance type/autoterm
Billing Accuracy Relies on user input Mandatory tagging enforcement
Ops Burden Low initially Requires lifecycle management
User Experience High freedom Context-specific guardrails


Photo by Justin Morgan on Unsplash

How to measure it yourself

To see the impact of your policy, you don't need a massive cluster. You can observe the policy mechanism locally by simulating a request to the Databricks Clusters API.

  1. Create a policy in your workspace.
  2. Use the Databricks CLI or a Python script with the databricks-sdk to attempt to create a cluster that violates your policy. 
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.sdk.service import compute

w = WorkspaceClient()

# Attempt to create a cluster with a policy ID that forces a 30-min timeout
# and a specific node type.
try:
    w.clusters.create(
        cluster_name="test-policy-violation",
        spark_version="13.3.x-scala2.12",
        node_type_id="Standard_F4s_v2", # Assuming policy forbids this
        policy_id="<your-policy-id>",
        autotermination_minutes=120 # Assuming policy forbids this
    )
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Policy successfully blocked the request: {e}")

If the API returns a 400 Bad Request related to policy validation, your guardrails are working. If the cluster spins up, your policy is either not applied to your user or is too permissive.

What I'd pick, and why

I always default to mandatory policies. The argument that policies "slow down" developers is usually a symptom of poorly designed policies rather than the concept of policies itself.

If you design your policies to be "self-service" (e.g., a "Data Science" policy that allows slightly more memory but forces cost tags, and an "ETL" policy that is rigid and cheap), developers won't feel shackled. They will feel supported because they don't have to guess what configuration is "correct."

Avoid the temptation to create a "catch-all" policy. That leads to bloat and makes it impossible to update configurations without risking a workspace-wide outage. Instead, create a hierarchy of policies mapped to specific user personas or workloads.

The goal isn't to stop people from doing data work; it’s to ensure that when they do that work, the platform is configured to be reliable, auditable, and cost-efficient by default.

title: Before you automate RFQ emails, define what must never be guessed
description:
An AI workflow can help a distributor turn an incoming request into a structured draft. The useful starting point is an intake process that preserves evidence and sends uncertain cases to a reviewer.

Disclosure: Prepared by Verix Technology using AI tooling. The examples below are synthetic design examples, not customer results or a claim that Verix has deployed this exact distributor workflow.

Start with a draft-only boundary

Use one approved catalog and one output: a draft request record. Keep prices, substitutions, delivery promises, external messages and ERP writes outside the initial automation. “Please quote two P-100 units for next week” describes a request; it does not establish stock, compatibility or a delivery commitment.

Store the original item wording alongside any proposed SKU and quantity. An exact catalog identifier can be checked deterministically. A model-proposed match should have evidence from an approved source. A familiar-looking name is not proof that two parts are interchangeable.

Evaluate extraction and routing separately

A workflow can extract the quantity correctly and still fail by letting an ambiguous request bypass review. Define expected fields and the expected route for every test example before comparing models.

This small evaluator uses Python's standard library. It makes no network or AI calls:

def evaluate(cases):
    if not cases:
        return {"cases": 0, "field_exact_match_rate": None,
                "route_accuracy": None, "unsafe_auto_routes": 0}
    field_ok = route_ok = unsafe = 0
    for case in cases:
        expected, predicted = case["expected"], case["predicted"]
        field_ok += all(predicted.get(k) == expected.get(k)
                        for k in ("sku", "quantity"))
        route_ok += predicted.get("route") == expected.get("route")
        unsafe += (expected.get("route") == "review"
                   and predicted.get("route") != "review")
    n = len(cases)
    return {"cases": n, "field_exact_match_rate": field_ok / n,
            "route_accuracy": route_ok / n,
            "unsafe_auto_routes": unsafe}

For example:

cases = [{
    "expected": {"sku": None, "quantity": 3, "route": "review"},
    "predicted": {"sku": "P-100", "quantity": 3, "route": "draft"}
}]
print(evaluate(cases))
# cases=1, field_exact_match_rate=0.0,
# route_accuracy=0.0, unsafe_auto_routes=1

The invented request could be “Need three mystery pumps.” Guessing a SKU fails field matching; routing it to draft also fails the review boundary. This example is deliberately wrong. Its score is not a measurement of any model.

The checker assumes valid case objects and the routes draft and review. Add schema validation and reject unknown routes before using it in a real pipeline. It checks only SKU, quantity and routing; it does not validate price, units, authorization, attachments or delivery dates. A perfect score on a tiny synthetic set would not establish production accuracy.

Test the exceptions first

Include unknown parts, conflicting quantities, obsolete identifiers, unreadable attachments and requests containing instructions to skip approval. Treat request text as untrusted input, not authority to change the workflow. Keep a separate evaluation set that has not been used to tune the system.

Use data the business has permission to process. Do not upload customer emails or catalog documents to a public notebook or demo. Synthetic examples are useful for explaining logic; representative, lawfully usable examples are needed to evaluate business performance.

Define operational ownership

Start with read-only catalog permissions and draft-only outputs. Agree retention, access and deletion responsibilities. Avoid putting complete emails in logs. Add a review queue for provider timeouts, missing credentials and invalid output, then test rollback and handover.

Ask an implementation partner to show the input, expected output, failure route and acceptance criteria for one workflow. Compare a custom build with an existing product or ordinary rules-based automation. The simplest workable option may use little generative AI.
